calibration.caveat: A supported rider (chase vehicle, no camping gear) in an unusually hot spring, riding this route in the opposite direction. Treat the speed spread as the honest range, not the temperatures.

source.author: UrbandaleDave (David Van Woert) with WDMDeb (escort)
source.heatCalibration: CRITICAL: the rider reports RECORD-SETTING heat in BOTH Arizona (p18-003) and Louisiana (p50-002). This entire journal was ridden in an unusually hot spring. Read every temperature figure as a high-end scenario, not a typical one. The operational rules (start before 7am, done by 2pm) still transfer.

records.summary: Last 15 mi into Alpine: sustained 3-8% with pitches to 10%
records.detail: Rider calls the final 15 mi 'brutal', very little flat or downhill, grades 3-8%, dismounted to walk where it hit 10%. Sustained 4-5 mph with repeated stops to get heart rate under 150. Day total 3,789 ft over 45.81 mi.
records.cyclistIntel: REVERSED: this is Nick's final descent into San Diego, ~3,800 ft over 46 mi. Not a climb for him. Brake check before leaving Alpine. Do not import the rider's day length.
records.quote: The last 15 miles were brutal. Very little flat or downhill.

photos.caption: The road just keeps going up and up.
photos.shows: Two-lane road climbing on a visible grade; yellow centerline, white fog line, cut embankment left, rural mailboxes and block retaining wall right

records.summary: First significant hill east of the city flats: ~300 ft vertical at 5-6%
records.detail: After the flat urban middle section, 'the first killer hill' — roughly 300 ft of vertical at mostly 5-6%. Position in the day suggests the transition out of the El Cajon / Santee basin toward the foothills.
records.cyclistIntel: Westbound this is a descent. Useful mainly as the marker for where the terrain stops being urban-flat.
records.quote: 300 feet vertical climb mostly at 5-6% grades.

records.summary: Traffic low and drivers courteous across the whole San Diego urban crossing
records.detail: Traffic 'for the most part was low' through San Diego neighborhoods; cars gave plenty of room, stopped to let riders cross intersections, a couple of thumbs-up. Rider notes this exceeded his expectations for California.
records.cyclistIntel: The urban crossing is not the stressful part of this segment; the grade is. Plan the day around the descent, not the traffic.
records.quote: Cars were friendly for the most part and gave us plenty of room

records.summary: No paved shoulder on the two-lane approach to Alpine — fog line only
records.detail: Not in the text; from two photographs on the Alpine / Japatul approach. Two-lane road, yellow centerline, white fog line with essentially nothing paved beyond it — a few inches to at most a foot or two of broken edge, then dirt, cut embankment or gravel. One frame shows the edge dropping to dirt in front of a block retaining wall.
records.cyclistIntel: Nick descends westbound at speed with no shoulder and no escape room. Ride in good light; expect to be in the lane rather than beside it.

photos.caption: Nice mountain scenery to look at as I catch my breath.
photos.shows: Two-lane road, yellow centerline, white fog line with no paved shoulder beyond it; chain-link fence, palms, rural lots; mountains behind

photos.caption: The road just keeps going up and up.
photos.shows: Fog line with roughly a foot of broken pavement edge, then dirt and a block retaining wall; no rideable shoulder

records.summary: Cracked and patched chipseal on the Alpine approach, incl. longitudinal cracks across the lane
records.detail: Photo evidence only. Aged chipseal with visible longitudinal and transverse cracking running across the travel lane and into the fog line, plus patching. Not broken up, but not smooth.
records.cyclistIntel: Matters because Nick takes this westbound as a descent — cracks running with the direction of travel are a handling risk at speed on a loaded touring bike.

photos.caption: Nice mountain scenery to look at as I catch my breath.
photos.shows: Aged chipseal with a long longitudinal crack and transverse cracking crossing the lane and fog line

records.summary: San Diego River Trail — car-free paved path, flat, from Ocean Beach inland
records.detail: First part of the day is a bike trail along the San Diego River. GPS track shows it running inland from Ocean Beach past Mission Bay before joining city streets. Flat, separated from traffic.
records.cyclistIntel: Gives Nick a car-free, flat final few miles into the Pacific terminus rather than city streets. Worth routing to deliberately for the finish.
records.quote: The first part of the route was a bike trail along the San Diego River.

records.summary: Homeless encampments along the San Diego River bike trail
records.detail: Rider notes people living along the bike trail. Reported as an observation of the trail's character; no incident, conflict or hazard described.
records.cyclistIntel: Nothing to plan around on this evidence. Recorded so a later report of an actual incident here has something to match against.
records.quote: lots of interesting homeless people hanging around along the bike trail

records.summary: Tailwind riding EASTBOUND out of San Diego in late March — headwind for Nick's westbound approach
records.detail: Rider lists 'a nice tailwind' among the day's positives travelling west-to-east Ocean Beach to Alpine on 30 March. Observed fact is an easterly-blowing wind on this stretch on that date; the inversion to Nick's direction is inference.
records.cyclistIntel: Corroboration 1 of 3 for prevailing westerlies on the final San Diego approach. Nick descends into a likely headwind on his last full day — the descent absorbs it, but do not bank on a fast finish.
records.quote: The positive was a nice tailwind, overcast and temps in the 50s and low 60s.
records.anchorNote: extent applied west→east per the source rule

records.summary: Late March on the San Diego coast: overcast, 50s to low 60s, chilly at the beach
records.detail: Overcast all day, 50s and low 60s; Pacific start 'a little chilly' with big surf. GPS records 61 F. All photographs show flat grey overcast.
records.cyclistIntel: Comfortable temps for a big descent, but cold enough at the coast that a windproof layer matters on a long downhill. Nick's arrival is a different season — treat as a seasonal datapoint, not a forecast.
records.quote: Overcast, a little chilly, big surfing waves.
records.anchorNote: extent applied west→east per the source rule

photos.caption: Dipping my rear tire in the Pacific Ocean.
photos.shows: Rider walking a loaded touring bike at the waterline; heavy grey overcast, large breaking surf, Ocean Beach Pier behind

records.summary: Night 1: unnamed campground in Alpine CA, reached by RV — tent policy unknown
records.detail: Journal says only 'our campground in Alpine' and that the support crew cooked there. No site name, facilities, cost, or tent policy. Party arrived by RV, so nothing was tested from a cyclist's position.
records.cyclistIntel: Establishes a legal overnight exists in Alpine — the natural last stop before the long descent into San Diego. Identify the site and confirm tent camping and walk-in availability by phone before it counts as an anchor.
records.quote: I was really glad to finally reach our campground in Alpine.

records.summary: 2,635 ft over 28.3 mi (~93 ft/mi) crossing the range — two big climbs with a sharp descent between
records.detail: 'Big steep climbs to get past the mountain range', rider estimates ~100 ft of climb per mile; GPS confirms 2,635 ft over 28.32 mi. Much of it at 4-5 mph in low gears. Elevation trace: ~3,000 ft to ~4,150 ft, sharp drop to 3,232 ft at 1:39, then a second climb back to ~4,000 ft. Speed exceeded 25 mph in only three short bursts.
records.cyclistIntel: REVERSED: the two big climbs become descents and the mid-day descent becomes a real climb. Materially less work westbound, but not a free ride. Westbound this pairs comfortably with more distance than their 28 mi.
records.quote: Only 28 miles but they packed in about 100 feet of climb for each mile.

photos.shows: Elevation profile rising ~3,000-4,150 ft, dropping to a marked 3,232 ft low at 1:39:05, then climbing back to ~4,000 ft; speed trace flat with brief 25-40 mph descent spikes

records.summary: Wide paved shoulder (4-6 ft) through the forested Cleveland National Forest section
records.detail: Not in the text; from a photograph at the start of the day. Two-lane road, yellow centerline, solid white fog line and roughly 4-6 ft of paved shoulder beyond it in good condition, guardrail on the opposite side. Marked improvement on the no-shoulder conditions lower down near Alpine.
records.cyclistIntel: Good news for the fast forested portion of Nick's descent — there is room to get out of the lane here. Not continuous; degrades to gravel further east.

photos.caption: The start of the day. Cold, wet and low visibility.
photos.shows: Approximately 4-6 ft of paved shoulder outside the fog line in sound condition; wet asphalt, guardrail far side, dense trees both sides

records.summary: Paved shoulder gives out to loose gravel on the open stretch near Boulevard
records.detail: Not in the text; from a photograph near the end of the day. Fog line with no paved surface beyond it — the verge is loose gravel and dirt, wide but unrideable on a loaded touring bike. A cyclist is visible riding in the traffic lane rather than on it. Fresh orange utility locate markings sprayed across pavement and verge, which may indicate planned utility or road work.
records.cyclistIntel: Nick is descending here at speed with no paved escape. With the wet-weather risk this is the stretch to take conservatively. Re-check the locate markings closer to the trip in case the road is torn up. Corroborated independently by d8g-006.

photos.caption: Almost to the finish line.
photos.shows: Fog line with loose gravel verge and no paved shoulder; cyclist in yellow riding in the traffic lane; support van on the gravel; fresh orange utility locate paint; open low scrub

records.summary: Very little traffic across the whole crossing, apart from Border Patrol vehicles
records.detail: 'Very little traffic other than Border Patrol vehicles' for the full 28 miles. This stretch runs within a few miles of the Mexican border so routine BP presence is expected. No stop, checkpoint or interaction reported.
records.cyclistIntel: Traffic is not the risk on this segment; grade, weather and shoulder are. Page establishes only that BP vehicles are around, not that a checkpoint exists — the westbound I-8 checkpoint question needs separate confirmation.
records.quote: Very little traffic other than Border Patrol vehicles.

records.summary: Cleveland National Forest is green and heavily treed, big trees around 3,600 ft
records.detail: Forest section described as very green and scenic. A photo caption places large trees at 3,600 ft; images show dense mature tree cover both sides of the road through this portion.
records.cyclistIntel: Shade and tree cover on the upper part of Nick's descent, which matters if he arrives in a hot season rather than the cold snap this rider hit. The open scrub near Boulevard has none.
records.quote: Lots of big trees at 3600 feet.

photos.caption: The start of the day. Cold, wet and low visibility.
photos.shows: Dense mature tree cover overhanging both sides of the road

records.summary: Wet pavement plus fog on the mountain crossing — a climbing nuisance for them, a descending risk for Nick
records.detail: CONDITIONAL ON WEATHER. Photographs show standing wet across the full road width and visibility closing to a few hundred feet in fog. The rider crossed at 4-5 mph uphill so it cost him nothing but comfort. Severity rated for the speed Nick will be doing in the opposite direction.
records.cyclistIntel: Nick takes this surface downhill. Wet chipseal, fog, sections with no paved shoulder and a headwind combine into the worst-case version of this segment. If the forecast is wet, start late rather than early and descend well inside his limits.

photos.caption: The start of the day. Cold, wet and low visibility.
photos.shows: Standing wet across the full road width, fog closing visibility to a few hundred feet

records.summary: Tecate Divide, 3,890 ft — signed high point near the Boulevard end
records.detail: From a photograph of the road sign reading 'Tecate Divide ELEV 3890 FT', captioned by the rider as the last high point of his day. Terrain at the sign is open, sandy and scrubby rather than forested, consistent with the eastern end of the crossing near Live Oak Springs / Boulevard.
records.cyclistIntel: REVERSED: this is Nick's FIRST high point of the day out of Boulevard, not his last — hit early, cold, before he is warmed up, then the forested descent follows. Good natural landmark for shaping the day.
records.quote: My attempt at a selfie at the last high point of the day.

photos.caption: My attempt at a selfie at the last high point of the day.
photos.shows: Green highway sign reading 'Tecate Divide ELEV 3890 FT'; rider in helmet, sunglasses, balaclava, yellow jacket; open sandy scrub, heavy overcast

records.summary: Wild turkeys in three places including the Boulevard campground, and a coyote near camp
records.detail: Turkeys at two points along the route plus four loitering at the KOA campground; riding partner saw a coyote close to the campground. Rider notes very little roadkill in California generally.
records.cyclistIntel: No action. Recorded so food storage at the Boulevard campground is a known consideration and any later report of aggressive wildlife here has a baseline.
records.quote: Until I got to the KOA Campground and find four of them just hanging around.

records.summary: Rain all day and SLEET at ~3,900 ft on 2 April — day average 43.1 F in Southern California
records.detail: Fog in the morning, then rain, then sleet; temps in the 40s and rain the entire day. GPS average 43.1 F, low 42.8 F at the 3,232 ft point; map header 54 F. Rider was glad he brought all his cold-weather gear and was still wearing it at the finish. Photos show heavy overcast and standing wet.
records.cyclistIntel: Strongest seasonal caution in the dataset. The California mountain section between Boulevard and Alpine sits at 3,000-4,200 ft and can deliver sleet in early April. Cold and wet gear is not optional here regardless of the coastal forecast. Pair with d8-004: same region hit 98.6 F four days later.
records.quote: The morning started off in a fog. Then rain, then sleet.

photos.caption: I am still wearing all the cold weather gear at the end. Glad I brought it all.

records.summary: Tailwind pushing them EASTBOUND up the climbs — headwind for Nick coming down
records.detail: 'A good tailwind that pushed me up the hills' listed as the day's main positive. Observed fact is a westerly wind through the mountain crossing on 2 April; the inversion is inference.
records.cyclistIntel: Corroboration 2 of 3 for prevailing westerlies on the California end. For Nick this is a headwind on a long descent — costs speed but adds braking help on wet pavement with no shoulder.
records.quote: The positive to this day was a good tailwind that pushed me up the hills.

records.summary: Night 4: KOA campground at Boulevard CA — rated 'very nice' by the rider
records.detail: Finished Day 4 at a KOA at Boulevard; wild turkeys on site, coyote nearby. On the following day's page the rider captions a photo 'Our KOA in Boulevard was very nice.' That photo shows a paved lot with two Sprinter RVs and a building behind — an RV-oriented site. 'Likely' facility values come from KOA chain norms, NOT from the page, and none of it was tested from a cyclist's position.
records.cyclistIntel: Leading California lodging anchor: named chain, on route, close to Jacumba on the imperial divergence. Phone to confirm tent sites, walk-in availability and cyclist rate. KOAs take reservations and can fill — book ahead, do not roll up.
records.quote: Our KOA in Boulevard was very nice.

photos.caption: A wet and chilly start to the day.
photos.shows: Paved lot with two Mercedes Sprinter RVs, low building behind, utility poles; wet ground, overcast; orange utility locate paint on the pavement

records.summary: THE WESTERN CRUX REVERSED: their 10-mi coast down I-8 from 3,200 to 600 ft is Nick's 10-mi climb at ~5%
records.detail: Route turns onto the shoulder of Interstate 8 for '10 miles of decent from 3200 feet to 600 feet', cruising 35-44 mph without pedalling the whole way. Roughly 2,600 ft of drop over 10 mi, sustained average near 4.9%. GPS speed trace confirms a solid block of 35-45 mph between ~1:06 and ~1:40, the only fast section of the day. This is the In-Ko-Pah grade below Jacumba.
records.cyclistIntel: Nick's hardest sustained climb on the California end: ~2,600 ft in 10 mi at about 5%, on an interstate shoulder, arriving at roughly mile 40-50 of his day AFTER the desert crossing, in desert heat, likely into a headwind. Single biggest reason not to plan a long day out of El Centro. Confirm whether his route takes the I-8 shoulder or Old Highway 80 up to Jacumba — see d8g-001, which shows Old 80 was also used that day.
records.quote: 10 miles of decent from 3200 feet to 600 feet. Cruising at 35 to 44 mph without turning the pedals for 10 miles!

photos.shows: Elevation trace holding near 3,800 ft then dropping sharply between ~1:23 and ~1:40 to a marked 349 ft at 2:12; speed trace a solid 35-45 mph block over the same interval

records.summary: The route rides the shoulder of Interstate 8 for the In-Ko-Pah grade
records.detail: 'The route turned on to the shoulder of I-8' and stayed on it for the full ten-mile descent. Bicycles are permitted on rural interstate shoulders in this part of California where no alternative exists. No difficulty reported; shoulder width, debris load and rumble strip not described.
records.cyclistIntel: Establishes the I-8 shoulder as a usable and apparently signed part of the route here, with no obvious alternative through the grade. Nick will be on it climbing at 4-6 mph rather than descending at 40 — far longer exposure to truck traffic and debris. Worth finding a self-supported account before relying on it.
records.quote: Then the route turned on to the shoulder of I-8.

records.summary: Whole day net ~3,650 ft downhill eastbound — roughly 4,600 ft of CLIMBING for Nick over 60 mi
records.detail: Derived from the page's own figures: began at about 3,600 ft, finished in El Centro at or just below sea level, recorded total ascent 961 ft over 59.96 mi. Net loss ~3,640 ft plus 961 ft regained implies about 4,600 ft of descent eastbound. Reversed, that is Nick's ascent, with only ~961 ft of descent to offset it. Their 14.7 mph average is the highest of the ride and tells you nothing about his.
records.cyclistIntel: Treat El Centro to Boulevard as a full hard day, not a 60-mile transit: ~4,600 ft of climbing, no services across the middle, likely headwind, and a 10-mile 5% interstate climb late. Strongly consider splitting it — which collides with the plan's zero spare days.
records.quote: Today's bicycling is like two rides separated by a glory ride on I-8.

photos.shows: GPS summary reading 59.96 mi, 4:05:18, 14.7 mph avg, 961 ft total ascent, 63.0 F and sunny

records.summary: Yuha Desert crossing has no towns, no shade and no facilities of any kind
records.detail: Desert section is flat sand, rock and occasional scrub. Lunch-stop caption is explicit: 'No towns, no shade, no picnic benches. This is the best we had.' Photograph shows the party eating on open sand with no structure, tree or feature in any direction. Supported party carrying an RV — never dependent on finding water here, so the absence is observed but its consequences were not.
records.cyclistIntel: El Centro and Calexico are the last full-service towns before the desert going westbound; nothing until Ocotillo. Nick carries all water for the desert crossing AND the 2,600 ft climb that follows, in desert heat, with no shade to wait out the middle of the day. This is the water-carry calculation for the western end.
records.quote: No towns, no shade, no picnic benches. This is the best we had.

photos.caption: Lunch break in the Yuha Desert. No towns, no shade, no picnic benches. This is the best we had.
photos.shows: Riders sitting on open sand with two bikes; flat sandy desert with sparse dry scrub in every direction, bare mountains on the horizon, no structure or shade anywhere in frame; full sun

records.summary: Border wall in view and heavy Border Patrol traffic for most of the second half of the day
records.detail: Rider calls the border wall 'the recurring theme of the second part of the ride' and reports lots of Border Patrol vehicles and repeated views of the wall, a first for them. A photograph at higher elevation shows the wall running as a continuous dark line across the middle distance. No stop, checkpoint, document check or hostility — only presence.
records.cyclistIntel: Second page in a row establishing routine BP presence without an actual checkpoint encounter. Nick's imperial divergence runs Calexico to Jacumba directly along this corridor — expect to be seen repeatedly, carry ID. The westbound I-8 checkpoint question remains unconfirmed by this journal.
records.quote: The recurring theme of the second part of the ride was the border wall. Lots of Border Patrol vehicles.

photos.caption: Pretty mountains and green brush earlier in the ride (higher elevation). And a border wall.
photos.shows: Rider with two loaded bikes on a gravel pullout; a continuous dark border wall running horizontally across the middle distance below bare mountains; desert scrub, broken cloud

records.summary: Abrupt palm-row boundary dividing desert from irrigated farmland, then a 4-6 mile solar farm
records.detail: Desert ends abruptly at a row of tall palm trees — bare desert to the west, irrigated green agriculture to the east. Beyond the first farms is a solar installation the rider estimates at four to six miles long and roughly as wide, the largest he has seen, after which irrigated agriculture resumes into Calexico and El Centro.
records.cyclistIntel: Unmistakable navigation landmark and day-shaping marker. For Nick westbound the palm row is the point where shade, farms and any chance of a water source end and the true desert begins — a good place to have already topped up. The solar farm stretch offers nothing: no shade, no buildings, no water.
records.quote: Divided by a row of tall palm trees there was desert to the west and green agriculture to the east.

records.summary: BLM boondocking reported as the only overnight option on the stretch east of El Centro
records.detail: FORWARD-LOOKING, not observed. Rider says tomorrow is 'a long stretch with only one real town and no services for miles' and that the RVs were fuelled and water tanks filled because 'the only option seems to be boondocking on BLM land.' Their plan and reading of the map, not experience. CONFIRMED the next day by p8-011.
records.cyclistIntel: Flags dispersed BLM camping as the expected lodging mode east of El Centro, directly relevant since the same land status applies to a cyclist. Verify against the planner's camping data and state laws rather than trusting this line.
records.quote: the only option seems to be boondocking on BLM land

records.summary: Tailwind across the Yuha Desert eastbound — a desert headwind for Nick, on the approach to the climb
records.detail: 'A nice tailwind' through the desert section, credited with making the crossing tolerable at 60 F. A 14.7 mph average across a day with almost no pedalling on the descent implies real assistance on the flat. Observed fact is a westerly through the Yuha on 3 April; the inversion is inference.
records.cyclistIntel: Corroboration 3 of 3 for prevailing westerlies on the California end, and the most costly. Nick crosses the Yuha into this wind with no shade and no water, then starts a 2,600 ft climb. A desert headwind here does not just slow him down, it changes his water requirement.
records.quote: The temperatures were in the 60's and we had a nice tailwind so for riding through a desert this wasn't too bad.

records.summary: Roughly 30 F swing in one day: 40 F and misty rain at 3,600 ft, 70s in the desert below
records.detail: Start delayed until after 9am waiting for overnight rain to stop and the temperature to clear the 30s; it reached 40 F with rain still around. Descended in misty rain which stopped about 500 ft lower, near 3,100 ft. GPS average 68.8 F with the trace climbing into the 70s once out of the mountains. Photos show heavy overcast and full winter kit at the start, clear blue sky in the desert.
records.cyclistIntel: GEAR ORDER INVERTS. They rode cold-to-hot; Nick rides hot-to-cold, starting in desert heat and finishing at 3,600 ft where it can be near freezing with rain (see p5-003). His cold gear needs to be accessible at the END of the day, not packed at the bottom — the opposite of instinct.
records.quote: We rode downhill from 3600 feet in a misty rain. Then 500 feet elevation lower the mist stopped.

photos.caption: A wet and chilly start to the day.
photos.shows: Two riders in full winter kit on loaded bikes beside two Mercedes Sprinter RVs on a wet paved lot; heavy flat overcast

records.summary: Night 5 in El Centro CA — site not named in the journal
records.detail: Day ends in El Centro; journal names no campground, park or site. Only related detail is that the RVs were refuelled and water tanks filled here for the following day, implying a serviced stop but not identifying it.
records.cyclistIntel: El Centro is a full-service town and the last one before the desert going westbound, so this night matters more as a resupply point than a lodging lead. Nothing here to call. Watch for the site name on a later page.

records.summary: Signed 'Blowing Sand Next 7 Miles' on CA-78 into Glamis — ~30 mph CROSSWIND that sandblasted face and legs
records.detail: CA-78 climbs a big hill to a CalTrans sign reading 'Blowing Sand Next 7 Miles', which the rider calls an understatement. He estimates the crosswind at around 30 mph and describes it as a sandblaster on his face and legs; a face mask helped. Conditions lasted the full stretch into Glamis. Independently corroborated by a non-riding crew member at Osborne Overlook the same period (d8g-004).
records.cyclistIntel: CROSSWIND DOES NOT INVERT. Unlike every head/tailwind in this dataset, this hits Nick the same way — except he descends westbound from Glamis toward Brawley, so he takes a 30 mph side gust at higher speed on a road with little shoulder and 65 mph traffic. First hazard that could justify waiting out conditions or changing the day. Eye protection and a face covering are required kit. Planner places Glamis at route mile 2637 — anchor this stretch just west of it.
records.quote: The cross wind had to be in the 30 mph neighborhood and it felt like like a sand blaster on my face and legs.
records.anchorNote: extent applied west→east per the source rule

photos.caption: Last bit of riding for the day.
photos.shows: Rider on CA-78 in a face covering; large sand dunes rising directly beside the road; sand visibly encroaching across the fog line onto the roadway edge; blowing haze

records.summary: Blown sand across the roadway edge and shoulder through the dunes section
records.detail: Not in the text; from a photograph on CA-78 near the dunes showing loose sand drifted across the fog line and covering what little shoulder exists, with dunes rising immediately beside the road. With the signed blowing-sand warning this is a persistent condition, not a one-off drift.
records.cyclistIntel: Sand over pavement is a traction problem, far worse descending than climbing. Nick comes through westbound losing elevation with a strong side wind pushing him toward the lane. Keep speed down; the rideable surface is narrower than the paint suggests.
records.anchorNote: extent applied west→east per the source rule

photos.caption: Last bit of riding for the day.
photos.shows: Loose sand drifted across the white fog line and over the narrow shoulder; dunes directly adjacent to the roadway

records.summary: CA-78 east of Brawley: rough, little shoulder, 65 mph limit, heavy RV-and-trailer traffic to the dunes
records.detail: Road after Brawley described as rough with little shoulder and a 65 mph speed limit, carrying 'lots of giant RV's pulling big trailers to the sand dunes area'; rider says plainly it was not a fun part of the ride. This was a Friday, when weekend OHV traffic heads out to Glamis.
records.cyclistIntel: Worst traffic reported in the journal. Traffic is DIRECTIONAL and day-dependent: Friday flow is eastbound toward the dunes, Sunday reverses. Nick riding westbound on a Friday meets it head-on. A midweek crossing avoids most of it — check his arrival day against the OHV weekend cycle rather than treating this as constant. This traffic is also the source of the debris in p10-002.
records.quote: After Brawley the road was rough with little shoulder and 65 mph.

records.summary: Old Highway 111 is very rough pavement but carries sparse traffic — a deliberate trade against New 111
records.detail: Rider took Old Highway 111, a two-lane running alongside New Highway 111 between El Centro and Brawley, described as a very rough road with sparse traffic. The pairing is the useful part: the old alignment trades pavement quality for a large reduction in traffic.
records.cyclistIntel: Good route intelligence for the Brawley-El Centro-Calexico leg of the imperial divergence. Rough pavement on a flat, low-elevation stretch is a fair trade for getting off a busy highway. Confirm which of the two the planner's geometry follows.
records.quote: We rode on Old Highway 111. A two lane next to New Highway 111. It was a very rough road but sparce traffic.

records.summary: Below sea level at Brawley (-112 ft) rising to roughly 400-500 ft at Glamis
records.detail: GPS elevation trace marks a low of -112 ft partway through and shows a gradual rise through the second half to roughly 400-500 ft, with 902 ft of total ascent over 44.24 mi. Rider notes CA-78 'climbed a big hill' immediately before the blowing-sand sign. Otherwise essentially flat.
records.cyclistIntel: Reversed, Nick loses this modest elevation heading west into Brawley — but precisely where the crosswind and sand are worst, which is the wrong place to be gaining speed. The climb is trivial in either direction; the wind is what matters.
records.quote: Highway 78 climbed a big hill with a sign "Blowing Sand Next 7 Miles."

records.summary: Brawley has fast food on the route — Wendy's, confirmed used
records.detail: Riders stopped at a Wendy's in Brawley. Confirms at minimum one chain fast-food outlet directly accessible from the route through town.
records.cyclistIntel: Brawley is the last real resupply before the dunes eastbound, and for Nick westbound the FIRST town with services after Glamis. Treat as a mandatory stop rather than optional — cold calories and water before or after the blowing-sand stretch.
records.quote: We stopped at a Wendy's at Brawley and each had a large Frostie. It hit the spot.

records.summary: Hard landmarks on CA-78: Mesquite Lake Cattle Manure Power Plant, and a Glamis/Palo Verde/Blythe distance sign
records.detail: Navigational fixes from photographs. A signed facility, the 'Mesquite Lake Cattle Manure Power Plant', sits directly on the route east of Brawley. A green highway sign reads Glamis 9, Palo Verde ~46, Blythe ~68 (middle figure partly obscured, treat as approximate). The Chocolate Mountains are the range visible from the Glamis camping area. Riders also stopped beside an alfalfa field near Brawley, placing irrigated farmland on the early part of the leg.
records.cyclistIntel: The distance sign gives real onward mileages to check against the planner's geometry once anchored. The power plant is an unmistakable fix. Irrigated alfalfa near Brawley puts the farmland-to-desert boundary east of town, matching the palm-row boundary in p6-008 west of it.
records.quote: The view from our camping spot. Those are the Chocolate Mountains.

photos.caption: Here's an idea that hasn't come to Iowa yet.
photos.shows: Signed wall reading 'Mesquite Lake Cattle Manure Power Plant' with industrial structures behind, marked 12-02; flat desert, clear sky

photos.caption: This was the scenery for a lot of miles.
photos.shows: Green highway sign reading Glamis 9 / Palo Verde ~46 / Blythe ~68; two-lane road with narrow gravel verge, dry scrub and sand

records.summary: Glamis is an active OHV destination — ATV and motorcycle crowds, fireworks after dark
records.detail: Motorcycles and ATVs charging through the sand at the Imperial Sand Dunes Recreation Area; the ATV crowd at another location setting off fireworks after dark. Rider hopes 'the ATV crowd sleeps in late.' Date was a Friday, when weekend OHV traffic arrives.
records.cyclistIntel: Glamis is not a quiet desert camp on a weekend. Expect vehicle noise, night activity and fireworks, plus heavy trailer traffic on the approach. Timing this stretch midweek changes the entire character of the place — traffic, noise, and how easy it is to find unoccupied flat ground.
records.quote: The ATV crowd in another location are shooting off fireworks. Looks like we missed the party.

records.summary: No organized camping at Imperial Sand Dunes — dispersed camping is the norm; confirms p6-010
records.detail: 'There is no organized camping in the Imperial Sand Dunes Rec Area. You just find a good flat area and set up camp.' Upgrades the forward-looking BLM boondocking note in p6-010 from unknown to observed. NOTE WHAT THE PAGE DOES NOT SAY: no mention of a permit, fee or designated-area requirement, and ISDRA is a managed recreation area rather than open BLM — the absence of a permit mention is a gap in the source, not evidence none exists. See also p10-009: the area borders a live-fire gunnery range.
records.cyclistIntel: Dispersed camping around Glamis is real and usable, which matters because Glamis sits at route mile 2637 with nothing else nearby. Before treating it as an anchor, verify the ISDRA permit and fee situation independently, and verify the gunnery range boundary. A supported party may have handled the permit off-page; the consequences of getting it wrong fall on a cyclist arriving at dusk.
records.quote: There is no organized camping in the Imperial Sand Dunes Rec Area. You just find a good flat area and set up camp.

records.summary: Headwind NORTHBOUND El Centro to Brawley — a TAILWIND for Nick heading south
records.detail: Headwind the whole way El Centro to Brawley, slow going. This leg runs roughly south to north, so the wind was out of the north — a different pattern from the westerlies recorded on the mountain and desert pages, and a reminder that compass direction matters, not just their direction versus his.
records.cyclistIntel: Rare good news that survives the inversion: Nick rides Brawley south toward Calexico, so this wind helps him. Do NOT fold into the prevailing-westerly bucket in consolidation — this is a north-south observation and belongs in its own bucket with p10-001.
records.quote: We did have a headwind all the way to Brawley so slow going.

records.summary: 84 F peak on 4 April in the Imperial Valley, average 76.6 F — first genuinely hot day
records.detail: GPS temperature trace starts around 55-60 F, crosses 84.2 F by 2:12 and averages 76.6 F. Riders started at 8:30 partly to avoid the morning rush. Two days after the page recording sleet at 3,900 ft.
records.cyclistIntel: The Imperial Valley hits the mid-80s in the first week of April, below sea level with no shade. Whatever season Nick crosses, treat this as the floor. With p6-004, the water-carry calculation for the California end should assume heat, not the mild numbers this journal happened to get.

photos.shows: Temperature trace rising from ~55 F to a marked 84.2 F at 2:12:21, averaging 76.6 F; elevation trace showing a marked low of -112 ft before rising toward 400-500 ft near Glamis

records.summary: Night 6: dispersed boondocking on open ground outside Glamis CA, Chocolate Mountains in view
records.detail: First boondocking night of their trip. Picked a flat area outside Glamis and set up; view of the Chocolate Mountains. Rider says it 'seems to work just fine.' No facilities described, and the party carried their own water in RV tanks filled at El Centro the day before — no water source here is established, and the absence is the important part. Tent suitability likely rather than yes: open flat desert suits a tent, but they were in an RV and no permit or fee information is given. Site borders the Chocolate Mountain aerial gunnery range (p10-009).
records.cyclistIntel: A genuine lodging option at route mile ~2637 where the planner has few. Nick must arrive carrying all his water — nothing here supplies it and Brawley is the nearest resupply. Verify ISDRA permit/fee requirements AND the gunnery range boundary before counting on it. Prefer a midweek arrival to avoid OHV crowds, noise and competition for flat ground.
records.quote: You just find a good flat area and set up camp. This is our first experience with boondocking. It seems to work just fine.

photos.caption: Our boondocking campground outside of Glamis CA.
The view from our camping spot. Those are the Chocolate Mountains.

records.summary: Day 5 used OLD HIGHWAY 80 near the border, not only the I-8 shoulder
records.detail: From the escort's photo gallery, captioned 'Day 5- biking on old hwy 80 near border' — rider on a two-lane road with the border wall climbing a hillside behind. The Day 5 narrative described turning onto the I-8 shoulder for the ten-mile In-Ko-Pah descent, so the day used BOTH: Old Highway 80 where it exists near the border, and the I-8 shoulder through the grade. The photo does not establish where the handoff occurs.
records.cyclistIntel: Resolves half the open question about the In-Ko-Pah corridor: the answer is not I-8 OR Old 80, it is both, with a transition point still to pin down. The planner should model the handoff rather than assuming one roadway for the segment. Old 80 in this photo has a sound paved surface and a usable shoulder — materially better than the interstate where it exists.
records.quote: Day 5- biking on old hwy 80 near border.

photos.caption: Day 5- biking on old hwy 80 near border.
photos.shows: Rider in yellow on a two-lane road with a sound paved shoulder; border wall running up a hillside behind; a metal-sided facility with portable toilets, white trailers and yellow equipment beside the road

records.summary: Wild burro herd beside Highway 78 — roughly ten animals
records.detail: Photo captioned 'Wild burrows along Hwy 78' showing about ten wild burros moving across an open rocky slope immediately beside the roadway. Dated to 2025-04-05 (Day 7) because the Day 7 narrative describes the escort photographing the herd from the RV. Wild burros run several hundred pounds and are unpredictable around traffic. Upgraded to a documented near-miss by p10-003.
records.cyclistIntel: Materially different from the turkeys and coyote recorded earlier. A burro herd adjacent to a 65 mph highway is a genuine collision and startle hazard, and they cross roads. Relevant riding and camping — burros investigate camps and go after water. Do not leave water containers accessible overnight along this stretch.
records.quote: Wild burrows along Hwy 78

photos.caption: Wild burrows along Hwy 78
photos.shows: Approximately ten wild burros moving across an open rocky desert slope beside the road; sparse creosote and desert scrub

records.summary: CA-78 east of Glamis has a sound paved shoulder (2-4 ft) — better than the dunes stretch west of it
records.detail: From a photo captioned 'Getting ready to take off from Glamis to Palo Verde Day 7', showing two riders and the support van on CA-78 with a clean paved shoulder of roughly two to four feet outside the fog line, sound surface, open desert and mountains under clear sky. Notably better than the sand-covered narrow shoulder photographed on the dunes stretch west of Glamis.
records.cyclistIntel: Sharpens the earlier finding: the shoulder problem on CA-78 is specific to the dunes section, not the whole highway. Anchor the bad stretch tightly rather than flagging all of 78. Note p10-006 shows it narrows again through the badlands further north.
records.quote: Getting ready to take off from Glamis to Palo Verde Day 7

photos.caption: Getting ready to take off from Glamis to Palo Verde Day 7
photos.shows: Two-lane road with roughly 2-4 ft of sound paved shoulder outside the fog line; two riders with loaded bikes, support van; open desert, low mountains, clear sky

records.summary: Narrow paved shoulder giving way to wide loose gravel on the Boulevard departure
records.detail: From a photo captioned 'Taking off from Boulevard Day 5 Apr 3th'. Two riders on the fog line with perhaps a foot of rough paved edge beyond it, then a broad band of loose gravel and stone. Pavement edge visibly ragged. Independently corroborates p5-006 — same character, adjacent stretch.
records.cyclistIntel: Second photographic confirmation that the Boulevard area has no usable paved shoulder. Nick passes here on a descent day. With the utility locate markings nearby, worth re-checking for roadworks closer to the trip.
records.quote: Taking off from Boulevard Day 5 Apr 3th

photos.caption: Taking off from Boulevard Day 5 Apr 3th
photos.shows: Riders on the fog line with roughly a foot of ragged paved edge, then a wide band of loose gravel and stone; arid scrub, low mountains, clear sky

records.summary: Border Patrol forward facility directly beside Old Highway 80, wall immediately adjacent
records.detail: A fenced compound sits directly off the roadway containing a large metal building, portable toilets, white trailers and yellow equipment, consistent with a Border Patrol forward operating site. The border barrier runs up the hillside a few hundred yards behind. Third page establishing routine BP infrastructure and presence along this corridor, still with no reported stop, checkpoint or document check.
records.cyclistIntel: Nick's imperial divergence puts him on this road. Carry ID and expect to be observed. The pattern across three pages is presence without incident — reassuring, but not the same as confirming how a lone self-supported cyclist is treated.

photos.caption: Day 5- biking on old hwy 80 near border.
photos.shows: Fenced compound with metal building, portable toilets, white trailers and yellow equipment beside the road; border barrier ascending the hillside behind

records.summary: Osborne Overlook — named paved viewpoint on CA-78 at Imperial Sand Dunes, independently reported as very windy
records.detail: Photo captioned 'Top of Osborne Overlook at Imperial Sand Dunes - WINDY!!' shows a support-crew member on a paved overlook platform with a vast dune field behind, clothing and hair visibly pushed by strong wind. Undated in the gallery, but Osborne Overlook sits on CA-78 near Glamis so it belongs to the Day 6 arrival or Day 7 departure. Second independent report of strong wind at the dunes, from a person who was not riding.
records.cyclistIntel: Corroborates the signed blowing-sand hazard (p8-001) from a different observer on a different occasion — strengthens it from one rider's bad day into a characteristic of the place. As a named paved overlook it is also a hard navigational fix and a possible regroup point. Worth identifying whether it has shade, water or restrooms — this photo establishes none of those.
records.quote: Top of Osborne Overlook at Imperial Sand Dunes - WINDY!!

photos.caption: Top of Osborne Overlook at Imperial Sand Dunes - WINDY!!
photos.shows: Paved overlook platform with a sticker-covered marker post; extensive dune field to the horizon; subject's clothing and hair pushed hard by wind

records.summary: Heavy accumulated road debris along CA-78 — years of material blown off trucks, RVs and trailers
records.detail: Riding at 5 mph into the wind with his head down, the rider passed the time cataloguing the trash along the roadside: 'every sort of thing that would blow off or break off trucks, rv's and trailers', which he believes has been accumulating for years. This corridor carries the heavy RV-and-trailer traffic to the dunes recorded in p8-003, which explains the source.
records.cyclistIntel: A puncture-and-flat corridor, not just an eyesore. Broken-off vehicle hardware means metal, wire and plastic in the exact strip a cyclist rides. Nick should expect to be scanning the shoulder rather than the horizon here, and carry more than one spare tube. Pair with p10-006: where the shoulder tightens, the debris and the only rideable line occupy the same space.
records.quote: There is every sort of thing that would blow off or break off trucks, rv's and trailers... I imagine the stuff has been accumulating for years.

records.summary: Herd of nine wild donkeys nearly ran in front of the bikes, then crossed the road ahead
records.detail: Upgrades the undated burro sighting (d8g-003) into a documented near-miss. Nine animals almost ran into the riders' path, were passed, then ran ahead and crossed the road in front of them. The escort photographed the same herd from the RV, which dates that gallery photo to this day.
records.cyclistIntel: A live collision hazard on CA-78 between Glamis and Palo Verde, not a wildlife sighting. They move as a group and cross without warning. A rider descending southbound toward Glamis — Nick's direction — has less time to react than these riders had grinding uphill at 5 mph. Also relevant at camp: burros come in after water.
records.quote: A herd of 9 wild donkeys almost ran in front of our bikes.

photos.caption: Donkeys!

records.summary: Big climb north out of Glamis then a long gentle descent — reversed, a long gentle climb then a big descent INTO Glamis
records.detail: Rider summarises the leg as 'north with a big climb followed by a long gentle downhill', with the descent beginning about halfway through the 39.9 miles. A photo captioned 'Plenty of ups and downs today' shows rolling terrain through eroded badlands rather than a single smooth grade, so the profile is lumpier than the summary suggests. NOTE: no GPS map or elevation chart was captured for this day — ascent, temperatures and the exact profile are unknown.
records.cyclistIntel: Reversed, Nick's day out of Palo Verde is a long gentle climb for the first half — likely with a tailwind on the observed pattern — then a substantial descent into Glamis. That descent puts him at speed exactly where the burro herd operates (p10-003) and where the debris is worst (p10-002), and delivers him into Glamis at the top of the blowing-sand section (p8-001). Sequence those four findings together when shaping this day.
records.quote: The route goes north with a big climb followed by a long gentle downhill.

photos.caption: Plenty of ups and downs today.
photos.shows: Two-lane road rising and falling through eroded desert badlands; double yellow centerline; roughly 1-2 ft of paved shoulder outside the fog line; two riders climbing

records.summary: Wide clean paved shoulder with rumble strip on the straight desert section of CA-78
records.detail: From the rider's handlebar-view photograph. Road runs dead straight across flat desert with a generous paved shoulder — well over the width of a bike lane — in sound condition, separated by a fog line with a rumble strip set inside it.
records.cyclistIntel: Confirms CA-78's shoulder problem is localised rather than general. Where the road is straight and flat there is real room. The rumble strip sits between the lane and the shoulder here, which is the good configuration — it does not eat the rideable surface.

photos.caption: This is the view from my cockpit.
photos.shows: Dead-straight two-lane road across flat desert; wide sound paved shoulder outside the fog line with a rumble strip inboard of it; distant mountains; ACA map visible in the handlebar map case

records.summary: Shoulder narrows to 1-2 ft through the rolling badlands section of CA-78
records.detail: From the 'Plenty of ups and downs today' photograph — the same highway through eroded terrain with only about one to two feet of paved surface outside the fog line and a cut bank rising immediately beside it. The riders are on or near the fog line rather than clear of the lane.
records.cyclistIntel: The narrow sections coincide with rolling terrain, where sightlines are shortest and Nick will be carrying descent speed southbound. Combine with p10-002 — in these stretches the only rideable line and the debris occupy the same strip, with no room to swerve.

photos.caption: Plenty of ups and downs today.
photos.shows: Roughly 1-2 ft of paved shoulder outside the fog line; cut bank and eroded badlands rising immediately beside the roadway; rolling grade limiting forward sightline

records.summary: A Palo Verde local directed them to a good boondocking spot unprompted
records.detail: A local in Palo Verde pointed them to a camping spot beside an oxbow lake, which the rider calls a really nice ending to a tough day. First recorded instance in this journal of local hospitality producing a lodging outcome.
records.cyclistIntel: A pattern rather than a one-off: in small towns along this stretch, asking locally produces better camping than a map does. Relevant because the planner's informal-lodging data is thin here. It also means the site in p10-N1 may not be findable without asking.
records.quote: The other fun thing was getting directed by a Palo Verde local to a boondocking spot.

records.summary: Open oxbow lake immediately beside the Palo Verde camp — surface water, untreated
records.detail: The camp sits next to an oxbow lake, photographed as a substantial body of open blue water fringed with tamarisk and reeds, a short walk from the site. Rider describes the setting as a lush garden. No potable source, tap or spigot mentioned anywhere on the page. This is Colorado River backwater in an agricultural valley, so assume farm runoff.
records.cyclistIntel: Surface water, not a water source. Genuinely useful as an emergency backstop and for washing, but needs filtering and probably chemical treatment given irrigation runoff. Do not let it substitute for carrying water into Palo Verde. Its value is that the planner shows very little between Glamis and Blythe.
records.quote: The spot is a lush garden next to an oxbow lake.

photos.caption: A very short walk from our camp.
photos.shows: Open oxbow lake with blue water, fringed by tamarisk and dry reeds, sandy shoreline; clear sky

records.summary: The Glamis camp sits close to a Navy bombing range, with helicopter activity overhead
records.detail: Photo caption: 'The spot in Glamis was close to a Navy bombing range. We saw several helicopters.' This is the Chocolate Mountain aerial gunnery range, which borders the Imperial Sand Dunes area. Adds to p8-N1.
records.cyclistIntel: Two consequences: noise and low-flying aircraft at the Glamis camp on top of the OHV crowd; and more importantly the gunnery range is closed land with live-fire restrictions, so 'find a flat spot' has a hard boundary the journal does not describe. Verify the range boundary before treating dispersed camping around Glamis as unrestricted.
records.quote: The spot in Glamis was close to a Navy bombing range. We saw several helicopters.

records.summary: 20+ mph NORTH wind — brutal headwind for them going north, a TAILWIND for Nick going south
records.detail: Wind blowing hard from the north on stepping out of the RV, holding above 20 mph all day. Made the opening climb 'as difficult as the steep stuff in the mountains' at 5 mph in granny gears, then flattened the long descent in the second half to a crawl. Second north-south leg to record a north wind, after p8-005.
records.cyclistIntel: Inverts in Nick's favour — he rides southbound, so a north wind pushes him. Do not bank on it: two observations in early April is a pattern, not a forecast, and the same corridor produced a 30 mph crosswind at the dunes two days earlier. The durable fact is that this region generates 20-30 mph winds routinely, so shape the day to survive a bad draw rather than exploit a good one. Keep in the north-south wind bucket, separate from the prevailing westerlies.
records.quote: The wind was over 20 mph so the long climb to start the day was as difficult as the steep stuff in the mountains.

photos.caption: The view of the Chocolate Mountains beyond the empty sands.
photos.shows: Plowed brown field with visible airborne dust streaming across it, green tree line beyond, Chocolate Mountains on the horizon — blowing dust corroborates sustained strong wind

records.summary: Night 7: dispersed camp beside an oxbow lake at Palo Verde CA — found by asking a local
records.detail: A Palo Verde local directed them to this spot. Rider describes it as a lush garden next to an oxbow lake and calls it a really nice ending to a tough day. Vegetation is dense tamarisk and reeds; the lake is a short walk from the site. No facilities and no potable water — the lake is surface water (p10-008). Land status not stated: whether BLM, county, or informally tolerated private ground is unknown, which matters more for a solo cyclist than for two RVs.
records.cyclistIntel: Best-sounding camp in the journal so far, in a stretch where the planner has almost nothing — and the only site recorded with actual SHADE. Two caveats before it becomes an anchor: it was found by asking a local rather than from any map, so its exact location needs pinning down; and its land status is unestablished. Arrive with water.
records.quote: The spot is a lush garden next to an oxbow lake. A really nice ending to a tough day of riding.

photos.caption: Our boondocking spot for the evening.
A very short walk from our camp.
photos.shows: Open oxbow lake with blue water fringed by tamarisk and reeds, sandy shore

records.summary: 11 miles of I-10 shoulder carpeted in shredded tire steel, screws and broken hardware
records.detail: Route puts you on the shoulder of I-10 for eleven miles and despite a fairly wide shoulder the rider had to concentrate the whole way on not running over 'all the shredded tires, broken bungie cords, screws, and other stuff.' A cockpit photograph shows debris and gravel across the shoulder with a semi passing close on the left. Same debris theme as CA-78 the day before, but with specifics that matter: screws and steel belt wire from blown truck tires are puncture-causing. LOCALISED: d10-001 shows the I-10 shoulder EAST of Quartzsite is clean, so this is likely the Ehrenberg truckstop concentrating tire failures at one point.
records.cyclistIntel: Highest-consequence hazard in the dataset for a self-supported rider, because a flat here means standing on an interstate shoulder with trucks at 75 mph. Nick takes this WESTBOUND AS A DESCENT at 2%, which is worse — less time to spot debris, higher impact energy. Most puncture-resistant tyre he owns, multiple tubes and a boot, daylight only. Anchor the eleven miles precisely; worth a warning fire in the app. Check whether Dome Rock Road (d8-007) parallels I-10 far enough west to avoid part of it.
records.quote: I had to concentrate on not running over all the shredded tires, broken bungie cords, screws, and other stuff.

photos.caption: My view riding on I-10.
photos.shows: Cockpit view on the I-10 shoulder; semi trailer passing close in the near lane; loose gravel and scattered debris across the shoulder surface; ACA map in the handlebar map case, Garmin GPS mounted

records.summary: I-10 shoulder is wide and legal for 11 miles, but trucks pass close in the adjacent lane
records.detail: Rider describes the I-10 shoulder as fairly wide and rides it eleven miles without incident. Photographs confirm a genuinely generous paved shoulder — several feet, well beyond a bike lane — with a signed 'Interstate 10 Pearl Harbor Memorial Highway' marker beside it. The cockpit photo also shows a semi trailer passing at close quarters. Surface is aged concrete or asphalt with cracking.
records.cyclistIntel: Second interstate-shoulder segment after the I-8 In-Ko-Pah grade, establishing the pattern: on this route, interstate shoulders are part of the official ACA alignment rather than an improvisation. Width is not the problem here — debris and truck wash are. Contrast with I-8, where Nick climbs slowly with long exposure; here he descends with short exposure but less reaction time.
records.quote: It was a fairly wide shoulder

photos.caption: Linda's view on the road.
photos.shows: Rider on a wide paved interstate shoulder beside a green 'INTERSTATE 10 Pearl Harbor Memorial Highway' sign; cracked pavement, gravel verge, bare mountains behind

records.summary: The 11-mile I-10 section is all uphill at a shallow 2% — reversed, an 11-mile descent for Nick
records.detail: Interstate section 'was all uphill but at least at a shallow 2% grade', not fun but manageable. GPS confirms: essentially flat at river level for the first two and a quarter hours, then a steady rise to a high point of 1,201 ft at 3:25, with 1,227 ft total ascent. The hottest reading of the day, 98.6 F, falls at exactly that high point.
records.cyclistIntel: Reversed, Nick descends eleven miles at 2% on the debris-covered interstate shoulder. A 2% grade on a loaded bike means 20-25 mph without pedalling, precisely the speed at which the screws and tyre wire in d8-001 become dangerous rather than annoying. RARE CASE WHERE THE INVERSION MAKES THINGS WORSE.
records.quote: This section was all uphill but at least at a shallow 2% grade.
records.anchorNote: extent applied west→east per the source rule

photos.shows: Elevation trace flat near river level until ~2:13 then climbing steadily to a marked 1,201 ft at 3:25; temperature trace peaking at 98.6 F at the same moment

records.summary: Dome Rock Road: 5 scenic miles off the interstate on a gentle slope into Quartzsite
records.detail: After leaving I-10 the route runs five miles down a gentle slope into Quartzsite on what the rider calls 'Dome Mountain Road' in the text but 'Dome Rock Road' in a photo caption on the same page. The caption spelling matches the road that exists there, so treat the body text as the error. Frontage-type road paralleling the interstate.
records.cyclistIntel: Reversed, this is Nick's gentle five-mile climb out of Quartzsite before joining I-10. Also the obvious candidate for avoiding some of the interstate debris section — CHECK WHETHER DOME ROCK ROAD PARALLELS I-10 FURTHER WEST than the five miles they used. Planner should geocode 'Dome Rock Road', not 'Dome Mountain Road'.
records.quote: the route went 5 miles down a gentle slope on Dome Mountain Road. Very scenic.
records.anchorNote: extent applied west→east per the source rule

photos.caption: I wonder how they came up with the name Dome Rock Road?

records.summary: Established boondocking area in the desert along Dome Rock Road outside Quartzsite
records.detail: 'Lots of boondockers scattered around the desert' along the five-mile Dome Rock Road stretch into Quartzsite. Quartzsite is a well-known long-term BLM dispersed camping destination; the density of people already doing it is what the observation establishes. No permit, fee or duration information given, and the riders themselves stayed at an RV park rather than joining them.
records.cyclistIntel: A real dispersed-camping option immediately on route at Quartzsite, corroborated by many people visibly doing it. Verify the BLM permit regime — Quartzsite has designated long-term and short-term visitor areas with different rules, none of it described here. Being surrounded by other campers is a meaningful safety plus for a solo rider compared with the isolated Glamis and Palo Verde sites.
records.quote: Lots of boondockers scattered around the desert there.
records.anchorNote: extent applied west→east per the source rule

records.summary: Irrigated produce farmland between Palo Verde and Blythe — alfalfa, cabbage, carrots, lettuce, onions
records.detail: First 25 miles run through irrigated farmland. Over preceding days the rider logged alfalfa, cabbage, carrots, lettuce and onion fields, the last strong enough to fill the air with onion smell. Cotton is supposedly grown here but they saw none.
records.cyclistIntel: Farmland means farm buildings, canals, occasional shade and people — materially different from the open desert either side, and worth having in the planner. It does NOT mean services: no store is named, and Blythe is the town that matters.
records.quote: we saw lots of alfalfa, some cabbage, carrots, lettuce, and onion fields that filled the air with onion smells

records.summary: Flying J truckstop with a Wendy's on the Arizona side of the Colorado River
records.detail: Lunch at a Wendy's inside a Flying J truckstop just across the state line, described as a beehive of activity because Arizona fuel runs about fifty cents cheaper than California one mile back, so everyone pulls off I-10 to fill up. Truckstops of this type carry water, food, restrooms and are typically open around the clock (not stated on the page).
records.cyclistIntel: Strong resupply anchor at the state line, roughly 25 miles into this leg. For Nick WESTBOUND it is the LAST substantial services before crossing back into California toward Palo Verde and the Glamis corridor, where the journal records nothing for two days. Fill everything here. Confirm 24-hour status.
records.quote: Lunch at a Wendy's at the Flying J truckstop was remarkable because of the beehive of activity.

records.summary: Colorado River crossing at Blythe/Ehrenberg, plus abundant irrigation canals through the farmland
records.detail: Route reaches the Colorado River 25 miles into the day and crosses into Arizona. A photograph from the bridge shows a wide body of blue-green water with sandbars, palms and developed banks. Rider separately notes 'a vast amount of water coming from the Colorado River to irrigation ditches' through the farmland approaching Blythe. All surface or agricultural water, not potable.
records.cyclistIntel: Marks the end of the dry country westbound and its beginning eastbound. Canals are visible, plentiful and full of agricultural runoff — usable as an emergency filtered source through the farmland belt and worth mapping as such, but the Flying J is the real water stop. Bridge crossings on the Colorado are natural, findable landmarks for anchoring.
records.quote: There is a vast amount of water coming from the Colorado River to irrigation ditches like this.

photos.caption: The Colorado River.
photos.shows: Wide blue-green river seen from a bridge with concrete railing; sandbars, red channel buoys, palms and low development on both banks

records.summary: 98.6 F peak on 6 April, day average 83.2 F — four days after an all-day average of 43 F with sleet
records.detail: GPS records a day average of 83.2 F and a peak of 98.6 F, reached at the top of the I-10 climb. Map header shows 66 F at the start, so the day gained more than thirty degrees. Set against p5-003 (43.1 F average with sleet at 3,900 ft), this journal swung fifty-five degrees in four days without leaving the region. QUALIFIED BY d9-002: the rider calls this heat unseasonable, so treat as a ceiling, not a baseline.
records.cyclistIntel: The low desert CAN hit 98 F in the first week of April, and the rider hit it while climbing. Use as a planning ceiling for water-carry, and note the operational response the riders themselves adopted: pre-7am starts. The peak lands in the afternoon at the top of a climb, which is the worst combination.

photos.shows: Temperature trace averaging 83.2 F with a marked 98.6 F at 3:25:02

records.summary: Dozens of Harleys on I-10 returning from Arizona Bike Week in Scottsdale
records.detail: At the Flying J the rider encountered dozens of motorcycles heading back from a large motorcycle rally in Scottsdale, describing them as loud. This was a Sunday, the event's return day. Event traffic on top of the usual Sunday interstate load.
records.cyclistIntel: Event-driven, not a standing condition — but I-10 through here carries surges. Arizona Bike Week runs in spring and Quartzsite itself hosts enormous RV gatherings in winter. Check both against Nick's arrival window; the difference between an ordinary weekday and a rally return day on an interstate shoulder is substantial.
records.quote: There were dozens of Harleys coming back from a big Bike Week in Scottsdale. Loud.

records.summary: Night 8: Quail Run RV Park, Quartzsite AZ
records.detail: Named on the following day's rest-day page. Party stayed two nights and chose it over the dispersed camping they had just ridden past on Dome Rock Road, consistent with wanting facilities before a rest day. Has a camp host. Laundry was done during the rest day but the page does not say whether on site. No facilities, cost or tent policy stated. Shade set to 'no' per the rider's general statement about Arizona RV parks (d10-005).
records.cyclistIntel: Callable lodging at Quartzsite. Confirm tents, showers and laundry. The dispersed BLM camping along Dome Rock Road (d8-008) is the stronger lead for a cyclist if the permit regime checks out — Quartzsite is unusual on this stretch for offering both.
records.quote: Word has spread through the Quail Run RV Park that we are riding cross country.

records.summary: Quartzsite RV community actively friendly to cross-country cyclists
records.detail: Once word spread that the party was riding cross country, a neighbour came over to talk — a man who was a bicycle messenger in Washington DC for eighteen years, has ridden across the country three times and did not own a car for twenty years. Rider describes the group as a friendly bunch of RVers.
records.cyclistIntel: Third consecutive stop where local people produced value — a Palo Verde local found them a camp (p10-007), a Quartzsite camp host and neighbour offered recommendations, a Salome local answered questions about the area (p15-002). For a solo self-supported rider this matters practically: these are the people who know which BLM areas are open, where water is, and what the road ahead is doing. Treat RV parks along this stretch as an information source, not just a place to sleep.
records.quote: This is a friendly group of RV'ers.

records.summary: Silly Al's Pizza in Quartzsite — sit-down food, recommended by the camp host
records.detail: Party went to Silly Al's Pizza for dinner on the rest day. Rider expects 'a good old fashioned tourist trap' but notes it came recommended by their camp host rather than a guidebook.
records.cyclistIntel: Concrete calorie stop in Quartzsite, useful because the towns either side on this route are thin. A place Nick can sit down and eat a large meal, which matters more on a self-supported trip than it did for a party with a cook.
records.quote: Tonight we are going to Silly Al's Pizza for dinner.

records.summary: Hi Jolly grave and the Quartzsite camel history
records.detail: The US government hired a Syrian camel handler named Hajid Ali, whose name locals turned into 'Hi Jolly'; he led camel caravans in the area for over thirty years before the railroads displaced them, and his grave is a local landmark. The party considered visiting it.
records.cyclistIntel: A point of interest in a town where the route otherwise offers nothing to look at, and a rest-day option if Nick takes one here. No routing consequence.
records.quote: He is a legend in these parts leading camel caravans for over 30 years before the railroads took over.

records.summary: CORRECTION: the rider calls the Arizona heat 'unseasonably hot' — the 98.6 F reading was an outlier, not the April norm
records.detail: Planning the next day's ride: 'It is unseasonably hot in Arizona so it will be an early start.' This qualifies d8-004, which recorded a 98.6 F peak and 83.2 F average. Those numbers stand as measured but were an anomaly for early April rather than a typical expectation.
records.cyclistIntel: Two things remain true and should not be softened: the low desert CAN hit 98 F in the first week of April, and the riders' own response was to start early. Keep the early-start conclusion and keep the figure as a planning CEILING, but do not treat it as the expected condition. The honest version is a very wide envelope — 43 F with sleet on 2 April (p5-003), 98.6 F on 6 April (d8-004) — and the plan needs to survive either end rather than target the middle.
records.quote: It is unseasonably hot in Arizona so it will be an early start.

records.summary: Rest-day cadence: one rest day after six riding days, used for laundry, cleaning and cooking ahead
records.detail: Day 9 is a full rest day with no agenda beyond chores — cleaning, laundry, pre-cooking meals. With the San Diego rest days on Days 2-3, the pattern is a rest day roughly every six riding days. Supported context: their rest day involves a kitchen and a cook, not the same set of tasks Nick will have.
records.cyclistIntel: Relevant to a plan with zero spare days across 53. This party built in a rest day at Quartzsite specifically because it has facilities. If Nick needs a maintenance stop on the Arizona end, Quartzsite is where this journal says the facilities are.
records.quote: Cleaning, laundry and pre-cooking meals for the next couple days.

records.summary: Night 9: second night at Quail Run RV Park, Quartzsite AZ (rest day)
records.detail: Second consecutive night at the same site, used as a rest day. Laundry was done during the day but the page does not say whether on site. Has a camp host. Community described as friendly and included an experienced long-distance cyclist. Nothing establishes tent policy — the party was in RVs throughout.
records.cyclistIntel: Named counterpart to d8-N1; both nights are the same site. Call to confirm tents, showers and laundry. The alternative immediately at hand is extensive BLM dispersed camping along Dome Rock Road (d8-008), the stronger option for a cyclist once the permit regime is checked.
records.quote: Word has spread through the Quail Run RV Park that we are riding cross country.

records.summary: I-10 EAST of Quartzsite is good — wide clean shoulder, light traffic, gradual grade
records.detail: Rider's verdict on the opening interstate section is unambiguous: 'The shoulder was good, the traffic was light, and the hill was gradual. For riding a bike on an interstate this wasn't too bad.' A cockpit photograph confirms a wide, sound paved shoulder in clean condition with a gravel verge and a single truck far ahead. Same interstate, two days after the eleven-mile stretch west of Quartzsite that was carpeted in screws and shredded tyre steel.
records.cyclistIntel: This NARROWS d8-001 rather than contradicting it. The debris problem belongs to the Ehrenberg-Quartzsite section specifically, not to I-10 as a road. Do not let the planner flag every I-10 mile as hazardous — anchor the bad eleven miles tightly and leave this section clean. Likely cause is the Ehrenberg truckstop concentrating traffic and tyre failures at one point.
records.quote: The shoulder was good, the traffic was light, and the hill was gradual. For riding a bike on an interstate this wasn't too bad.

photos.caption: Morning on Interstate 10.
photos.shows: Cockpit view on a wide, clean paved interstate shoulder in sound condition; gravel verge right, one truck distant in the far lane; open desert, low mountains, clear morning sky

records.summary: Three-stage shallow profile: long climb, long descent, long climb — 1,768 ft over 43.9 mi
records.detail: GPS elevation trace confirms the shape previewed on the rest-day page: steady rise from about 400 ft to roughly 1,300 ft by 1:23, a long decline to a trough near 2:46, then a sustained climb to the day's high around 4:30 before easing. Total ascent 1,768 ft. Average speed was only 8.4 mph over 5:12:47 for grades the rider calls gradual — slower than the 11.2 mph on Day 8 with similar terrain. The page offers no explanation and mentions no wind, so the cause is NOT established. Average heart rate 114 bpm.
records.cyclistIntel: Reversed, Nick's Wenden-Quartzsite day is descent, climb, descent, finishing with the gradual drop into Quartzsite on I-10. The unexplained slow average is the thing to watch — if later pages reveal a headwind pattern on this US-60 corridor, this day is the first evidence. Do not assume shallow grades make it a fast day in either direction.
records.quote: More desert scenery. Flat, flat, flat then hills happen.

photos.shows: Elevation trace rising ~400-1,300 ft by 1:23, declining to a trough near 2:46, then climbing to the day's high around 4:30; speed trace averaging 8.4 mph with brief 25 mph spikes; heart rate averaging 114 bpm

records.summary: US-60 corridor northeast of Brenda is lightly travelled and empty
records.detail: After leaving the interstate the route follows a lightly travelled highway through Vicksburg Junction, Salome and Harcuvar to Wenden. Rider: they 'had a lot of time to look at the saguaro cactuses. Not much else out there.'
records.cyclistIntel: Good riding conditions but an empty corridor — light traffic also means few services, no shade and nobody around if something goes wrong. Salome is the exception and has a bar/restaurant with real shade (p15-001). Enter this stretch self-sufficient rather than planning to resupply in it.
records.quote: The next section was on a lightly traveled highway.

records.summary: First roadrunner sighting; roadkill coyote on the highway
records.detail: Rider saw his first roadrunner, moving too fast to photograph, and separately passed a flattened coyote carcass. Both on the US-60 corridor. Neither is a hazard to a cyclist.
records.cyclistIntel: No action. Recorded so the wildlife picture along this corridor stays continuous and so a later report of an actual animal incident here has a baseline.
records.quote: We saw our first roadrunner. It was running fast and I couldn't get a photo.

records.summary: First saguaro cactus of the trip on the US-60 corridor — the transition into Sonoran desert
records.detail: Rider notes saguaro cactuses along the lightly travelled highway section. Saguaros mark the change from the Colorado Desert scrub of the Imperial Valley and Quartzsite area into Sonoran desert proper.
records.cyclistIntel: A real ecological boundary, legible from the saddle. Saguaro country also means the first meaningful vertical structures since the Imperial Valley — though a saguaro's shadow is not much shade.
records.quote: We had a lot of time to look at the saguaro cactuses. Not much else out there.

records.summary: NO SHADE at Arizona RV parks — stated flatly, and a serious problem for a tent in 80-100 F
records.detail: Photo caption on the night's campsite: 'Our campsite tonight. There is no such thing as shade in Arizona RV parks.' Said about their own site at the Wenden KOA and generalised by the rider to Arizona RV parks as a class. Same page records riding in the 80s; earlier pages recorded a 98.6 F peak.
records.cyclistIntel: Most useful lodging observation in the journal, and it comes from an offhand caption. An RV in full sun runs air conditioning; a tent in full sun in Arizona is unusable from late morning until evening. Nick cannot treat an Arizona RV park as a place to rest through the heat of the day, only a place to sleep at night. Where he needs midday shade, look at town parks, libraries, ramadas and picnic shelters instead — Don's Cactus Bar in Salome (p15-001) is the first confirmed example on route. 'shade' is now a field on every site record.
records.quote: There is no such thing as shade in Arizona RV parks.

photos.caption: Our campsite tonight. There is no such thing as shade in Arizona RV parks.

records.summary: Second consecutive day requiring a pre-7am start because of heat; riding in the 80s
records.detail: On the road by 7am specifically because the day was forecast sunny and warm; rider notes riding 'in the 80's'. The following day is previewed as longer and hotter with another early start. Settled pattern across three consecutive pages, even though the heat itself was described as unseasonable (d9-002). The escort's companion page (p15-004) confirms it cooled down at night.
records.cyclistIntel: The operational lesson transfers regardless of whether the temperatures were typical: on this stretch the working practice is to be riding at first light and done by early afternoon. Knock-on effects for a self-supported plan — camp is struck in the dark, and the midday shade problem in d10-005 becomes unavoidable rather than optional.
records.quote: Today was sunny and warm so an early start was a good idea. On the road by 7am.

records.summary: Night 10: KOA RV park at Wenden AZ — has a pool, has no shade
records.detail: A KOA with a swimming pool, which the rider says felt great after riding in the 80s. Same page states there is no shade at the site or, generalised, at Arizona RV parks at all. Facility values marked likely come from KOA chain norms rather than the page; the pool and the absence of shade are both stated directly. Second KOA of the trip after Boulevard — the chain is proving to be the reliable named option on this route.
records.cyclistIntel: A pool is a significant amenity in this heat and worth planning a day around. The absence of shade is the counterweight — Nick can cool off in the water but has nowhere to sit out the afternoon. Call-ahead list with the standard questions plus one more: whether any site has a shade structure.
records.quote: The KOA RV park we are at has a pool. It felt great.

photos.caption: Awww, it feels so good after biking in the 80's.

records.summary: DON'S CACTUS BAR, Salome AZ — genuine covered shade, food, drink, and a fan, directly on route
records.detail: Escort's companion page for Day 10 (page 15/68, written by WDMDeb). The crew cooled off at Don's Cactus Bar in Salome while waiting for the riders: margaritas, chips and salsa, with a restaurant beside the bar. A slow morning became 'a hopping place by noon, with all the locals stopping in for a drink, or eating at the restaurant beside the bar. The parking lot was full.' Captions: 'Enjoying the shade' and 'Carly enjoying the cool concrete' (Carly appears to be the party's dog). The photograph shows a large open-air covered structure — corrugated metal roof on timber beams, arched masonry opening, ceiling fan, string lights, a red vinyl bar, tables and chairs, cool concrete floor, Coke machine, Dick Wick Hall memorabilia.
records.cyclistIntel: THE ANSWER TO d10-005. This is the first confirmed midday shade shelter on the Arizona stretch — covered, open-air, with a fan, cold drinks, food, a bathroom presumably, and cool concrete to lie on. Exactly what an Arizona RV park cannot offer. Salome sits on the US-60 corridor which d10-003 describes as otherwise empty. Anchor it precisely: this is a place to time a day around, not just a place to eat. Confirm opening hours and days — it was busy at noon on a Tuesday.
records.quote: While we were waiting for the guys, we decided to cool off at Don's Cactus Bar in Salome. The margaritas, chips, and salsa hit the spot.

photos.caption: Don's Cactus Bar, Salome
photos.shows: Large open-air covered patio: corrugated metal roof on timber beams, arched masonry opening to the desert, ceiling fan, string lights, red vinyl bar, wooden tables and mesh chairs, bare concrete floor, Coke machine, Jack Daniels and Dick Wick Hall signage, US and POW/MIA flags

photos.caption: Enjoying the shade
