Carly enjoying the cool concrete

records.summary: Salome locals at Don's Cactus Bar were helpful and answered questions about the area
records.detail: The waitress was 'very helpful' and one local 'answered lots of questions we had about the area.' Recorded on the escort's page. Fourth consecutive stop where local people produced useful information, after Palo Verde, Quartzsite camp host, and the Quartzsite neighbour.
records.cyclistIntel: A reliable pattern on this stretch now: the bar or the camp host is the best available source on road conditions, water and open BLM ground ahead. For a solo rider crossing an empty corridor, Don's is both the shade stop and the intelligence stop.
records.quote: The waitress was very helpful, and 1 guy answered lots of questions we had about the area.

records.summary: Salome main street is very wide with aged cracked asphalt and no shoulder markings
records.detail: From a photograph captioned 'Guys coming in to Salome' showing the two riders crossing a very wide expanse of aged, cracked asphalt through the town — low buildings, palms, parked RVs, no lane or shoulder markings visible in frame. Wide open roadway rather than a marked bike-relevant shoulder.
records.cyclistIntel: Low-consequence but worth knowing: through-town riding at Salome is on a broad unmarked surface with cars able to pass anywhere. Cracked pavement rather than smooth. Not a hazard at town speeds.
records.quote: Guys coming in to Salome

photos.caption: Guys coming in to Salome
photos.shows: Two cyclists crossing a very wide expanse of aged cracked asphalt; low white buildings, palm, utility poles, parked RVs; no lane or shoulder markings visible; harsh midday light

records.summary: Hot again by noon at Salome, cooling down at night — corroborates the early-start pattern
records.detail: Escort's page opens 'Another hot day in the desert!' and closes 'It's starting to cool down a little tonight, so better get some shut eye before an early morning start.' Independent confirmation of d10-004 from a second observer, and it establishes that the nights do cool.
records.cyclistIntel: Useful nuance: the heat is a daytime problem, not a round-the-clock one. Nights cool enough to sleep, which makes the pre-dawn start viable rather than merely necessary. The unusable window is roughly late morning to evening — which is when a shade stop like Don's earns its place.
records.quote: It's starting to cool down a little tonight,so better get some shut eye before an early morning start

records.summary: WENDEN U.S. 60 COUNTRY MARKET AND HARDWARE — groceries, hardware, liquor, and a LAUNDROMAT, on route in Wenden
records.detail: Established from a photograph captioned 'Taking off from Wenden' on page 16 (escort's Day 11 page). A large lit sign reads 'WENDEN U.S. 60 COUNTRY MARKET AND HARDWARE'; the storefront carries 'LIQUOR BEER WINE' and a smaller sign reading 'PIKE LIQUORS / LAUNDROMAT'. The riders are photographed departing past it in low morning sun with long shadows, corroborating the pre-7am start pattern. Not mentioned in the text at all — this is entirely photo evidence.
records.cyclistIntel: Significant find on an otherwise empty corridor: a general store with groceries AND hardware AND a laundromat, directly on US-60 in Wenden, next to the KOA the party used (d10-N1). Hardware matters for a self-supported rider — zip ties, fasteners, tape, fuel. Laundry matters because the Arizona RV parks have no confirmed laundry. This makes Wenden a genuine service node rather than just a campground. Confirm hours and days; small-town Arizona markets often close early and may not open Sundays.
records.quote: Taking off from Wenden

photos.caption: Taking off from Wenden
photos.shows: Lit sign 'WENDEN U.S. 60 COUNTRY MARKET AND HARDWARE'; storefront lettered 'WENDEN U.S. 60 COUNTRY MARKET' with 'LIQUOR BEER WINE' window signage and a 'PIKE LIQUORS / LAUNDROMAT' sign below; two loaded riders departing on the roadway in low morning sun with long shadows; support RV and van parked outside

records.summary: Wickenburg AZ is a full-service town — CVS pharmacy, Goodwill, groceries, sit-down restaurant
records.detail: Escort's page records buying groceries, eating lunch with the riders at Rancho Bar 7 ('excellent chicken salad sandwich'), and a Goodwill and CVS with a shared parking lot. Also sightseeing through historical Wickenburg. First substantial town with a pharmacy recorded anywhere on the Arizona stretch of this journal.
records.cyclistIntel: The best resupply point in Arizona so far and the first with a PHARMACY, which matters for a self-supported rider — sunscreen, electrolytes, first aid, prescriptions. Groceries plus a sit-down restaurant plus a thrift store for replacing worn kit. Coming from the west, Wickenburg is the first real town after the empty US-60 corridor; treat it as a planned resupply, not an incidental stop.
records.quote: Then we got some more groceries, ate lunch with the boys at Rancho Bar 7 (excellent chicken salad sandwich)

records.summary: Locals continue to engage — a 96-year-old on an electric trike in Wickenburg
records.detail: Escort reports 'We are visiting with lots of locals' and recounts meeting a 96-year-old man riding an electric upright tricycle in the Goodwill/CVS parking lot, a retired mechanical engineering professor from Tempe, originally from Wisconsin, whose trike they nicknamed 'truck Badger'. Fifth consecutive stop where locals engaged with the party.
records.cyclistIntel: No routing consequence, but it extends a consistent pattern across the whole Arizona and California stretch: this corridor's small towns are receptive rather than indifferent to touring cyclists. Reinforces the practical point in p15-002 — locals are the best available source on road and water conditions ahead.
records.quote: We are visiting with lots of locals.

photos.caption: Our 96 year old local riding his "truck Badger"

records.summary: Historical downtown Wickenburg with street statuary, worth walking
records.detail: Escort did 'some sightseeing throughout historical Wickenburg' and notes 'The statutes are so cool!' — the town's downtown historical district and its street sculptures.
records.cyclistIntel: A rest-stop option in the one Arizona town on this stretch with real amenities. Combined with p16-002, Wickenburg is the natural place to take a half day if Nick needs one on the Arizona end.
records.quote: The statutes are so cool!

records.summary: Desert pattern confirmed by a second observer: hot by day, cool at night, and hydration is the limiting factor
records.detail: Escort's page: 'We can tell we're in the desert - hot during the day and cool at night. I can't seem to drink enough water!!' Written by a non-riding crew member with air conditioning and unlimited RV water — which makes the hydration complaint more striking, not less. Independently corroborates p15-004 and d10-004.
records.cyclistIntel: THE HYDRATION POINT IS THE ONE TO CARRY. A supported crew member with unlimited water could not drink enough in this climate. Nick will be carrying his, on a bike, working. Every water-carry figure for the Arizona and California low desert should be built assuming intake demand well above normal, on top of the no-shade problem (d10-005) and the 98.6 F ceiling (d8-004). The cool nights are the offset that makes pre-dawn starts workable.
records.quote: hot during the day and cool at night. I can't seem to drink enough water!!

records.summary: Night 11: HORSPITALITY RV PARK, on US-60 east of Wickenburg AZ
records.detail: Named directly: 'our home for the night - Horspitality RV Park along the trail Hwy 60 East'. Located on US-60 east of Wickenburg, so on the onward route rather than back in town. No facilities, cost or tent policy given. Party in RVs throughout.
records.cyclistIntel: Named and callable, and positioned east of Wickenburg — meaning for Nick travelling WESTBOUND it comes BEFORE the town, so he would hit the campground first and the resupply second. Worth knowing when sequencing a day. Add to the call-ahead list: tents, showers, laundry, and shade (the rider's flat statement in d10-005 is that Arizona RV parks have none, so assume no shade until told otherwise).
records.quote: time to head to our home for the night -Horspitality RV Park along the trail Hwy 60 East

records.summary: First 20 miles east of Wenden are VERY rough chipseal — 'sucked the energy right out of us'
records.detail: Rider is unambiguous: 'The first 20 miles of road was very rough chipseal. So rough it sucked the energy right out of us.' This is US-60 east of Wenden. Worth pairing with d10-002: the previous day's average was an unexplained 8.4 mph on shallow grades, and rough chipseal on this same corridor is a plausible cause that the earlier page simply did not mention.
records.cyclistIntel: A 20-mile energy tax with no hazard attached — nothing to dodge, just a surface that costs you speed and legs for the better part of two hours. Plan the day's mileage assuming a slower average through here rather than budgeting off the gradient. For Nick WESTBOUND this is the LAST 20 miles into Wenden, arriving tired, which is worse than hitting it fresh as they did. Wider tyres at lower pressure are the mitigation.
records.quote: The first 20 miles of road was very rough chipseal. So rough it sucked the energy right out of us.

records.summary: Lots of GLASS on the shoulder east of Wenden, requiring active dodging
records.detail: 'Oh, and there was a lot of glass on the shoulder that we had to dodge. No flats, that's a positive!' Same 20-mile stretch of US-60 as the rough chipseal. Third debris finding in the dataset after CA-78 (p10-002) and the I-10 stretch west of Quartzsite (d8-001), and the first where the material is specifically glass. Note the Wenden market sells liquor, beer and wine (p16-001), which is a plausible local source.
records.cyclistIntel: Glass plus rough chipseal on the same 20 miles is a bad combination: the surface is already jarring, so spotting and steering around glass is harder, and rough chipseal disguises it. They escaped without a flat but were actively dodging the whole way. Ride this stretch scanning the shoulder rather than the scenery, and consider taking the lane where traffic allows — d10-003 records this corridor as lightly travelled.
records.quote: there was a lot of glass on the shoulder that we had to dodge. No flats, that's a positive!

records.summary: Long steady gentle climb Wenden to Wickenburg: 1,750 ft to a 2,594 ft high point, 912 ft ascent over 49 mi
records.detail: Rider calls it 'One long, straight, flat ride through an unchanging landscape' — but the GPS elevation trace shows a continuous gentle rise from about 1,750 ft to a marked 2,594 ft at 3:47, then a drop into Wickenburg. 912 ft total ascent over 48.93 mi at 11.4 mph. It FEELS flat and is not. Photographs show saguaro on the hillsides and an early-morning onion field near Wenden, placing irrigated farmland at the western end of the leg. NOTE: the GPS activity is titled 'Salome to Wickenburg' while the page is titled 'Wenden to Wickenburg'; the map start pin is at Wenden.
records.cyclistIntel: An invisible gradient is worth flagging precisely because the rider could not feel it — combined with 20 miles of rough chipseal it explains a day that reads as harder than its numbers. Reversed, Nick gets a gentle net descent from Wickenburg toward Wenden, which partly offsets hitting the rough chipseal at the end of his day.
records.quote: Today's ride is interesting because it was so uninteresting. One long, straight, flat ride through an unchanging landscape.

photos.shows: Elevation trace rising steadily from ~1,750 ft to a marked 2,594 ft at 3:47:16 then dropping; speed averaging 11.4 mph; GPS summary 48.93 mi, 4:18:05, 912 ft ascent, 61.0 F

photos.caption: Lots of cactuses.
photos.shows: Dozens of mature saguaro scattered across a rocky desert hillside with creosote and low scrub

records.summary: Almost no wildlife on the Wenden-Wickenburg leg — crows and a second flattened coyote
records.detail: 'The only wildlife were crows and another flattened cayote.' Second roadkill coyote in two days on the US-60 corridor after d10-007. Notable mainly as the contrast with the burro and turkey activity further west.
records.cyclistIntel: No action. The wildlife risk on this corridor is materially lower than on CA-78, where the burro herd operates (p10-003). Worth having in the planner so the warning layer does not fire uniformly across the desert.
records.quote: The only wildlife were crows and another flattened cayote.

records.summary: Met a 16-rider Adventure Cycling organized group riding NICK'S DIRECTION — St. Augustine 15 Feb, almost finished 9 April
records.detail: 'We met a group of 16 riders going the opposite way. They were on an Adventure Cycling organized ride that left St. Augustine FL on February 15 and were almost done.' Opposite to this journal means EAST-TO-WEST — the same direction Nick rides. One wore a RAGBRAI jersey. St. Augustine on 15 February to nearly finished on 9 April is roughly 53 days elapsed for the full St. Augustine to San Diego route.
records.cyclistIntel: BEST FEASIBILITY DATAPOINT IN THE DATASET. An organized ACA group covered St. Augustine to near-San Diego in about 53-56 days riding Nick's direction. Nick's plan is 53 days from PENSACOLA, which is several hundred miles shorter — so his schedule sits in the same range as a supported organized tour on a longer route, and is not obviously unrealistic. It also confirms a mid-February departure puts you here in early April, which is the weather window every page in this dataset describes. Two caveats: an organized group has vehicle support and no rest-day flexibility problems, and Nick's plan has zero spare days.
records.quote: They were on an Adventure Cycling organized ride that left St. Augustine FL on February 15 and were almost done.

records.summary: Wickenburg historical downtown: the Jail Tree (200-year-old mesquite), Wickenburg Massacre marker, rodeo and cowboy statuary
records.detail: Rider found Wickenburg 'surprisingly interesting' with 'a lot of community pride in their rodeo and cowboy heritage. Statues all over downtown.' Two specific fixes from photographs: the Jail Tree, a roughly 200-year-old mesquite that prisoners were chained to, and a stone-set Arizona Highway Department plaque commemorating the Wickenburg Massacre of 5 November 1871, when the Wickenburg-Ehrenberg stage was ambushed. Corroborates the escort's account (p16-004).
records.cyclistIntel: Wickenburg is the one town on the Arizona stretch worth stopping in for its own sake, and it pairs with the resupply in p16-002 to make it the natural half-day or rest stop. Incidentally, the massacre marker names the Wickenburg-Ehrenberg stage road — essentially the same corridor the route follows between the Colorado River and Wickenburg.
records.quote: Dave and Mike chained to the Jail Tree. It's a 200 year old mesquite tree.

photos.caption: Interesting history in Wickenburg.
photos.shows: Cast plaque set in a stone wall reading 'WICKENBURG MASSACRE — IN THIS VICINITY, NOV 5, 1871, WICKENBURG-EHRENBURG STAGE AMBUSHED BY APACHE MOHAVE INDIANS' with named victims; Arizona Highway Department, 1937

records.summary: 60 F at the early start, 98.6 F peak, day average 86.9 F — second 98.6 F day in four
records.detail: Photo caption: 'Early start, already 60 degrees. It got to 90 degrees at the end of the ride.' The GPS temperature trace disagrees with the rider's estimate, recording a peak of 98.6 F at 3:47 and a day average of 86.9 F — so the felt figure was 90 and the measured figure was nearly 99. Second day at 98.6 F after d8-004, and the highest DAY AVERAGE recorded so far. The escort's companion page confirms it cooled at night (p16-005).
records.cyclistIntel: The day average is the number that matters here: 86.9 F sustained is harder than a brief 98 F spike, and it climbed all day, peaking at the high point at the end of the ride. Note also that the rider UNDERESTIMATED the heat by nearly nine degrees — a reminder not to trust felt temperature when planning water. With d9-002 calling the heat unseasonable, treat this as ceiling; but two 98.6 F days in four says the ceiling is reachable.
records.quote: Early start, already 60 degrees. It got to 90 degrees at the end of the ride.

photos.shows: Temperature trace climbing all day to a marked 98.6 F at 3:47:16, averaging 86.9 F

records.summary: Smooth shoulder and good roads Wickenburg to the Phoenix basin — explicit contrast with the previous day
records.detail: Rider: 'The shoulder of the road was smooth and downhill. It was nice to be able to look around at the river to our right instead of holding on for dear life on a rough surface. Almost the entire day was downhill or flat and on nice roads.' The relief is the point — this is the same rider who described 20 miles of energy-sapping chipseal the day before (p17-001). A photograph shows a sound two-lane with roughly 2-3 ft of paved shoulder through saguaro country.
records.cyclistIntel: Confirms the rough-surface problem on this corridor is specific to the Wenden-Aguila stretch, not general to US-60. From Wickenburg toward Phoenix the surface is good and the shoulder usable. Anchor the bad 20 miles tightly rather than flagging the corridor.
records.quote: The shoulder of the road was smooth and downhill.

photos.shows: Rider on a two-lane road with roughly 2-3 ft of sound paved shoulder outside the fog line; saguaro and palo verde, clear sky, low morning sun, rider still in a jacket

records.summary: Net ~1,000 ft descent Wickenburg into the Phoenix basin — reversed, a gentle all-day CLIMB for Nick
records.detail: 'Almost the entire day was downhill or flat.' GPS elevation trace confirms: 2,075 ft near Wickenburg at 52:26 declining steadily to roughly 1,000-1,100 ft by the end, with only 804 ft of total ascent over 49.10 mi at 12.8 mph — their second-fastest average of the trip.
records.cyclistIntel: REVERSED: Nick climbs roughly 1,000 ft net from the Phoenix basin up to Wickenburg across 49 miles. Gentle, but all day and in the direction of increasing heat exposure as the day goes on, and their 12.8 mph average tells him nothing. Combined with p17-003, Nick's Phoenix-to-Wenden run is a two-day continuous gentle ascent ending in 20 miles of rough chipseal.
records.quote: Almost the entire day was downhill or flat and on nice roads.

photos.shows: Elevation trace declining from a marked 2,075 ft at 52:26 to roughly 1,000-1,100 ft at the end; GPS summary 49.10 mi, 3:49:18, 12.8 mph, 804 ft ascent, 68.0 F

records.summary: OFF-ROUTE detour into Sun City West, and Google's 'bike safe route' through the metro took forever
records.detail: 'We rode off route to visit friends in Sun City West. It took forever to follow the bike safe route Google gave us. And it was in the 90's.' The rider also badly underestimated the remaining distance — 'Its only 8 miles or so' became 20. This portion is NOT the ACA alignment; the map shows the track leaving the corridor and dropping south into the Surprise / Sun City West area.
records.cyclistIntel: Two useful things despite being off route. First, mark this segment as not-ACA so it does not contaminate the route geometry check. Second, and more valuable: Google's bicycle routing through the Phoenix metro produced a circuitous route that took far longer than expected, in 90-degree heat. Nick crosses this metro area on his own alignment — do not trust a consumer bike-routing detour here to be short, and do not plan a metro crossing on the assumption that urban miles are easy miles.
records.quote: It took forever to follow the bike safe route Google gave us. And it was in the 90's.
records.anchorNote: extent applied west→east per the source rule

records.summary: A river runs alongside the road southeast of Wickenburg (Hassayampa corridor)
records.detail: Rider notes it was 'nice to be able to look around at the river to our right' on the descent out of Wickenburg. Almost certainly the Hassayampa. The page establishes only that a river is visible from the road — nothing about whether it is flowing, accessible, or of any use. Arizona desert rivers on this corridor are frequently dry at the surface.
records.cyclistIntel: Recorded as a landmark and a POSSIBLE emergency water lead, deliberately at low confidence. Do NOT enter it in the planner as a water source: no flow, access or quality information exists, and desert rivers here run dry for most of the year. Verify independently if it matters.
records.quote: look around at the river to our right

records.summary: Truckstop lunch stop between Wickenburg and the Phoenix metro
records.detail: 'Truckstop lunch breaks are always interesting' — they stopped at a truckstop for lunch somewhere on the leg, with an extended anecdote about the people-watching. The page does not name it or give its location beyond being between Wickenburg and the metro; the map shows waypoint markers near Morristown and Circle City.
records.cyclistIntel: A services point exists on this leg but is not identified — worth pinning down, since it sits between Wickenburg and the metro edge. Truckstops are the reliable form of resupply on this route: water, food, restrooms, usually long hours. Second truckstop lunch of the journal after the Flying J at Ehrenberg (d8-005).
records.quote: Truckstop lunch breaks are always interesting.

records.summary: Photo evidence: Horspitality RV Park is raw desert vegetation with no shade structure
records.detail: A morning photograph captioned 'Early morning at the Horspitality RV Park' shows the site as open Sonoran desert — saguaro, palo verde, mesquite and dry grass, with an RV just visible at the edge of frame. No trees over the sites, no ramada, no shade structure anywhere in view. Directly corroborates the rider's general statement about Arizona RV parks (d10-005) for this specific named site.
records.cyclistIntel: Resolves the shade field on p16-N1 from unknown to no. Horspitality is a place to sleep at night, not somewhere to wait out an afternoon in a tent. The rider's generalisation now has photographic support at two named Arizona sites, which makes it safe to assume no shade at any Arizona RV park on this route until a specific site says otherwise.
records.quote: Early morning at the Horspitality RV Park. They really like their cowboy culture in Wickenburg.

photos.caption: Early morning at the Horspitality RV Park. They really like their cowboy culture in Wickenburg.
photos.shows: Open Sonoran desert with saguaro, palo verde, mesquite and dry bunchgrass; distant mountains; an RV at the right edge of frame; no trees over sites, no ramada or shade structure anywhere in view; clear sky

records.summary: RECORD HIGHS in the Phoenix area for the time of year — 90s after lunch, day average 86.3 F
records.detail: 'We left Wickenburg early since the Pheonix area is having record highs for this time of year.' GPS records a day average of 86.3 F, 77.0 F at 52 minutes in, and the temperature trace climbing all afternoon. Rider: 'After the lunch break it officially became hot... And it was in the 90's.' Third consecutive day-average above 83 F. Note this sharpens d9-002: the heat is not merely unseasonable, it was record-setting.
records.cyclistIntel: IMPORTANT CALIBRATION. This journal's Arizona heat readings are record highs, not normal April, so they are a genuine outlier — but they are also a real, recorded, survivable condition on this exact route, which makes them the right ceiling to plan water and shade against. The riders' response was consistent every single day: leave before dawn, be done by early afternoon. That operational rule is the transferable finding, not the specific numbers.
records.quote: We left Wickenburg early since the Pheonix area is having record highs for this time of year.

photos.shows: Temperature trace rising from a marked 77.0 F at 52:26 through the afternoon, averaging 86.3 F

records.summary: Night 12: Sun City West AZ, hosted by friends — OFF ROUTE
records.detail: The party detoured off route to Sun City West to visit friends Don and Rhonda, who 'brought us some cool drinks, toured us around his area, and fed us pizza cooked in his Big Green Egg.' The page does not say where the RVs were parked for the night. Private hospitality, not a replicable site.
records.cyclistIntel: NOT A LODGING LEAD — private friends, off route. Recorded only to keep the overnight chain unbroken. The transferable point is that the Phoenix metro detour cost them roughly 20 unplanned miles in 90-degree heat (p18-004); a social stop in this metro is not a short one.
records.quote: our friends Don and Rhonda brought us some cool drinks, toured us around his area, and fed us pizza cooked in his Big Green Egg

records.summary: 21 miles of CAR-FREE paved bike trail across Phoenix — New River Trail then a canal trail
records.detail: 'It was 21 miles of bike trail that followed a river and then a canal. It was a very nice bike trail.' Photographs show a wide smooth concrete path with a yellow centerline, block wall on one side and desert landscaping on the other, with young trees casting partial shade; then an asphalt path running directly alongside a full flowing canal. The trail begins at the signed New River Trailhead at Fletcher Heights in Peoria. Rider's only complaint is that Central Iowa's trail system is better.
records.cyclistIntel: MAJOR find for the metro crossing: 21 continuous car-free miles through Phoenix on the official ACA alignment. For Nick this is 21 miles with no traffic risk at all in the middle of the largest urban area on his route. It also has intermittent tree shade, which the Arizona RV parks do not (d10-005). The catch is navigation — see p20-002.
records.quote: It was 21 miles of bike trail that followed a river and then a canal.

photos.caption: It's so nice to be on a bike trail.
photos.shows: Wide smooth concrete shared-use path with yellow centerline; block wall right, desert landscaping left, young trees casting partial shade; survey marks on the surface

photos.caption: The trail went from following a dried up riverbed to a canal.
photos.shows: Asphalt path running directly beside a full flowing concrete-lined canal; palms, power lines, low houses; clear sky

records.summary: The Phoenix bike path DISAPPEARS AND REAPPEARS half a block away — two independent touring cyclists both lost the route
records.detail: Rider met another fully loaded Southern Tier rider taking a break on the canal trail who 'was as bewildered as I was on how to follow the bike path that disappears then reappears a half block away.' Two separate experienced touring cyclists, independently, could not follow the alignment. This is a navigation failure, not a road-condition problem.
records.cyclistIntel: THE HIGHEST-VALUE WARNING IN THE PHOENIX SECTION. The trail itself is excellent but the alignment is discontinuous in a way that maps do not convey, and getting lost here means unplanned city miles in 97 F heat (p20-003) — exactly what cost the previous day 20 extra miles (p18-004). Nick should have the trail loaded as a GPS track rather than relying on signage or turn cues, and the app should flag the discontinuities specifically. Worth finding a rider's GPX of this section rather than trusting the reconstructed geometry.
records.quote: He was as bewildered as I was on how to follow the bike path that disappears then reappears a half block away.

records.summary: Phoenix suburban roads after the trail were lightly travelled
records.detail: 'The rest of the route was lightly traveled city roads. I really got to see a lot of suburbia Phoenix. Some run down, some really nice.' Roughly 34 miles of the 55-mile day on city streets after the trail section ends, through Scottsdale, Tempe and Mesa.
records.cyclistIntel: Reassuring: the ACA alignment through the Phoenix metro deliberately uses quiet streets rather than arterials. Combined with the 21 trail miles, the metro crossing is a low-traffic day — the real costs here are heat and navigation, not cars.
records.quote: The rest of the route was lightly traveled city roads.

records.summary: New River Trailhead at Fletcher Heights, Peoria — signed trailhead, trees, adjacent commercial buildings
records.detail: Photograph shows a substantial stone-and-steel monument sign reading 'NEW RIVER TRAILHEAD AT FLETCHER HEIGHTS' with a City of Peoria emblem, mature shade trees, paved plaza and commercial buildings behind including a dental practice. This is where the rider joined the trail. The page does not mention water, restrooms or parking, but a signed municipal trailhead of this scale commonly has them.
records.cyclistIntel: The western entry point to the Phoenix trail system and a hard navigational fix for anchoring the trail span. Has real tree shade, which is scarce on this route. Worth confirming whether it has a water fountain and restrooms — if so it becomes a genuine service point at the metro edge, which matters given Nick arrives here off the desert.
records.quote: Start of the bike trail.

photos.caption: Start of the bike trail.
photos.shows: Stone-and-steel monument sign 'NEW RIVER TRAILHEAD AT FLETCHER HEIGHTS' with City of Peoria emblem; mature shade trees, paved plaza, commercial buildings behind including 'BLACK MOUNTAIN ENDODONTICS'; loaded touring bike and rider in a SPAM jersey

records.summary: Flowing irrigation canal runs alongside the trail for miles through the metro
records.detail: The trail follows a dried-up riverbed and then a canal. The photograph shows a concrete-lined canal carrying a substantial flow of water immediately beside the path, with no fencing visible in frame. This is Salt River Project irrigation water, not potable, and canal banks in Phoenix are generally posted against entry.
records.cyclistIntel: Recorded as a landmark and last-resort emergency source only, deliberately at unknown confidence. Do NOT enter as a water source: untreated irrigation water, likely posted, steep concrete sides that are genuinely dangerous to enter. In an urban area Nick has far better options — the value here is that the canal makes the trail easy to identify and follow.
records.quote: The trail went from following a dried up riverbed to a canal.

photos.caption: The trail went from following a dried up riverbed to a canal.
photos.shows: Concrete-lined canal carrying substantial flow immediately beside the asphalt path; no fencing visible; palms and power lines

records.summary: ACA Southern Tier map 1 ends and map 2 begins in the Phoenix metro
records.detail: Photo caption: 'It was here that we celebrated completing the first Adventure Cycling map and moving to the second map.' Places the boundary between ACA Southern Tier sections 1 and 2 in the Phoenix/Mesa area. Confirms again (with p10-010) that this journal follows the official ACA alignment.
records.cyclistIntel: Useful structural fact for cross-referencing: ACA map 1 covers San Diego to roughly Phoenix. If Nick ever buys official ACA data for part of the route rather than all of it, this is where the section boundary falls — and the two hardest segments found so far (the In-Ko-Pah grade and the I-10 debris stretch) both sit inside map 1.
records.quote: It was here that we celebrated completing the first Adventure Cycling map and moving to the second map.

records.summary: THREE other Southern Tier riders met in a single day in the Phoenix metro
records.detail: An unnamed fully loaded Southern Tier rider on the canal trail, then Donna from Minneapolis and Becky from Ohio, who caught up and rode with him for about 20 miles. All three riding the same west-to-east direction as this journal. With the 16-rider ACA organized group met two days earlier going the OPPOSITE way (p17-005), that is 19 other Southern Tier cyclists encountered in three days.
records.cyclistIntel: The route is genuinely busy in the first half of April — which is good news for a solo rider: company, shared information, and help available if something breaks. It also means the lodging and water points in this dataset are being used by other cyclists at the same time of year, so popular spots may be competitive.
records.quote: we struck up a conversation and found out we all were on the same quest.

photos.caption: Me, Becky from Ohio and Donna from Minneapolis. It was here that we celebrated completing the first Adventure Cycling map and moving to the second map.

records.summary: DATA CAVEAT: the rider was driven from the RV park to the trail start, so the GPS track is short of the full route
records.detail: 'Linda gave me a ride from the RV Park to where the route takes a bike trail through Phoenix.' The recorded 54.81 mi activity therefore begins at the trailhead, not at the previous night's lodging, and the gap between them was covered by vehicle. Page title says Peoria to Mesa; the GPS start pin is in north Peoria.
records.cyclistIntel: Do not treat this day's mileage as a complete route segment when reconciling against the planner's geometry — there is an unrecorded vehicle-shuttled gap at the start. A recurring risk with a supported journal: mileages measure what the rider pedalled, not what the route covers.
records.quote: Linda gave me a ride from the RV Park to where the route takes a bike trail through Phoenix.

records.summary: DAY AVERAGE 97.4 F crossing Phoenix, with trace peaks above 115 F — hottest day in the dataset by far
records.detail: GPS records a day average of 97.4 F over 4:41:42, starting near 78 F and climbing all day, with several spikes on the trace above 115 F. Map header 75 F at the start. The high peaks are likely sensor readings in direct sun and radiant heat off concrete paths and city pavement rather than shade air temperature — but that is exactly the heat a cyclist is actually in. Set against the record-highs note the previous day (p18-003), and the 43.1 F sleet day ten days earlier (p5-003).
records.cyclistIntel: THE URBAN HEAT ISLAND IS A SEPARATE PROBLEM FROM DESERT HEAT. Concrete trails and city pavement radiate, so the Phoenix crossing runs hotter than the open desert either side of it — a 97.4 F day average versus 86 F in the country. Combined with p20-002, the failure mode here is getting lost in the metro during the hottest part of the day. Nick should cross Phoenix starting at first light, with the trail loaded as a track, and treat the metro as a heat hazard rather than a rest from the desert.
records.road: New River Trail / canal trail / city streets

photos.shows: Temperature trace starting near 78 F and climbing all day with multiple spikes above 115 F, averaging 97.4 F; elevation trace 1,050 ft rising to a marked 1,577 ft at 4:38; speed averaging 11.7 mph

records.summary: Night 14 in Mesa AZ — site not named
records.detail: Day ends in Mesa; the page names no site. Rider signs off 'Tomorrow I leave the city behind and head back into the hilly desert.' Night 13 is also unrecorded — page 19 has not been processed and the mileage totals show Day 13 as a zero-mile rest day in the Peoria / Sun City West area.
records.cyclistIntel: No lead. Mesa is a large suburb with commercial lodging, so this is a low-value gap. Worth noting that nights 13 and 14 are the first real holes in the overnight chain since the San Diego rest days.
records.quote: Tomorrow I leave the city behind and head back into the hilly desert.

records.summary: AZ-87 Beeline Highway has little to NO paved shoulder on the climbs — 'I was very close to the traffic'
records.detail: The rider makes this the explicit point of a photo caption: 'Contemplating getting back on the road after a major climb. This shows how narrow some of the shoulders were today. I was very close to the traffic.' Two photographs confirm it — he is standing on a wide DIRT AND GRAVEL verge with roughly a foot of paved surface outside the fog line, and a second frame shows him climbing on the fog line with a sedan passing close around a blind curve. A third photo shows steel guardrail running immediately beside the traffic lane, where there is no verge to escape onto at all.
records.cyclistIntel: THIS IS ON NICK'S AZ_CENTRAL DIVERGENCE (Globe - Tonto Basin - Gilbert), so it is his road, not the classic ACA alignment. Worst shoulder-plus-speed combination in the dataset: no paved shoulder, blind curves, a highway carrying Payson-bound and recreational traffic, and — reversed — Nick DESCENDING it at up to 40 mph rather than crawling up at 5. Where guardrail replaces the gravel verge there is no bail-out. Anchor the narrow sections tightly if possible; this warrants a warning in the app on both grade and shoulder.
records.quote: This shows how narrow some of the shoulders were today. I was very close to the traffic.
records.anchorNote: extent applied west→east per the source rule

photos.caption: Contemplating getting back on the road after a major climb. This shows how narrow some of the shoulders were today. I was very close to the traffic.
photos.shows: Rider standing on a wide dirt-and-gravel verge; roughly a foot of paved surface outside the white fog line; fresh dark asphalt, yellow centerline, road curving away between rocky saguaro-covered slopes

photos.caption: Note the disappearing car. I just finished a climb that capped off at a 10% grade.
photos.shows: Rider climbing on the fog line with a silver sedan passing close on a blind right-hand curve; no paved shoulder; steep cut slope right

photos.caption: Lots of cactuses but also other green plants at this high altitude.
photos.shows: Steel guardrail running immediately beside the traffic lane with no verge outside it; saguaro-covered hillside beyond

records.summary: 5,436 ft of climbing in 56.3 mi out of Phoenix on AZ-87, with a pitch capping at 10% — hardest day in the dataset
records.detail: 'I kept slogging up steep hills then screaming down the other side. Then repeat. The 5400 feet of vertical climb today is more than some 7 day rides I have done.' GPS confirms 5,436 ft over 56.33 mi in 6:07:48 at 9.2 mph — the slowest average of the trip. The elevation trace climbs from about 1,000 ft to roughly 4,200 ft with roughly eleven marked climb waypoints, a drop, then a partial recovery. One climb 'capped off at a 10% grade'. Rider's heart rate reached close to 150 on the climbs. Route is AZ-87 north out of the Mesa area through Tonto National Forest.
records.cyclistIntel: ON NICK'S AZ_CENTRAL DIVERGENCE — this is the real cost of the Globe/Tonto Basin/Gilbert routing and the planner should know it. Reversed, Nick has roughly 3,500 ft of climbing and 5,400 ft of descending across this leg: a rolling net-downhill day, but with substantial climbing and, more importantly, repeated steep descents on a road with no shoulder (p21-002). Their 9.2 mph tells him nothing about his speed, but the 6-hour moving time tells him this is a full day either direction.
records.quote: The 5400 feet of vertical climb today is more than some 7 day rides I have done.
records.anchorNote: extent applied west→east per the source rule

photos.shows: GPS summary 56.33 mi, 6:07:48, 9.2 mph, 5,436 ft total ascent, 70.0 F; elevation trace 1,000 ft to ~4,200 ft with about eleven marked climb waypoints; speed trace with a marked 40.6 mph at 2:31:25

records.summary: Repeated steep descents on AZ-87 with 40.6 mph recorded — reversed, this is Nick's principal descent risk in Arizona
records.detail: 'I kept slogging up steep hills then screaming down the other side.' The speed trace shows numerous spikes above 25 mph and a marked peak of 40.6 mph at 2:31:25. These descents happen on the same road recorded in p21-002 as having no paved shoulder, blind curves and sections of guardrail hard against the traffic lane.
records.cyclistIntel: Combine with p21-002 before shaping this day. Nick travels the reverse direction, so the descents he takes are the reverse of their climbs — and by their own numbers there are roughly 5,400 ft of them. High speed, no shoulder, blind curves, close traffic, and a loaded touring bike. This is the segment where his brakes, tyres and daylight all matter most in Arizona. Do not schedule it at the end of a long day or in fading light.
records.quote: I kept slogging up steep hills then screaming down the other side. Then repeat.
records.anchorNote: extent applied west→east per the source rule

records.summary: AZ-87 carries heavy weekend recreational traffic, plus a car fire that closed lanes with a large emergency response
records.detail: Two elements. First, Sunday recreational traffic: at 9am a large parking lot at the Salt River was 'filling up fast' with kayakers, tubers and paddleboarders, and AZ-87 is the main Phoenix-to-Payson highway. Second, a specific incident — a car fire on the far side of Highway 87 that was 'a big ball of flames' when the support RV passed and burnt out by the time the rider reached it, with 'so many firefighters, highway patrol and sheriffs' that he did not feel he should stop.
records.cyclistIntel: The recreational traffic is the durable finding: this is a weekend destination highway with no shoulder (p21-002), which makes a Sunday crossing materially worse than a weekday one. Same midweek-timing logic as Glamis (p8-010). The car fire is a one-off, but it does establish that emergency response on this corridor is fast and heavy — worth knowing on a road where Nick will be descending fast with no escape room.
records.quote: There was a big parking lot filling up fast at 9am with kayakers, tubers, and stand up boards.
records.anchorNote: extent applied west→east per the source rule

records.summary: High desert transition on AZ-87 — saguaro giving way to small pines and grasses with altitude
records.detail: 'The high desert gave a more interesting landscape, mixing Saguaro cactuses with small pines and more grasses.' Photographs show densely saguaro-covered hillsides at lower elevation and green riparian growth along the Salt River, under overcast skies. The change tracks the climb from roughly 1,000 ft to over 4,000 ft.
records.cyclistIntel: A genuine ecological and climate boundary rather than travelogue: pines and grasses mean cooler air and the first real shade since the Cleveland National Forest in California. Relevant for a rider fleeing 97 F metro heat — climbing out of the Phoenix basin buys temperature relief as well as costing elevation.
records.quote: The high desert gave a more interesting landscape, mixing Saguaro cactuses with small pines and more grasses.

photos.caption: More majestic scenery with the Salt River in the foreground.
photos.shows: Dense green riparian vegetation along a stretch of open water below tall reddish cliffs and rocky peaks; overcast sky

records.summary: Salt River recreation access on AZ-87 — large parking lot, busy with kayakers and tubers by 9am
records.detail: 'The Salt River can be seen between the goalposts. There was a big parking lot filling up fast at 9am with kayakers, tubers, and stand up boards.' A developed recreation site with a substantial parking lot directly on the route, with open flowing water. Photographs show a real river with significant flow through green riparian vegetation. The page does not mention restrooms, water fountains or a fee, but a developed Tonto National Forest river access of this scale usually has toilets and often a day-use fee.
records.cyclistIntel: Best water and facilities candidate on this leg, roughly a third of the way in, and the only developed site recorded between Mesa and Jake's Corner. Worth confirming whether it has potable water and restrooms — if so it becomes the mid-day anchor for a 56-mile day with 5,400 ft of climbing. Note the crowds are a Sunday phenomenon; on a weekday it may be quiet or gated.
records.quote: There was a big parking lot filling up fast at 9am with kayakers, tubers, and stand up boards.

photos.caption: Another Salt River shot.
photos.shows: Open river water with substantial flow through dense green riparian growth below rocky cliffs

records.summary: JAKE'S CORNER BIKER BAR — hot food (brisket), beer, and a patio with a real SHADE TREE
records.detail: 'Happy to have brisket and a beer at the biker bar.' A second caption records 'A tree in the patio area of the biker bar at Jake's Corner' — an actual mature shade tree over an outdoor patio. Jake's Corner sits at the junction area near Tonto Basin, at the top of the day's climbing.
records.cyclistIntel: Second confirmed shade-and-food stop in Arizona after Don's Cactus Bar in Salome (p15-001), and it sits at the end of the hardest climbing day in the dataset — which for Nick, travelling the other way, means it is at the START of his big descent. Hot food, cold beer, covered outdoor seating and a tree. Anchor it precisely and confirm hours; a rural Arizona bar may not open early. This plus the biker-bar clientele also means people to ask about road conditions on AZ-87 ahead.
records.quote: A tree in the patio area of the biker bar at Jake's Corner.

photos.caption: A tree in the patio area of the biker bar at Jake's Corner.
Happy to have brisket and a beer at the biker bar.

records.summary: DATA CAVEAT: the support crew carried two other Southern Tier riders' bags over the climbs
records.detail: 'Linda convinced them she could carry their bags to Jake's Corner which was after all the big climbs. Donna and Becky made it to Jakes Corner 15 minutes before I did.' The two independent riders met the previous day were effectively supported over this leg by this journal's crew.
records.cyclistIntel: Matters for interpreting the only other-rider pace data in the dataset: Donna and Becky's time over this segment was set unloaded, so it is not a self-supported benchmark. A recurring hazard of mining a supported journal — even the independent riders in it got help.
records.quote: Linda convinced them she could carry their bags to Jake's Corner which was after all the big climbs.

records.summary: OVERCAST day, average 84.7 F — and the rider credits the cloud for making it manageable
records.detail: Every photograph shows flat grey overcast. GPS records a day average of 84.7 F, down from 97.4 F crossing Phoenix the previous day, despite this being by far the harder ride. Rider signs off: 'If it is overcast like today it should be a good day.' Twelve degrees cooler than the metro crossing, partly cloud and partly the 3,000 ft of elevation gained.
records.cyclistIntel: Useful counterfactual: 5,436 ft of climbing was survivable at 84.7 F under cloud. In clear-sky conditions at the 97 F recorded the day before, this same day would be a different proposition entirely. When Nick plans this leg — on his az_central divergence — cloud cover and elevation are the two variables that make it workable, and he gets the elevation benefit going the other way only at the start of his day.
records.quote: If it is overcast like today it should be a good day.
records.anchorNote: extent applied west→east per the source rule

photos.shows: Temperature trace averaging 84.7 F, rising through the day but staying below the previous day's level; all photographs show flat grey overcast

records.summary: Night 15: JAKE'S CORNER RV PARK, AZ-87 — named on the following day's departure caption
records.detail: The day ends at Jake's Corner, where the party ate at the biker bar. The page does not name a campground or RV park. Shade marked likely on the strength of the mature tree photographed in the bar's patio area and the pine-and-grass vegetation at this elevation — the first Arizona overnight where shade is plausible. NAME RESOLVED from the Day 16 page: 'Leaving Jakes Corner RV Park at 6:45am.'
records.cyclistIntel: Positioned exactly where Nick needs a stop on his az_central divergence: at the top of the AZ-87 climbing, with hot food and shade adjacent. Worth identifying what lodging actually exists there — the page implies something took two RVs. If it takes tents, this is a strong candidate anchor for the Tonto Basin leg, which the planner currently struggles with.

records.summary: MILE 227 + ELEVATION 3883 sign at the top of the big climb above Roosevelt Lake
records.detail: Photograph shows a loaded touring bike leaning against a green ADOT sign reading 'ELEVATION 3883' with a 'MILE 227' milepost directly below it. Two-lane highway, narrow paved shoulder with a gravel/grass verge, rocky high-desert terrain. The elevation matches the caption on the day's summit photo — Roosevelt Lake sits near 2,100 ft and the rider records 'nearly 1800 feet of vertical ascent', landing at ~3,900 ft. So this sign IS the top of the big hill.
records.cyclistIntel: HIGHEST-PRECISION ANCHOR IN THE DATASET. Arizona mileposts on state routes are statewide-continuous and published by ADOT, so MP 227 resolves to an exact coordinate from public data — no interpretation needed. Use it as the fixed point for the whole Roosevelt Lake to Globe segment, and as a control for the anchoring pilot. The road is ambiguous (the route runs AZ-188 south from Roosevelt Lake to US-60 near Globe) — resolve against ADOT milepost data for both and take whichever puts MP 227 at 3,883 ft.

photos.shows: Green ADOT sign 'ELEVATION 3883' above a green 'MILE 227' milepost; loaded touring bike with bar bag and three bottles leaning on the post; two-lane highway with narrow paved shoulder and gravel verge; rocky high desert, scattered cloud

records.summary: 5.35 miles of unbroken 6-7% climbing out of Roosevelt Lake — ~1,800 ft, topping at 3,883 ft
records.detail: 'After Roosevelt Lake came the big hill. 5.35 miles of nothing but climbing 6% to 7% grades. It took a lot out of me.' Summit caption: 'Nearly 1800 feet of vertical ascent in 5.35 miles. It was slow and hot.' The top is pinned exactly by the MILE 227 / ELEVATION 3883 sign (anchor:mp227-az). Comes at the end of a 62-mile day, after 40 miles of gentle descending. The support crew again carried two other riders' luggage specifically because of this hill.
records.cyclistIntel: ON NICK'S AZ_CENTRAL DIVERGENCE, second half. Reversed, this is a 5.35-mile DESCENT at 6-7% dropping him into Roosevelt Lake early in his day — fast, and one of the few big descents in the dataset that is precisely anchored at the top. It also means his day out of Globe starts with a steep drop and then turns into 40 miles of gentle climbing to Jake's Corner (p22-002), which is the harder half for him and the easier half for them. Note their own crew judged this hill worth removing luggage for.
records.quote: 5.35 miles of nothing but climbing 6% to 7% grades. It took a lot out of me.

photos.caption: The top of the big hill. Nearly 1800 feet of vertical ascent in 5.35 miles. It was slow and hot.

records.summary: First 40 miles Jake's Corner to Roosevelt Lake are gentle downhill — reversed, 40 mi of gentle climbing for Nick
records.detail: 'The first 40 miles of the ride today were very fun. Gentle downhill, no wind and cool temperatures.' Jake's Corner sits near 3,200 ft, Roosevelt Lake near 2,100 ft, so roughly 1,100 ft of net loss spread over 40 miles. No GPS map or charts were captured for this day, so total ascent, average speed and temperatures are unknown.
records.cyclistIntel: Reversed this is the long half of Nick's day: 40 miles of gentle but continuous climbing from Roosevelt Lake up to Jake's Corner, arriving at the top of the AZ-87 descent. Gentle grades over 40 miles in Arizona heat is a different problem from a short steep climb — it is a water and pacing question, not a gearing one. Their 'very fun' does not transfer.
records.quote: The first 40 miles of the ride today were very fun. Gentle downhill, no wind and cool temperatures.

records.summary: TONTO NATIONAL FOREST VISITORS CENTER at Roosevelt Lake — indoor, staffed, on route
records.detail: 'Also near Roosevelt Lake is the Visitors Center for the Tonto National Forest. It was a small visitors center with nice displays of the history, the animals and the plants in the area.' Small but staffed and indoor. The page does not mention water, restrooms or hours, but a Forest Service visitor centre of this type normally has potable water and toilets.
records.cyclistIntel: Potentially the best mid-route facility on the whole az_central divergence, and it sits at the BOTTOM of the 5.35-mile climb — meaning for Nick it is the natural stop before 40 miles of gentle ascent, or the first shelter after his steep descent. Indoor means air conditioning, which no Arizona RV park in this dataset offers. Confirm water, toilets, hours and seasonal closures; Forest Service visitor centres often close midweek or off-season.
records.quote: a small visitors center with nice displays of the history, the animals and the plants in the area

records.summary: Roosevelt Lake Bridge — signature steel arch, rideable, on the route
records.detail: Two photographs. One long shot shows a white steel through-arch bridge spanning a lake inlet between rocky slopes, with a guardrail and a shoreline showing a pronounced drawdown ring. The second shows two riders on the bridge deck itself: two travel lanes, yellow centerline, a narrow paved shoulder outside the white fog line and a solid concrete barrier immediately beyond it. Riders are in the traffic lane, not on the shoulder.
records.cyclistIntel: An unmistakable, uniquely-shaped, mapped structure — ideal anchoring fix, better than any place name on this segment. Also a minor hazard note: the deck has a narrow shoulder with a hard barrier and no escape room, so it is a short pinch point rather than an open crossing. The drawdown ring visible on the shoreline is a reminder that lake-edge water access varies by season.

photos.caption: The Bridge at Roosevelt Lake.
photos.shows: White steel through-arch bridge spanning a lake inlet between rocky desert slopes; pronounced drawdown ring on the shoreline; guardrail in foreground

photos.caption: Me following Donna off the bridge.
photos.shows: Bridge deck with two travel lanes, yellow centerline, narrow paved shoulder outside the fog line and a solid concrete barrier immediately beyond; riders in the traffic lane

records.summary: Cliff dwelling sites near Roosevelt Lake (Tonto National Monument) — off-bike, hiking access
records.detail: 'While I continued on with the biking Linda explored some cliff dwelling sites.' The support crew hiked to them; the rider did not stop. This is the Tonto National Monument area adjacent to Roosevelt Lake on AZ-188. Access is on foot up a trail, so it is a dismount-and-hike stop rather than a roadside view.
records.cyclistIntel: A genuine point of interest immediately on the divergence, but it costs a hike in heat with a loaded bike to leave somewhere. Worth knowing it exists rather than planning around it. It also implies a developed site with parking, which usually means water and toilets — worth confirming alongside the visitor centre.
records.quote: While I continued on with the biking Linda explored some cliff dwelling sites.

photos.caption: Linda exploring cliff dwellings.

records.summary: Globe AZ has downtown Mexican restaurants — camp-host recommended, seated seven
records.detail: 'Our camp host recommended a Mexican restaurant in downtown Globe. We had seven of us from all over the midwest.' Unnamed, but a sit-down restaurant in downtown Globe able to take a party of seven. Globe is the largest town on this section of the divergence.
records.cyclistIntel: Globe is the resupply and food anchor at the eastern end of the az_central divergence, and it sits at the top of Nick's 5.35-mile descent to Roosevelt Lake. Camp host again the source of the recommendation — sixth consecutive stop where local knowledge produced something useful.
records.quote: Our camp host recommended a Mexican restaurant in downtown Globe.

records.summary: Seven Southern Tier riders converged for dinner in Globe — a rolling cohort forms
records.detail: Tim from Wisconsin caught the rider halfway up the big hill; his wife Beth had separately met the support crew hiking to the cliff dwellings. Dinner in Globe had seven people: Dave, Donna from Minneapolis, Tim and Beth from Wisconsin, Bruce and Becky from Ohio, plus Linda. Note this corrects an earlier record — 'Becky from Ohio' is travelling with Bruce.
records.cyclistIntel: Confirms the April cohort effect: riders leaving the coast within a few days of each other converge repeatedly and coordinate. For a solo self-supported rider this is the strongest argument for a season-typical departure — company, shared road intel, and help if something breaks. Same caveat as before: this journal's crew keeps hauling other riders' luggage, so nobody's pace here is a clean self-supported benchmark.
records.quote: The chatter never stopped because we kept finding so many common experiences.

photos.caption: The group of like minded people. Behind me is Donna from Minneapolis. Next to Linda is Tim and Beth from Wisconsin. At the other end are Bruce and Becky from Ohio.

records.summary: Cool with no wind for the first 40 miles, then 'slow and hot' on the climb
records.detail: 'Gentle downhill, no wind and cool temperatures' for the first 40 miles; the summit caption on the 5.35-mile climb reads 'It was slow and hot.' No GPS temperature data was captured for this day, so no figures. Departure was 6:45am — the pre-7am start pattern holds for a fifth consecutive day.
records.cyclistIntel: The pattern that matters: cool early, hot by the time the climbing starts. Reversed, Nick's steep descent comes early and cool, and his 40 miles of gentle climbing land in the heat of the day — the worse arrangement of the two. Argues for splitting Globe to Jake's Corner or starting it very early.
records.quote: It was slow and hot.
records.anchorNote: extent applied west→east per the source rule

records.summary: Night 16: Globe AZ, campground with a camp host — site not named
records.detail: Day ends in Globe. The page establishes there is a camp host (who made the restaurant recommendation) but names no site. Seven Southern Tier riders were in town the same night, so multiple lodging options presumably exist.
records.cyclistIntel: Globe is the eastern anchor of the az_central divergence and clearly has campground lodging with a host, but the site is unidentified. Worth pinning down — Globe is where Nick's steep descent to Roosevelt Lake begins, so it is a natural overnight for him too.

records.summary: SAN CARLOS APACHE RESERVATION crossing on US-70 — roughly 40 mi where camping is not an option, and this journal shows it is crossable in one day
records.detail: The GPS map labels SAN CARLOS RESERVATION across the middle of the route and the track runs through it on US-70 via San Carlos, Calva and Bylas. The party had lunch at Bylas and did NOT stop there — they continued a further ~30 mi to Thatcher, making 74.21 mi for the day. The page says nothing about permits or camping law; the constraint comes from the planner's own existing note that roadside camping is illegal on San Carlos Apache land.
records.cyclistIntel: THIS DIRECTLY ADDRESSES THE D39 BYLAS PROBLEM — the hardest unsolved night in the plan. The answer this journal demonstrates is: do not try to sleep on the reservation, cross it. Globe to Bylas is roughly 45 mi and Bylas to Thatcher roughly 30 mi, and a supported rider covered the whole 74 mi in 6:19 moving time at 11.7 mph on a mostly flat road with a wide shoulder. Bylas works as a lunch and water stop rather than an overnight. Pair with p23-007: Thatcher City Park grants permission, has shade and bathrooms, and is the far-side anchor. That turns D39 from 'genuinely hard' into 'a long but ordinary day with a known endpoint'.
records.quote: Tim and I leaving Bylas after a lunch break.

records.summary: THATCHER CITY PARK — boondocking by City Manager permission, SHADED, with nice bathrooms nearby
records.detail: 'Our accommodations for tonight are boondocking at the Thatcher City Park. Thanks to the staff at Taylor Freeze. They called the City Manager and got permission for us. Shaded, nice bathrooms nearby.' Permission was arranged on the spot by local business staff phoning the City Manager. Three things stated directly: permission is obtainable, the site is shaded, and there are good bathrooms adjacent.
records.cyclistIntel: BEST LODGING FIND IN THE DATASET. It is the far-side anchor for the San Carlos Reservation crossing, it is SHADED — the only shaded municipal site recorded anywhere on this route — and it has real bathrooms. Permission is discretionary rather than posted, so the play is to ask: Taylor Freeze in Pima (p23-006) is the proven route to the City Manager, and a solo self-supported cyclist is an easier ask than two RVs. Confirm the current City Manager's policy before relying on it, and have a fallback. This is the record to feed into the planner's informal-lodging layer as a lead, labelled 'a lead, not a booking'.
records.quote: Shaded, nice bathrooms nearby.

records.summary: TAYLOR FREEZE, Pima AZ — family-run ice cream stand, and the people who unlock Thatcher City Park
records.detail: 'The mother and daughter that run the Taylor Freeze. Boy the chocolate shake hit the spot.' The same staff phoned the Thatcher City Manager and obtained camping permission for the party. A second caption reads 'Dave and Tim coming into Pima. Motivated by ice cream.' Pima sits between Bylas and Thatcher on US-70.
records.cyclistIntel: Two functions, and the second is worth more than the first. Cold calories after crossing the reservation, and — more importantly — this is the specific local contact that produced the Thatcher City Park permission. Sixth consecutive instance in this journal of local knowledge producing an outcome no map contains. For a solo rider arriving hot off a 45-mile reservation crossing, this is the stop to make.
records.quote: Thanks to the staff at Taylor Freeze. They called the City Manager and got permission for us.

photos.caption: The mother and daughter that run the Taylor Freeze. Boy the chocolate shake hit the spot.
Dave and Tim coming into Pima. Motivated by ice cream.
photos.shows: Two riders on a quiet street entering a bollarded path signed 'NO MOTOR VEHICLES'; mature green trees, metal-roofed buildings, mountains behind

records.summary: US-70 across the Gila valley has a WIDE, SMOOTH shoulder — but photo shows rumble strip cut into it in places
records.detail: 'The traffic thinned out, the shoulder was wide and smooth, and the road was mostly flat.' A photograph of the open highway confirms a generously wide paved shoulder on a straight run toward an escarpment. HOWEVER a second roadside photograph shows the fog line with a row of rumble-strip indentations cut INTO the paved shoulder itself, which narrows the usable width wherever that treatment occurs. The text and the photo are not in conflict — the shoulder is wide, and at least some of it is rumbled.
records.cyclistIntel: Best shoulder recorded on the Arizona stretch, which matters because this is the reservation crossing where stopping is not an option. The rumble-strip caveat is the thing to verify: where a rumble strip sits inside the shoulder rather than between shoulder and lane, it eats the rideable line and forces a rider outboard or into the lane. Worth a second source before calling the whole 74 mi comfortable.
records.quote: the shoulder was wide and smooth, and the road was mostly flat

photos.caption: Long rolling hills with lots of mountain scenery.
photos.shows: Straight two-lane highway with a wide paved shoulder running toward a long flat-topped escarpment; trucks distant; power lines; scrub and low trees

photos.caption: More scenery. The Gila River is in the background where the line of trees are.
photos.shows: Roadside view showing yellow centerline, white fog line, and a row of rumble-strip indentations cut into the paved shoulder; dry grass verge, green tree line marking the river beyond, mountains behind

records.summary: Heavy 65 mph traffic on the descent out of Globe, thinning after the first stretch
records.detail: 'The day started out downhill with lots of 65mph traffic. The traffic thinned out...' The GPS speed trace confirms the fast section — spikes to 25-30 mph through the first hour and a half, matching the elevation drop out of Globe. So the rider was descending at speed alongside 65 mph traffic.
records.cyclistIntel: Reversed, Nick CLIMBS this section into Globe at the end of his day, slowly, alongside the same 65 mph traffic — longer exposure, though less speed differential risk on his part. The traffic is concentrated near Globe and thins across the reservation, so it is a first-and-last-few-miles problem rather than a whole-day one.
records.quote: The day started out downhill with lots of 65mph traffic.

records.summary: Net descent Globe to Thatcher: ~3,500 ft down to 2,913 ft, front-loaded, then 3 hours of near-flat
records.detail: Read from the elevation trace: starts near 3,400-3,500 ft with a brief rise, then a sustained drop between about 1:23 and 1:50 to roughly 2,400 ft, then rolling bumps through 3:20, then a long almost-flat gentle rise to a marked 2,913 ft at the finish. Total ascent only 2,060 ft across 74.21 mi. Roughly thirteen climb waypoints are clustered in the FIRST HALF; the second half has none.
records.cyclistIntel: The day has two completely different halves and the planner should model them separately: a rolling, descending, traffic-heavy first half out of Globe, then roughly 35 miles of near-flat valley riding on a wide shoulder. Reversed, Nick gets the easy flat half FIRST out of Thatcher and the rolling climb into Globe at the end of a 74-mile day in afternoon heat — the worse arrangement. That argues for him splitting this differently than they did, or starting very early.
records.quote: It was rolling hills that reminded Linda of Iowa, just not any corn or soybean fields.

photos.shows: Elevation trace: ~3,450 ft start with brief rise, sustained drop 1:23-1:50 to ~2,400 ft, rolling bumps to 3:20, then near-flat gentle rise to a marked 2,913 ft at 6:15; about thirteen climb waypoint markers all in the first half

records.summary: The route follows the Gila River for most of the Globe-to-Thatcher run
records.detail: 'We followed the Gila River most of the way.' A photo caption identifies the river by its tree line: 'The Gila River is in the background where the line of trees are.' So the river is nearby but set back from the road behind vegetation, not immediately at the roadside. Terrain has grasses and more trees than anything since California.
records.cyclistIntel: Recorded as a landmark and a possible emergency source, not a water point. The river runs behind a tree line rather than beside the road, so access is not casual, and Gila water below Safford carries agricultural and historic mining runoff. Its real value is as a navigational and vegetation cue — the tree line marks the route. Get water in Bylas, Pima or Thatcher instead.
records.quote: We followed the Gila River most of the way.

records.summary: Towns roughly every 20 miles across the Gila valley — the densest services on the Arizona stretch
records.detail: 'Linda and Beth met us at the towns roughly 20 miles apart.' Named on the map and in the text along US-70: San Carlos, Calva, Bylas, Pima, Thatcher, with Safford at the far end. A marked contrast with the empty US-60 corridor further west.
records.cyclistIntel: Materially better resupply spacing than anything since the Colorado River. Twenty-mile intervals means a rider can carry less water and top up repeatedly, which is what makes a 74-mile day across the reservation feasible. Note the rider's own closing line contradicts this for the day AFTER — 'There just aren't many options in this part of the Arizona desert' — so the town density ends somewhere east of Safford.
records.quote: Linda and Beth met us at the towns roughly 20 miles apart.

records.summary: Day average 88.5 F rising to 96.8 F at the finish — hottest sustained average outside the Phoenix crossing
records.detail: GPS temperature trace starts near 55-60 F and climbs steadily all day, averaging 88.5 F with 96.8 F recorded at the end of the ride and peaks above 100 F in the late afternoon. Map header 70.0 F. Fifth consecutive day at or above an 84 F average.
records.cyclistIntel: The heat lands on the second, flat half of the day — which for Nick, riding the reverse, is the FIRST half out of Thatcher. He then climbs into Globe in the worst of it. On a 74-mile reservation crossing with no camping option, heat management is the whole problem: leave in the dark, use the 20-mile town spacing to keep topping up, and treat Bylas as a shade-and-water checkpoint rather than a lunch destination.

photos.shows: Temperature trace rising from ~55-60 F to a marked 96.8 F at the finish, averaging 88.5 F, with peaks above 100 F between 4:51 and 5:33

records.summary: Afternoon headwinds riding SOUTHEAST down the Gila valley — a tailwind for Nick
records.detail: 'Some headwinds in the afternoon.' The route runs northwest to southeast along the Gila valley, so the wind was out of the southeast. Valley-aligned afternoon winds of this kind are usually a daily thermal pattern rather than weather.
records.cyclistIntel: Inverts in Nick's favour — he rides northwest up the valley, so an afternoon southeasterly pushes him. But it also means his easy flat half comes with help and his rolling climb into Globe comes at the end regardless. File in the valley-wind bucket, separate from both the California westerlies and the Imperial north-south winds; three distinct wind regimes now.
records.quote: Some headwinds in the afternoon.

records.summary: SOURCE CHANGE from Day 17: the second rider and one crew member leave; the journal becomes a solo rider with one supporter
records.detail: Dave's riding partner Mike withdrew from the trip on medical grounds and was hospitalised; Deb, the escort who wrote several of the pages processed so far, left with him. Dave continued alone, supported by Linda in one RV, and rode this day in company with Tim, an independent Southern Tier rider met the previous day.
records.cyclistIntel: PROVENANCE, not route intel. From Day 17 onward: expect no more WDMDeb escort pages, so the two-pages-per-day pattern ends and photo volume may drop. The support level also reduces from two RVs and two crew to one of each, which slightly narrows the supported-rider caveat but does not remove it. Company from other riders becomes a more frequent feature.
records.quote: I am, however, continuing the ride.

records.summary: Night 17: THATCHER CITY PARK by permission — shaded, bathrooms, free
records.detail: Boondocking in the municipal park with explicit permission from the Thatcher City Manager, obtained by phone by the staff at Taylor Freeze in Pima on the party's behalf. Stated directly: shaded, with nice bathrooms nearby. Toilets confirmed; potable water marked likely on the strength of good bathrooms in a city park. Permission was discretionary and same-day, not a standing policy.
records.cyclistIntel: The single most useful overnight in the dataset. Shaded, free, has toilets, and sits exactly where a rider needs it — the far side of the San Carlos Reservation crossing. Tents are a much easier ask than two RVs, so a solo cyclist's odds are better than theirs were. Approach: ask at a local business or call the City Manager directly, and do it before arriving rather than at dusk. Enter into the planner's informal-lodging layer flagged 'a lead, not a booking'.
records.quote: Our accommodations for tonight are boondocking at the Thatcher City Park... Shaded, nice bathrooms nearby.

records.summary: GOATHEAD SAND BURRS start near El Paso — warned by riders coming the OTHER way, i.e. Nick's direction
records.detail: 'We met up with a young couple doing the East to West Southern Tier. They warned us of the Goat's Head sand burrs starting near El Paso.' Goatheads (puncturevine, Tribulus terrestris) are hard woody thorns that lie on shoulders and verges and reliably destroy unprotected tyres. The warning came from riders travelling east-to-west who had already come through it — the same direction Nick rides. The rider recognises them from the Cowboy Trail in Nebraska.
records.cyclistIntel: MOST VALUABLE FORWARD WARNING IN THE DATASET, and it comes from riders in NICK'S DIRECTION rather than this journal's. Goatheads are a flat-tyre epidemic, not a single puncture: they embed in the casing and keep working through. Mitigations are gear decisions Nick has to make BEFORE he starts — sealant, tyre liners or heavy touring tyres — and behavioural ones: never ride the dirt verge, never walk a bike off pavement, and check tyres at every stop. Note the extent is unknown from this source: 'starting near El Paso' means the eastern edge. Find where they end.
records.quote: They warned us of the Goat's Head sand burrs starting near El Paso.

records.summary: Thatcher to Lordsburg is a 43-or-75 mile day — Duncan then nothing until Lordsburg
records.detail: 'There weren't many options for civilization today. Either ride 43 miles or ride 75 miles. We chose the 75 miles to a KOA.' Duncan sits at roughly 43 mi and Lordsburg at 77.45 mi, with the New Mexico line at about 50 mi and only Virden between. A binary day-length choice, not a spectrum.
records.cyclistIntel: This is a HARD PLANNING CONSTRAINT, not a preference, and both endpoints are on Nick's nm_az divergence (Silver City-Lordsburg-Duncan). The 43-mile option at Duncan has a shaded city park and a historic hotel (p24-003, p24-004); the 75-mile option ends at a KOA. For a self-supported rider in 88 F average heat, 43 to Duncan then a shorter run into Lordsburg is the safer split — and it sets up the brutal Lordsburg-to-Silver-City climb (p25-001) on fresher legs.
records.quote: Either ride 43 miles or ride 75 miles.
records.anchorNote: extent applied west→east per the source rule

records.summary: DUNCAN AZ — shaded picnic tables in the city park, sprinklers running, visitor centre, intact downtown
records.detail: 'The gem of the day was our lunch stop in Duncan AZ. Its downtown area still looked good and we ate lunch at a shaded picnic table in their lovely city park.' A photo caption adds: 'The City of Duncan was sprinkling its park. It was hot. I did the natural thing' — he ran through the sprinklers. There is a staffed visitor centre with a talkative attendant. Roughly 43 mi into the Thatcher-Lordsburg leg.
records.cyclistIntel: Third confirmed SHADE stop in the dataset after Don's Cactus Bar and Jake's Corner, and the best of the three for a cyclist: a public city park, shaded picnic tables, running sprinklers to cool off in, and a visitor centre for local knowledge. Free and unticketed. Directly on Nick's nm_az divergence and exactly at the 43-mile decision point in p24-002. Anchor it precisely — this is a place to build a day around.
records.quote: we ate lunch at a shaded picnic table in their lovely city park

photos.caption: The City of Duncan was sprinkling its park. It was hot. I did the natural thing.

records.summary: THE SIMPSON INN, Duncan AZ — historic hotel just off Main Street, used by other Southern Tier riders
records.detail: 'Linda and Beth also toured the Simpson Inn. It is an old, historic hotel just off Main Street run by a Buddist and an Episcopalian. We later found out our other Southern Tier friends, Donna and Becky, were staying there that evening.' Two independent Southern Tier cyclists actually stayed there the same night, which is the strongest form of evidence for a lodging lead in this dataset — a cyclist-tested bed rather than an RV park.
records.cyclistIntel: The only recorded lodging on this whole route that was USED BY SELF-SUPPORTED CYCLISTS rather than by the RV party — so it escapes the support caveat entirely. Named, in a town with a shaded city park, at the 43-mile decision point on Nick's nm_az divergence. Worth calling for cyclist rates and bike storage. A bed the night before the 4,200 ft Silver City climb is worth real money.
records.quote: our other Southern Tier friends, Donna and Becky, were staying there that evening

records.summary: Thatcher to Lordsburg: 2,438 ft over 77 mi, net 2,500 to 4,196 ft — one big climb, one big descent, rest gently up
records.detail: 'One big climb, one big decent and a lot of flat or slightly uphill.' Elevation trace confirms a steady net rise from about 2,500 ft to a marked 4,196 ft at the finish, with roughly seven climb waypoints all in the first three and a half hours and the speed trace showing its only fast section around 3:28 (the descent toward Duncan). The map's speed banding turns red/orange in the Duncan area, confirming that as the fast stretch.
records.cyclistIntel: Reversed, Nick loses ~1,700 ft net across this leg with one substantial climb in the second half. Easier westbound, but 77 miles is 77 miles and the services constraint in p24-002 governs the day regardless of direction. The gentle continuous rise eastbound means a gentle continuous descent for him, which is the good half of the trade.
records.quote: One big climb, one big decent and a lot of flat or slightly uphill.
records.anchorNote: extent applied west→east per the source rule

photos.shows: GPS summary 77.45 mi, 6:56:39, 11.2 mph, 2,438 ft ascent, 64.0 F; elevation trace 2,500 ft rising to a marked 4,196 ft, seven climb waypoints in the first 3.5 hours; map speed banding red/orange near Duncan

records.summary: Small towns on this route have a morning rush hour heading OUT of town — about an hour of work trucks
records.detail: 'Each of these overnight towns we stay in seem to have a rush hour in the morning. Rushing out of town not into it. After an hour or so all the work trucks were past us so we had pretty light traffic to deal with.' Observed as a pattern across multiple overnight towns, not a single day.
records.cyclistIntel: Genuinely useful and generalisable: the pre-dawn start that the heat forces also puts a rider directly into an hour of outbound work traffic on a two-lane highway. The two constraints pull against each other. Practical answer is to expect the first hour to be the busiest of the day and to be lit and visible for it — not to start later, because the heat penalty is worse.
records.quote: Each of these overnight towns we stay in seem to have a rush hour in the morning. Rushing out of town not into it.

records.summary: Favourable wind for the last 15 miles into Lordsburg, riding east
records.detail: 'The wind was favorable the last 15 mile (good thing, we were getting tired) so we made it all the way to Lordsburg.' Riding roughly eastbound, so a westerly. It is what made the 75-mile option possible rather than the 43.
records.cyclistIntel: Inverts against Nick — a westerly on this stretch is a headwind for him on his first 15 miles OUT of Lordsburg. Since Lordsburg is where the 4,200 ft Silver City climb ends for them and begins for him in reverse, a headwind there is on the flat approach rather than the climb. Note how load-bearing this wind was for their day length: without it they take the 43-mile option.
records.quote: The wind was favorable the last 15 mile (good thing, we were getting tired)
records.anchorNote: extent applied west→east per the source rule

records.summary: Day average 88.5 F, 91.4 F at the finish — 6:30am start forced by the heat
records.detail: 'Because of the high temperatures here Tim and I were on the road by 6:30am.' GPS records an 88.5 F day average with 91.4 F at the end and peaks above 95 F through the afternoon; map header 64.0 F at the start. Sixth consecutive day at or above an 84 F average.
