records.cyclistIntel: The 6:30am start is now the settled operating rule across six days and two states, and it collides with the outbound-traffic surge in p24-001. Also worth noting the rider's stated water consumption on the following page — 5 to 6 bottles a day WITH vehicle resupply (p25-009). That is the number to plan Nick's carry against.
records.quote: Because of the high temperatures here Tim and I were on the road by 6:30am.
records.anchorNote: extent applied west→east per the source rule

records.summary: Arizona / New Mexico state line on US-70, about 50 mi east of Thatcher
records.detail: 'At about 50 miles of riding we hit the New Mexico border. Another state down!' A photo caption reads 'Welcome to New Mexico!'. The map shows the state line as a dashed vertical boundary crossed between Duncan and Virden. Third state line of the trip.
records.cyclistIntel: Hard, unambiguous, mapped anchor — state lines are the easiest possible fix and this one comes with a stated distance-into-day (50 mi of 77.45). Combined with Duncan at ~43 mi, it gives two ordered distance fixes on the same leg, which is exactly what the anchoring pass needs to calibrate.

photos.caption: Welcome to New Mexico!
New Mexico desert is slightly different than Arizona desert. Fewer cactii, more sage brush.
photos.shows: Loaded touring bike on a gravel shoulder above open high desert; sparse dry grass and sage, distant low mountains, deep blue sky

records.summary: Night 18: KOA at Lordsburg NM
records.detail: 'We chose the 75 miles to a KOA.' Third KOA of the trip after Boulevard and Wenden. No facilities, cost or tent policy stated; 'likely' values come from KOA chain norms, not the page.
records.cyclistIntel: Callable, and positioned at the eastern end of the 43-or-75 mile choice — and critically, at the FOOT of the 15-mile 2,000 ft climb to Silver City (p25-001). For Nick riding the other way it is where that descent delivers him. Add to the call-ahead list: tents, showers, shade. The KOA chain is now the single most reliable named lodging on this route with three confirmed sites.
records.quote: We chose the 75 miles to a KOA.

records.summary: 15-mile climb out of Lordsburg gaining over 2,000 ft, pitches to 8% — first 15 mi of the day
records.detail: 'The day started off with a 15 mile climb that went up over 2,000 feet.' Grades reached 8%. The ELEVATION-OVER-DISTANCE chart on this page gives it precisely: 4,210 ft at mile 0, rising steadily to about 5,700 ft by mile 12 and roughly 6,250 ft by mile 15-16. So the gradient steepens through the middle of the climb rather than being uniform. A passing motorist shouted an obscene question at the rider mid-climb, which he took as fair comment once the grade hit 8%.
records.cyclistIntel: REVERSED THIS IS A 15-MILE DESCENT DROPPING 2,000 FT INTO LORDSBURG — one of the longest sustained descents on Nick's whole route, and on his nm_az divergence. The over-distance profile means it can be anchored by mile rather than by place name, which makes it one of the few spans in the dataset that should resolve tightly. Note the pitch: 8% sections mean real braking on a loaded bike.
records.quote: The day started off with a 15 mile climb that went up over 2,000 feet.
records.anchorNote: extent applied west→east per the source rule

photos.shows: Elevation-over-DISTANCE chart: 4,210 ft at mile 0 rising to ~5,700 ft by mile 12 and ~6,250 ft by mile 15-16

records.summary: 4,209 ft of climbing in only 48 miles — and it stays rolling at 6,000+ ft after the first climb
records.detail: 'Everything you could ask for except 4200 feet of climbing.' 4,209 ft over 48.04 mi at 9.7 mph. The over-distance profile shows the terrain never settles after mile 15: a dip to 5,900 at mile 18, up to 6,350 at mile 21, rolling 6,000-6,300 through mile 33, a drop to 5,730 at mile 37, then rolling back to 6,030 at the finish. 'After that we got some downhills along with the uphills but everything was steep.' Roughly fourteen climb waypoints across the day.
records.cyclistIntel: Second-hardest climbing day in the dataset after AZ-87, in the fewest miles. Reversed, Nick gets the same rolling high-desert section (it is symmetrical) plus the 15-mile descent, so his version is materially easier — perhaps 2,200 ft of climbing instead of 4,200. But 'everything was steep' applies in both directions, and the rolling section sits at 6,000+ ft where the air is thinner.
records.quote: After that we got some downhills along with the uphills but everything was steep.
records.anchorNote: extent applied west→east per the source rule

photos.shows: GPS summary 48.04 mi, 4:55:49, 9.7 mph, 4,209 ft ascent, 63.0 F; over-distance elevation showing rolling 5,730-6,350 ft between miles 15 and 48; about fourteen climb waypoints

records.summary: NM-90 is smooth with VERY LITTLE trash on the shoulders — the cleanest road recorded so far
records.detail: 'the road was smooth with very little trash on the shoulders'. Stated as one of the day's explicit positives. A photograph confirms a sound paved shoulder with a clean surface on a curve marked with chevron signs. Direct contrast with the three debris corridors recorded in California and Arizona.
records.cyclistIntel: Worth recording as a POSITIVE span so the app does not warn uniformly. New Mexico's high-desert roads appear materially cleaner than the Arizona corridors that carry dune and interstate traffic. That said, this is also 100 miles west of where the goathead warning (p24-005) begins — clean shoulders here say nothing about further east.
records.quote: the road was smooth with very little trash on the shoulders

photos.caption: Beautiful blue sky, green trees. And a road that just disappears down the hill.
photos.shows: Two-lane road with a sound clean paved shoulder curving through high desert; chevron curve-warning signs ahead; sparse juniper and dry grass, deep blue sky

records.summary: Heavy traffic coming into Silver City; open road otherwise quiet
records.detail: 'The other shout came in heavy traffic in Silver City.' The town approach carries real traffic; the open NM-90 sections between Lordsburg and Silver City are not described as busy. Two shouted comments from passing cars during the day, one hostile-in-jest on the big climb and one friendly in town — no aggressive driving reported.
records.cyclistIntel: Reversed, this is Nick's first few miles OUT of Silver City rather than his last few in — better, since he is fresh and it is early. Note the two car interactions were verbal and non-threatening, which is the pattern across this whole journal: no hostility recorded anywhere in three states.
records.quote: The other shout came in heavy traffic in Silver City.

records.summary: Above 6,000 ft the hillsides turn to pine and green trees — first real forest since California
records.detail: 'Getting up over 6,000 elevation did make for a nice change of scenery. The hillsides are full of pine trees and other green trees. Sand, rocks and cactii are interesting but I was ready for some green.' Marks the transition out of desert into pinyon-juniper and pine at elevation.
records.cyclistIntel: Real shade and cooler air, which is why this day averaged in the 70s while the previous six averaged 84-97 F. Elevation is the only reliable heat relief on this route. For Nick this section is a genuine respite between the Arizona desert and whatever the Texas stretch brings.
records.quote: The hillsides are full of pine trees and other green trees.
records.anchorNote: extent applied west→east per the source rule

records.summary: CONTINENTAL DIVIDE crossing on NM-90 between Lordsburg and Silver City — signed
records.detail: 'We crossed the Continental Divide today. I was so beat from the climbing that I didn't even stop for a photo of the sign.' So a sign exists but was not photographed. The crossing falls somewhere in the rolling 6,000-6,350 ft section between miles 15 and 40 of the day per the over-distance profile — most plausibly at one of the two local high points at mile 21 (6,350 ft) or mile 33 (6,320 ft).
records.cyclistIntel: A major, permanently mapped, signed geographic feature — excellent anchor once its exact location is fixed from public data rather than this page. Also a milestone worth having in the app for its own sake: the highest hydrological boundary on the route. Cross-reference the two candidate high points against the actual Divide crossing on NM-90.

records.summary: Tyrone Mine — vast open-pit copper complex, 10 miles south of Silver City, visible from the road
records.detail: 'We passed by The Tyrone Mine. It is a large open-pit copper mining complex located 10 miles south of Silver City. It was vast in size. I would have loved to go to the top and look down.' The rider gives the distance from Silver City explicitly.
records.cyclistIntel: Anchor-grade fix with a stated offset — 10 miles south of Silver City on NM-90 — so it calibrates the last third of this leg without needing the resolver to interpret anything. Enormous, mapped, and unmistakable from the saddle.
records.anchorNote: 10 mi south of Silver City

records.summary: McComas Incident historical marker, roadside on NM-90
records.detail: Photograph of a timber-framed brown New Mexico state marker headed 'McCOMAS INCIDENT', describing the March 1883 killing of Judge and Mrs H. C. McComas by Chiricahua Apaches led by Chatto, and the failed manhunt for their captive six-year-old son. Roadside pull-off with the highway visible behind.
records.cyclistIntel: State historical markers are surveyed, permanent and individually documented, which makes them among the best available anchors on a rural highway. Also a natural stop with a pull-off. No services implied.

photos.caption: The Wild West was here!
photos.shows: Timber-framed brown state historical marker headed 'McCOMAS INCIDENT' with explanatory text; dry grass, roadside pull-off, highway behind

records.summary: HYDRATION NUMBER: the rider drinks 5 to 6 bottles a day — WITH vehicle resupply
records.detail: 'I tried to lighten my load by leaving the trunk bag behind and only carrying three water bottles. I have been drinking 5 to 6 bottles each day. We get resupplied by Linda and Beth.' So his consumption is 5-6 bottles but his CARRY is three, because a vehicle refills him mid-day. Roughly 120-140 fl oz consumed per day at 48-77 mi in 80-95 F.
records.cyclistIntel: THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT NUMBER FOR NICK IN THE WHOLE DATASET, and it needs inverting carefully. This rider consumes 5-6 bottles and carries 3. Nick consumes a comparable amount and must CARRY ALL OF IT between water points. On the stretches where this dataset records no water — the Yuha Desert, the Glamis corridor, the 43-or-75 mile Thatcher-Lordsburg leg — that is a 5-6 bottle carry, roughly 8-9 lb of water, on top of full touring load. Combine with the escort's 'I can't seem to drink enough water!!' (p16-005) and the 99.8-mile dry stretch already known in west Texas. This is the input for the water-carry calculator.
records.quote: I have been drinking 5 to 6 bottles each day. We get resupplied by Linda and Beth.

records.summary: Good TAILWIND on the big climb eastbound — a headwind for Nick on the 15-mile descent
records.detail: 'there was a good tailwind' listed among the day's positives, riding roughly northeast from Lordsburg to Silver City. High winds had been forecast the previous evening. The observed fact is a following wind on this leg on 17 April; the inversion is inference.
records.cyclistIntel: Inverts against Nick, but usefully: a headwind on a 15-mile 2,000 ft descent with 8% pitches is braking assistance rather than a penalty. Fourth distinct wind regime now recorded — California westerlies, Imperial north-south, Gila valley afternoon southeasterlies, and now southwest New Mexico. Keep them in separate buckets; there is no single prevailing pattern for this route.
records.quote: there was a good tailwind

records.summary: Mid-80s maximum, day average in the 70s — first cool day in a week, and elevation is why
records.detail: 'The temperatures topped out in the mid 80's.' GPS records a day average in the 70s (partially obscured) with 86.0 F marked as the peak; map header 63.0 F. The previous six days averaged 84-97 F. The difference is elevation: this day spent most of its time above 6,000 ft. Start was 8am rather than the usual 6:30, because the heat did not force it.
records.cyclistIntel: Demonstrates the one reliable lever against heat on this route: gain elevation. It also shows the operating rule relaxing — a later start became affordable. For Nick, the high-desert section between Silver City and Lordsburg is the cool part of the southwestern leg, sandwiched between Arizona desert and whatever comes east of El Paso.
records.quote: The temperatures topped out in the mid 80's.

records.summary: Nights 19-20: SILVER CITY KOA, NM — laundry $4.50/load, no shade, at 6,100 ft
records.detail: Day ends in Silver City; no site named. 'Tomorrow is a much needed rest day' — so night 20 is here too. Silver City sits at roughly 6,000 ft and is the largest town between Lordsburg and the Rio Grande. NAME RESOLVED from the Day 21 page (campfire 'in the KOA campgrounds', shower room). Laundry $4.50 wash and dry. No shade per the rider's regional statement (p26-001).
records.cyclistIntel: No lead, but Silver City is clearly the natural rest and resupply town on the New Mexico end — largest town, high enough to be cool, and it sits at the top of the 15-mile climb. Second rest day of the run falls here, six riding days after the Quartzsite rest day, which holds the one-in-six cadence exactly.
records.quote: Tomorrow is a much needed rest day.

records.summary: EMORY PASS, 8,228 ft — signed Official Scenic Historic Marker, and the HIGHEST POINT ON THE ENTIRE SOUTHERN TIER
records.detail: Photograph of a timber-framed Official Scenic Historic Marker reading 'EMORY PASS / BLACK RANGE MOUNTAINS / ELEVATION: 8,228 ft', with text describing Tertiary volcanic and Paleozoic sedimentary rocks, the Caballo Mountains 15 miles east, Hillsboro Peak at 10,165 ft as the range high point, and an 1846 crossing by an Army officer. The rider states independently that this day 'took us to over 8,200 feet elevation' and calls Emory Pass 'the highest point on this whole ride'.
records.cyclistIntel: THE ROUTE HIGH POINT, signed, surveyed, permanently marked, with an elevation printed on it. Best anchor in the dataset alongside MILE 227. Everything about this segment can be calibrated from it. Note the asymmetry, which matters enormously for Nick: they climbed the LONG WEST SIDE from Silver City (43 mi, 4,685 ft) and descended the SHORT EAST SIDE to Kingston. Nick does the reverse — he climbs the short steep east side from Kingston, roughly 2,050 ft, then gets the long descent into Silver City.

photos.shows: Timber-framed Official Scenic Historic Marker 'EMORY PASS / BLACK RANGE MOUNTAINS / ELEVATION: 8,228 ft'; two riders in full winter kit with loaded bikes, gloves and balaclavas; pines, gravel pull-off, broken grey cloud

records.summary: Silver City to Emory Pass: 4,685 ft of climbing in 43 mi to 8,228 ft — the rider's own pick as hardest day of the transcontinental
records.detail: 'This day's ride took us to over 8,200 feet elevation and almost 4,700 feet of climbing so it possibly is the most challenging day of the entire transcontinental ride.' 43.12 mi in 5:06:07 at 8.5 mph — slowest average recorded. The over-time elevation profile shows rolling 6,000-6,750 ft for the first 1:23, a drop to a marked 5,694 ft at 1:52, then a CONTINUOUS unbroken climb from 5,694 ft to about 8,200 ft between 1:52 and 4:40, then a sharp descent to ~6,180 ft at Kingston. So the real climb is one sustained ~2,500 ft push occupying nearly three hours.
records.cyclistIntel: REVERSED THIS IS MUCH BETTER FOR NICK. They climbed the long west side and descended the short east side; he climbs the SHORT EAST SIDE from Kingston — roughly 2,050 ft over about 9 miles, call it 4-5% average, steeper but a fraction of the work — then gets the long rolling descent west to Silver City. Their 4,685 ft is not his number. His number is closer to 2,000 ft plus whatever he has already climbed getting to Kingston (p29-001).
records.quote: possibly is the most challenging day of the entire transcontinental ride

photos.shows: GPS summary 43.12 mi, 5:06:07, 8.5 mph, 4,685 ft ascent, 41.0 F; over-time elevation showing a marked 5,694 ft low at 1:52:17 then continuous climb to ~8,200 ft by 4:40 and a sharp drop to ~6,180 ft

records.summary: SNOW on 19 April at Emory Pass — start in the low 30s, day average around 38 F
records.detail: 'The day started cold, low 30's in Silver City. The forecast was for wind and rain. We didn't have rain but we did have snow. Not enough to accumulate but pretty bothersome.' GPS temperature trace runs mostly between 35 and 50 F with 42.8 F marked and an average around 38 F. All riders wore heavy layers; the summit photograph shows full winter kit, gloves and balaclavas. This is 19 April, six days after a 97.4 F day average crossing Phoenix.
records.cyclistIntel: THE FULL TEMPERATURE ENVELOPE OF THIS ROUTE IS NOW ~60 DEGREES INSIDE THREE WEEKS: 97.4 F average in Phoenix on 12 April, ~38 F average with snow at Emory Pass on 19 April. Nick crosses the route high point at 8,228 ft and must carry genuine cold-weather kit for it no matter how hot the desert was two days earlier. Note the rider's own conclusion, which is counterintuitive and important: the cold made the climb EASIER — fewer cars, simple heat regulation, no overheating. Bad weather at Emory Pass is not automatically bad news.
records.quote: We didn't have rain but we did have snow. Not enough to accumulate but pretty bothersome.

photos.shows: Temperature trace running 35-50 F, marked 42.8 F, averaging around 38 F; riders in winter jackets, gloves and balaclavas at the summit

records.summary: Strong TAILWIND up the west side of Emory Pass — a headwind for Nick on his east-side climb
records.detail: 'The wind was strong but it was a tailwind. Hooray, it really helped as we slowly made our way up to Emory Pass.' Forecast had been for wind and rain. The rider credits the tailwind, along with the cold and overcast, with getting him over the top in one day when he had doubted he could.
records.cyclistIntel: Inverts against Nick, and this one costs him. A strong westerly at Emory Pass means a headwind on his short steep east-side climb — the one part of the pass that is steep. Their own account says the tailwind was load-bearing for finishing in one day; Nick should assume the opposite and not plan the pass as a bolt-on to a long day. Fifth distinct wind regime recorded (Black Range / Emory Pass).
records.quote: The wind was strong but it was a tailwind.

records.summary: Cold weather cut traffic on the Emory Pass road to 'just a handful' of cars
records.detail: 'The cold temperatures reduced the number of cars on the mountain road to just a handful.' NM-152 over the Black Range is a scenic mountain road, so traffic is presumably weather- and season-dependent rather than commuter-driven.
records.cyclistIntel: Useful inverse relationship: the conditions that make the pass physically harder make it much safer. A warm clear weekend would bring recreational traffic onto a narrow mountain road; a cold overcast day empties it. Worth pairing with the shoulder question, which this page does not answer — nobody describes the shoulder on NM-152, and on a pass road it is likely narrow to absent. Needs a second source.
records.quote: The cold temperatures reduced the number of cars on the mountain road to just a handful.

records.summary: Night 21: boondocked at KINGSTON NM, just east of Emory Pass
records.detail: 'After summit photos Tim and I had a blissful ride down the other side and boondocked at Kingston.' A photo caption reads 'Oue overnight campground.' Kingston sits at roughly 6,180 ft on the east side of the Black Range, a tiny former mining settlement. Shade marked likely on the strength of the pine and mixed forest at this elevation. No facilities described.
records.cyclistIntel: Critically positioned for Nick: Kingston is the base of his EAST-SIDE climb to Emory Pass, so this is where he wants to sleep before the route high point rather than after it. Dispersed camping works here, at elevation, in forest — which means shade and cool nights, unlike everything in Arizona. Identify what is actually available (the rider's own RV needed hookups he did not get here, which is why he calls it boondocking). Verify land status and whether Kingston has any water.
records.quote: had a blissful ride down the other side and boondocked at Kingston

photos.caption: Oue overnight campground.

records.summary: Kingston to Radium Springs: 71.56 mi with only 1,076 ft ascent — the long drop off the Black Range into the Rio Grande valley
records.detail: GPS: 71.56 mi, 5:18:00, 13.5 mph, 1,076 ft total ascent, 37.0 F. Kingston sits near 6,180 ft and Radium Springs near 4,100 ft, so net loss ~2,080 ft implies roughly 3,150 ft of descent against 1,076 ft of climbing. Fastest average of the entire journal. Map route runs east from Kingston through Hillsboro, then northeast to the Caballo / Arrey / Garfield / Hatch area, then south down the Rio Grande valley through Salem to Radium Springs, with the I-25 corridor alongside.
records.cyclistIntel: REVERSED THIS IS NICK'S APPROACH TO THE ROUTE HIGH POINT: 71 miles and roughly 3,150 ft of climbing from Radium Springs up the Rio Grande valley and into the Black Range to Kingston — and then Emory Pass the next day. That is two consecutive climbing days totalling ~5,200 ft, and the second one tops out at 8,228 ft where it snowed in April. Do not let their 13.5 mph average anywhere near the planning for this. Strong candidate for splitting.

photos.shows: GPS summary 71.56 mi, 5:18:00, 13.5 mph, 1,076 ft ascent, 37.0 F; map route Kingston-Hillsboro-Caballo/Arrey/Garfield/Hatch-Salem-Radium Springs; context labels Elephant Butte, Truth or Consequences, Las Cruces, Mesilla, Dona Ana, White Sands Missile Range, Deming

records.summary: CRITICAL DATA CAVEAT: their day lengths were set by RV HOOKUP needs, not by cycling logic
records.detail: The rider states it outright on the rest-day page: 'being in a Class C motorhome we really try to stay at campgrounds where we can hook up power, water and sewer. Part of the reason for the last few long difficult days was to get ourselves to good campgrounds where we can hook up. Boondocking is ok for one or two days.' He also notes campgrounds sit on the outskirts of towns, and that once the RV is set up they will not tear down to go out.
records.cyclistIntel: THIS INVALIDATES THEIR DAY BOUNDARIES AS ANY GUIDE FOR NICK, and it confirms it from the source's own mouth. The 74-mile and 77-mile days were long because a Class C motorhome needed a full-hookup site, not because that is a sensible cycling distance. A self-supported cyclist has the opposite constraint set: he can stop almost anywhere, and has no reason to overshoot a good stopping point to reach a sewer connection. Use their MILE-ANCHORED observations; discard their itinerary entirely. Reinforces the whole three-class anchoring design.
records.quote: Part of the reason for the last few long difficult days was to get ourselves to good campgrounds where we can hook up.

records.summary: NO SHADE IN ANY SOUTHWEST CAMPGROUND — the rider generalises it across the whole region, not just Arizona
records.detail: 'Here in the southwest there is no shade in any of the campgrounds.' Written on a rest day in New Mexico at 6,100 ft, reviewing three weeks and three states. This broadens the earlier Arizona-specific statement (d10-005) into a regional rule, now supported by photographic evidence at two named Arizona sites and stated across California, Arizona and New Mexico.
records.cyclistIntel: Treat 'commercial campground in the southwest' as 'no shade' by default across all three states, not just Arizona. The confirmed exceptions in this dataset are all NON-commercial: Thatcher City Park (shaded, by permission), the Palo Verde oxbow site, Kingston at elevation, and the two bar patios at Salome and Jake's Corner. For a tent in heat, the municipal park and the roadside bar beat the RV park every time.
records.quote: Here in the southwest there is no shade in any of the campgrounds.

records.summary: Campground availability pattern: Sunday-Thursday plenty of room, WEEKENDS FILL UP
records.detail: 'It's offseason so Sunday-Thursday there is plenty of room. Weekends seem to fill up.' He also notes every park has lots of permanent campers, staff are always friendly and talkative, and there is usually a faint sewer smell somewhere. Observed across roughly a dozen campgrounds in three states in April.
records.cyclistIntel: Directly actionable for a rider who cannot book far ahead. Midweek arrivals find space; weekend arrivals may not. This now compounds with two other weekend findings — Glamis OHV crowds and the AZ-87 recreational traffic — into a single planning rule: WEEKENDS ARE WORSE ON THIS ROUTE for traffic, noise and lodging alike. Also note the friendly-talkative staff observation, which pairs with six recorded instances of local knowledge producing something no map contains.
records.quote: It's offseason so Sunday-Thursday there is plenty of room. Weekends seem to fill up.

records.summary: Silver City KOA has laundry at $4.50 per load wash and dry
records.detail: 'Plenty of laundry at $4.50 a load wash & dry.' Stated on the rest day at the Silver City KOA (named on the following page's campfire account). Also gives a rare price datapoint.
records.cyclistIntel: First confirmed laundry with a price anywhere in the dataset. Silver City is the natural New Mexico rest and resupply town — largest town on the leg, at 6,100 ft so genuinely cool, and it sits between the 15-mile Lordsburg climb and Emory Pass. If Nick takes a maintenance day on the New Mexico end, this is where the facilities are.
records.quote: Plenty of laundry at $4.50 a load wash & dry.

records.summary: Six-plus Southern Tier and touring cyclists around a campfire at the Silver City KOA
records.detail: 'there were several people sitting around a campfire in the KOA campgrounds... Linda was there. And our Southern Tier friends Donna and Becky, Beth and two other avid cyclists Shelley and Suzanne.' Confirms the Silver City KOA as the site for nights 19 and 20 and shows the April cohort still travelling together 800 miles in.
records.cyclistIntel: Names the Silver City overnight, and confirms the cohort effect persists across three states and three weeks. For a solo rider that is a real safety and information asset — and it says these lodging points are shared, so popular ones are competitive, especially at weekends (p26-002).
records.quote: our Southern Tier friends Donna and Becky, Beth and two other avid cyclists Shelley and Suzanne

records.summary: The rider's own comparison of RV touring vs self-supported tenting — from someone doing one and watching the other
records.detail: On the rest day he sets the two side by side. For tenting: 'Tent camping can give you the warm feeling of being close to nature and is very flexible. If needed you find a secluded spot on BLM land and you are home. If you have bad weather you can look for a motel. But tenting is limited in the food and clothing options that can be carried every day.' For the RV: better sleep, better nutrition, climate control, a bathroom four steps away — but heavy setup, campgrounds on the outskirts of town, limited dining options, and a need for full hookups. He also notes 'The guys doing self supported transcontinental rides only have a couple clothes changes.'
records.cyclistIntel: Useful because it makes the source's bias explicit and quantifies the difference in Nick's favour on one axis: FLEXIBILITY. The rider identifies dispersed BLM camping and the motel bail-out as the tenting advantages, and food and clothing capacity as the disadvantages. Combined with p26-004, the conclusion is that Nick's stopping options are strictly wider than this journal's, so any place they could not reach or could not use is still potentially available to him.
records.quote: If needed you find a secluded spot on BLM land and you are home.

records.summary: IRON CREEK CAMPGROUND, Gila National Forest — signed USFS campground THREE MILES from the Emory Pass summit
records.detail: Photograph shows a brown USFS sign reading 'Iron Creek CAMPGROUND / GILA National Forest / U.S. Department of Agriculture' with A PITCHED TENT visible behind it among ponderosa pines. Caption: 'We stopped for lunch at this campground three miles from the top of the mountain. My original plan was to stop here but the rest stop made it possible to climb the last 1000 feet of ascent.' So the rider's own Plan A was to overnight here and split the pass across two days.
records.cyclistIntel: MAJOR FIND FOR THE ROUTE HIGH POINT. A named, signed, Forest Service campground with confirmed tent use, three miles below the 8,228 ft summit, in pine forest — so shade, cool nights and legal camping all at once. It is also the rider's own stated fallback for splitting Emory Pass into two days, which is exactly the option Nick may want. Note for HIS direction: three miles WEST of the summit means he reaches it AFTER cresting the pass on his descent toward Silver City, not before his climb. His pre-pass option remains Kingston (p28-N1). Verify season of operation, fee and whether water is on.

photos.shows: Brown USFS sign 'Iron Creek CAMPGROUND / GILA National Forest'; a pitched tent among ponderosa pines behind it; rider in winter kit with loaded touring bike; pine needle ground, dry grass

records.summary: CATTLE STANDING ON THE ROADWAY on the Emory Pass mountain road — open range, in falling snow
records.detail: Photo caption: 'Ditch cows on the mountainside. It is snowing at this point.' The photograph shows roughly seven cattle including calves standing on and beside a two-lane mountain road with a rock cut on one side, occupying most of one lane and drifting across the centreline. Wet pavement, no shoulder visible. This is open-range country on NM-152.
records.cyclistIntel: A serious hazard combination on this specific road: full-grown cattle standing in a traffic lane, on a mountain road with rock cuts, no shoulder, blind curves and — for Nick in the reverse direction — a long DESCENT. Cattle do not move for bicycles and calves make cows unpredictable. This is the fourth animal hazard in the dataset and the largest. Descend the west side of Emory Pass expecting livestock in the road, not just cars.
records.quote: Ditch cows on the mountainside. It is snowing at this point.

photos.caption: Ditch cows on the mountainside. It is snowing at this point.
photos.shows: About seven cattle including calves standing on and across a two-lane mountain road, occupying most of one lane; rock cut rising on the right, wet pavement, no shoulder, road curving out of sight

records.summary: NM-152 over the Black Range: narrow paved shoulder, roughly a foot, with a fog line and no verge
records.detail: Not stated in the text; established from two photographs on the mountain section. Both show a two-lane road with a yellow centerline and a white fog line with only about a foot of paved surface beyond it, then pine-needle ground or rock cut. Riders are on or just inside the fog line. Surface is sound and smooth.
records.cyclistIntel: Fills the gap left by p28-005, which established light traffic but said nothing about the shoulder. The answer is: effectively none. That is tolerable at climbing speed with a handful of cars, which is what they had — but Nick DESCENDS this side, at speed, with cattle in the road (p29-002) and no escape room. Pair the three findings before shaping the day: no shoulder, livestock, and a long fast descent.

photos.caption: Struggling uphill.
photos.shows: Two riders in full winter kit climbing a two-lane forest road; yellow centerline, white fog line with roughly a foot of paved shoulder beyond it, then pine needles and dry grass; ponderosa pines both sides

records.summary: Hanover Copper Mine — huge open pit directly on NM-152 east of Silver City
records.detail: Photo caption: '4/19 a huge open pit copper mine. Hanover Copper Mine. Tim and I stopped for a rest here. Beth and Linda made hot chocolate for us.' A second caption, 'How much would a set of these tires cost?', refers to the enormous haul-truck tyres displayed at such sites. Used as a rest stop on the climb out of Silver City. Second major open-pit mine on this leg after Tyrone (anchor:tyrone-mine), plus the Chino Mine visible on the map.
records.cyclistIntel: Anchor-grade landmark — vast, permanently mapped, unmistakable — and a natural rest point with a pull-off on the long west-side approach to Emory Pass. For Nick this falls late in his descent toward Silver City. Note this leg passes three major open-pit mines (Chino, Hanover, Tyrone), which makes the corridor easy to identify but also means heavy haul and industrial traffic is plausible on weekdays.

photos.caption: 4/19 a huge open pit copper mine. Hanover Copper Mine. Tim and I stopped for a rest here. Beth and Linda made hot chocolate for us. Wow, was that good.
How much would a set of these tires cost?

records.summary: Kingston to Radium Springs: ~6,400 ft down to ~3,200 ft over 71.6 mi — downhill cruise, one uphill, then a long slight descent
records.detail: 'Downhill cruise, one uphill, then a long slight downhill with decent temperatures and a big blue sky.' Elevation trace confirms: starts near 6,400 ft, dips, a small bump at roughly 50 minutes, then a continuous decline to about 3,200 ft, essentially flat for the last two and a half hours. 1,076 ft total ascent over 71.56 mi at 13.5 mph — fastest average of the journal. Only three climb waypoints all day. The rider notes his legs felt good despite the previous day's 4,685 ft.
records.cyclistIntel: REVERSED THIS IS NICK'S 71-MILE, ~3,200 FT APPROACH to Kingston and the route high point — and the profile matters: for him it is two and a half hours of near-flat valley riding FIRST, then a sustained climb into the Black Range at the end of the day. That is the wrong order, and it lands him at Kingston tired before an 8,228 ft pass the next morning. Strong candidate for splitting at Hillsboro or Caballo. Their 13.5 mph is meaningless for him.
records.quote: Downhill cruise, one uphill, then a long slight downhill with decent temperatures and a big blue sky.

photos.shows: Elevation trace from ~6,400 ft declining with a small bump near 50 min to ~3,200 ft, near-flat for the final 2.5 hours; only three climb waypoints; speed averaging 13.5 mph; temperature averaging 66.9 F

records.summary: Huge pecan groves in the Rio Grande valley — flooded once a month for irrigation
records.detail: 'We were back to agricultural areas with huge pecan tree groves. More cattle, houses and towns so we had different things to look at.' A photo caption adds the operational detail: 'Pecan groves. They flood them once a month.' So the valley floor south of Hatch carries large-scale flood-irrigated orchards.
records.cyclistIntel: Two things. Pecan groves are MATURE TREES IN ROWS — genuine shade at road level, the first available since the New Mexico high country and unlike anything in the Arizona desert. And monthly flood irrigation means canals, standpipes and headgates throughout, so surface water is abundant though agricultural and untreated. Neither is a water source, but a shaded orchard road in the Rio Grande valley is a real asset for a hot afternoon.
records.quote: Pecan groves. They flood them once a month.

photos.caption: Pecan groves. They flood them once a month.

records.summary: Mid-30s at Kingston to a 66.9 F day average — 30-plus degree swing coming off the Black Range
records.detail: 'The morning in Kingston was chilly, in the mid 30's when we took off.' GPS records a day average of 66.9 F with the temperature trace climbing steadily from near 40 F to the 70s as the route loses 3,200 ft into the Rio Grande valley. Map header 37.0 F. The previous day averaged around 38 F with snow.
records.cyclistIntel: Elevation, not season, is the temperature control on this route — the same lesson as the Boulevard-to-El Centro day in California, and the same GEAR ORDER problem inverted. Nick rides valley-to-mountain here, so he starts warm in the Rio Grande pecan groves and finishes cold at Kingston at 6,180 ft, then crosses an 8,228 ft pass where it snowed in April. Cold kit accessible at the END of the day, again.
records.quote: The morning in Kingston was chilly, in the mid 30's when we took off.

records.summary: Night 22: Radium Springs NM area — the rider leaves the route here to visit friends; site not named
records.detail: At Radium Springs the party turned north to visit New Mexico friends while Tim and Beth continued south on the route. No site named. 'We will be taking several days off to visit with friends and family.'
records.cyclistIntel: No lead. Recorded to close the chain and to mark the point where this journal leaves the Southern Tier. Radium Springs sits just north of Las Cruces, so the route from here runs south to Las Cruces / Mesilla and on toward El Paso — where the goathead warning (p24-005) begins.
records.quote: we headed North and they continued South

records.summary: THE RIO GRANDE IS DRY SAND at Las Cruces — 'Nothing but sand'
records.detail: Photo caption: 'This is a view of the Rio Grande River outside of Las Cruces. Nothing but sand.' The photograph shows a wide riverbed of bare wind-rippled sand from bank to bank, with tamarisk on the margins and no water anywhere in frame, shot from a bridge. Upstream flow on this reach is controlled by Elephant Butte releases for irrigation, so the channel is dry outside release season.
records.cyclistIntel: CRITICAL NEGATIVE WATER FINDING. On a map the Rio Grande looks like the most reliable water on the southwestern half of the route. It is not — at Las Cruces in late April it is bare sand. Do NOT enter the Rio Grande as a water source in the planner, and do not let any day plan depend on reaching it. Water on this reach comes from towns and from the irrigation canals that the pecan groves use, not from the river. This is the same class of finding as the waterless free campgrounds in New Mexico already in the plan.
records.quote: This is a view of the Rio Grande River outside of Las Cruces. Nothing but sand.

photos.caption: This is a view of the Rio Grande River outside of Las Cruces. Nothing but sand.
photos.shows: Wide riverbed of bare wind-rippled sand from bank to bank seen from a bridge parapet; tamarisk and scrub on the margins; no water anywhere in frame; deep blue sky

records.summary: PECAN GROVES BLOCK THE WIND — dense hedgerows right against the road sheltered the first 30 miles from a strong SW wind
records.detail: 'The wind was strong from the SW but the pecan groves were very close to the road and worked to block the wind for the first 30 miles.' A photograph confirms it: a wall of dense pecan canopy trimmed flush and rising perhaps 30 feet, immediately at the road edge with no setback, running continuously along the shoulder.
records.cyclistIntel: GENUINELY USEFUL AND NON-OBVIOUS. On a route where wind is the dominant variable, thirty miles of natural windbreak is worth more than a tailwind you cannot count on. The groves also give shade at road level (p29-005). For Nick riding north up this valley the same shelter applies whichever way the wind blows. Worth marking the pecan corridor as a distinct span in the planner — it is the only sheltered stretch identified anywhere in 900 miles.
records.quote: the pecan groves were very close to the road and worked to block the wind for the first 30 miles

photos.caption: The pecan trees are right up against the road. Nice to see lots of green and nice to have the wind block.
photos.shows: Continuous wall of dense trimmed pecan canopy rising ~30 ft immediately at the road edge with no setback; two-lane road with yellow centerline, cracked pavement edge, rider in the lane; car approaching

records.summary: FIRST FLAT AT ~966 MILES — and the tyre that prevented earlier ones took 40 minutes to change with no shade
records.detail: 'I had my first flat tire of the trip today. I didn't find any wires or sand burrs in the tire so I am crossing my fingers whatever flatted me isn't still in the tire.' Photo caption: 'Boy was that tire hard to change. Very stiff sidewalls. My friend Doug warned me my tough Continental Total Contact tires would be a bear. He was right. 40 minutes with just a telephone pole for shade.' So: heavy puncture-resistant touring tyres, one flat in 966 miles across the debris corridors of CA-78, I-10 and the glass east of Wenden — and a 40-minute roadside repair when it finally happened.
records.cyclistIntel: THE GEAR DECISION, WITH BOTH SIDES OF THE TRADE MEASURED. Heavy armoured tyres bought him ~966 miles through three separate debris corridors with a single flat. The cost is a 40-minute change in full sun with a telephone pole for shade. For Nick that trade is clearly right — the debris findings in this dataset are severe and a flat on the I-10 shoulder is dangerous, not just slow — but he should PRACTISE the change before departure and carry proper levers. Note this is also the pre-El Paso stretch, i.e. BEFORE the goathead zone (p24-005) even begins.
records.quote: 40 minutes with just a telephone pole for shade.

photos.caption: Boy was that tire hard to change. Very stiff sidewalls.
photos.shows: Touring bike inverted-leaning against a utility pole with rear wheel removed on a gravel verge; five water bottles visible on frame and fork mounts; narrow pole shadow the only shade; irrigated field opposite

records.summary: Rio Grande levee bike path into El Paso — paved and car-free, but a flood-control maintenance road 'not maintained for public use'
records.detail: 'The route included a very nice bike path that paralleled the Rio Grande.' A photograph shows a smooth concrete path running along a levee, and the regulatory sign beside it reads: 'MOTORIZED TRAFFIC PROHIBITED... ALL PROHIBITED USES ARE CONSIDERED TRESPASS. This is a Flood Control Project Subject to Flooding. U.S. Government Property. US International Boundary and Water Commission. USIBWC Levee and Maintenance Road. NOT MAINTAINED FOR PUBLIC USE. ONLY NON-MOTORIZED AND AUTHORIZED USE ALLOWED. ENTER AT YOUR OWN RISK.' So bicycles are explicitly permitted, but it is a federal levee road rather than a park trail.
records.cyclistIntel: Excellent car-free approach into El Paso — the second such find after the Phoenix canal trails. But read the sign: it is a working flood-control levee, explicitly NOT maintained for public use, and subject to flooding. Expect no sweeping, no repairs and possible closure or debris after rain. Also note it runs the international boundary, so Border Patrol presence should be assumed. Load it as a track; a path with no maintenance obligation is exactly the kind that disappears (compare p20-002 in Phoenix).
records.quote: The route included a very nice bike path that paralleled the Rio Grande.

photos.caption: A real bike path!
photos.shows: Smooth concrete path running along a levee into open scrub; regulatory sign 'MOTORIZED TRAFFIC PROHIBITED / Flood Control Project Subject to Flooding / USIBWC Levee and Maintenance Road / NOT MAINTAINED FOR PUBLIC USE / ENTER AT YOUR OWN RISK' with pictogram panel permitting bicycles and pedestrians; loaded bike leaning on a rock

records.summary: Big uphill on a very busy El Paso street — the rider took to the SIDEWALK
records.detail: 'Then a big uphill on a very busy street. I rode on the sidewalk for that part. A few sketchy neighborhoods, the UTEP campus and I made it to the Roadrunner RV Park.' The GPS elevation trace confirms the climb: after roughly four hours of gentle descent the profile jumps from about 3,700 ft to a peak near 4,150 ft between 4:26 and 4:50, with three climb waypoints, then drops to a marked 3,797 ft at the finish. The speed trace shows its only fast spikes in that same window.
records.cyclistIntel: An experienced touring rider chose the sidewalk over the road here, which is the strongest possible signal about the street. Climbing slowly in heavy urban traffic on a grade is the worst combination in city riding. For Nick, WESTBOUND, this becomes a fast DESCENT on a busy street — different risk, arguably worse, and the sidewalk is not an option at speed. Anchor it: it sits in the last ten miles into El Paso near the UTEP campus. Worth finding an alternative line through this specific climb.
records.quote: Then a big uphill on a very busy street. I rode on the sidewalk for that part.

photos.shows: Elevation trace gently declining ~4,100 to ~3,700 ft over four hours, then a sharp rise to ~4,150 ft between 4:26 and 4:50 with three climb waypoints, then a drop to a marked 3,797 ft

records.summary: Las Cruces is good to cycle through — 'Good roads, bike lanes, flat'
records.detail: Photo caption: 'Starting out. Las Cruces was a very nice town to bike through. Good roads, bike lanes, flat.' A second photograph shows the rider at a 'JCT 157 / LAS CRUCES VIA I-25' junction sign on a quiet tree-shaded road with a gravel verge.
records.cyclistIntel: Worth recording as a positive so the app does not warn generically on urban sections. Las Cruces has actual bike infrastructure, which distinguishes it from the El Paso approach ten miles later (p32-005). It is also the last substantial city before the Texas border and sits at the northern end of the sheltered pecan corridor — a natural resupply and regroup point for Nick heading north out of El Paso.
records.quote: Las Cruces was a very nice town to bike through. Good roads, bike lanes, flat.

photos.caption: Starting out. Las Cruces was a very nice town to bike through. Good roads, bike lanes, flat.
photos.shows: Rider with loaded bike beside a 'JCT NM-157' shield and a green 'LAS CRUCES VIA I-25' sign; quiet two-lane road, mature trees, wall and gravel verge, morning light

records.summary: They rode 73.5 mi deliberately to get PAST El Paso and avoid the next morning's commute
records.detail: 'We had an ambitious agenda of getting through to the east side of El Paso today instead of fighting the morning commute tomorrow. 73.5 miles was tough but worth it.' A deliberate day-length choice driven by urban traffic timing rather than by terrain or lodging.
records.cyclistIntel: Transferable tactic, and the mirror image of the small-town outbound rush hour already recorded (p24-001). In a big city the play is to be through it before the commute, which for Nick travelling WESTBOUND means clearing El Paso heading out rather than in. Note this is the same rider who elsewhere overshot good stopping points to reach RV hookups, so treat the distance as his constraint and the tactic as the finding.
records.quote: getting through to the east side of El Paso today instead of fighting the morning commute tomorrow

records.summary: Day average 87.8 F with a trace spike above 100 F — heat is back on the Texas border
records.detail: GPS records an 87.8 F day average, 82.4 F marked, and a spike above 100 F at roughly 1:40 into the ride. Map header 66.0 F at the start. Eight days after snow at Emory Pass, the route is back into high-80s averages at ~3,800 ft on the Rio Grande.
records.cyclistIntel: The elevation-controls-temperature rule holds: down off the Black Range and back into the high 80s. Note the rider's flat repair took 40 minutes in this, 'with just a telephone pole for shade' (p32-003) — a concrete illustration of why the no-shade findings matter operationally. Nick should assume any roadside mechanical on this stretch happens in full sun at 90 F.
records.anchorNote: extent applied west→east per the source rule

photos.shows: Temperature trace averaging 87.8 F with a spike above 100 F near 1:40 and a marked 82.4 F

records.summary: Border wall visible again at El Paso, plus a pedestrian bridge into Mexico busy with foot traffic
records.detail: 'Tomorrow the route follows the border south. Today I saw The Wall again and a foot bridge between Texas and Mexico that was filled with people walking to Mexico.' Fourth stretch in the dataset with the border barrier in view, after the Jacumba, Calexico and Old Highway 80 sections in California.
records.cyclistIntel: Confirms the route runs the international boundary through El Paso and continues along it southeast. Same practical guidance as the California border sections: expect Border Patrol presence and carry ID. Still no checkpoint encounter recorded anywhere in this journal across four border stretches.
records.quote: a foot bridge between Texas and Mexico that was filled with people walking to Mexico

records.summary: Night 30: ROADRUNNER RV PARK, east side of El Paso TX
records.detail: Named directly. On the east side of El Paso, reached after the busy-street climb and the UTEP campus. No facilities, cost or tent policy given.
records.cyclistIntel: Callable, and positioned east of the city — so for Nick WESTBOUND it comes BEFORE the El Paso crossing, which makes it the natural staging point for clearing the city early. Add to the call-ahead list: tents, showers, shade. Note El Paso is also where the goathead zone begins (p24-005), so it is the last sensible place to check tyres and add sealant before that stretch.
records.quote: I made it to the Roadrunner RV Park

records.summary: GOATHEADS CONFIRMED with the exact mechanism: they are in the GRAVEL, not on the asphalt — and shade-seeking is the trap
records.detail: 'I got another flat. Two days in a row is a little much. I know exactly what happened this time. I pulled off the nice clean road at Tornillo to get to some shade next to a broken down ice machine. There had to be sand burrs in the gravel since I had no trouble until getting ready to leave from my break. Linda met me there and also had sand burrs picked up by her shoes. Two sand burr needles were removed from my front tire... From now on I will be very careful when leaving the asphalt.' The road itself he describes as 'nice clean'. This confirms and sharpens the warning received four days earlier from east-to-west riders (p24-005).
records.cyclistIntel: THE MOST ACTIONABLE HAZARD IN THE DATASET, because the mechanism is now precise. The pavement is safe; every unpaved surface from El Paso east is suspect. The trap is exactly what a rider in 95 F heat will want to do — pull onto gravel for shade. Rules for Nick: stop only on pavement, never wheel the bike onto gravel or dirt, never set the bike down off-asphalt, and check tyres before rolling after any stop. Also note his supporter picked them up on her SHOES, so they transfer into a tent, a groundsheet and bare feet. Sealant plus armoured tyres does not solve a thorn you carry into camp. *** AMENDED BY p35-002: dust devils in west Texas LIFT goatheads and deposit them on the road, on the bike and on bare skin. Staying on asphalt is necessary but NOT sufficient. Sealant and eye protection become mandatory east of El Paso. ***
records.quote: From now on I will be very careful when leaving the asphalt.

photos.caption: The shade was nice but I would rather not have had to remove sand burrs and change the tire.

records.summary: DOGS START AT THE TEXAS LINE — chased twice on his first full day in Texas, after 1,028 miles with none
records.detail: 'Now that I am riding in Texas, I of course was chased by dogs on two different occasions. I had a headstart in both cases and could outrun them (flat and tailwind helps). I didn't resort to the airhorn I have in my handlebar bag ready to startle a dog if it gets too close.' First dog incidents anywhere in the journal, on day one of Texas riding, in agricultural country with ranches and houses along the road. He carries an AIRHORN in his handlebar bag specifically for this.
records.cyclistIntel: A CLEAN PATTERN BOUNDARY: zero dogs in 1,028 miles across California, Arizona and New Mexico desert; two chases on the first Texas farming day. The trigger is inhabited agricultural land, not the state line as such — so expect this all the way east. CRITICAL INVERSION: he outran them because the terrain was flat AND he had a tailwind. Nick rides the opposite direction, so on this stretch he faces the same dogs INTO a headwind and cannot outrun them. That makes a deterrent mandatory rather than optional for him — the airhorn in an accessible bar bag is the specific, tested answer from this source.
records.quote: I of course was chased by dogs on two different occasions... I didn't resort to the airhorn I have in my handlebar bag

records.summary: Day average 94.6 F on the Texas border — highest sustained average outside the Phoenix crossing
records.detail: GPS records a 94.6 F day average over 4:38:48, with the temperature trace above 90 F for most of the ride and touching roughly 105 F. Map header 73.0 F at the start. Riding began late, at 9:30am, because of an RV repair — so he was on the road through the hottest part of the day rather than ahead of it.
records.cyclistIntel: Second-hottest day average in the dataset after the 97.4 F Phoenix crossing, and it shows what happens when the pre-dawn start slips: the 9:30am departure put him in full afternoon heat on a 62-mile day. The heat also drives the goathead problem in p33-001 — the reason he left the asphalt at all was to find shade. Heat and thorns are one coupled hazard on this stretch, not two.
records.anchorNote: extent applied west→east per the source rule

photos.shows: Temperature trace above 90 F for most of the ride, peaking near 105 F, averaging 94.6 F; elevation trace nearly flat from ~3,800 ft to a marked 3,573 ft at 3:13 and level to the end

records.summary: Nice clean roads and dead flat along the Texas border corridor — 367 ft of ascent in 62 miles
records.detail: 'The roads today were nice and the wind was to my back or side. And super flat the entire day. I actually got to look around and enjoy the scenery instead of concentrating on a bad road or a tough hill.' GPS confirms: 367 ft of total ascent over 61.68 mi at 13.3 mph, second-fastest average of the journal, with the elevation trace essentially level from about 3,800 ft to a marked 3,573 ft.
records.cyclistIntel: Genuinely easy riding — flattest and cleanest surface recorded anywhere on the route so far, through irrigated farmland with pecan groves, alfalfa and goat farms. Record it as a POSITIVE span so the planner does not warn generically across Texas. The hazards on this stretch are the ones you cannot see from the road profile: thorns off the pavement, dogs from the houses, and 95 F heat.
records.quote: The roads today were nice and the wind was to my back or side. And super flat the entire day.

photos.caption: Alfalfa field. Green!

records.summary: Border always to the west with heavy Border Patrol presence, but the wall is too far off to see
records.detail: 'The border with Mexico was always just to our west. We could see the mountains in Mexico and the green ribbon that is the Rio Grande but we were too far away to see any wall or fence. Lots of boarder patrol vehicles on this route.' Fifth border stretch in the journal. The Rio Grande here is described as a green ribbon rather than the dry sand photographed at Las Cruces the day before, so it carries water on this reach.
records.cyclistIntel: Expect sustained Border Patrol traffic on this corridor — the fifth such stretch and still no checkpoint encounter recorded anywhere in the journal. Carry ID. Note the Rio Grande contrast: dry sand at Las Cruces (p32-001), a green ribbon here. River presence on this route is release-dependent and cannot be assumed either way.
records.quote: Lots of boarder patrol vehicles on this route.

records.summary: Fort Hancock TX has a post office — but the town 'looked like it had seen better days'
records.detail: 'Stopped at the post office in Fort Hancock. Nice post office but the town looked like it had seen better days.' A post office is confirmed; nothing else is named. Fort Hancock sits roughly 50 miles southeast of El Paso on the border corridor.
records.cyclistIntel: A confirmed US Post Office matters more than it looks on a self-supported trip — it is a mail-drop point for resupplying consumables (tubes, tyres, sealant, chain) which on this stretch is exactly what the goathead problem consumes. Do NOT assume groceries, water or food here: the rider describes a town past its best and names only the post office. Treat it as a mail and shade stop, not a resupply.
records.quote: Nice post office but the town looked like it had seen better days.

photos.caption: Stopped at the post office in Fort Hancock. Nice post office but the town looked like it had seen better days.

records.summary: Irrigation reservoirs and ditches throughout the border farmland — surface water, plentiful, untreated
records.detail: 'We passed a couple of pretty lakes which were really just irrigation reservoirs.' Irrigation ditches along the route hold enough water to support Cattle Egrets, Great Blue Herons and a Sand Hill Crane. Pecan groves and alfalfa fields the whole way, plus goat farms.
records.cyclistIntel: Abundant surface water through the farmland belt, all agricultural and untreated — an emergency filtered backstop, not a source. The wildlife is the tell that it is permanent rather than seasonal. Real water comes from towns; note that Fort Hancock (p33-006) is not confirmed to have any. Also: irrigated farmland means the pecan-grove shade and windbreak effect (p32-002, p29-005) continues into Texas.
records.quote: We passed a couple of pretty lakes which were really just irrigation reservoirs.

photos.caption: We passed a couple of pretty lakes which were really just irrigation reservoirs.

records.summary: GPS routing error sent the support vehicle down a bad road and broke part of the RV
records.detail: 'We broke a pad off the hydralic leveling system (Garmin's fault, it sent us down a bad road) so we stopped at Lowe's in El Paso to come up with a make-do.' The repair delayed the ride start to 9:30am, which is what put the rider into the day's worst heat (p33-003).
records.cyclistIntel: Two transferable points. Consumer GPS routing on this corridor put a vehicle onto a road bad enough to cause damage — the same class of failure as Google's circuitous Phoenix bike routing (p18-004) and the vanishing Phoenix bike path (p20-002). Do not trust turn-by-turn here; carry the route as a track. And second: a mechanical delay cascaded into a heat problem, because on this route the schedule has almost no slack before the afternoon becomes dangerous.
records.quote: Garmin's fault, it sent us down a bad road

records.summary: PREVIEW: next day is the I-10 shoulder for a long steady climb before levelling out
records.detail: FORWARD-LOOKING, not observed: 'Tomorrow promises traveling on the shoulder of I-10 for a long steady climb before leveling out. Hopefully I will get an early start to beat most of the interstate traffic.' Recorded at unknown confidence pending the Day 32 page. Note this journal's previews have been reliable on terrain and unreliable on endpoints (p10-008).
records.cyclistIntel: Flags a third interstate-shoulder segment after the I-8 In-Ko-Pah grade and the I-10 stretch west of Quartzsite. Both earlier ones carried severe debris, and this one sits INSIDE the confirmed goathead zone — the worst combination yet. Confirm and replace from the next page, and pay particular attention to what he says about the shoulder surface.
records.quote: Tomorrow promises traveling on the shoulder of I-10 for a long steady climb before leveling out.

records.summary: Night 31: behind a TRUCK STOP on I-10 in a big gravel lot — and gravel is where the goatheads are
records.detail: 'Not many choices for camping in this area. We are behind a truck stop on I-10 in a big gravel lot. I assume when we get up tomorrow morning we will have more company.' Water, showers and toilets marked likely on the strength of it being a full interstate truck stop, not from the page. No shade. Surface is gravel. RETROSPECTIVE FROM THE NEXT PAGE: 'Before nightfall the line of trucks (and our little camper) filled the lot. We had big rigs within 5 feet of us on both sides, running their engines all night. The white noise was actually not so bad. It drowned out the interstate noise.' So the lot fills completely after dark.
records.cyclistIntel: WORST TENT PROSPECT IN THE DATASET, and for a specific reason: the only camping option in the area is a GRAVEL LOT, and this same page establishes that gravel here carries goatheads (p33-001) — the rider's own supporter picked them up on her shoes that afternoon. Pitching a tent and a groundsheet on that surface, and walking on it barefoot, is a different proposition from parking an RV. Truck stops do offer real advantages for a cyclist though: water, showers, toilets, food, 24-hour lighting and people around. If Nick uses this, sweep a pitch, keep shoes on, and check tyres and groundsheet before packing. Identify the specific truck stop and look hard for an alternative in this stretch. ALSO: the lot FILLS with big rigs after dark, engines running all night, with only about 5 ft of clearance between vehicles. Tolerable inside an RV; for a tent that is idling diesel exhaust at head height on both sides, and a real risk of being unseen by a manoeuvring truck. Pitch at the edge of the lot, not in it, and arrive early enough to choose.
records.quote: Not many choices for camping in this area. We are behind a truck stop on I-10 in a big gravel lot.

photos.caption: Not many choices for camping in this area. We are behind a truck stop on I-10 in a big gravel lot.

records.summary: I-10 in west Texas is 'a slalom course between shreds of tires' — third interstate debris field, inside the goathead zone
records.detail: 'The entire day was either on I-10 or on the rough chip seal access road. As before, riding on the interstate was a slalom course between shreds of tires. And the noise is loud.' His 'as before' refers to the eleven-mile I-10 stretch west of Quartzsite (d8-001), so he is explicitly reporting the same condition. Third interstate-shoulder debris field in the dataset, and the first one that also sits inside the confirmed goathead zone (p33-001).
records.cyclistIntel: Shredded truck tyres mean steel belt wire, which is the classic slow-puncture cause, and here it compounds with goatheads off the pavement — so there is nowhere clean to stop. Same rules as d8-001, tightened: armoured tyres, multiple tubes, daylight only, and do NOT pull onto the gravel verge to fix anything if there is any alternative. Note this rider had already had two flats in the preceding two days.
records.quote: riding on the interstate was a slalom course between shreds of tires
records.anchorNote: extent applied west→east per the source rule

records.summary: DIRECT EVIDENCE FOR NICK'S DIRECTION: riders going east-to-west were FIGHTING the big wind Dave was riding with
records.detail: 'On the lonely access road Linda found two new friends. Mark and Janet, from Maine, were riding the opposite direction from me.' Photo caption: 'Mark and Janet. They had to fight the big wind I was benefitting from.' Opposite direction means east-to-west — Nick's direction. So this is not an inference from Dave's tailwind; it is an observation of loaded touring cyclists in Nick's direction struggling into a strong headwind in west Texas.
records.cyclistIntel: THE STRONGEST WIND FINDING IN THE DATASET, because it removes the inversion guesswork. Every other wind record here required inferring Nick's experience from Dave's. This one shows it directly: riders in Nick's direction, on this corridor, fighting a big wind. West Texas on I-10 should be planned as a headwind corridor, with day lengths set accordingly. Sixth distinct wind regime recorded, and the only one confirmed from Nick's own direction of travel.
records.quote: They had to fight the big wind I was benefitting from.
records.anchorNote: extent applied west→east per the source rule

photos.caption: Mark and Janet. They had to fight the big wind I was benefitting from.
photos.shows: Three cyclists on a rough concrete/chipseal access road; two loaded touring bikes with front and rear panniers; I-10 with trucks passing behind, gravel stockpile, bare desert butte, clear sky

records.summary: On I-10 the TRUCKERS moved over; the CARS did not
records.detail: 'Most truckers were very considerate and moved to the outside lane. The cars weren't so considerate.' Observed across a full day on the interstate shoulder in west Texas.
records.cyclistIntel: Counterintuitive and worth having in the planner, because the instinctive fear on an interstate is the trucks. The actual risk is passenger cars. That changes the mitigation: the danger is not predictable big vehicles giving room, it is inattentive drivers at 80 mph who do not move over — so maximum rear visibility and a mirror matter more than road position. Consistent across three interstate segments now; no aggressive behaviour reported anywhere in this journal.
records.quote: Most truckers were very considerate and moved to the outside lane. The cars weren't so considerate.
records.anchorNote: extent applied west→east per the source rule

records.summary: The alternative to I-10 is a ROUGH CHIP SEAL access road — quieter is not on offer
records.detail: 'The entire day was either on I-10 or on the rough chip seal access road... When the course jumped off the interstate to the parallel access road the interstate was still close enough to be noisy and dominate the view.' A photograph of the access road shows aged, patched concrete-and-chipseal surface with a ragged edge and gravel verge. So the route alternates between the interstate shoulder and a rough frontage road, and neither escapes the noise.
records.cyclistIntel: Important expectation-setting: on this stretch there is no good option, only a choice between smooth-but-debris-strewn interstate and rough-but-slower frontage road. Rough chipseal has already cost this rider dearly once — 20 miles east of Wenden 'sucked the energy right out of us' (p17-001). Budget a slower average for the access-road portions and expect interstate noise for the whole day regardless of which surface he is on.
records.quote: the rough chip seal access road
records.anchorNote: extent applied west→east per the source rule

photos.caption: Mark and Janet. They had to fight the big wind I was benefitting from.
photos.shows: Aged patched concrete/chipseal access road surface with a ragged edge and gravel verge; I-10 and trucks immediately alongside

records.summary: Heavy Border Patrol presence continues; culverts under I-10 may be occupied
records.detail: 'We are still seeing a lot of Border Patrol vehicles. It makes sense as we can see Mexico in the distance. Linda was looking in a large culvert under I-10 at the flood level sign when she spotted some people under there in the shadows.' A photo caption shows 'A culvert under the interstate similar to the one Linda saw people in.' Sixth border stretch in the journal; still no checkpoint encounter recorded.
records.cyclistIntel: Practical, non-speculative point: large culverts under I-10 look like the only shade on this corridor and a cyclist may be tempted to use one for a heat break. They are not reliably unoccupied. Plan shade around towns, truck stops and structures instead, and carry ID given the sustained Border Patrol presence. No incident of any kind is reported here.
records.quote: she spotted some people under there in the shadows
records.anchorNote: extent applied west→east per the source rule

photos.caption: A culvert under the interstate similar to the one Linda saw people in.

records.summary: Steady rise from ~3,600 ft to 4,678 ft over 53 mi — 1,631 ft, the start of the west Texas high plateau
records.detail: GPS: 52.86 mi, 4:01:21, 13.1 mph, 1,631 ft ascent. Elevation trace climbs from about 3,600 ft to a marked 4,678 ft at 3:38, with a broad crest near 1:40 and a slight drop into Van Horn. Six climb waypoints, four of them in the first hour. This confirms the previous day's preview of 'a long steady climb before leveling out' (p33-009).
records.cyclistIntel: Gentle by this route's standards and it buys temperature relief — the day averaged 73.9 F against 94.6 F the day before, largely on 1,000 ft of elevation. Reversed, Nick descends this into the hotter, flatter border farmland. Note his direction gets the elevation loss and the temperature gain at the same time, which is the wrong combination.
records.anchorNote: extent applied west→east per the source rule

photos.shows: Elevation trace ~3,600 ft rising to a marked 4,678 ft at 3:38:44 with a broad crest near 1:40; six climb waypoints, four in the first hour; temperature averaging 73.9 F with 87.8 F marked; speed averaging 13.1 mph

records.summary: VAN HORN TX — real town with restaurants; Van Horn Cattle Company confirmed (steaks)
records.detail: 'Linda and I went out to dinner to the Van Horn Cattle Company. Your choices were steaks or steaks. In small print on the back of the menu were hamburgers, chicken sandwiches, etc.' Van Horn sits at the I-10 / US-90 junction at roughly 4,600 ft. A photograph shows welded metal sculpture in town.
records.cyclistIntel: First substantial town since El Paso, 115 miles back, and the junction where the route leaves I-10 for US-90 toward Marfa. Confirmed sit-down food. Treat Van Horn as a mandatory resupply and tyre-check stop: it is at the end of the I-10 debris slalom and the start of the Marfa leg. Also the last chance to deal with anything the goatheads and tyre shreds have done.
records.quote: Your choices were steaks or steaks.

photos.caption: In Van Horn. Someone with welding skills and a different eye than I have.

records.summary: Sierra Blanca train depot — meeting point of the SECOND transcontinental railway
records.detail: Photo caption: 'The train depot in Sierra Blanca. This was the meeting point for the second transcontinental railway.' A fixed, historically significant structure directly on the route between the I-10 truck stop and Van Horn.
records.cyclistIntel: Good mid-leg anchor on a stretch with very few fixed references — the corridor is otherwise interstate, frontage road and desert. Sierra Blanca is also the only named settlement between Esperanza and Van Horn, so worth checking independently whether it has water or a store; this page does not say.

photos.caption: The train depot in Sierra Blanca. This was the meeting point for the second transcontinental railway.

records.summary: PREVIEW: Marfa TX is well regarded by every Southern Tier rider ahead of them
records.detail: FORWARD-LOOKING: 'We are looking forward to making it to Marfa tomorrow. It is an artist colony in the desert that everyone before us has enjoyed.' Reported as consensus among the riders ahead on the route rather than the author's own experience, so recorded at unknown confidence pending the next page.
records.cyclistIntel: Worth flagging early because it is the first place on the route described as universally recommended by other Southern Tier cyclists. Confirm from the Day 33 page and look for what specifically makes it good — lodging, food, or a rider-friendly business. An artist town in far west Texas is also a plausible candidate for the kind of discretionary-permission camping that worked at Thatcher (p23-007).
records.quote: It is an artist colony in the desert that everyone before us has enjoyed.

records.summary: Night 32: Van Horn TX — site not named
records.detail: Day ends in Van Horn; the page names no campground or RV park, only the restaurant they ate at. Van Horn is a real town on the I-10 / US-90 junction with commercial lodging.
records.cyclistIntel: No specific lead, but Van Horn is a genuine town with services at the point where the route leaves the interstate — a natural stopping point regardless of which site. Worth identifying what exists there since it is the only substantial option in 115 miles.

records.summary: DUST DEVILS CARRY THE GOATHEADS — one storm put a burr in his LEG and two in his TIRE while he was on the pavement
records.detail: 'All day these dust devil storms were out in the desert.' Then: 'I was caught in one dust devil storm. I had to close my eyes, the sand was stinging all my exposed skin. Afterwards I had one sand burr in my leg and two in my tire.' A photograph shows a goathead burr embedded in the tread of his tyre; another shows three dust devils standing over the desert simultaneously. He was riding, not parked on gravel.
records.cyclistIntel: THIS BREAKS THE MITIGATION I RECORDED YESTERDAY. p33-001 concluded that goatheads live in the gravel and staying on asphalt keeps you clean. That is now only half true — dust devils lift them and deposit them on the road, on the bike and on bare skin. So in west Texas: tyre sealant becomes genuinely important rather than optional, exposed skin is a target, and eye protection is mandatory because he had to shut his eyes while riding. Also note the compound failure mode — blinded, stung, and picking up thorns, all at once, on a no-services stretch with a headwind. Wraparound glasses, a buff, and sealant in both tyres.
records.quote: I had to close my eyes, the sand was stinging all my exposed skin. Afterwards I had one sand burr in my leg and two in my tire.

photos.caption: All day these dust devil storms were out in the desert.
photos.shows: Three distinct dust devils standing simultaneously over open desert grassland below a low mountain ridge; clear sky

photos.caption: I was caught in one dust devil storm.
photos.shows: Close-up of a goathead burr with multiple hard spines embedded in the tread of a touring tyre

records.summary: THE WEST TEXAS NO-SERVICES STRETCH: 73 mi today with one tiny town, then 50+ mi with none
records.detail: 'This part of the ride has long sections of no services so today was over 73 miles and tomorrow will be over 50 no services miles. Very few dwellings, very few intersections. Only one town to pass through.' The one town is Valentine (p35-004), which is very small and whose only recorded business is a bar with limited hours. The map confirms it: between Van Horn and Marfa the only labelled settlements on US-90 are Valentine, Quebec and Ryan.
records.cyclistIntel: THIS IS ALMOST CERTAINLY THE 99.8-MILE DRY STRETCH ALREADY IN THE PLANNER at route mile 1689-1789 — first firsthand account of it. Two consecutive no-services days, back to back, in 80-95 F heat, with a headwind, dust devils and goatheads. Against the rider's measured 5-6 bottles a day WITH vehicle resupply (p25-009), Nick has to carry the whole thing. Van Horn (p34-005) and Marfa are the bracketing resupply points and both are confirmed real towns. Valentine cannot be relied on. Anchor this span tightly — it is the single most dangerous water gap on the route.
records.quote: This part of the ride has long sections of "no services" so today was over 73 miles and tomorrow will be over 50 no services miles.

records.summary: VALENTINE TX — the only town in 73 miles, and its one business is a dive bar with limited hours
records.detail: 'Valentine is a very small town but has a bar that was written up in Bon Appetite magazine. The Valentine Texas Bar wasn't open when I passed through but Linda hung around until it was. It is a real cowboy dive bar.' Photographs show the interior with a bobcat mount and a bartender named Rachel, plus a sign reading 'You can hitch up your horse or your Tesla at the Valentine Texas Bar.' A further caption: 'I'm bummed. I am too early for the bar to open.' The rider passed through and got nothing.
records.cyclistIntel: DIRECTLY ADDRESSES THE D28 VALENTINE GAP — one of the six nights in the plan with no lodging anchor. The honest answer this page gives is discouraging: Valentine is very small, the only business recorded is a bar, and that bar was CLOSED to a cyclist arriving in the morning. Do not plan on Valentine for water, food or lodging on the strength of it being the only dot on the map. If Nick must stop there, the bar is the place to ask about water and a patch of ground — the Thatcher precedent (p23-007) says small-town discretion is how these get solved — but arrive when it is open and have a fallback. Verify opening days and hours.
records.quote: The Valentine Texas Bar wasn't open when I passed through

photos.caption: Rachel at The Valentine Texas Bar. Nice bobcat in the background.
You can hitch up your horse or your Tesla at the Valentine Texas Bar.
I'm bummed. I am too early for the bar to open.

records.summary: EL COSMICO, Marfa TX — named eclectic campground with dry camping, hammocks, and an outdoor cold shower
records.detail: 'In Marfa we are dry camping in the parking lot of El Cosmico. The place is an eclectic mishmash of funky old trailers, yurts, tee pees, and canvas sided huts. They have hammocks to hang out in and an outdoor gathering place so all the hippies can commune. The shower was an outdoor shower with cold water. It reminded me of my RAGBRAI experiences.' So: a commercial campground with alternative accommodation, communal space, and cold outdoor showers.
records.cyclistIntel: THE MOST CYCLIST-FRIENDLY COMMERCIAL SITE IN THE DATASET. A place built around tents, yurts and teepees is by definition tent-accepting — unlike every RV park recorded so far, where tent policy has been the open question every time. Hammocks and a communal gathering space mean shade and somewhere to sit out the heat, which the southwest campgrounds do not offer (p26-001). A cold shower after a 73-mile no-services day in 95 F is worth a lot. It also brackets the dry stretch on the east side. Call for tent rates; Marfa is a destination town so book ahead, especially at a weekend (p26-002).
records.quote: The place is an eclectic mishmash of funky old trailers, yurts, tee pees, and canvas sided huts.

records.summary: HEADWIND all day going southeast — west Texas wind is strong and hits BOTH directions
records.detail: 'The route today moves south and east. Away from the hubbub of I-10, but directly into the wind. I knew I had been lucky so far with wind direction, today it caught up to me. Slow going in the headwind.' His average fell to 11.0 mph over 6:41:06 despite only 1,243 ft of climbing. Read against the previous day, when he had a big tailwind heading east on I-10 while riders going west fought it (p34-004), the wind evidently shifted — so this corridor is not a one-directional wind regime.
records.cyclistIntel: IMPORTANT CORRECTION TO THE OPTIMISTIC READ. p34-004 showed riders in Nick's direction fighting a headwind, which suggested west Texas is simply bad for him. This page shows the same corridor delivering a headwind to a rider going the OTHER way a day later. The honest conclusion: west Texas wind is strong and directionally unreliable, so plan the no-services days to survive a headwind rather than hoping for help. Note the compounding — headwind, 73 miles, no services, dust devils, 95 F.
records.quote: directly into the wind. I knew I had been lucky so far with wind direction, today it caught up to me.

records.summary: Four pronghorn antelope — first animal larger than a ground squirrel since the burros in California
records.detail: 'Other interesting things along the route were seeing four pronghorn antelope, the first wildlife of the trip larger than a ground squirrel.'
