A photograph shows two pronghorn in open grassland beyond a railway line and fence, with mountains behind. Note the fence and railway between them and the road.
records.cyclistIntel: Low hazard as recorded — they were behind fencing and beyond the railway, not in the road like the burros (p10-003) or the cattle on Emory Pass (p29-002). Worth logging so the wildlife layer stays continuous, and as a marker that this is open-range grassland rather than desert scrub. Pronghorn do cross roads and are fast; note but do not over-warn.
records.quote: four pronghorn antelope, the first wildlife of the trip larger than a ground squirrel

photos.caption: A fuzzy picture of Pronghorn Antelope.
photos.shows: Two pronghorn antelope standing in open dry grassland beyond a railway line and fence; mountains behind

records.summary: Border Patrol aerostat blimp flying over US-90
records.detail: 'Also seeing a blimp in the air over the highway. It seems Border Patrol has a lot of tools in their toolchest.' A tethered surveillance aerostat, photographed. Seventh consecutive border-adjacent stretch in the journal and still no checkpoint encounter of any kind recorded.
records.cyclistIntel: No action beyond the standing advice: carry ID on every border-corridor stretch. Notable only as a marker of how comprehensively this corridor is monitored — seven stretches across four states with sustained presence and zero reported interactions with cyclists.
records.quote: It seems Border Patrol has a lot of tools in their toolchest.

photos.caption: Border Patrol blimp.

records.summary: Long gentle rise Van Horn to Marfa: 3,900 ft to 4,903 ft, only 1,243 ft of ascent over 73 mi
records.detail: GPS: 73.46 mi, 6:41:06, 11.0 mph, 1,243 ft ascent. Elevation trace rises almost imperceptibly from about 3,900 ft, steepening slightly after 2:05, to a marked 4,903 ft at 5:50 before easing into Marfa. No climb waypoints at all. The 11.0 mph average on such gentle terrain is entirely the headwind (p35-003).
records.cyclistIntel: Terrain is not the problem on this leg — wind, heat and the services gap are. Reversed, Nick descends gently from Marfa to Van Horn, which is the good direction for the elevation but means he crosses the no-services stretch from the Marfa side, so El Cosmico is his last real stop before it rather than his reward after.

photos.shows: Elevation trace rising gently from ~3,900 ft to a marked 4,903 ft at 5:50:05, no climb waypoints; speed averaging 11.0 mph; temperature averaging 80.7 F with 95.0 F marked

records.summary: Day average 80.7 F with 95 F peak, at nearly 5,000 ft — cooler than the border but still hot
records.detail: GPS records an 80.7 F day average with 95.0 F marked and the trace above 90 F through the afternoon. Map header 52.0 F at the start, so a 40-plus degree swing. Marfa sits near 4,900 ft, which is what keeps the average down.
records.cyclistIntel: Elevation again doing the work — 80.7 F here against 94.6 F on the border two days earlier. But the peak still hit 95 F, and it hit during the no-services stretch with dust devils. The relevant number for water planning is the peak, not the average.

records.summary: PRADA MARFA art installation, roadside on US-90 near Valentine
records.detail: 'Linda was able to spot several pieces of art along the highway, including the world famous Prada Marfa.' Photo captions: 'An art piece. Prada Marfa.', 'Inside Prada Marfa.', 'They wouldn't let me in, my bank account wasn't big enough.' A permanent, internationally known roadside sculpture directly beside the highway.
records.cyclistIntel: Excellent anchor — permanent, precisely located, individually mapped and impossible to miss from the road. On a 73-mile stretch with almost no fixed references, this and the Giant installation are the two best positional fixes. No services; it is a sculpture in the desert with no shade or water.

photos.caption: An art piece. Prada Marfa.

records.summary: 'Giant' cast art installation with an oversized James Dean, roadside near Marfa
records.detail: Photo captions: 'An art installation, the cast of Giant' and 'A really big James Dean. Giant was his last movie.' The 1956 film was shot at Marfa. A fixed roadside installation.
records.cyclistIntel: Second permanent roadside art anchor on this leg. Useful as a positional fix approaching Marfa, and as a marker that the rider is close to the town and the end of the no-services stretch.

photos.caption: An art installation, the cast of "Giant"

records.summary: Night 33: EL COSMICO, Marfa TX — dry camping in the lot, tent-native site, outdoor cold shower
records.detail: Dry camping in the El Cosmico parking lot — no hookups, which is why the rider calls it dry camping. The site itself is built around funky old trailers, yurts, teepees and canvas-sided huts with hammocks and a communal outdoor gathering space, so tents are unambiguously part of what it does. Shower is outdoor and cold. Marfa sits near 4,900 ft.
records.cyclistIntel: BEST COMMERCIAL SITE FOR A TENT IN THE ENTIRE DATASET, and the first where tent acceptance is not in question. Shade and communal space, which the southwest RV parks lack. Positioned at the EAST end of the west Texas no-services stretch — so for Nick travelling west it is the last proper stop BEFORE two consecutive no-services days, making it the place to fill every bottle and check every tyre. Marfa is a destination town; book ahead and avoid weekends.
records.quote: In Marfa we are dry camping in the parking lot of El Cosmico.

records.summary: TIME-OF-DAY TRAFFIC MODEL for west Texas desert roads: cars/work trucks 7:30-9am, semis 8:30-10am, road empty after 10am
records.detail: 'On these desert roads I have noticed there are a lot of cars and work trucks from 7:30am to 9am, then the semi's are heavy from 8:30 to 10am. I ride the shoulder no matter how rough it is. Then after 10am the road is mine with just occasional traffic so I can ride in the road where it is much smoother.' Stated as a generalised pattern from many days of observation, with an explicit behavioural response: rough shoulder during the busy window, smooth traffic lane afterwards.
records.cyclistIntel: MOST OPERATIONALLY USEFUL FINDING IN THE DATASET, and it creates a REAL CONFLICT Nick has to resolve. Every heat record here says start before dawn. This says the 7:30-10am window is when the traffic is, and that the shoulder — which on this stretch alternates between smooth asphalt and rough chipseal (p36-002) — is where you have to be during it. So a pre-dawn start buys cool air but spends it riding the rough shoulder in traffic, while a later start gets the smooth empty lane and the heat. The resolution is probably: ride the cool early window on the shoulder regardless, and use the after-10am empty road for the miles that remain. But the planner should model BOTH constraints, not just heat.
records.quote: Then after 10am the road is mine with just occasional traffic so I can ride in the road where it is much smoother.

records.summary: SURFACE QUALITY CHANGES AT THE COUNTY LINE — smooth asphalt shoulder becomes rough chipseal, abruptly
records.detail: 'The wind was calm, sun shining and a very smooth asphalt shoulder to ride on for the morning rush hour. I was riding faster than my typical average. Life was good. I crossed the county line and, boom, rough chipseal to ride on.' A hard, structural transition at a jurisdictional boundary rather than a gradual degradation. Presterio/Jeff Davis into Brewster County on US-90 east of Marfa.
records.cyclistIntel: GENUINELY VALUABLE STRUCTURAL INSIGHT: in Texas, shoulder surface is a county-maintenance artifact, so it changes at county lines and stays consistent within them. That makes it PREDICTABLE and anchorable — county boundaries are precise, mapped and permanent. Worth building the planner's Texas surface expectations around county lines rather than trying to anchor every rough patch individually. Also explains the earlier Wenden chipseal (p17-001) and the I-10 access road (p34-002) as the same phenomenon.
records.quote: I crossed the county line and, boom, rough chipseal to ride on.

records.summary: PAISANO PASS, 5,101 ft — high point between Marfa and Alpine on US-90
records.detail: Named by the rider: 'On the downhill side of Paisano Pass I scared up four deer.' The GPS elevation trace marks 5,101 ft at 1:25:08, which is the day's high point, with three climb waypoints clustered around it. Highest point on the Texas portion of the route recorded so far.
records.cyclistIntel: Named, mapped pass with an elevation confirmed by the GPS trace — good anchor on a stretch otherwise short of fixed references. It sits roughly a quarter of the way from Marfa to Marathon, which brackets the Alpine resupply nicely. Reversed, Nick climbs to it from the Alpine side and descends toward Marfa.

photos.shows: Elevation trace marking 5,101 ft at 1:25:08 as the day's high point, with three climb waypoints around it

records.summary: ALPINE TX — the midway oasis: Magoo's Restaurant, a lumberyard, real town services
records.detail: 'I started to feel sluggish and slow until I hit the midway point, Alpine TX.' Linda got a local tip on a breakfast joint that 'did not steer us wrong' — Magoo's Restaurant, photographed. She then used the local lumberyard, where staff and a customer found scrap wood and screwed metal plates to it to fix the RV's leveller. So: restaurants, a lumberyard, and notably helpful people. Alpine sits at the US-90 / TX-118 junction.
records.cyclistIntel: The 'one nice oasis' of the page title, and the only real town between Marfa and Marathon. Roughly the midpoint of a 58-mile day, immediately after Paisano Pass. Restaurant confirmed by name. The lumberyard matters as a repair resource — it is the kind of place that produces a fix for a broken rack or fender when a bike shop does not exist. Seventh consecutive instance of local knowledge producing an outcome. Treat Alpine as the mandatory mid-day stop on this leg.
records.quote: I am getting ready to leave after a good meal and good conversation at Magoo's Restaurant in Alpine.

photos.caption: I am getting ready to leave after a good meal and good conversation at Magoo's Restaurant in Alpine.

records.summary: Deer near the road on both sides of Paisano Pass — two separate groups of four, jumping fences
records.detail: 'Just outside Alpine she spotted four deer near the road. They turned and gracefully jumped a fence and disappeared. On the downhill side of Paisano Pass I scared up four deer that ran and jumped a fence. Weird.' Two independent sightings the same day, both of four animals close enough to the roadway to be startled by a passing cyclist.
records.cyclistIntel: Deer are the most dangerous roadside animal on this route so far — faster and more erratic than the burros or cattle, and they bolt rather than stand. Both sightings were within a few miles of Paisano Pass, on the grassland side of the desert transition. Nick descends the Alpine side of the pass; a deer bolting across at descent speed is a genuine collision risk. Dawn and dusk are their active periods, which collides with the early-start rule.
records.quote: On the downhill side of Paisano Pass I scared up four deer that ran and jumped a fence.

records.summary: AFTERNOON WINDS PICK UP as a daily pattern — 30 mph constant with 50 mph gusts by evening
records.detail: 'A few miles outside Alpine the road turned to the southeast just in time for the afternoon winds to pick up from the northwest. Tailwind! Big tailwind! I flew the remaining 20 miles.' That evening at Big Bend: 'The wind was blowing at a constant 30 mph with gusts I estimate to be 50. Not a good evening to sit outside.' The morning had been calm. So the durable pattern is a daily thermal cycle: calm early, building through the afternoon, strong by evening.
records.cyclistIntel: THE DURABLE WIND FINDING FOR WEST TEXAS is the DAILY CYCLE, not the direction. Mornings calm, afternoons strong, evenings 30 mph with 50 mph gusts. Direction has been unreliable across three consecutive days — SE headwind (p35-003), NW tailwind here, westerly two days before (p34-004). So plan to do the hard miles in the calm morning and treat any afternoon wind as a coin flip that could cost or gain 3-4 mph. It also means tent pitching in the evening happens in 30 mph wind — stake everything.
records.quote: The wind was blowing at a constant 30 mph with gusts I estimate to be 50.

records.summary: ROUGHLY 20 JAVELINAS rooting in the TENT CAMPING AREA at Big Bend, plus wild burros by the camper
records.detail: 'I did go for a short hike at dusk. On the way back there were javelinas in the campground I walked through and wild burros grazing near our camper. I gave them both a wide berth.' Photo caption: 'A dark and blurry picture of javelinas. There were maybe 20 of them rooting around in the tent camping area. No, I did not try to get closer for a better picture.' The photograph shows javelinas among picnic tables and trees on grass at dusk.
records.cyclistIntel: Note precisely where they were: the TENT camping area, at dusk, about twenty of them. Javelinas have poor eyesight, travel in groups, will raid food and can be aggressive if surprised or cornered — a real consideration for someone sleeping at ground level rather than in an RV. Hard food storage and nothing scented in or near the tent. Combined with the wild burros, this is the second site in the dataset where large animals come into camp after water and food (see p8-N1 Glamis). NOTE: this is Big Bend NP, which is OFF ROUTE — but javelinas range across all of far west Texas, so treat the behaviour as regional rather than site-specific.
records.quote: There were maybe 20 of them rooting around in the tent camping area.

photos.caption: A dark and blurry picture of javelinas. There were maybe 20 of them rooting around in the tent camping area.
photos.shows: Several javelinas rooting on grass among picnic tables and mature trees at dusk in a developed campground

records.summary: Big Bend NP campsites walked into unreserved in early May — OFF ROUTE, reached by vehicle from Marathon
records.detail: 'Linda and I were able to drive south to Big Bend National Park and just waltz into an RV campsite. Generally in a national park all campsites are reserved months in advance.' They also visited the park visitor centre with exhibits and a film. IMPORTANT: they DROVE there from Marathon — this is not on the cycling route and the rider did not ride it.
records.cyclistIntel: OFF-ROUTE, recorded for completeness and one transferable point: national park campsites in this region were walk-in available on a Friday in early May, against the usual expectation of months-ahead reservations. That is a shoulder-season availability datapoint consistent with p26-002 (midweek and offseason have room). Big Bend itself is roughly 70 miles south of the route from Marathon — a substantial detour a self-supported cyclist would need two extra days for.
records.quote: just waltz into an RV campsite. Generally in a national park all campsites are reserved months in advance.

records.summary: Marfa to Marathon: over Paisano Pass at 5,101 ft then a long descent — 1,188 ft ascent over 58 mi
records.detail: GPS: 57.93 mi, 4:42:32, 12.3 mph, 1,188 ft ascent. Elevation trace rises from Marfa to a marked 5,101 ft at 1:25 (Paisano Pass), then declines steadily through Alpine to roughly 4,000 ft at Marathon, with a slight rise at the very end. Three climb waypoints, all before the pass. The speed trace shows its fastest section in the final 45 minutes — the big tailwind (p36-005).
records.cyclistIntel: Reversed, Nick climbs gently from Marathon to Alpine, then over Paisano Pass, then descends to Marfa. Modest terrain; the variables here are the county-line surface change, the traffic window and the afternoon wind, not the gradient. Alpine at the midpoint splits it neatly into two ~29-mile halves.

photos.shows: Elevation trace rising to a marked 5,101 ft at 1:25:08 then declining to ~4,000 ft; three climb waypoints all before the pass; speed averaging 12.3 mph with the fastest section in the final 45 min; temperature averaging 72.5 F

records.summary: Crisp 51 F start, day average 72.5 F, and the first real clouds in weeks
records.detail: 'It was a crisp start to the day at 51 degrees. The wind was calm, sun shining.' GPS day average 72.5 F, map header 57.0 F — the coolest riding day since Emory Pass. Photo captions note 'Real clouds! Linda and I are so used to nothing but big blue skys it was nice to see some thunderheads' and 'The clouds stuck right to the mountains, none came to the desert.' Evening at Big Bend was cloudy and very windy.
records.cyclistIntel: A genuinely pleasant day, and worth recording as such so the planner is not uniformly grim about Texas. The elevation here (4,000-5,100 ft) is what makes it liveable. Note the thunderhead observation: clouds building over the mountains but not reaching the desert — relevant because mountain thunderstorms in this region can produce wind and flash flooding on roads well away from the cloud itself.
records.quote: It was a crisp start to the day at 51 degrees.

photos.caption: Real clouds! Linda and I are so used to nothing but big blue skys it was nice to see some thunderheads.
photos.shows: Large cumulus and thunderhead build-up over a long layered escarpment; hazy desert foreground

records.summary: Marfa Lights viewing area — signed roadside stop on US-90 east of Marfa
records.detail: Photo caption: 'A roadside stop where you are supposed to be able to see The Marfa Lights. An unexplained phenomena where eerie lights appear in the desert. It gets a lot of people gathered here at night for the chance to see them.' A permanent, signed, developed pull-off directly on the route.
records.cyclistIntel: Anchor plus a possible facility: a developed roadside viewing area on a highway with very little else usually has restrooms and shade structure. Worth confirming, because it sits on the leg immediately after the west Texas no-services stretch. It also gets crowds at night, which means it is not a discreet place to camp.

records.summary: Night 34: Big Bend National Park campground — OFF ROUTE, reached by vehicle from Marathon
records.detail: They drove roughly 70 miles south from Marathon to Big Bend and got an unreserved site. The photographed campground has mature trees, grass and picnic tables, so shade and tent camping are clearly available. Evening wind was a constant 30 mph with gusts near 50. About twenty javelinas were in the tent camping area at dusk and wild burros were grazing by the camper.
records.cyclistIntel: NOT A ROUTE OVERNIGHT — Nick would need two extra days to ride there and back, and the plan has zero spare. Recorded to keep the chain unbroken and for the availability datapoint. If he ever did detour, the site has real shade and water but comes with javelinas in the tent area and severe evening wind.
records.quote: just waltz into an RV campsite

records.summary: 15-20 mph HEADWIND all day: 9.9 mph average on a 'generally all downhill' 54-mile day, then 24 mph steady overnight
records.detail: 'I started early this Sunday morning to try to beat the wind. It was just a little headwind in the early morning but that changed as the day went on. The headwinds were 15-20 mph so it was a slow slog to Sanderson even though it was generally all downhill. 54 miles is tough in these winds.' GPS confirms 9.9 mph over 5:29:16 with only 656 ft of ascent and a net 1,700 ft LOSS. That evening: 'the wind is blowing at a steady 24 mph with gusts that rock the Winnebago. It may be tough sleeping tonight for us, but at least we aren't trying to sleep in a tent in this weather.'
records.cyclistIntel: THE CLEAREST DEMONSTRATION IN THE DATASET OF WHAT WIND COSTS. A net-downhill 54-mile day took five and a half hours at 9.9 mph. That is the number to plan west Texas days against — not the terrain. Note also that starting early did NOT beat it; the wind was already there and built. And the rider says the quiet part out loud: an RV rocking in 24 mph steady with gusts is a tent night nobody wants. For Nick that is the real exposure — Sanderson is where he needs a wind-sheltered pitch, not an open lot.
records.quote: at least we aren't trying to sleep in a tent in this weather

photos.shows: GPS summary 54.29 mi, 5:29:16, 9.9 mph, 656 ft ascent, 57.0 F; elevation trace from ~4,200 ft through a marked 4,310 ft at 2:13 then declining steadily to ~2,600 ft; speed trace uniformly slow with a marked 8.2 mph mid-ride

records.summary: WILDLIFE BOUNDARY: mule deer, two javelinas and six pronghorn in ONE day — 'more than California, Arizona and New Mexico combined'
records.detail: 'Early on, just after leaving the Marathon Motel & RV Park, I scared up a mule deer that bounced across the road. Then in a few miles two Javelinas were hanging around the road. A little further down the road I spotted six Pronghorn Antelope in the desert. That is more wildlife sightings than California, Arizona and New Mexico combined!' Photographs show a javelina grazing on the roadside and pronghorn in open grassland. The mule deer crossed the road; the javelinas were at the roadside.
records.cyclistIntel: A clean regional boundary the rider identifies himself: large animals on and beside the road become common from Marathon east. Three species in 54 miles, two of them ON or AT the roadway. Mule deer bolt across without warning and javelinas are unpredictable at close range. This compounds with p36-004 (deer both sides of Paisano Pass) and p36-007 (javelinas in a tent area). From here east, treat roadside wildlife as a standing hazard rather than a novelty, and expect it worst at dawn and dusk — which is exactly when the heat rules push him to be riding.
records.quote: That is more wildlife sightings than California, Arizona and New Mexico combined!

photos.caption: One of a pair of Javelinas grazing on the roadside.
photos.shows: Single javelina walking on open rocky ground immediately beside the roadway

photos.caption: Two of the six Pronghorn Antelope I spotted.
photos.shows: Pronghorn in open dry grassland

records.summary: NO CELL RECEPTION between Marathon and Sanderson — the support crew's tracking app stopped working
records.detail: 'Linda stopped a couple times to check on my 9 mph progress. There was no cell reception out there so she couldn't use the tracking app.' A supported party with a vehicle could not maintain contact across this 54-mile stretch.
records.cyclistIntel: SERIOUS FOR A SOLO SELF-SUPPORTED RIDER, and it stacks badly with everything else on this leg: no services, 15-20 mph headwinds, large animals on the road, and now no way to call for help. If something breaks or he goes down between Marathon and Sanderson, there is no phone. Worth carrying a satellite messenger for the west Texas stretch specifically, and worth telling someone the day plan before starting. Also means no live weather check mid-ride in a region where the wind builds unpredictably.
records.quote: There was no cell reception out there so she couldn't use the tracking app.

records.summary: Roadside picnic area with a SHADE SHELTER, concrete table and seats between Marathon and Sanderson
records.detail: 'Lunch at a roadside picnic area. Shade! A seat and table! I did have to hold on to my plate or my lunch would have blown away.' The photograph shows a proper TxDOT-style covered shelter — metal roof on steel posts over a concrete slab with a fixed concrete table and bench seats, plus a litter bin, in open desert with ocotillo around it. His exclamation marks say how rare this is. No water source is mentioned.
records.cyclistIntel: Real shade with a table on a no-services stretch — genuinely valuable given the shade findings across this whole route. BUT the planner already knows TxDOT picnic areas have NO WATER, and this page does not contradict that: he ate food Linda brought. So treat it as a heat-break and lunch point only, never a water point. Pair with the no-cell finding — a picnic area is also the most likely place to be found if something goes wrong. Anchor it if it can be located.
records.quote: Lunch at a roadside picnic area. Shade! A seat and table!

photos.caption: Lunch at a roadside picnic area. Shade! A seat and table!
photos.shows: TxDOT-style covered picnic shelter: metal roof on steel posts over a concrete slab with fixed concrete table and bench seats; litter bin; ocotillo and open desert; highway behind

records.summary: SANDERSON TX — Z Bar Trading Company (hardware plus metal art), Visitors Center, fuel
records.detail: 'When we got close to Sanderson she went ahead, got diesel fuel, checked out the Visitors Center, and went up the street to Z Bar Trading Company. It is a store with a lot of metal art in front. It turned out to also be a hardware store so Linda told her tale of woe about our missing leveler foot. Travis had exactly the right thing to help us.' So Sanderson has fuel, a visitor centre and a hardware store with helpful staff.
records.cyclistIntel: Second hardware store in the dataset after the Alpine lumberyard, and both produced a fix. On a stretch with no bike shops for hundreds of miles, a hardware store is the repair resource — bolts, zip ties, hose clamps, tape. Sanderson sits at the east end of the Marathon leg and is the only town in 54 miles. Treat it as a resupply and repair anchor. Eighth consecutive instance of local people producing an outcome no map contains.
records.quote: It turned out to also be a hardware store... Travis had exactly the right thing to help us.

records.summary: Marathon to Sanderson loses ~1,700 ft — but reversed, Nick climbs it, and into the prevailing afternoon wind
records.detail: Elevation trace runs from about 4,200 ft through a marked 4,310 ft high point at 2:13 then declines steadily to roughly 2,600 ft at Sanderson. Only 656 ft of total ascent across 54.29 mi. Two climb waypoints, both in the first half. The rider calls it 'generally all downhill' and still averaged 9.9 mph because of the headwind.
records.cyclistIntel: Reversed, Nick CLIMBS about 1,700 ft net from Sanderson up to Marathon across 54 miles. Gentle gradient, but the wind on this leg is the dominant force and this journal shows it can strip 3-4 mph regardless of direction. Plan Sanderson to Marathon as a full day, not a transit — no services, no cell, wildlife on the road, and a net climb.
records.quote: it was generally all downhill

records.summary: Met a woman riding WEST (Nick's direction) and Sam attempting the Southern Tier in 30 DAYS with RV support
records.detail: 'I met a young woman biking west. We talked a bit about what each of us could expect ahead and then we were on our way. Linda and I also met Sam from Chicago who was attempting to do the Southern Tier Ride in 30 days. He also had his wife driving an RV and his two young daughters.' Two more riders, one of them in Nick's direction.
records.cyclistIntel: Two useful reference points. First, riders going Nick's direction are still on this corridor in early May, and the standard practice among them is to swap what is ahead — worth doing. Second, Sam's 30-day attempt is the aggressive end of the range: roughly 100 miles a day, with vehicle support. Set against the ACA group's ~53 days (p17-005) and this rider's pace, Nick's 53-day plan sits comfortably in the normal band rather than the fast one.
records.quote: Sam from Chicago who was attempting to do the Southern Tier Ride in 30 days

records.summary: OFF ROUTE (Big Bend NP): burros confirmed in the tent camping area a second time, and a coyote in camp range
records.detail: Rest-day page at Big Bend. Photo captions: 'Burros in the tent camping area' and 'A burro eating a prickly pear cactus. That is one tough burro.' Plus a clear photograph of a coyote in scrub. This is the second consecutive night at this campground with large animals in the TENT area, after roughly twenty javelinas the evening before (p36-007).
records.cyclistIntel: OFF ROUTE — Big Bend is ~70 mi south of the route. Recorded because the animal behaviour is regional, not site-specific: in far west Texas, burros, javelinas and coyotes all come into developed campgrounds and specifically into tent areas, on consecutive nights. A burro that eats prickly pear will certainly chew through a pannier for food. Hard food storage everywhere in this region.
records.quote: Burros in the tent camping area.

photos.caption: Coyote pic.
photos.shows: Coyote standing alert in rocky desert scrub, close to camera

records.summary: SECOND CONFIRMATION the Rio Grande runs dry — walked across it on foot at Santa Elena Canyon
records.detail: OFF ROUTE, Big Bend NP. Photo caption: 'This is Linda, returning from her trip to Mexico. She went to the other side of the dry Rio Grande for different picture angles for the Santa Elena Canyon.' So the river bed was dry enough to walk across into Mexico and back. Independently corroborates the bare-sand riverbed photographed at Las Cruces (p32-001), 300 miles upstream.
records.cyclistIntel: Reinforces the single most important negative water finding: the Rio Grande cannot be treated as water on this route. Two separate points, 300 miles apart, both dry enough to walk across. Note this contrasts with the 'green ribbon' seen from the Texas border corridor (p33-005) — flow on this river is release-dependent and varies by reach and season, so it is unpredictable in both directions and should never appear as a source in the planner.
records.quote: the other side of the dry Rio Grande
records.from: Santa Elena Canyon, Big Bend NP

records.summary: Night 36: Sanderson TX — site not named, and a 24 mph wind with gusts all night
records.detail: Day ends in Sanderson; no site named. Wind that night was a steady 24 mph with gusts strong enough to rock the RV, and the rider explicitly notes he would not want to be in a tent in it.
records.cyclistIntel: No specific lead, but the requirement is clear: Sanderson needs a WIND-SHELTERED pitch, not an open site. Given the town has a visitor centre and a helpful hardware store (p38-004), it is the kind of small Texas town where asking might produce a sheltered spot — the Thatcher City Park precedent (p23-007). Identify what exists there; it is the only town in 54 miles in either direction.
records.quote: the wind is blowing at a steady 24 mph with gusts that rock the Winnebago

records.summary: Night 35: MARATHON MOTEL & RV PARK, Marathon TX
records.detail: Named on the Day 36 page: 'just after leaving the Marathon Motel & RV Park'. The party spent the Day 35 rest day at Big Bend and returned to Marathon for the night before riding on. Has both motel rooms and RV sites.
records.cyclistIntel: Callable, and useful because it has MOTEL ROOMS as well as sites — a bail-out option in a region where the evening wind hits 24-30 mph with gusts and a tent is genuinely unpleasant (p38-001). Marathon is the western bracket of the Sanderson no-services leg. Add to the call-ahead list: tents, shade, and room rates.
records.quote: just after leaving the Marathon Motel & RV Park

records.summary: WORST-CASE BENCHMARK: 8.7 mph over 60 mi — slowest day in 50 years of riding, NINE HOURS elapsed, pedalling downhill
records.detail: 'Today I averaged 8.7 miles per hour over the 60 miles. I think that is the slowest I have ever ridden in 50 years. On the flip side, I can claim I have never ridden 60 miles into such a stiff headwind. It was a constant slow push. Even downhill I had to pedal. It took me 9 hours to get to Langtry.' He started at 6:40am specifically to beat it — 'It was only 12mph then but it got up to the 20's by the afternoon.' GPS: 6:58:05 MOVING time against 9 hours elapsed, so roughly two hours of stops, and a photo caption confirms why: 'I was making a lot of stops like this one to catch my breath.' Note the terrain was net downhill with 1,736 ft of rolling ascent.
records.cyclistIntel: THIS IS THE WORST-CASE NUMBER FOR THE WHOLE ROUTE and the planner should hold it as the floor: 8.7 mph, and 9 hours elapsed for 60 miles. Two things transfer. First, a stiff headwind makes DOWNHILL require pedalling — the gradient stops helping entirely. Second, and easy to miss: headwind days need roughly 30% MORE elapsed time than moving time because of recovery stops. If Nick's planner budgets days on moving average, west Texas headwind days will overrun by hours. Starting at 6:40am did not beat it; the wind was already 12 mph and built all day.
records.quote: I think that is the slowest I have ever ridden in 50 years... Even downhill I had to pedal.

photos.shows: GPS summary 60.29 mi, 6:58:05, 8.7 mph, 1,736 ft ascent; elevation trace declining from ~2,800 ft to ~1,300 ft with nine climb waypoints across the day and a marked 1,759 ft at 5:50; speed trace uniformly slow, marked 8.6 mph

photos.caption: Thick clouds kept the temperature down but didn't slow the headwind. I was making a lot of stops like this one to catch my breath.
photos.shows: Covered picnic shelter with concrete table beside an accessible-parking area, bike leaning against it; overcast sky, mesquite scrub

records.summary: JUDGE ROY BEAN TRAVEL CENTER, Langtry TX — first-class visitor centre with gardens, in a town with nothing else
records.detail: 'Langtry was a railroad town in the old days so now it doesn't have much left. Except for the Judge Roy Bean Travel Center. It was really nice. They had the original saloon and Bean's home. They also had a really first class visitor center and gardens. So out of place in such a run down town.' Photographs show the actual Jersey Lilly Saloon and Bean's home, 'The Opera House'. This is a Texas state travel information centre.
records.cyclistIntel: MAJOR SERVICES FIND. Texas state travel centres reliably have restrooms, drinking water, shade and staff — and this one has irrigated gardens, which in far west Texas means real shade and real water. It sits in a town the rider says has nothing else, at the end of a 60-mile two-town day. For Nick this is the water and heat-shelter anchor for the Langtry stretch. Confirm opening hours and days; state centres typically keep daytime hours and may close on some holidays, which would leave Langtry with nothing.
records.quote: They also had a really first class visitor center and gardens. So out of place in such a run down town.

photos.caption: This is the actual Jersey Lilly Saloon that Judge Roy Bean held court in.
Judge Roy Bean's home, "The Opera House".

records.summary: Only TWO towns in 60 miles between Sanderson and Langtry — and Langtry 'doesn't have much left'
records.detail: 'It took me 9 hours to get to Langtry which was only the second town for the entire day.' The map shows Dryden as the only settlement between them. Langtry itself is described as a run-down former railroad town whose one asset is the state travel centre (p39-002).
records.cyclistIntel: Third consecutive no-services day in west Texas after Van Horn-Marfa and Marathon-Sanderson. Two towns in 60 miles, one of them essentially just a visitor centre. With the 8.7 mph headwind benchmark, that is a nine-hour day carrying everything. Sanderson has the hardware store and fuel; Langtry has water and shade at the travel centre. Dryden needs independent verification — nothing in this journal establishes it has anything.
records.quote: Langtry which was only the second town for the entire day

records.summary: HUMIDITY ARRIVES — 'very unusual day for the desert. It was humid and misty', 65 F at 6am
records.detail: 'It was a very unusual day for the desert. It was humid and misty. Temperature 65 degrees at 6am.' A photo caption: 'The streetlights show the humidity in the air.' Thick cloud all day held the temperature to a 73.2 F average with 87.8 F marked. The rider says twice that it reminded him of Iowa in July on RAGBRAI — both the humidity and the rolling terrain.
records.cyclistIntel: POSSIBLE CLIMATE TRANSITION MARKER. Every previous day in this dataset has been arid. This is the first humid one, at roughly 1,300 ft elevation approaching the Pecos, and the rider — who has crossed the whole desert — calls it unusual. If this is the western edge of Gulf moisture influence, it matters for Nick in the OPPOSITE way: riding east to west, this is roughly where he LEAVES the humidity and ENTERS the true desert, which is a gear and hydration inflection point. Watch the next few pages to see whether the humidity persists or was a one-day anomaly.
records.quote: It was a very unusual day for the desert. It was humid and misty.

photos.caption: The streetlights show the humidity in the air.
photos.shows: Pre-dawn street scene with visible haloes around streetlights indicating airborne moisture; rider with loaded bike and rear light beside a 40 mph sign and a large sculpted dinosaur figure

records.summary: Deer in two separate places on the pre-dawn start — third consecutive Texas day with deer
records.detail: 'Leaving early, I saw deer in two places.' Third consecutive day in Texas with deer sightings, after Paisano Pass (p36-004) and the mule deer out of Marathon (p38-002). All of them at or near dawn on early starts.
records.cyclistIntel: The pattern is now firm and it is a scheduling problem: deer are active at dawn, and the heat rules force a dawn start. Nick cannot avoid the overlap, so the mitigation is speed and light — a bright front light even in daylight, and moderate speed on descents through the first hour. Deer bolt across rather than standing like the cattle or burros further west.
records.quote: Leaving early, I saw deer in two places.

records.summary: Rolling hills all day — 1,736 ft of ascent while losing 1,500 ft net, nine separate climbs
records.detail: 'The terrain was rolling hills. I thought I was in Iowa in July on RAGBRAI again.' Elevation trace declines from about 2,800 ft to roughly 1,300 ft but with nine marked climb waypoints spread evenly across the day and 1,736 ft of total ascent — so it is genuinely lumpy rather than a descent. A marked 1,759 ft appears at 5:50.
records.cyclistIntel: Reversed, Nick climbs about 1,500 ft net from Langtry to Sanderson PLUS the same rolling profile — call it 3,200 ft of climbing over 60 miles, with no services and possibly a headwind. That is a materially harder day in his direction than in theirs, and theirs took nine hours. Strong candidate for splitting if anything exists at Dryden.
records.quote: The terrain was rolling hills.

records.summary: US-90 here has a wide paved shoulder with a rumble strip set on the fog line
records.detail: Established from a photograph of another rider ahead on the road: a wide paved shoulder outside a white fog line, with a continuous line of rumble-strip indentations running along the fog line itself, and a broad clean paved surface beyond. Surface looks sound. Two-lane road with yellow centreline.
records.cyclistIntel: Good news on width — real room outside the lane. The rumble strip sits ON the fog line rather than inside the shoulder, which is the acceptable configuration: it does not eat the rideable surface, but it does mean drifting left is jarring, and crossing it to take the lane requires deliberate effort. Better than the Boulevard and Alpine sections in California and Arizona.

photos.caption: Riding with my head down to deal with the wind. And a Turkey Vulture circling above.
photos.shows: Rider ahead on a two-lane road; wide sound paved shoulder outside the white fog line with a continuous rumble strip running along the fog line; turkey vulture circling overhead; hazy overcast

records.summary: Night 37: dry camping at the VASHTI SKILES COMMUNITY CENTER lot, Langtry TX — no internet
records.detail: 'We are boondocking in the same place at Langtry' — the same spot as Sam, another Southern Tier rider travelling with his family in an RV. The site is not named. Water, toilets and shade marked likely because the Judge Roy Bean Travel Center with its gardens is in this same small town (p39-002), not because the page establishes them at the camp itself. SITE NAMED from the Day 38 page photo: 'Our dry camp spot in Langtry. No internet.' The photograph shows the RV parked on a gravel lot in front of a white metal-roofed building signed 'VASHTI SKILES COMMUNITY CENTER', with a historical marker out front and mesquite trees around.
records.cyclistIntel: Two independent touring parties boondocked here the same night, which is decent evidence that informal camping at Langtry is tolerated and findable. Combined with the state travel centre for water, shade and toilets, Langtry works as an overnight despite the town having little else. Pin down the actual spot — with two parties using it, it is probably an obvious piece of ground near the travel centre or the old town.
records.quote: We are boondocking in the same place at Langtry.

records.summary: TEXAS HIGHWAY PATROL STOPPED HIM and told him to ride the EIGHT-INCH shoulder on a 75 mph highway
records.detail: 'A Texas Highway Patrol Officer pulled me over. It certainly wasn't for speeding, the speed limit on this highway is 75. He told me I shouldn't ride in the lane of the highway, that I need to ride on the shoulder. A lot of thoughts went through my head about the 8 inches he was telling me to ride on, that there were two lanes and cars can easily pass, and I was wearing brightly colored clothing and had red blinking lights so cars will see me from a distance. I said Thank you for your advice and rode on the narrow rough shoulder until his car disappeared over the hill.' Note: advice, not a citation — but delivered as an instruction by a state trooper.
records.cyclistIntel: THE ONLY LAW-ENFORCEMENT INTERACTION IN 1,370 MILES, and it matters because it is a live risk for Nick. Texas law does require riding as near as practicable to the right edge, with exceptions including when the lane is too narrow to share safely — the trooper's reading did not include the exception. Practical guidance: on Texas highways with a token shoulder, expect this can happen, be maximally visible (he credits bright clothing and blinking lights), be courteous, and know the actual statute. Also note what it reveals about the road: an 8-inch shoulder on a 75 mph two-lane, which is a shoulder finding in its own right. Worth researching Texas Transportation Code 551.103 before departure.
records.quote: the 8 inches he was telling me to ride on

records.summary: THE WIND DELTA, MEASURED: 95 miles at 14.7 mph with a tailwind, the day after 60 miles at 8.7 mph into one
records.detail: 'Yesterday was really tough so I set my sights on 60 miles to Del Rio. Today, however, the wind was to my back and I was just flying... I covered 95 miles in the same time as the 60 yesterday.' GPS: 95.31 mi, 6:28:37, 14.7 mph, 2,425 ft ascent — against 60.29 mi at 8.7 mph the previous day. Same rider, same bike, same region, consecutive days.
records.cyclistIntel: THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT PLANNING NUMBER IN THE DATASET. Wind alone moved this rider's daily range from 60 miles to 95 miles — a 69% swing in average speed, 8.7 to 14.7 mph. That is far larger than any terrain effect recorded anywhere on the route. For a plan with ZERO spare days across 53, this is the dominant risk: a run of headwind days in west Texas could cost several days, and a run of tailwinds cannot bank them back because Nick has no slack to absorb the bad ones. The planner should model west Texas day lengths as a range of 60-95 miles driven by wind, not as a fixed figure — and the schedule needs contingency it currently does not have.
records.quote: I covered 95 miles in the same time as the 60 yesterday.

photos.shows: GPS summary 95.31 mi, 6:28:37, 14.7 mph, 2,425 ft ascent with a trophy icon; elevation rolling 1,000-1,644 ft with about eleven climb waypoints all in the first half, then declining; temperature averaging 89.6 F

records.summary: ROADKILL EXPLOSION in Texas — deer, coyote, skunk, raccoon, opossum, birds, even a turkey vulture
records.detail: 'California, Arizona and New Mexico didn't seem to have much roadkill to look at. The last two days of Texas has had a big increase in bodies. Deer, coyote, skunk, raccoon, opossum, cactus wrens. Even one turkey vulture. Texas deer roadkill is different from Iowa deer roadkill. In Texas the entire insides are missing. Only a hollowed out ribcage. There must be efficient scavengers in this part of the world.'
records.cyclistIntel: Two practical consequences beyond the unpleasantness. Carcasses are obstacles on the shoulder — the exact strip Nick rides, and on a road where a trooper may insist he stay in eight inches of it (p40-002). And heavy roadkill means heavy scavenger activity ON the road: vultures feeding on pavement flush late and low, and a turkey vulture among the dead says even they get hit. Pair with the live-animal findings (p38-002, p39-005): from Marathon east, animals dead and alive are a continuous roadside factor.
records.quote: The last two days of Texas has had a big increase in bodies.

records.summary: PECOS RIVER canyon crossing on US-90 — high bridge over a deep canyon
records.detail: 'We crossed the Pecos River today. A very impressive canyon.' Two photographs show a deep limestone canyon with green-blue water below and steep walls. The Pecos High Bridge on US-90 is one of the highest highway bridges in Texas. The GPS elevation trace shows the sharp dip and rise around this point, and the speed trace has its fastest spike of the day there.
records.cyclistIntel: Superb anchor — a major named river crossing on a signature bridge, precisely mapped and unmistakable. Also a terrain note: canyon crossings mean a short steep drop and climb on either side, and the speed spike confirms it. Amistad National Recreation Area lies just downstream, which the map shows the route skirting.

photos.caption: The Pecos River canyon,
photos.shows: Deep limestone canyon with blue-green water below and steep layered walls

records.summary: Greening begins east of the Pecos — 'Things are getting greener, trees are getting taller'
records.detail: 'Things are getting greener, trees are getting taller. Maybe soon I will see something other than desolate desert.' The GPS map shows the terrain shading from bare tan west of the Pecos to green east of it. Follows the first humid day two days earlier (p39-004).
records.cyclistIntel: The desert-to-green transition is now confirmed over three consecutive days and it brackets the Pecos River. For Nick riding WESTWARD this is where the green ends and the true desert begins — the single most important environmental boundary on his route after the mountains. Everything west of the Pecos means no shade, no water, no services and thorns; everything east means trees, creeks and towns. Worth marking as a hard transition in the planner.
records.quote: Things are getting greener, trees are getting taller.

records.summary: Night 38: campground at Brackettville TX, shared with another Southern Tier family
records.detail: 'Since I went the extra miles we were able to camp in the same campground as Sam and Katie.' A real campground rather than a boondocking spot, but unnamed. Brackettville sits at the US-90 / TX-131 junction.
records.cyclistIntel: Two touring parties in the same campground, so it accommodates travellers. Unnamed, so needs identifying. Note the day-length logic: he reached Brackettville only because of a 95-mile tailwind day — on a headwind day this is out of reach from Langtry and Del Rio becomes the stop instead. Both need to be in the planner as alternatives.
records.quote: we were able to camp in the same campground as Sam and Katie

records.summary: CANYON BBQ & GRILL, Camp Wood TX on Highway 55 — the manager phoned the owner and let them camp in the parking lot
records.detail: 'Linda went ahead to Camp Wood TX and asked at the BBQ restaurant if there were any options in town for RV camping. There really weren't, but the manager of the restaurant called the owner and arranged to let us stay in their parking lot. Very good food, very friendly workers, and they went the extra mile to help us. If you are passing through Camp Wood be sure to stop by Canyon BBQ & Grill, right on Highway 55.' The rider names it and recommends it explicitly.
records.cyclistIntel: THIRD DISCRETIONARY-PERMISSION LODGING WIN, after Thatcher City Park (p23-007) and the Langtry community centre lot. The pattern is now unmistakable and it is the most valuable lodging insight in the dataset: in small Texas towns with no formal camping, ASK AT A LOCAL BUSINESS — a restaurant, a bar, a hardware store — and someone will make a call. A solo cyclist with a tent is a far easier ask than a Class C motorhome, so Nick's odds are better than theirs were. Named, on Highway 55, food confirmed good. Camp Wood is also the last town before the Three Sisters climbs.
records.quote: the manager of the restaurant called the owner and arranged to let us stay in their parking lot

records.summary: A HERD OF ROUGHLY TWENTY DEER in one sighting, plus turkey and rabbit — Hill Country wildlife density
records.detail: 'I saw a herd of 20 or so deer, a rabbit, a turkey, and plenty of turkey buzzards.' Twenty animals in a single group, in the greening Hill Country approach. Fourth consecutive Texas day with deer, and by far the largest group.
records.cyclistIntel: Escalating sharply: two deer at Paisano Pass, one mule deer at Marathon, deer in two places at Sanderson, now a herd of twenty. Texas Hill Country has one of the densest whitetail populations in the country and this confirms it from the saddle. A herd that size means animals on both sides of the road and unpredictable crossings. Dawn and dusk are worst, which is exactly when the heat forces riding. This is now the highest-frequency animal hazard on the route.
records.quote: I saw a herd of 20 or so deer

records.summary: Very rough chipseal Brackettville to Camp Wood, but very little traffic
records.detail: 'A little bit of climbing, calm winds, very rough chipseal roads, and very little traffic.' 49.94 mi at 11.1 mph with 1,355 ft of ascent on calm-wind day — so the modest average is the surface, not the wind. A cockpit photograph shows a dead-straight two-lane with a narrow to non-existent paved edge and a gravel verge.
records.cyclistIntel: Rough chipseal again, and worth noting the pattern that has now held across three states: on this route the quiet roads are the rough ones and the smooth roads carry the traffic. It also confirms the county-line surface hypothesis (p36-002) — this is a different county from the smooth US-90 shoulder the day before. Budget slower averages on the Hill Country approach even in calm conditions.
records.quote: very rough chipseal roads, and very little traffic

photos.caption: The road goes on forever.
photos.shows: Cockpit view of a dead-straight two-lane road with a narrow to absent paved edge and gravel verge; fenced scrub, deep blue sky

records.summary: FIRST FLOWING WATER OF THE TRIP — 'And some flowing water in a creek!'
records.detail: 'The big thing I noticed today is the change in the terrain. A little flatter and a lot greener. Green grass and large trees. What a change in just a couple days riding... And some flowing water in a creek!' The exclamation mark is the point — after 1,400 miles this is the first creek with water in it. The Nueces River runs through Camp Wood.
records.cyclistIntel: A genuine environmental milestone and the clearest possible marker of the transition out of the arid west. From here east, surface water exists. For Nick riding WESTWARD, Camp Wood is roughly where flowing water stops and he enters 700-plus miles where every drop is carried or bought. Combined with p40-004 (greening at the Pecos), the desert boundary for his direction sits between Camp Wood and the Pecos.
records.quote: And some flowing water in a creek!

records.summary: SHADE RETURNS — 'Green trees! Shade!' — large trees and green grass in the Hill Country approach
records.detail: 'A little flatter and a lot greener. Green grass and large trees. What a change in just a couple days riding.' A photo caption reads 'Green trees! Shade! An Emu!' and the photograph shows the rider stopped under a large spreading mesquite with dense green trees behind — genuine roadside shade.
records.cyclistIntel: The shade problem that has run through this entire dataset — no shade in southwest campgrounds, 40-minute tyre changes with a telephone pole for shelter, seeking gravel for shade and picking up goatheads — ends here. From the Hill Country east, roadside shade exists. That changes midday strategy completely, and for Nick westward it is where he must start planning shade deliberately instead of finding it.
records.quote: Green trees! Shade! An Emu!

photos.caption: Green trees! Shade! An Emu!
photos.shows: Rider and loaded touring bike stopped in the shade of a large spreading mesquite; dense green trees behind, green grass, an emu standing behind a wire fence

records.summary: Only ONE intersection in 50 miles between Brackettville and Camp Wood
records.detail: 'When I stopped for some shade and a snack at the only intersection on today's route I realized I wasn't alone. A very curious Emu was standing on the other side of a fence looking at me.' So a single intersection across the whole 50-mile leg, and no services mentioned at it. Camp Wood at the far end had no formal camping either (p41-004).
records.cyclistIntel: Still effectively a no-services stretch even though the landscape is greening — green does not mean populated. Brackettville and Camp Wood are the brackets. Note the improvement though: he got SHADE at his snack stop, which is the first time in the Texas run that a mid-route stop offered any. Carry food and water for the full 50.
records.quote: the only intersection on today's route

records.summary: Cell and internet 'near non-existent' across the whole west Texas run
records.detail: 'Internet and cell phone service has been near non-existant so I may not be able to post tomorrow.' Stated as a regional condition rather than a single dead spot, and consistent with the total absence of reception between Marathon and Sanderson (p38-003) and 'No internet' at the Langtry camp. Spans roughly Marathon to Camp Wood, some 300 miles.
records.cyclistIntel: Now a REGIONAL finding, not a local one: assume no communications across west Texas from Marathon to the Hill Country. For a solo self-supported rider that means no navigation reload, no weather check, no emergency call, and no way to tell anyone where he is — across the stretch that also has the worst wind, the fewest services and animals on the road. A satellite messenger is the obvious answer, and this is the section that justifies it.
records.quote: Internet and cell phone service has been near non-existant

records.summary: Humid 65 F morning to a 90.6 F day average — heat and humidity together now
records.detail: 'It was humid and 65 degrees when I left in the morning. It got very warm in the afternoon, I'm glad I stopped and didn't try to bite off another 20 miles.' GPS: 90.6 F day average with 95.0 F marked. Second consecutive humid day, so the humidity noted at Langtry was not a one-day anomaly.
records.cyclistIntel: IMPORTANT COMPOUND CHANGE: the desert was hot and dry; the Hill Country is hot and HUMID. Humid heat is physiologically harder — sweat evaporates less, so cooling fails at lower temperatures and fluid needs rise further. The rider deliberately stopped at 50 miles rather than push 70, and he was supported. Nick should expect his sustainable daily distance to FALL entering the humid east even as shade and water become available.
records.quote: It got very warm in the afternoon, I'm glad I stopped and didn't try to bite off another 20 miles.

records.summary: PREVIEW: the Three Sisters — 'one of the toughest climbing days on the whole ride'
records.detail: FORWARD-LOOKING. The page title is 'An Easy Day Before The Three Sisters' and the rider writes: 'Tomorrow promises to be one of the toughest climbing days on the whole ride. I will be starting early.' The Three Sisters are three steep climbs on TX-335/336/337 in the Texas Hill Country. Recorded at unknown confidence pending the next page.
records.cyclistIntel: Flags a major climbing day immediately after Camp Wood, in humid 90 F heat. Note this rider has already ridden AZ-87 (5,436 ft), Emory Pass (8,228 ft, 4,685 ft of climbing) and the Lordsburg climb (4,209 ft) — so for him to call the Three Sisters one of the toughest on the whole ride is significant. Confirm from the next page and get the numbers. Camp Wood is the staging town.
records.quote: Tomorrow promises to be one of the toughest climbing days on the whole ride.

records.summary: Night 39: Canyon BBQ & Grill parking lot, Camp Wood TX — by permission from the owner
records.detail: Camp Wood has no formal RV camping. The restaurant manager phoned the owner and arranged permission to use the parking lot. Very good food and friendly staff; the rider recommends the place by name. Water and toilets marked likely because it is an operating restaurant, not from the page.
records.cyclistIntel: Strong lead of the ASK-LOCALLY class, and the third one to work. A restaurant lot beats a truck-stop gravel lot substantially: food, toilets, people around, no goatheads, and probably shade now that the trees have returned. Camp Wood is the staging town for the Three Sisters, so this is exactly where a rider wants a comfortable night. Enter into the informal-lodging layer as 'a lead, not a booking' — permission was discretionary and same-day.
records.quote: If you are passing through Camp Wood be sure to stop by Canyon BBQ & Grill, right on Highway 55.

records.summary: THE THREE SISTERS: four big climbs in ~20 miles, 4,921 ft total in 74 mi — the rider's PERSONAL ALL-TIME BEST, more than Emory Pass
records.detail: 'Today's ride was all about getting over the Three Sisters: Actually four really big climbs within about 20 miles. I had 4,921 feet of vertical ascent today which is my personal all time best. More than going over the 8,000 foot Emerson Pass.' (He means Emory Pass, which was 4,685 ft.) 'In between 4mph ascents and 30mph descents I really enjoyed looking out over the Texas Hill Country.' GPS: 74.34 mi, 7:34:26, 9.8 mph, 4,921 ft. The elevation trace shows the signature Three Sisters shape — repeated sharp drops and steep re-climbs between about 1,200 and 2,400 ft, with roughly twenty climb waypoints across the day and a marked 2,385 ft at 5:26. A photographed sign reads 'STEEP GRADES / 12 MILES' and he captions it 'The sign didn't lie.'
records.cyclistIntel: THE BIGGEST CLIMBING DAY IN THE WHOLE DATASET — more total ascent than Emory Pass at 8,228 ft, and more than AZ-87 out of Phoenix. It is on TX-337 in the Hill Country and it is symmetrical, so unlike Emory Pass NICK GETS NO DISCOUNT FOR DIRECTION: roughly 4,900 ft either way. Signed as 12 miles of steep grades. 4 mph up and 30 mph down, on rough chipseal with no shoulder (p42-002, p42-003). Camp Wood and Hunt are the bracketing towns, both with confirmed permission-camping. This is a day to plan short and start early, and a strong candidate for splitting at Leakey or Vanderpool.
records.quote: 4,921 feet of vertical ascent today which is my personal all time best. More than going over the 8,000 foot Emerson Pass.

photos.caption: The sign didn't lie.
photos.shows: Yellow diamond warning sign reading 'STEEP GRADES' above a supplementary plate reading '12 MILES'; guardrail with delineator posts, dense green hill-country brush

Elevation trace between ~1,200 and 2,400 ft with repeated sharp drops and steep re-climbs, roughly twenty climb waypoints, marked 2,385 ft at 5:26:15; speed trace alternating deep troughs and 25-40 mph spikes; averaging 9.8 mph

records.summary: The entire Three Sisters route is chipseal, 'mostly very rough' — on the steepest terrain of the trip
records.detail: 'The road was all chipseal. Mostly very rough.' Stated flatly about the whole 74 miles, including the four big climbs. Third consecutive Hill Country day on rough chipseal after Brackettville to Camp Wood (p41-001).
records.cyclistIntel: Rough chipseal is bad on the flat; on 4 mph climbs it steals what little momentum there is, and on 30 mph descents it is a handling and comfort problem that also masks debris. This is the worst surface-plus-gradient combination in the dataset. Widest tyres Nick has and lower pressure for this day specifically. Note the county-line pattern (p36-002) means the surface may improve abruptly at a boundary — worth checking which Hill Country counties maintain better.
records.quote: The road was all chipseal. Mostly very rough.

records.summary: NO SHOULDER on the Three Sisters — fog line to gravel, on 30 mph descents with blind curves
records.detail: Not stated in the text; established from photographs. One shows a two-lane road with a double yellow centreline and essentially no paved surface outside the edge line, dropping straight to a grass and gravel verge, with a chevron curve-warning sign ahead. Another shows the rider climbing with no shoulder at all and an orange marker post at the pavement edge. A third shows guardrail hard against the roadway at the steep-grades sign.
records.cyclistIntel: Combine with p42-001 before planning this day: four steep climbs, 30 mph descents, blind curves, rough chipseal, and no shoulder or escape room. Guardrail sections have none at all. This is the highest-consequence descent risk in Texas, matching AZ-87 in Arizona. Recreational traffic on a signed scenic route (the Texas Hill Country Trail) makes weekends worse — same midweek logic as Glamis and AZ-87.

photos.caption: A place I had never visited. This is a nice part of the country.
photos.shows: Two-lane road with double yellow centreline and no paved shoulder, dropping straight to grass and gravel verge; chevron curve-warning sign ahead; green hill country

photos.caption: Head down and suffering up a hill.
photos.shows: Rider climbing on a two-lane road with no paved shoulder; orange marker post at the pavement edge; dense green brush

records.summary: THE HUNT STORE, Hunt TX (est. 1946) — meat market, jerky, diner, and the Hunt Locals Club on the patio
records.detail: 'When I finally reached Hunt I saw the RV in the parking lot behind The Hunt Store. When I pulled in I received a standing ovation from Linda and a crew of local folks who gather at the patio every day... We sat with them and shot the breeze like we had known each other for years.' He names nine of them and thanks the store for 'a very good meal, and for allowing us to park in their lot overnight.' A photograph shows the storefront lettered 'THE HUNT STORE / EST. 1946 / MEAT MARKET JERKY DIN[ER]' with a covered patio and benches, and a hand-painted club sign reading 'Members & Non-members Only'.
records.cyclistIntel: FOURTH DISCRETIONARY-PERMISSION LODGING WIN and the warmest reception in the journal — a standing ovation from strangers at the end of the hardest climbing day of the trip. A general store with a meat market, jerky counter and diner is a genuine resupply, not just a meal. Covered patio means shade. And the daily locals' gathering is the single best local-knowledge source a cyclist could ask for, right at the eastern foot of the Three Sisters. Named, est. 1946, on the Guadalupe at Hunt. Ask at the counter.
records.quote: Thanks to The Hunt Store for welcoming us in, for a very good meal, and for allowing us to park in their lot overnight.

photos.caption: Thanks to The Hunt Store for welcoming us in.
photos.shows: Weathered timber storefront signed 'THE HUNT STORE / EST. 1946 / MEAT MARKET JERKY DIN[ER]' with cedar-post covered porch, benches and people sitting; wet ground reflecting lights after rain

photos.caption: The official sign for the group. "Members & Non-members Only".

records.summary: Highway 39 follows the GUADALUPE RIVER into Hunt — flowing water, summer camps and shade
records.detail: 'The last part of the ride followed the Guadalupe River. It is a pretty river and Highway 39 had a lot of big, nicely cared for summer camps along it. Also lots of very nice homes on the river.' A real flowing river alongside the road for the final miles, in a developed and populated corridor.
records.cyclistIntel: Second flowing water in two days after the first creek at Camp Wood (p41-002) — the arid west is definitively behind. Practical value: a populated river corridor means houses, camps, shade trees and people, which is the opposite of everything west of the Pecos. Note summer camps mean SEASONAL traffic and possibly seasonal water access; in summer this corridor will be busy with camp vehicles. For Nick westbound, Hunt is where the last reliable green ends.
records.quote: The last part of the ride followed the Guadalupe River.

records.summary: Deer, turkey, fox, coyote, Great Blue Heron and introduced MOUFLON SHEEP in one day
records.detail: 'Wildlife report: Deer, turkey, fox, Great Blue Heron, and of course Turkey Vultures. Linda saw a coyote.' Plus a photographed caption: 'Mouflon Sheep. Originally from southern Italy and introduced to Texas.' Fifth consecutive Texas day with deer, and the most species-diverse day of the journal.
records.cyclistIntel: Hill Country wildlife density is now clearly the highest on the route. Exotic game species like mouflon are common here because of the ranching industry, which means high fences in places and animals near the road. The compounding risk is the same as p42-003: animals plus 30 mph descents plus no shoulder plus blind curves. Keep descent speeds moderate through the Sisters.
records.quote: Wildlife report: Deer, turkey, fox, Great Blue Heron, and of course Turkey Vultures.

photos.caption: Mouflon Sheep. Originally from southern Italy and introduced to Texas.

records.summary: 'The land of no Verizon' — carrier named for the west Texas and Hill Country dead zone
records.detail: 'Internet is tough to get, we have been in the land of no Verizon.' The rider names his carrier, which sharpens the regional no-service finding (p41-009, p38-003) from 'no signal' to 'no Verizon signal' across roughly Marathon to the Hill Country.
records.cyclistIntel: ACTIONABLE IN A WAY THE EARLIER RECORDS WERE NOT: the dead zone is carrier-specific, so Nick should check his own carrier's coverage on this corridor rather than assuming the same outcome. AT&T and T-Mobile have different footprints in rural Texas. If his carrier is also weak here, a satellite messenger becomes the answer for the 300-mile stretch — which is also the stretch with the worst wind, fewest services and most wildlife.
records.quote: we have been in the land of no Verizon

records.summary: 78.4 F day average and RAIN in the evening — first rain since California
records.detail: GPS day average 78.4 F, map header 61.0 F with cloud, so materially cooler than the 90.6 F of the previous day. 'It is raining this evening. If it continues to rain through the morning it might be a short day.' The Hunt Store photograph shows wet ground reflecting the lights. First rain recorded since the California mountain crossing on Day 4, and the first in Texas.
records.cyclistIntel: Marks the arrival of Gulf weather. From here east, rain becomes a factor the desert never presented — which changes what matters: wet chipseal descents on the Sisters, no shade being replaced by no dry shelter, and a rider deciding day length by the morning forecast rather than the heat. Note the cooler average too: cloud cover here does what elevation did further west.
records.quote: It is raining this evening. If it continues to rain through the morning it might be a short day.

records.summary: TEXAS HILL COUNTRY TRAIL — signed scenic driving route the course follows through the Sisters
records.detail: Photograph of a blue-and-white sign with a whitetail buck reading 'TEXAS HILL COUNTRY TRAIL' with a directional arrow, at a roadside pull-off with parked vehicles and a building behind. A signed and mapped state scenic route.
records.cyclistIntel: Useful anchor, and a warning: a signed scenic route means recreational traffic, motorcycles and sightseeing drivers on exactly the roads with no shoulder and blind curves (p42-003). The Three Sisters are a well-known motorcycling destination. Strongly favour a midweek crossing. The sign is also at a pull-off with a building — worth identifying whether it has services.

photos.shows: Blue and white sign with a whitetail buck silhouette reading 'TEXAS HILL COUNTRY TRAIL' with directional arrow; roadside pull-off, parked pickups, building behind, storm cloud building

records.summary: Night 40: THE HUNT STORE parking lot, Hunt TX — by permission, with a diner and a standing ovation
records.detail: Permission from the store to park in their lot overnight, plus a very good meal. The store has a covered cedar-post porch and patio where local people gather daily. Est. 1946; meat market, jerky and diner. It rained that evening. No Verizon service.
records.cyclistIntel: The best-positioned overnight in Texas: the eastern foot of the Three Sisters, with food, resupply, covered shade and a friendly crowd, by permission. Fourth confirmed instance of the ask-locally pattern working. For Nick this pairs with Canyon BBQ at Camp Wood (p41-N1) to bracket the hardest climbing day of the route with two permission stops — meaning he could split the Sisters and have a known endpoint either side. Enter as 'a lead, not a booking'.
records.quote: for allowing us to park in their lot overnight

records.summary: FREDERICKSBURG TX — first full-service town since El Paso, with a HOSPITAL, brewery, shaded patios and a real downtown
records.detail: 'The town is steeped in German heritage and has a vibrant downtown district. We sat in a shaded patio and listened to live music. We had a flight of beers at the Fredericksburg Brewery. We had ice cream.' A photograph of the rider on Main Street shows a blue hospital 'H' direction sign at the intersection, and Katie was in town getting RV maintenance done — so vehicle service exists too.
records.cyclistIntel: THE BEST-EQUIPPED TOWN ON THE ROUTE SINCE EL PASO, 570 miles back. First HOSPITAL recorded anywhere in this dataset, which matters for a solo rider in a region with heavy wildlife, no shoulders and steep descents. Vehicle and mechanical services, groceries, restaurants, brewery, shaded patios. Fredericksburg is the obvious rest-day and maintenance town for the Texas Hill Country, and it sits immediately after the two hardest climbing days on the route (the Three Sisters and this one). Worth planning a stop here even at the cost of a short day.
records.quote: The town is steeped in German heritage and has a vibrant downtown district.

photos.shows: Rider on Fredericksburg Main Street with front light on; traffic signals, a blue hospital 'H' direction sign at the intersection, low commercial buildings, mature trees

photos.caption: A flight of beers and a big soft pretzle. A nice way to cap off the day.

records.summary: Numerous steep short hills — 'not monsters like yesterday but they were numerous and steep', 2,037 ft in 48 mi
records.detail: 'Today was a shorter day but not necessarily an easy day. The hills weren't monsters like yesterday but they were numerous and steep. I did end up with more than 2,000 feet of vertical climb.' GPS: 48.11 mi, 4:29:51, 10.7 mph, 2,037 ft. The elevation trace shows continuous short rollers between about 1,500 and 2,100 ft with a broad higher plateau in the middle third and roughly nine climb waypoints. A photograph shows a typical back road pitching down and away with another rise beyond.
records.cyclistIntel: A different problem from the Three Sisters and worth modelling separately: not four big climbs but dozens of short steep ones, which on a loaded touring bike is arguably more tiring because there is no rhythm. 42 ft of climbing per mile on a day the rider calls short. Symmetrical rollers, so no direction discount. Expect a 10-11 mph average through the Hill Country regardless of wind.
records.quote: The hills weren't monsters like yesterday but they were numerous and steep.

photos.caption: Rolling, green hills.
photos.shows: Narrow two-lane back road dropping steeply away and rising again beyond; no paved shoulder, grass verge, wire fence, dense green oak and cedar; big cumulus sky; a rider in yellow visible far ahead

records.summary: Hill Country back roads have no paved shoulder at all — pavement edge straight to grass
records.detail: Established from photographs. The back-country road shown has a centre line, no edge line at all in places, and pavement running directly into grass and wire fencing. Narrow enough that two vehicles passing would need the full width. The rider describes it as 'real back country' with 'lots of cattle and fancy looking ranch houses'.
records.cyclistIntel: Third consecutive Hill Country day with no shoulder (p42-003, p41-001). The mitigating factor here is genuinely low traffic on back roads between ranches — but the same low-traffic roads are the narrow ones with blind crests, and the Texas trooper precedent (p40-002) shows a rider can be told to move over onto pavement that does not exist. Best defence is visibility: the rider runs a front light in daylight, which the Fredericksburg photograph confirms.
records.quote: The route took me into some real back country today.

records.summary: Headwinds again — third consecutive Hill Country day with wind against him
records.detail: 'Even though I had headwinds and hills I was entertained the whole way.' 10.7 mph average over 48 miles with 2,037 ft of climbing. Follows the headwind day into Camp Wood and the calm-but-rough day before it.
records.cyclistIntel: Wind persists east of the desert. The Hill Country pattern that is emerging: 10-11 mph averages regardless, because either the hills or the wind or the chipseal takes the difference. Plan Hill Country days at 45-55 miles rather than the 60-75 that worked in flatter country.
records.quote: Even though I had headwinds and hills I was entertained the whole way.

records.summary: Exotic game ranches with tall fences — 'a collection of different kinds of deer behind a really tall fence'
records.detail: 'Linda spotted this collection of different kinds of deer behind a really tall fence.' Follows the mouflon sheep the previous day (p42-006). High game fences are characteristic of Hill Country exotic-game ranching.
records.cyclistIntel: Slightly reassuring rather than alarming: tall game fences keep the exotics IN, which is why the roadside sightings here are fenced animals rather than loose ones. The genuine hazard remains native whitetail, which are not contained — see the herd of twenty two days earlier (p41-003). Note that game fences also mean no roadside escape route where they run right to the pavement.
records.quote: a collection of different kinds of deer behind a really tall fence

records.summary: STONEHENGE II at The Point, Hill Country Arts Foundation, Ingram TX — full-scale replica beside the route
records.detail: Photo caption 'They moved Stonehenge to Texas.' The photograph shows a stone monument sign reading 'THE POINT / HILL COUNTRY ARTS FOUNDATION' with an electronic marquee, and a full-scale Stonehenge replica standing on mown grass behind it, backed by hill-country trees.
records.cyclistIntel: Unmistakable, permanently sited, mapped landmark a few miles east of Hunt — a good anchor for the start of this leg. It is also an arts-foundation campus with a theatre, so it likely has parking, restrooms and shade; worth confirming, since it sits between Hunt and Kerrville on a corridor where those matter less now but still count.

photos.caption: They moved Stonehenge to Texas.
photos.shows: Limestone monument sign 'THE POINT / HILL COUNTRY ARTS FOUNDATION' with electronic marquee; full-scale Stonehenge replica of upright and lintel stones on mown grass behind; hill-country tree line, clear blue sky

records.summary: Night 41: Fredericksburg TX — site not named, in a full-service town
records.detail: Day ends in Fredericksburg; no site named. The town has a vibrant downtown, brewery, restaurants, a hospital and RV maintenance services. Another Southern Tier rider's family was in town the same day for RV work.
records.cyclistIntel: No specific lead, but Fredericksburg is a tourist destination with plenty of commercial lodging and campgrounds — the constraint here is likely PRICE and weekend availability rather than existence. This was a Friday, and the weekend-fills pattern (p26-002) applies to a destination town more than anywhere else on the route. Book ahead if stopping here at a weekend.

records.summary: GOOD ROADS AT LAST — 'up to par with Iowa roads, not bone rattling chip seal'
records.detail: 'And the roads were up to par with Iowa roads, not bone rattling chip seal.' Ends a three-day run of rough chipseal through the Hill Country (Brackettville-Camp Wood, the Three Sisters, and the Hunt-Fredericksburg back roads). A photograph confirms a sound asphalt surface with a white edge line and roughly two to three feet of paved shoulder beyond it.
records.cyclistIntel: First genuinely good pavement recorded east of the Pecos, and it arrives around Fredericksburg heading toward Johnson City. Consistent with the county-line maintenance pattern (p36-002) — Gillespie and Blanco counties evidently maintain better than the counties west of them. Record as a POSITIVE span so the planner does not warn generically across the Hill Country: the rough surface belongs to the Sisters corridor specifically, not the whole region.
records.quote: the roads were up to par with Iowa roads, not bone rattling chip seal

photos.caption: There were some nice downhills.
photos.shows: Sound asphalt two-lane with yellow centreline, white edge line and roughly 2-3 ft of paved shoulder, then grass verge; long green rolling hills ahead, oaks and pasture

records.summary: Long rolling hills — 2,195 ft in 46 mi, but longer and less steep than the Sisters
records.detail: 'The hills were again green but they were longer and not as steep or tall as the past few days. It felt like western Iowa on the first two days of every RAGBRAI. Long rolling hills, green and scenic.' GPS: 46.16 mi, 3:54:07, 11.8 mph, 2,195 ft. The elevation trace declines gently overall from a marked 1,760 ft with continuous long undulations, and roughly SIXTEEN climb waypoints across the day — so the count is high even though no single climb is severe.
records.cyclistIntel: Third distinct Texas climbing profile now recorded: the Sisters (four monsters), the Hunt day (dozens of short steep ones), and this (long gentle rollers). 48 ft per mile but at 11.8 mph — the best average of any Hill Country day, which shows that gradient shape matters as much as total ascent. Symmetrical, so no direction discount. Plan Hill Country at 46-50 miles per day and expect 10-12 mph.
records.quote: Long rolling hills, green and scenic.

photos.caption: Green and rolling.
photos.shows: Two-lane road undulating away through green pasture and oak groves; a car in the middle distance; long views, scattered cumulus

records.summary: SATURDAY MEANT LIGHT TRAFFIC here — the opposite of the weekend pattern further west
records.detail: 'It was Saturday so traffic was light.' Directly contrary to the weekend findings earlier on the route: Glamis OHV crowds (p8-010), AZ-87 recreational traffic (p21-007), and the Texas Hill Country Trail scenic corridor (anchor:hill-country-trail).
records.cyclistIntel: IMPORTANT NUANCE that stops the weekend rule being applied blindly.
