Weekends are worse where the road IS the destination — OHV areas, scenic motorcycling routes, national park approaches. Weekends are BETTER on ordinary working roads, because the commuter and work-truck traffic (p36-001) disappears. So the planner should treat weekend effects as location-specific, not regional: bad at Glamis, AZ-87 and the Sisters; good on farm and commuter corridors like this one.
records.quote: It was Saturday so traffic was light.

records.summary: Paved shoulder returns — roughly 2-3 ft outside the edge line on the Johnson City run
records.detail: Established from two photographs. One shows a sound asphalt two-lane with a white edge line and two to three feet of paved shoulder beyond it. Another shows the rider on a road with a wide but coarse chipseal/gravel shoulder. So shoulder provision is inconsistent but present, a marked improvement on the three preceding days where there was none at all.
records.cyclistIntel: Meaningful upgrade from the Sisters corridor, where the pavement ran straight into grass. Two to three feet is not generous but it is somewhere to be. Combined with light Saturday traffic and good surface, this is the most comfortable riding recorded in Texas so far. Note the inconsistency — some sections revert to coarse gravel shoulder.

photos.caption: I'm still riding upright. I must be ok.
photos.shows: Rider on a two-lane road with a wide coarse chipseal and gravel shoulder; yellow centreline, pasture and oaks, big cumulus sky

records.summary: LBJ BOYHOOD HOME National Historical Park, Johnson City — NPS site with ranger-led tours
records.detail: 'The shorter day allowed Linda and me to go visit the LBJ Childhood Home National Historical Site. We got a tour by Ranger Douglas.' A photograph shows the white clapboard house behind a picket fence with mature shade trees, on a paved street with an NPS interpretive sign. Part of Lyndon B. Johnson National Historical Park.
records.cyclistIntel: A National Park Service visitor site directly in Johnson City, which reliably means restrooms, drinking water, shade and staff — the same value as the Judge Roy Bean travel centre at Langtry (p39-002) but in a town that also has other services. Free or low-cost, staffed, and a genuine rest-day option. Confirm hours; NPS historic homes typically keep daytime hours with seasonal variation.
records.quote: We got a tour by Ranger Douglas.

photos.caption: LBJ's childhood home.
photos.shows: White clapboard house with green shutters and a wraparound porch behind a white picket fence; mature shade trees, NPS interpretive sign, paved street and stone kerb

records.summary: Longhorn cattle in tree groves, and turkey vultures still constant
records.detail: 'It's a poor photo but these are longhorns standing in a grove of trees.' Plus 'I can't get away from the Turkey Vultures.' Fenced ranch cattle rather than loose animals; turkey vultures have appeared on every Texas day since Sanderson.
records.cyclistIntel: Low hazard — fenced cattle, not the open-range livestock that stood in the road on Emory Pass (p29-002). Turkey vultures matter slightly: they feed on roadkill on the pavement and flush late and low, and Texas roadkill is heavy (p40-003). Otherwise no action.
records.quote: I can't get away from the Turkey Vultures.

records.summary: PEDERNALES FALLS STATE PARK sits at the day's endpoint east of Johnson City — inferred from the GPS map, not stated
records.detail: The GPS map's red endpoint pin falls east of Johnson City in the immediate vicinity of the labelled 'Pedernales Falls State Park', and the track continues past Johnson City toward it. The page itself never mentions the park or names where they slept, so this is INFERRED FROM THE MAP ONLY and recorded at unknown confidence.
records.cyclistIntel: Worth chasing rather than trusting. A Texas state park on the route would be a strong lodging anchor — state parks reliably take tents, have water, showers and shade, and can be reserved. But this journal does not confirm they used it or that it is on the cycling route rather than a vehicle detour. Verify independently: if Pedernales Falls SP is accessible from the route, it is a much better option than anything in the last 400 miles.

photos.shows: GPS map with the red endpoint pin east of Johnson City adjacent to the labelled Pedernales Falls State Park; the Pedernales River runs alongside the route

records.summary: Night 42: Johnson City TX area — site not named; GPS endpoint near Pedernales Falls State Park
records.detail: The page names Johnson City as the destination and describes visiting the LBJ site, but never names a campground. The GPS track ends east of Johnson City near Pedernales Falls State Park (p44-007).
records.cyclistIntel: No confirmed lead, but the location is promising — Johnson City has an NPS site for water and shade, and a state park may be within reach. Worth resolving because it sits between the Hill Country climbs and the Austin metro crossing.

records.summary: MELLOW JOHNNY'S BIKE SHOP, downtown Austin — the FIRST bike shop recorded in 1,638 miles
records.detail: 'we went downtown. We saw the Texas State Capitol Building then visited Mellow Johnnie's Bike Shop. It's Lance Armstrong's shop and has a lot of his bikes and memorabilia from his Tour De France years.' A photograph shows the rider in front of a display of seven yellow jerseys.
records.cyclistIntel: THE ABSENCE IS THE FINDING. This is the first bicycle shop named anywhere in this journal, at mile 1,638 — meaning across San Diego, the Imperial Valley, Quartzsite, Phoenix, Globe, Silver City, El Paso, Van Horn, Marfa, Del Rio and the whole Hill Country, not one bike shop appears. Whether that is because none exist or because a supported rider never needed one, Nick cannot assume mechanical help. It explains why the hardware stores at Alpine, Sanderson and the Camp Wood lumberyard kept mattering. Austin is the first place to get real bike service, buy tyres, and replace anything the goatheads and chipseal have destroyed. Plan a maintenance stop here. Confirm the shop still trades under this name.
records.quote: visited Mellow Johnnie's Bike Shop

photos.caption: I am in front of Lance's seven yellow jerseys.

records.summary: LOW-WATER CROSSING on a rural Hill Country road — only an inch or two deep, but the road is broken and it floods
records.detail: 'I had a water crossing today. Luckily it was just an inch or two.' The photograph shows a narrow rural road dipping through a creek bed with standing water spanning the full width, a yellow depth-marker post at the edge, and badly broken, patched and potholed pavement on the approach and exit. The surrounding country is wooded creek bottom.
records.cyclistIntel: Hill Country roads use low-water crossings instead of bridges, and they are exactly what the name implies — passable most of the time and impassable after rain. This one was benign; the depth marker exists because it is not always. Note it rained two nights earlier (p42-007) and this is what an inch of runoff looks like. For Nick: check forecasts before committing to a back-road day here, expect broken pavement at every crossing, and never ride into moving water. The crossings are also unavoidable — they are on the route, not a detour.
records.quote: I had a water crossing today. Luckily it was just an inch or two.

photos.caption: I had a water crossing today. Luckily it was just an inch or two.
photos.shows: Narrow rural road dipping through a wooded creek bed with standing water across the full width; yellow depth-marker post at the edge; badly broken, patched and potholed pavement on approach and exit

records.summary: Austin's bike trails and downtown bike lanes are excellent — 'The route took great pains to show off' them
records.detail: 'The rest of the trip was negotiating the city streets and bike trails of Austin. The route took great pains to show off the bike trails and downtown bike lanes. They were all very nice.' Photographs show a wide smooth concrete shared-use path running under a highway bridge alongside the Colorado River, with railings.
records.cyclistIntel: Third car-free metro crossing on the route after the Phoenix canal trails (p20-001) and the El Paso levee path (p32-004), and the rider rates this the best. The ACA alignment deliberately routes onto it. Unlike the Phoenix path, nothing here suggests the alignment vanishes — but load it as a GPX anyway, since the Phoenix lesson was that urban trail routing is where riders get lost (p20-002).
records.quote: The route took great pains to show off the bike trails and downtown bike lanes. They were all very nice.
records.road: Austin bike trails / downtown bike lanes
records.anchorNote: extent applied west→east per the source rule

photos.caption: Pedestrian bridge over the Colorado River. It was really crowded.
photos.shows: Wide smooth concrete shared-use path under a highway bridge beside the Colorado River, steel railings, many pedestrians with strollers and dogs

records.summary: AUSTIN PATHS ARE PACKED on a fine weekend — 'slow going dodging all the folks'
records.detail: 'It being a decent temperature and Sunday, everyone and their brother were using the paths. It was slow going dodging all the folks.' The photograph of the Colorado River pedestrian bridge shows a continuous stream of walkers, strollers and dogs. His average for the day was 11.0 mph despite the last 22 miles being essentially flat and dropping to 475 ft.
records.cyclistIntel: COMPLETES THE WEEKEND PICTURE, and it cuts the opposite way from the day before. Rural working roads are QUIETER at weekends (p44-003); recreational destinations are BUSIER — and that now includes urban shared-use paths, not just OHV areas and scenic byways. So the rule is about what the road is FOR, not what day it is. For Austin specifically: crossing on a fine weekend afternoon means walking pace on the best sections. Cross early or midweek.
records.quote: everyone and their brother were using the paths. It was slow going dodging all the folks.

records.summary: Last Hill Country climbing day: 2,595 ft in 52 mi, then dropping from ~1,300 ft to 475 ft into Austin
records.detail: 'today was over 2,500 of climbing in 52 miles.' GPS: 52.04 mi, 4:43:15, 11.0 mph, 2,595 ft. The elevation trace holds around 1,100-1,300 ft with continuous rollers and about thirteen climb waypoints through the first three hours, then falls away steadily after 3:20 to a marked 475 ft at 4:39. Fifth consecutive day with 2,000+ ft of climbing.
records.cyclistIntel: Marks the eastern edge of the Hill Country. Five consecutive days at 2,000-4,900 ft of climbing (Days 39-43) totalling roughly 13,000 ft — that is the real cost of this section and it should be modelled as a block, not as individual days. Reversed, Nick CLIMBS 800-plus feet out of Austin into the Hill Country and then has five hard days ahead of him rather than behind. Austin is where he should arrive rested, not leave tired.
records.quote: today was over 2,500 of climbing in 52 miles

photos.shows: Elevation trace holding 1,100-1,300 ft with continuous rollers and ~13 climb waypoints through 3:20, then falling steadily to a marked 475 ft at 4:39; speed averaging 11.0 mph; temperature averaging 73.8 F

records.summary: Clean three-part structure to the day: 20 mi cow country, 10 mi estate homes, 22 mi city
records.detail: 'The first 20 miles were rural cow country. The next 10 miles was rural but big, fancy homes. The rest of the trip was negotiating the city streets and bike trails of Austin.' A tidy account of the rural-to-metro gradient west of Austin, matching the map's progression through Dripping Springs, Bee Cave and West Lake Hills.
records.cyclistIntel: Useful for day planning: the last 22 miles into Austin are urban, so services, water and food are continuous from roughly Bee Cave onward — but so are traffic lights and path crowds. The first 20 miles are the ones to carry water for. For Nick outbound, the reverse: use the estate-homes and cow-country stretch as the transition and top up before leaving the metro edge.
records.quote: The first 20 miles were rural cow country.

records.summary: AUSTIN — full metro services: bike shop, Texas State Capitol, Terry Black's BBQ, KOA campground
records.detail: Done riding by 1:30pm, then downtown for the Texas State Capitol, Mellow Johnny's bike shop and Terry Black's BBQ, which was 'packed with people and for good reason, it was delicious.' Overnight at a KOA campground.
records.cyclistIntel: The largest city on the route since Phoenix and the best-equipped anywhere in this dataset. Everything a self-supported rider needs: bike service, medical, groceries, transport options if something goes badly wrong, and a KOA. Fourth KOA of the journal, so the chain remains the reliable named lodging. If Nick needs one planned maintenance day in Texas, Austin is where the parts and the mechanics are.
records.quote: Then we went for some Texas BBQ at Terry Black's BBQ.

records.summary: Colorado River crossings in Austin, including a dedicated pedestrian/bike bridge
records.detail: Two captions: 'Pedestrian bridge over the Colorado River. It was really crowded' and 'Another crossing of the Colorado River.' The photographed bridge is a wide concrete shared-use deck slung beneath a highway bridge with steel railings, busy with pedestrians.
records.cyclistIntel: Hard urban anchor, and a practical note: the route crosses the Colorado twice in Austin, at least once on a dedicated non-motorised bridge under a road deck. That is both the safest way across and the most congested point on a fine weekend (p45-003). Good positional fix for the metro section.

records.summary: Night 43: KOA campground, Austin TX
records.detail: 'before we went to our KOA campground we went downtown.' Fourth KOA of the trip after Boulevard, Wenden and Lordsburg. Not further named. The GPS endpoint pin sits southeast of downtown near Del Valle, which is where Austin's KOA is located. Facility values from chain norms, not the page.
records.cyclistIntel: Callable and in the one city on this stretch with full services. Note the position — southeast of downtown, so on the EAST side of the metro, which for Nick travelling westbound means he reaches it before the city crossing rather than after. Given the path congestion finding, staging there and crossing Austin early in the morning is the sensible play.
records.quote: before we went to our KOA campground

records.summary: THREE dog encounters in one day — and TWO countermeasures that both worked: a bellowed 'NO!' and an AIR HORN
records.detail: 'Finally the route turned to a less busy road with several houses close to the road. This is Texas. First I was chased by a German Shepherd. I bellowed out NO!!! which was actually very effective. Next I saw, in my rear view mirror, four dogs running hard to catch me. I used my air horn on them. I never saw the dogs again so the blast horn was a success. The last dog was a pit bull that responded to a noisy NO.' Three separate incidents in a single day, on a rural road with houses close to the roadway. He spotted the pack of four in a REAR VIEW MIRROR.
records.cyclistIntel: THE DEFINITIVE DOG RECORD, and everything about it is actionable. (1) A loud bellowed 'NO' worked on two of three, including a pit bull — free, instant, no hands off the bars. (2) An AIR HORN turned back a pack of four; he carries it in his handlebar bag where he can reach it (p33-002). (3) A REAR VIEW MIRROR is what let him see the pack coming, which is the difference between reacting and being ambushed. All three are cheap and Nick should have all three. Critical inversion: on the earlier Texas day he outran dogs only because he had a tailwind and flat ground (p33-002) — Nick cannot count on that, so the deterrents are his primary defence, not his backup. The trigger is consistent: rural roads with houses close to the pavement, i.e. all of east Texas and beyond.
records.quote: I bellowed out NO!!! which was actually very effective... I used my air horn on them... the blast horn was a success.

records.summary: BASTROP STATE PARK is directly ON the route — and the course runs through TWO connected state parks
records.detail: 'The route went through two state parks. Very scenic but also very sharp climbs.' A photograph shows the rider's bike at the signed entrance: 'BASTROP STATE PARK / TEXAS PARKS & WILDLIFE DEPARTMENT / 100 PARK ROAD 1A', with the historic CCC stone gate pillars and mature pines. A second caption references 'The Overlook at the state park'. The second park is almost certainly Buescher, which connects to Bastrop by Park Road 1C.
records.cyclistIntel: FIRST STATE PARK CONFIRMED ON THE ROUTE ITSELF, and it changes the lodging picture entirely. Texas state parks reliably take tents, have potable water, showers, toilets, shade and reservable sites — everything that has been missing or uncertain for 1,700 miles. The route runs THROUGH it rather than past it. That makes Bastrop/Buescher a proper anchor rather than a lead, and the first one Nick can book online with confidence. Reserve ahead; Texas state parks near Austin fill at weekends. The cost is the 'very sharp climbs' the rider notes inside the parks.
records.quote: The route went through two state parks.

photos.caption: Riding through state parks!
photos.shows: Signed park entrance 'BASTROP STATE PARK / TEXAS PARKS & WILDLIFE DEPARTMENT / 100 PARK ROAD 1A' with historic CCC-era stone gate pillars; loaded touring bike on smooth park road, mature pines and mown grass, morning light

records.summary: Busy no-shoulder road out of Austin — his tactic was to BAIL OFF THE ROAD into the weeds and let traffic pass
records.detail: 'The day started out on a very busy road with no shoulders. I learned to just bail out, stop in the weeds and let a string of traffic by. It took a while.' So the shoulder was absent, the traffic was heavy enough that he could not simply hold his line, and the working solution was repeatedly leaving the roadway entirely. This is the eastern exit from the Austin metro.
records.cyclistIntel: An experienced rider dismounting into the weeds repeatedly is the strongest signal in the dataset about a road's rideability. Note the compound problem for Nick: 'stop in the weeds' is exactly the behaviour that picks up goatheads (p33-001) — though he is now east of the worst of that. This is the WESTBOUND ENTRY to Austin in Nick's direction, so he hits it approaching the city, likely tired, possibly in afternoon traffic. Worth finding an alternative line for the metro edge, and worth crossing early like the Phoenix lesson (p20-003).
records.quote: I learned to just bail out, stop in the weeds and let a string of traffic by. It took a while.

records.summary: The ACA alignment ADDS SIGNIFICANT MILES to avoid busy highways east of the state parks
records.detail: 'After the state parks, the route took great pains to avoid the busy highways. It added a lot of miles and I was bushed when I met up with Linda in Burton.' A 90.93-mile day where a direct line would be materially shorter. Note the same phrasing he used approvingly about the Austin bike trails the day before — here the extra distance cost him.
records.cyclistIntel: IMPORTANT EXPECTATION-SETTING for the planner's mileage model: the official ACA route is deliberately longer than the direct route through populated country, because it routes onto quiet roads. That is the right trade for safety but it means Nick's daily distances will exceed what a map's point-to-point suggests, and it compounds with the dog exposure — quiet rural roads with houses close to the pavement are exactly where the dogs are (p46-001). Check the planner's reconstructed geometry against this: if it took direct lines anywhere through east Texas, the mileage is understated.
records.quote: the route took great pains to avoid the busy highways. It added a lot of miles

records.summary: 3,442 ft over 90.9 mi at low elevation — relentless short rollers plus 'very sharp climbs' in the state parks
records.detail: GPS: 90.93 mi, 7:43:25, 11.8 mph, 3,442 ft ascent. The elevation trace runs entirely between about 240 and 720 ft — genuinely low country now — but with continuous short undulation and roughly EIGHTEEN climb waypoints across the day, ending at a marked 383 ft. The rider singles out the state park sections for 'very sharp climbs'.
records.cyclistIntel: Out of the Hill Country by elevation but not by effort: 38 ft of climbing per mile at 500 ft above sea level. Sixth consecutive day above 2,000 ft of ascent. The pattern for east Texas is now clear — no big climbs, but no rest either, and the sharpest pitches are inside the state parks. Plan on 11-12 mph and do not let the low elevation numbers suggest an easy day.
records.quote: Very scenic but also very sharp climbs.

photos.shows: Elevation trace confined between ~240 and 720 ft with continuous short rollers and ~18 climb waypoints, ending at a marked 383 ft; speed averaging 11.8 mph; temperature averaging 81.2 F with peaks near 100 F

records.summary: 81.2 F average with peaks near 100 F, and a forecast heat spike drove a 90-mile push
records.detail: 'He called with the warning that the temperatures are supposed to be way up on Thursday and I should ride as much as I can for the next three days. This, combined with very few RV camping options, led to today's 90+ miles.' The withdrawn riding partner is now doing remote weather forecasting for him. GPS records an 81.2 F day average with the trace touching roughly 100 F in the afternoon.
records.cyclistIntel: Two transferable points. First, the tactic: bank miles ahead of a forecast heat spike rather than riding into it — which only works if the schedule has slack, and Nick's has none. Second, note what actually forced the 90 miles: a heat forecast AND 'very few RV camping options'. The second constraint is theirs, not Nick's; a cyclist with a tent has more stopping choices, so he would not be obliged to ride 91 miles here. Another instance of their itinerary being driven by the vehicle (p26-004).
records.quote: the temperatures are supposed to be way up on Thursday and I should ride as much as I can for the next three days

records.summary: Wildfire scars in the Bastrop state parks — charred trees among wildflowers, from the 2011 and 2015 fires
records.detail: Photo caption: 'Wild flowers and charred trees. The wild fires were 2011 and 2015.' The Bastrop County Complex fire of 2011 destroyed most of the Lost Pines forest in Bastrop State Park. The photograph shows standing dead trunks among regrowth and flowering ground cover.
records.cyclistIntel: Mostly context, with one practical edge: burn-scar areas have reduced canopy, so the shade inside these parks is patchier than mature pine forest would suggest. Worth knowing if Nick is counting on the state parks for midday shelter as well as camping. The regrowth also means the park's character may have changed again by the time he rides it.
records.quote: Wild flowers and charred trees. The wild fires were 2011 and 2015.

records.summary: Night 44: Burton TX — site not named, and camping options were explicitly scarce
records.detail: Day ends at Burton after 90.93 miles. No site named. The rider states plainly that 'very few RV camping options' was one of the two reasons the day ran to 90+ miles, so the stretch between the state parks and Burton is thin for vehicle camping.
records.cyclistIntel: The useful finding is the GAP, not the site: between Bastrop/Buescher State Parks and Burton there is little formal camping. But that constraint is RV-shaped — Nick has the state parks behind him (bookable, tents, water, showers) and the ask-locally pattern ahead, which has worked four times in Texas. He does not need to ride 91 miles here. Identify what Burton actually has, and treat the state parks as the real anchor for this leg.
records.quote: very few RV camping options

records.summary: THE OPERATING RULE, STATED PLAINLY: up early, off the bike by 2:00pm, because it is humid and hitting the 90s
records.detail: 'It is more humid in this area and the temperatures are hitting the 90's in the afternoon. We are getting up early and trying to be done biking at 2:00ish.' GPS records an 86.8 F day average with the trace peaking near 100 F after 3:30 into the ride — so the afternoon he is avoiding is real. This is the same rule that emerged in Arizona (p10-004) now restated for humid east Texas.
records.cyclistIntel: THE SINGLE CLEAREST OPERATIONAL RULE IN THE DATASET, and it holds across two very different climates: pre-dawn start, finish by early afternoon. In the desert the reason was dry heat; here it is humid heat, which is physiologically harder. That constrains day length more than terrain does — roughly seven hours of riding window, so 55-70 miles at east Texas averages. It also collides with the traffic-window finding (p36-001) and the dawn wildlife pattern (p39-005), which Nick has to accept rather than solve. The planner should treat 'done by 2pm' as a hard constraint on day length from El Paso east.
records.quote: We are getting up early and trying to be done biking at 2:00ish.

records.summary: PIT STOP RV PARK outside Anderson TX — air-conditioned laundry and the machines take NO QUARTERS
records.detail: 'We ended up at the Pit Stop RV Park outside of Anderson. After the superintendent fixed our electrical hookup we found the laundry building. It was big, clean and nicely air conditioned. And the machines didn't need quarters. We did all our laundry. The little pleasures of life on the road.' Named, with an on-site superintendent who fixed a hookup problem.
records.cyclistIntel: Best-documented facilities of any commercial site in the dataset: big, clean, AIR-CONDITIONED laundry with free machines. Air conditioning matters enormously here — it is the only recorded indoor cool space at a campground anywhere on the route, and in humid 90s heat that is a genuine mid-day refuge, not just a convenience. Named and callable. Ask about tents; the journal never establishes tent policy at any RV park, but a site with a resident superintendent is the kind where asking works. Second confirmed laundry after Silver City KOA at $4.50 a load — this one is free.
records.quote: It was big, clean and nicely air conditioned. And the machines didn't need quarters.

records.summary: Narrow roads with SOFT verges — the support vehicle went into a ditch simply turning around
records.detail: Photo captions: 'This is what happens when you need a photo and turn around on a very narrow road' and 'There are some really good people in Texas. This road crew had Linda pulled out of the ditch 5 minutes after she landed there.' A separate photograph shows the typical surface — sound pavement, white edge line, then a band of loose gravel and soft grass verge, with a 'PASS WITH CARE' sign.
records.cyclistIntel: IMPORTANT QUALIFIER ON THE BAIL-OUT TACTIC. The day before, the rider's answer to a busy no-shoulder road was to 'bail out, stop in the weeds' (p46-003). This page shows the verges here are soft enough to trap a vehicle. For a loaded touring bike that means leaving the pavement at speed is a crash risk, not a safety valve — pick the bail-out spot deliberately, at low speed, on gravel rather than grass. Also note the flip side, which recurs throughout this journal: a road crew had her out in five minutes.
records.quote: This road crew had Linda pulled out of the ditch 5 minutes after she landed there.

photos.caption: Typical of the scenery today.
photos.shows: Two-lane road with sound pavement, yellow centreline, white edge line then a band of loose gravel and soft grass verge; 'PASS WITH CARE' sign; broad green pasture, oaks, a car approaching

records.summary: Out of the Texas Hills — 2,362 ft over 60 mi, now between 120 and 600 ft elevation, hills longer and less steep
records.detail: 'The hills are getting longer and not as steep, I think we are moving out of the Texas Hills. Today's roads were good and the wind was kind of at my back.' GPS: 59.90 mi, 5:03:11, 11.9 mph, 2,362 ft. Elevation trace runs between roughly 120 and 600 ft with a marked 208 ft low at 2:57 and about seventeen climb waypoints. Seventh consecutive day above 2,000 ft of ascent.
records.cyclistIntel: The gradients are easing but the total is not — 39 ft per mile at 400 ft above sea level. That is the east Texas signature: no climbs worth naming, no rest either. Seven straight days of 2,000-4,900 ft (Days 39-45) is roughly 20,000 ft of climbing across the Hill Country and its eastern approaches. Model it as a block. Reversed, Nick rides into it rather than out of it.
records.quote: The hills are getting longer and not as steep, I think we are moving out of the Texas Hills.

photos.shows: Elevation trace between ~120 and 600 ft with continuous rollers, a marked 208 ft at 2:57:52 and ~17 climb waypoints; speed averaging 11.9 mph; temperature averaging 86.8 F peaking near 100 F after 3:30

records.summary: Heavy roadkill including ARMADILLOS, and no live wildlife seen at all
records.detail: 'Today we saw lots of big broad pastures and big broad houses. Cattle and horses. I didn't really see any wildlife today. Lots of road kill, including armadillos.' First armadillos of the journal. Notable inversion of the previous week: five straight days of live deer, javelina and pronghorn sightings, then a day with none but plenty of carcasses.
records.cyclistIntel: Armadillo carcasses are a shoulder obstacle — armoured, roughly football-sized and slow to decompose, so they sit in the rideable strip. Combined with the general roadkill increase from the Pecos east (p40-003), expect to be steering around bodies on the shoulder in populated country. The absence of live sightings suggests this is fenced ranch land rather than open range, which is better for collision risk.
records.quote: Lots of road kill, including armadillos.

records.summary: COW TALK STEAK HOUSE — packed local restaurant that got him through the last 20 miles
records.detail: 'Linda met me for lunch at the Cow Talk Steak House. It was packed. The food was good and got me through the remaining 20 miles of the ride.' Location not stated precisely; the map places the mid-route towns as Independence, Washington and Navasota, so it is most likely in or near Navasota, roughly 40 miles into the day.
records.cyclistIntel: A substantial sit-down meal at roughly the two-thirds point of a 60-mile day, and the rider credits it with finishing. Worth pinning down which town it is in, because mid-route hot food is scarce on this route and this is only the second named lunch-stop restaurant in Texas after Magoo's in Alpine. Packed at lunchtime on a Tuesday suggests reliable hours.
records.quote: The food was good and got me through the remaining 20 miles of the ride.

records.summary: They call the SOUTHERN TIER HALFWAY POINT at 1,788.8 miles — which implies a longer total than ACA publishes
records.detail: 'Woo Hoo! We have passed the half way point of the Southern Tier Route.' Their cumulative at that moment is 1,788.8 miles, which would put the full route near 3,578 miles. The ACA Southern Tier is generally published at roughly 3,000-3,100 miles San Diego to St Augustine. The discrepancy is unexplained — their cumulative includes at least one off-route detour (the Sun City West day) and possibly other variations.
records.cyclistIntel: DO NOT take 3,578 as the route length. Recorded because a halfway claim is a useful cross-check and this one does not reconcile. Either their cumulative includes off-route miles, or the ACA alignment as currently mapped is materially longer than the published figure — which would matter for Nick, since his own plan is built on 2,972.5 route miles. Worth checking the planner's total against current ACA mileage rather than an older published number.
records.quote: We have passed the half way point of the Southern Tier Route.

records.summary: BRAZOS RIVER crossing, near Washington / Navasota TX
records.detail: Photo caption: 'The Brazos River.' A major named river crossing on the route between Washington-on-the-Brazos and Navasota. The elevation trace shows the day's low point of 208 ft at roughly the same time, consistent with a river bottom.
records.cyclistIntel: Major mapped river crossing — reliable anchor, and the elevation low of the day gives a second independent fix on the same point. Note the pattern from the Pecos and Colorado crossings: river bottoms mean a dip and climb either side.

photos.caption: The Brazos River.
photos.shows: Wide green-brown river seen from a bridge with dense riparian trees on both banks

records.summary: Grimes County Courthouse, Anderson TX — 'quite a building'
records.detail: 'The town of Independence had interesting history and the courthouse in Anderson was quite a building.' Photographed. County courthouses in Texas are typically the tallest structure in a small county seat and are individually mapped and dated.
records.cyclistIntel: Good positional fix in the town nearest the night's lodging (Pit Stop RV Park). Texas county seats reliably have a courthouse square with shade trees, benches and public restrooms — worth checking, since Anderson is otherwise a small town and the courthouse square is the likeliest public facility.

photos.caption: The Grimes County Courthouse in Anderson.

records.summary: Night 45: PIT STOP RV PARK, outside Anderson TX — free air-conditioned laundry, on-site superintendent
records.detail: Named directly. The superintendent fixed their electrical hookup, so staff are on site and responsive. The laundry building is big, clean, air-conditioned and free. Electrical and water hookups confirmed by the fact they used them.
records.cyclistIntel: Callable, staffed and unusually well equipped for this route. The air-conditioned laundry is the standout — the only indoor cool space recorded at any campground in 1,789 miles, which in humid 90s heat is a real refuge for the hours between arriving and sleeping. Ask about tents. Positioned near Anderson, roughly 60 miles east of the Bastrop/Buescher state parks, so it fits as the next anchor after them.
records.quote: We ended up at the Pit Stop RV Park outside of Anderson.

records.summary: SAM HOUSTON NATIONAL FOREST — the route runs through it, with tall pines and real shade
records.detail: 'Today's ride spent a good portion of the day going through the Sam Huston National Forest. It was good to see tall pine trees and have a little shade. What a difference a few miles make.' Caption: 'The Sam Huston National Forest was a pleasant surprise. It reminded me of Northern Minnesota.' Photographs show dense mature pine on both sides of the road with the canopy closing overhead in places.
records.cyclistIntel: POTENTIALLY A MAJOR LODGING OPTION NICK HAS AND THEY DID NOT USE. National forests generally permit dispersed camping, and the route runs through this one for a good part of a day — which matters enormously because the same page says commercial RV parks here are 20+ miles off route (p48-002). They could not use dispersed camping because they needed mains electricity for air conditioning; Nick has no such constraint. Verify Sam Houston NF dispersed-camping rules and designated areas before relying on it, but this is the first national forest on route since the Gila and Tonto, and it comes with shade, which is now the scarce resource.
records.quote: It was good to see tall pine trees and have a little shade.

photos.caption: The Sam Huston National Forest was a pleasant surprise.
photos.shows: Two-lane road running straight through dense mature pine forest with the canopy closing overhead; yellow centreline, white edge line, narrow paved shoulder then grass verge; low sun through cloud

records.summary: RV PARKS RUN 20+ MILES OFF ROUTE in east Texas — three consecutive days of it, and it is driving their day lengths
records.detail: 'Since the afternoons are now in the 90's and humid we are trying to stick with RV parks that have electricity. Boondocking would be miserable right now since I am too cheap to run the generator for 10 hours straight. It is really tough finding RV parks in this part of Texas. Yesterday we were 20 miles away from where I ended the ride. Tonight we were lucky, we are camping right on the route. Tomorrow we will be at least 20 miles away from the nearest RV park.'
records.cyclistIntel: READ THIS CAREFULLY, BECAUSE IT IS NOT NICK'S PROBLEM. Two separate facts are tangled together. (1) Formal commercial campgrounds are genuinely scarce and often 20+ miles off route in east Texas — that part transfers. (2) But their requirement is MAINS ELECTRICITY for air conditioning, which is why boondocking is off the table for them and why their days keep running long. Nick needs none of that. His options here are the national forest (p48-001), the state parks behind him, and the ask-locally pattern that has worked four times in Texas. So do NOT copy their day lengths through east Texas — this and the 90-mile Burton day were both shaped by a generator, not by cycling.
records.quote: It is really tough finding RV parks in this part of Texas.

records.summary: 72 F and STEAMY HUMID at 6:45am, peaking 96.8 F — the humidity is now there before dawn
records.detail: 'The morning at 6:45am was already 72 degrees and steamy humid. There was, however, a little bit of cloud cover so it didn't get as hot as it could have.' GPS temperature trace starts near 72 F, climbs through the day and is marked 96.8 F, averaging in the mid-80s. Compare the desert: 51-65 F starts were normal there.
records.cyclistIntel: THIS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT SHIFT SINCE LEAVING THE DESERT. In Arizona and west Texas the pre-dawn start bought genuinely cool air. Here it does not — 72 F and steamy at 6:45am means there is no cool window at all, so the early start no longer buys comfort, only a shorter exposure to the worst of it. Humid heat also limits evaporative cooling, so fluid needs rise while sustainable pace falls. Nick should expect east Texas day lengths to be shorter than the desert despite easier terrain, and should not assume the pre-dawn trick works the same way here.
records.quote: The morning at 6:45am was already 72 degrees and steamy humid.

photos.shows: Temperature trace starting near 72 F, climbing steadily and marked 96.8 F; elevation trace 0-480 ft with ~17 climb waypoints, marked 171 ft near the end; speed averaging 12.0 mph

records.summary: COLDSPRING TX — THE MASON JAR ('best burger I have had on this trip') and Rosalie's Cottage
records.detail: 'I made good time and had over 50 miles in the morning before I met Linda for lunch in Cold Springs. I found her hanging out with the ladies in Rosalie's Cottage. We went a few doors down to The Mason Jar and had an excellent cheeseburger to get me through the next 20 miles.' Captions: 'Apparently at The Mason Jar any hour can be happy hour' and 'It was the best burger I have had on this trip.' Coldspring is the San Jacinto County seat, roughly 50 miles into the day.
records.cyclistIntel: Named restaurant with the rider's highest food praise of the whole journey, at the 50-mile mark of a 69-mile day, with a second business (Rosalie's Cottage) a few doors away — so a walkable small-town centre with more than one option. Coldspring is also a county seat, which per the Anderson pattern means a courthouse square with likely shade and public restrooms. Best mid-route services point recorded in east Texas so far.
records.quote: It was the best burger I have had on this trip.

photos.caption: Apparently at The Mason Jar any hour can be happy hour.

records.summary: Shoulder provision is INCONSISTENT through the forest — 3-4 ft of paved shoulder in places, narrow to none elsewhere
records.detail: Established from four photographs on the same day. Two show a genuinely usable paved shoulder of roughly three to four feet outside the white edge line, with wet pavement and mown grass verge. Two others show the same road type with only a narrow paved edge, and one shows guardrail sections with the pavement running close to it. Surface throughout looks sound rather than chipseal.
records.cyclistIntel: Materially better than the Hill Country, where there was no shoulder at all for three days — but it comes and goes, so do not plan on it. Where it exists it is real room; where guardrail appears there is none. The good news is the surface: sound asphalt rather than the bone-rattling chipseal of the Sisters corridor, consistent with the county-maintenance pattern (p36-002).

photos.shows: Rider on a forest road with roughly 3-4 ft of sound paved shoulder outside the white edge line; wet pavement, mown grass verge, dense mixed forest both sides, a car approaching

photos.caption: Still some hills.
photos.shows: Forest road dipping and rising with guardrail on both sides at the low point; narrow paved edge, no usable shoulder through the guardrail section

records.summary: Hills lower but still 2,415 ft over 69 mi — eighth consecutive day above 2,000 ft of ascent
records.detail: 'The hills are getting lower, we are definitely leaving the Texas Hill Country.' GPS: 68.80 mi, 5:43:59, 12.0 mph, 2,415 ft. Elevation trace now runs between about 100 and 480 ft with a marked 171 ft near the end and roughly seventeen climb waypoints. Eighth straight day at 2,000+ ft (Days 39-46).
records.cyclistIntel: 35 ft of climbing per mile at 300 ft above sea level. The Texas signature holds: nothing named, no rest. Eight consecutive days now totalling well over 22,000 ft from Brackettville to Goodrich — that is the number to plan the Texas crossing against, and it is invisible if you only look at a map's relief. Reversed, Nick rides into it westbound with the Hill Country and the Sisters still ahead.
records.quote: The hills are getting lower, we are definitely leaving the Texas Hill Country.

records.summary: Southwest wind gave a push riding east, plus helpful cloud cover
records.detail: 'And a wind from the southwest gave me a little push.' Plus 'There was, however, a little bit of cloud cover so it didn't get as hot as it could have.' He covered over 50 miles before lunch and averaged 12.0 mph.
records.cyclistIntel: Inverts against Nick — a southwesterly is a headwind for him riding west through east Texas. Note how modest the effect is here compared with west Texas: this is a 'little push' rather than the 60-to-95-mile swing seen at Langtry (p40-001). Wind matters less east of the Pecos, where trees and terrain break it up; humidity and heat replace it as the limiting factor.
records.quote: a wind from the southwest gave me a little push

records.summary: Night 46: RV park RIGHT ON THE ROUTE near Goodrich TX — unnamed, and they call it luck
records.detail: 'Tonight we were lucky, we are camping right on the route.' Not named. Mains electricity confirmed, since that was their explicit requirement. A photograph shows the rider on a gravel drive with a 10 mph speed-limit sign and mown grass, mature trees around — consistent with a small wooded RV park. Goodrich is on US-190 near Livingston.
records.cyclistIntel: Worth identifying precisely, because the rider calls being ON the route lucky — the two nights either side were 20 miles off it. A named on-route site here would be a genuinely useful anchor. Shade likely, given the trees in the photograph and the pine country. Ask about tents. Note the alternative Nick has that they did not consider: Sam Houston National Forest dispersed camping, roughly 20 miles back (p48-001).
records.quote: Tonight we were lucky, we are camping right on the route.

photos.shows: Rider on a gravel drive with a '10 MPH' speed limit sign, mown grass, mature trees and a paved road behind — small wooded RV park

records.summary: SEVEN DOG CHASES IN ONE DAY — the airhorn used twice and confirmed 'pretty effective' again
records.detail: 'I got chased by dogs seven times today. Two got close enough that I used the airhorn. It is pretty effective.' Peak dog day of the entire journey, in the Big Thicket / east Texas piney woods on a 94-mile day. Escalation across Texas is now unmistakable: zero dogs in 1,028 miles of desert, two chases on his first Texas farming day (p33-002), three in one day near Bastrop (p46-001), now seven.
records.cyclistIntel: THE DOG PROBLEM PEAKS IN EAST TEXAS AND THE COUNTERMEASURE HOLDS. Seven chases, two requiring the horn, no incident. Two things to take from it. First, frequency: on a long day through populated piney woods, expect this repeatedly, not once — so the deterrent has to be reachable without stopping, which is why he keeps it in the handlebar bag. Second, the triage: five of seven needed nothing (outrun or ignored), two needed the horn. That matches the earlier pattern where a bellowed 'NO' handled most of them. For Nick the inversion still bites — he cannot rely on outrunning them into a headwind — so horn plus voice plus mirror, all three.
records.quote: I got chased by dogs seven times today. Two got close enough that I used the airhorn. It is pretty effective.

records.summary: LOGGING TRUCKS through the Big Thicket — heavy timber traffic on two-lane roads
records.detail: 'We saw a lot of logging activity today. When the logging trucks went past I could smell the pine. It smelt like Christmas.' The Big Thicket section is a working pine plantation, which Linda confirmed at the National Preserve visitor centre — so the timber traffic is industrial and continuous, not incidental.
records.cyclistIntel: A new traffic class and a serious one. Loaded logging trucks are heavy, wide, and shed bark and debris; they also run on schedules that do not respect the quiet-after-10am pattern (p36-001). The mitigation here is that the shoulder on this stretch is genuinely wide (p49-003), which is not true of the Hill Country roads. Note the compound: seven dog chases on the same day means repeated distraction on a road with heavy trucks. Weekday timber traffic will be worse than weekend.
records.quote: We saw a lot of logging activity today. When the logging trucks went past I could smell the pine.

photos.caption: There is a lot of logging activity and trucks filled with fragrant pine logs.

records.summary: WIDE paved shoulder with a rumble strip on the edge line — best shoulder recorded in Texas
records.detail: Established from two photographs on this leg. Both show a sound asphalt two-lane with a double yellow centreline, a white edge line with a continuous rumble strip cut ALONG it, and a genuinely wide paved shoulder beyond — several feet, clean, with mown grass verge past that. Dense pine plantation both sides. Surface is smooth asphalt, not chipseal.
records.cyclistIntel: BEST SHOULDER IN TEXAS, and the configuration is right: the rumble strip sits on the edge line rather than inside the shoulder, so it does not eat the rideable surface. Real room to be clear of the logging trucks (p49-002). This is what makes a 94-mile day possible here. Note the contrast with the Hill Country three days earlier, where there was no shoulder at all — Texas shoulder provision varies enormously and is worth anchoring per segment rather than per state.

photos.caption: Tall trees on both sides.
photos.shows: Sound asphalt two-lane with double yellow centreline, white edge line and a wide clean paved shoulder beyond; dense young pine plantation both sides, overcast
Same road type showing a continuous rumble strip cut along the white edge line with wide paved shoulder outside it; mown grass verge, pine plantation, overcast

records.summary: FLATTEST DAY OF THE JOURNEY by ratio — 1,529 ft over 94.26 mi, just 16 ft per mile
records.detail: GPS: 94.26 mi, 7:40:25, 12.3 mph, 1,529 ft ascent. Elevation trace runs between roughly 120 and 360 ft with a marked 240 ft at 1:20 and only ONE climb waypoint on the entire day. This ends an eight-day run of 2,000+ ft days (Days 39-46).
records.cyclistIntel: The Texas hills are done. 16 ft per mile against 38-66 ft per mile through the Hill Country. This is what makes 94 miles feasible in humid 85 F heat, and it is the profile Nick should expect from here east — the constraint shifts entirely from terrain to heat, humidity, dogs and traffic. Reversed, this is Nick's easy approach BEFORE the Texas climbing begins, so it is the stretch to bank miles on rather than the stretch to rest on.

photos.shows: Elevation trace confined between ~120 and 360 ft with a marked 240 ft at 1:20:27 and only one climb waypoint all day; speed averaging 12.3 mph; temperature averaging 85.5 F with peaks near 100 F

records.summary: BIG THICKET NATIONAL PRESERVE Visitors Center — and the 'forest' is a working pine plantation
records.detail: 'Today the route went through The Big Thicket region of Texas. There were a lot of really big pine trees on both sides of the road. That's all I could see. Linda visited The Big Thicket National Preserve Visitors Center. She found out it was a pine plantation.' A photograph shows a signed 'BIG THICKET' board beside a concrete path running along the highway.
records.cyclistIntel: An NPS visitor centre on route, which per the pattern (Judge Roy Bean at Langtry, LBJ at Johnson City) reliably means water, restrooms, shade and staff — valuable on a 94-mile day in humid heat. The pine-plantation detail is worth keeping honest: the wall of trees is managed timber, which explains the logging traffic and means the 'forest' offers no dispersed camping the way Sam Houston NF might. Confirm the visitor centre's hours and location relative to the route.
records.quote: She found out it was a pine plantation.

photos.caption: This is an actual bike trail. In the middle of the boondocks.
photos.shows: Concrete shared-use path running alongside a two-lane highway with a signed 'BIG THICKET' notice board, mown grass, pine and hardwood behind; drainage grate in the foreground

records.summary: 94 miles ridden to reach 'the only RV park in the area' — he nearly hitched a ride at 70
records.detail: 'I thought I was going to quit riding after 70 miles and hitch a ride to the only RV park in the area. I was feeling good so I finished out the 94 miles to Kirbyville.' Third consecutive day where the day length was set by RV park availability rather than by cycling (p46-006, p48-002). He was prepared to abandon riding and get in the vehicle to reach lodging.
records.cyclistIntel: ANOTHER DAY LENGTH THAT IS NOT NICK'S. 94 miles because there was one RV park; a cyclist with a tent, a national forest behind him and four successful ask-locally precedents in Texas has no such forcing. The transferable part is narrower: formal campgrounds in east Texas are genuinely sparse and can be the only option for 90+ miles. Plan Nick's east Texas nights on the informal pattern plus state and national forest land, and treat commercial parks as a bonus.
records.quote: I thought I was going to quit riding after 70 miles and hitch a ride to the only RV park in the area.

records.summary: Cloudy all morning and the rider is grateful — 85.5 F average, peaks near 100 F
records.detail: 'It was cloudy all morning. Good thing since it was hot enough without the sun.' GPS records an 85.5 F day average with the trace crossing 90 F by mid-ride and touching roughly 100 F. Start at 6:30am. Fourth consecutive day above an 85 F average in humid conditions.
records.cyclistIntel: Cloud cover is now doing what elevation did in the west — it is the only relief available, and it is not something you can plan around. Note the pattern across these east Texas days: every one has had either cloud or a wind push, and the rider notices when he gets neither. In humid heat at 85-100 F, a clear windless day on this stretch would be materially harder than anything the numbers suggest.
records.quote: It was cloudy all morning. Good thing since it was hot enough without the sun.

records.summary: Almost no wildlife in the plantation — one deer in the whole Big Thicket region
records.detail: 'I only saw one deer in the region.' Plus 'There were lots of Cattle Egrets today. A good share of them were hanging out close to the cattle. The cattle are scaring up bugs?' and captions noting fenced exotic deer-like animals and a curious longhorn. So: fenced livestock and birds, one wild deer across 94 miles.
records.cyclistIntel: Notable contrast with the Hill Country, where a herd of twenty appeared in a day. A managed pine plantation supports little game, so the wildlife collision risk drops sharply through the Big Thicket even as the DOG risk peaks (p49-001). Useful for the warning layer: it should fire on dogs here, not deer.
records.quote: I only saw one deer in the region.

records.summary: TEXAS TOOK 17 DAYS AND ROUGHLY 990 MILES — the state is a third of the whole route
records.detail: 'The sun has riz. The sun has set, and here we is, in Texas yet. This was what a volunteer at Big Bend NP told Linda. This has been true for the past 17 days but today is the last. Tonight is our last night in this big state. Tomorrow, Louisiana!' They entered Texas at El Paso on Day 30 with 965.9 cumulative miles and leave after Day 47 at 1,951.9 — so roughly 986 miles of Texas.
records.cyclistIntel: SCALE CHECK FOR THE PLAN. Texas alone is roughly 990 route miles and took this rider 17 riding days at an average of 58 miles a day, including one rest day, two 90+ mile days and the Three Sisters. For Nick that is about a third of his entire trip in one state, and it contains the goatheads, the worst wind, the no-services stretches, the dogs, the biggest climbing day and the only 300-mile communications dead zone. If any part of the 53-day plan needs contingency, it is Texas.
records.quote: here we is, in Texas yet

records.summary: Night 47: Kirbyville TX — the only RV park in the area, unnamed; last night in Texas
records.detail: Described as 'the only RV park in the area' and the reason the day ran to 94.26 miles. Not named. Mains electricity implied, since that was their stated requirement. Kirbyville is in Jasper County near the Louisiana line.
records.cyclistIntel: Worth identifying since it is apparently the sole option across a 90-mile stretch — but remember that is an RV constraint. Kirbyville is a real town, so a cyclist has motel and ask-locally options too. Position is useful: last stop before the Louisiana line, so a good place to resupply and check the bike before a new state.
records.quote: the only RV park in the area

records.summary: RIDER'S OWN MILEAGE: Texas alone was 1,011.0 miles; California + Arizona + New Mexico combined were 965.9
records.detail: 'Texas is one big state when biking the Southern Tier Route. California/Arizona/New Mexico combined were 965.9 miles. Texas alone was 1,011.0 miles.' His own figures, which supersede the ~986 mi estimate derived earlier from cumulative totals.
records.cyclistIntel: AUTHORITATIVE SCALE CHECK. Texas is a third of the route by itself and larger than the three western states put together. For Nick that means the state containing the goatheads, the worst wind, the no-services stretches, the dog escalation, the biggest climbing day and the only communications dead zone is also the longest single leg of his trip. If the 53-day plan gets contingency anywhere, it goes here.
records.quote: Texas alone was 1,011.0 miles.

records.summary: 78 F and 93% HUMIDITY at 6:15am — and locals say these temperatures are flirting with RECORD HIGHS
records.detail: 'Today it was 78 degrees and 93% humidity at 6:15 when I stepped out to disconnect water and electricity.' Caption: 'As long as afternoon highs are 90+ I am starting before 7am. The locals are saying these are flirting with record highs for this time of year.' GPS day average 86.5 F with the trace above 90 F all afternoon. This is the SECOND region where he reports record-setting heat, after Arizona (p18-003).
records.cyclistIntel: TWO THINGS, AND THE SECOND IS A CALIBRATION WARNING. First: 93% humidity at 6:15am is the extreme humidity reading of the dataset — there is no cool window at all in Louisiana, so the pre-dawn start buys only a shorter exposure. Second and more important: the rider has now reported RECORD HIGHS in both Arizona and Louisiana, which means this entire journal was ridden in an unusually hot spring. Every temperature figure in this dataset should be read as a high-end scenario rather than a typical one — including my own severity ratings on the weather records. Keep the operational rules (start before 7am, done by 2pm) and treat the numbers as a ceiling.
records.quote: 78 degrees and 93% humidity at 6:15... The locals are saying these are flirting with record highs for this time of year.

records.summary: HYDRATION ESCALATES: a GALLON of sweet tea at one lunch stop, on top of bottles
records.detail: 'After lunch the sun was out and the winds picked up (in my face). It was a little slower but all the BBQ and the gallon of sweet tea I drank let me finish the final 18 miles.' Set against his stated desert consumption of 5-6 bottles a day with vehicle resupply (p25-009), the humid Gulf states are pushing intake higher again.
records.cyclistIntel: The water problem changes character rather than going away. In the desert the constraint was AVAILABILITY — carrying enough between sources. Here water is everywhere but the demand is higher because humid heat blocks evaporative cooling. Nick will not need the desert carry capacity in Louisiana, but he will need to drink more than feels normal and should plan calorie-plus-electrolyte stops rather than just water. A gallon at one sitting is a striking number from a supported rider.
records.quote: all the BBQ and the gallon of sweet tea I drank let me finish the final 18 miles

records.summary: DEAD SNAKES on the roadside as bayou country begins — no alligators yet
records.detail: 'I have seen a few dead snakes on the side of the road (sorry, no pictures). Haven't seen any alligators yet.' Plus 'I have been passed by several pickup trucks pulling odd looking side-by-sides with about 4 feet of clearance' — swamp buggies, which indicate the terrain either side of the road. A local photograph shows a 99-pound alligator snapping turtle over 100 years old, caught the previous week on the Sabine River.
records.cyclistIntel: New hazard class entering the Gulf states. Dead snakes on the shoulder mean LIVE snakes crossing it, and in Louisiana that includes venomous species — cottonmouths in particular sun themselves on warm pavement and near standing water. Practical rules: do not step off the pavement into vegetation, look before putting a foot down at a stop, and be careful about roadside relief breaks. The snapping turtle is a curiosity but reinforces the point that anything near the water bites. No alligator sightings yet; expect them further east.
records.quote: I have seen a few dead snakes on the side of the road

photos.caption: Local man with the 99 pound Alligator Snapping Turtle he caught when he was fishing for catfish.

records.summary: BAYOU COUNTRY BEGINS — 'coffee brown water sitting everywhere', standing water on both sides
records.detail: 'The road is still miles and miles of really tall Loblolly Pine trees. No expansive vistas to see. The change now is seeing so much water. It is looking like bayou country with coffee brown water sitting everywhere.' Also 'May 16 and the corn here is 5 feet tall' — a fully humid growing season.
records.cyclistIntel: The complete inversion of the western half of this dataset. Where the Rio Grande was dry sand and the Yuha Desert had nothing, here water is standing on both sides of the road continuously. None of it is potable — it is bayou and swamp water — so it changes nothing about carrying, but it does mean the water-scarcity warnings must switch OFF east of the Sabine and be replaced by humidity, snakes and standing-water hazards. Marks a hard regional boundary in the planner: for Nick riding west, this is where water stops being free.
records.quote: It is looking like bayou country with coffee brown water sitting everywhere.

records.summary: Tall loblolly pines give continuous SHADE, and the road is very flat — 955 ft over 66 mi
records.detail: 'The trees were so tall I had shade. It was very flat so I was able to keep up my 12 mph cooling breeze.' GPS: 66.00 mi, 5:26:15, 12.1 mph, 955 ft ascent — 14 ft per mile, flatter even than the previous day. Elevation trace essentially level with a marked 202 ft at 3:33 and one climb waypoint. No vistas; the pine wall is continuous.
records.cyclistIntel: Two useful things. Continuous roadside shade is now the norm — the exact opposite of the 1,500 miles behind him, and it makes the humid heat survivable. And note his own tactic: at 12 mph he generates his own 'cooling breeze', so on flat shaded roads maintaining pace is a cooling strategy rather than an effort cost. That inverts the desert logic where slowing down saved you.
records.quote: The trees were so tall I had shade. It was very flat so I was able to keep up my 12 mph cooling breeze.

records.summary: SABINE RIVER — the Texas/Louisiana state line, crossed on a signed bridge
records.detail: 'I crossed the state line at the Sabine River before 9am.' A photograph shows the bridge approach with a green 'Sabine River' sign and a yellow 'SPEED LIMIT 55' warning, steel guardrail, and the brown river visible beyond. FIFTH STATE of the journey.
records.cyclistIntel: Hard, unambiguous anchor — a signed named river crossing that is also a state line, so it is doubly fixed. Note the bridge itself: guardrail hard against a narrow shoulder, which is the standard pinch-point pattern for river crossings on this route (compare Roosevelt Lake, p29 anchor). Short exposure, but no escape room on the deck.

photos.caption: The west bank of the Sabine River. My last glance at Texas.
photos.shows: Bridge approach with green 'Sabine River' sign and yellow 'SPEED LIMIT 55' plaque; steel guardrail beside a narrow shoulder; brown river and dense green banks beyond; broken cloud

records.summary: DE RIDDER LA — The Big Thicket BBQ, the 1910 Gothic Jailhouse, and a huge Canfor lumber mill
records.detail: 'Linda and I rendezvoused for lunch in De Ridder, LA. We walked to The Big Thicket BBQ and had really good Texas style BBQ. It was a neat place in a big old house. On the walk to the restaurant we stopped at the Gothic Jailhouse. A jailhouse built in 1910 as a showpiece.' Also 'This is where all the piney smelling logging trucks were headed. A huge Canfor lumber milling plant in De Ridder.' The town's information centre turns out to be the Sheriff's office. 'Myths and Legends' trail signs mark the area.
records.cyclistIntel: First real town in Louisiana and a good one — named restaurant, walkable centre, historic landmark, roughly 48 miles into the day. The Canfor mill explains the logging-truck traffic recorded the previous day and means industrial vehicle traffic converges here. Note the information centre being inside the Sheriff's office: unusual, but it means a staffed public building for questions and probably restrooms.
records.quote: We walked to The Big Thicket BBQ and had really good Texas style BBQ.

photos.caption: The Gothic Jailhouse in De Ridder LA. Supposedly haunted.
This is where all the piney smelling logging trucks were headed. A huge Canfor lumber milling plant in De Ridder.

records.summary: Sun out and headwind picked up after lunch — the afternoon wind pattern holds into Louisiana
records.detail: 'After lunch the sun was out and the winds picked up (in my face). It was a little slower but all the BBQ and the gallon of sweet tea I drank let me finish the final 18 miles.' Morning was shaded and calm; afternoon brought sun and a headwind. Same daily cycle first identified in west Texas (p36-005).
records.cyclistIntel: The afternoon-wind cycle is now confirmed across three very different regions — Arizona, west Texas and Louisiana. It is a daily thermal pattern, not weather, and it reinforces the operating rule: the productive hours are the calm shaded morning. Direction remains unreliable, so plan to be finishing rather than starting when it builds.
records.quote: After lunch the sun was out and the winds picked up (in my face).

records.summary: Night 48: small five-site RV park at SUGARTOWN LA, 18 miles east of De Ridder
records.detail: 'We are camping tonight in a five spot rv park 18 miles outside of town. Quiet little place that was a pleasant surprise.' Five sites only, unnamed, at Sugartown on LA-26. Water and electricity confirmed by the fact he disconnected both in the morning.
records.cyclistIntel: Tiny and unnamed but on route and pleasant. With only five sites it could easily be full, so not a site to depend on — but a five-space rural park is exactly the kind of place where a cyclist with a tent gets squeezed in when an RV cannot. Shade likely given the pine country. Worth identifying; it is the first Louisiana lodging in the dataset.
records.quote: a five spot rv park 18 miles outside of town. Quiet little place that was a pleasant surprise.

records.summary: Stiflingly humid Louisiana day: 76F / 83% humidity at DAWN, avg 89.9F, peak 104.0F mid-afternoon
records.detail: Day began at 76F with 83% relative humidity before sunrise. GPS temperature trace averaged 89.9F over 7:17 of riding and touched 104.0F at 3:48:42 into the ride. Rider described the air as 'stiflingly humid'.
records.cyclistIntel: Louisiana humidity, not the air temperature, is the limiter here. 76F at dawn with 83% RH means there is NO cool morning window to exploit the way there is in West Texas or Arizona — sweat does not evaporate, so cooling fails and the effective load is far above the dry-air equivalent. The done-by-2pm rule that works in the desert does not buy Nick as much here because the start is already warm; what it does buy is avoiding the 100F+ afternoon spike. Plan Louisiana days as EARLY starts for the humidity, not for the temperature. NOTE: this journal was ridden in an unusually hot spring (see source heatCalibration) — treat these figures as a high-end scenario, not a Louisiana baseline.
records.quote: stiflingly humid

records.summary: 86 miles with under 600 ft of total gain — essentially dead flat, and the only real incline all day is the Atchafalaya River bridge
records.detail: GPS reported 584 ft of ascent across 86.21 miles. The rider singled out the Atchafalaya River bridge as 'the first steep incline I had seen in three days'. Everything else was rice, crawfish, corn and sugar cane fields at near sea level.
records.cyclistIntel: This is the flattest sustained stretch in the whole journal and it runs for three-plus days. For Nick riding east-to-west this is the OPPOSITE of a warning — it is a bankable mileage opportunity early in his trip while his legs are still green. The bridges over the Atchafalaya and Mississippi are the only gradient, and they are short. Flat also means NO shade, NO descent to coast on, and continuous pedalling, so the fatigue here is heat-and-monotony fatigue, not climbing fatigue. Direction is irrelevant on terrain this flat — no inversion discount applies.
records.quote: the first steep incline I had seen in three days
records.anchorNote: extent applied west→east per the source rule

records.summary: Atchafalaya River bridge — the single named gradient on an 86-mile flat day
records.detail: Called out by the rider as the only steep incline in three days of riding. Carries most of the day's 584 ft of gain.
records.cyclistIntel: Short, isolated bridge climb. Worth knowing about only because it is the one place Nick will need a gear on this stretch, and because bridge decks in Louisiana routinely have narrow or absent shoulders with a raised curb and expansion joints. Approach it expecting a pinch point rather than a climb.
records.road: UNRESOLVED — verify which crossing the ACA route uses

records.summary: THREE dog chases in one day — air horn used on one, and it worked
records.detail: Rider was chased three separate times on this day. He used the air horn on one of them and noted with satisfaction that the owner could hear it: 'It's really satisfying when you know the owner can hear the loud horn.'
records.cyclistIntel: Louisiana rural-road dog density is the highest recorded anywhere in this journal — three chases in a single 86-mile day, against isolated single incidents in Texas and none in the desert. This CONFIRMS the air horn as a working countermeasure and adds a second benefit: it is loud enough to reach the owner's house, which is the only thing that changes behaviour long-term. For Nick, the operational rule for rural Louisiana and Mississippi is: air horn mounted where it can be reached without looking down, rear-view mirror in use, and the bellowed 'NO' as the first response. Do NOT try to outsprint them on flat road with loaded bags. Dogs do not invert with direction — this hazard is identical whichever way Nick rides it.
records.quote: It's really satisfying when you know the owner can hear the loud horn.
records.anchorNote: extent applied west→east per the source rule

records.summary: BUNKIE LA — Miss Leslie at Griffin's Antiques & Main Street Market opened on a CLOSED Sunday for apple pie; rider explicitly recommends her to Southern Tier riders
records.detail: The rider singles out Miss Leslie by name and recommends the stop to other Southern Tier cyclists. She opened up on a day the shop was closed. Apple pie; leftovers eaten for breakfast the next morning (see page 54 photo).
records.cyclistIntel: A named, human, verified-friendly stop in a small town — the highest-value kind of resupply intel because it does not appear on any map or app. Bunkie is a real town with services. Worth routing through deliberately rather than past. Caveat: this depends on one person still being there in Nick's riding year; treat as a lead to check, not a guaranteed service.
records.quote: Miss Leslie

records.summary: '57 Chevy mounted on the roof of a Bunkie gas station
records.detail: Landmark noted in passing at Bunkie.
records.cyclistIntel: Useful as a visual confirmation waypoint — if Nick sees the car on the roof he is in Bunkie and at the Miss Leslie stop.

records.summary: Agricultural transition: rice and crawfish fields give way to corn and sugar cane; first Spanish moss of the trip
records.detail: The rider tracked the crop change across the day and noted the first Spanish moss he had seen on the ride.
records.cyclistIntel: Not a hazard but a genuinely useful positional cue set. Crawfish ponds and flooded rice mean standing water alongside the road, which in May-June Louisiana means mosquitoes at dawn and dusk and higher humidity at road level. First Spanish moss marks entry into the true Gulf coastal zone. For Nick riding westbound these cues run in reverse: he loses the moss and moves from cane and corn back into rice and crawfish as he heads toward the Atchafalaya Basin.

records.summary: MORGANZA FLOODWAY — standing flood water across the area from torrential rain days earlier
records.detail: The rider arrived at the Morganza Floodway to find standing flood water left from torrential rain several days before. The Raccourci Old River dike was also noted.
records.cyclistIntel: The Morganza Floodway is by design a place that floods, and this shows it holds water for DAYS after a rain event, not hours. For Nick this is a genuine route-continuity risk, not just wet feet: standing water on a low floodway road can be deep, can hide debris and dropoffs, and can close the road outright. This is the one place on the Louisiana flats where Nick should check conditions before committing to the day, especially in spring. Build a bail-out into the day plan that crosses the floodway rather than one that has no alternative. Not direction-dependent.

records.summary: Another RV-driven day length: three options weighed were a 53-mi boondock behind a truck stop, 86 mi to a real RV park, or stop midway and drive back
records.detail: The support crew weighed a 53-mile stop boondocking behind a truck stop alongside parked stock trucks, an 86-mile push to a proper RV park, or stopping the rider midway and driving back. They took the 86.
records.cyclistIntel: The 86-mile day length here was chosen by RV hookup availability, NOT by what the cycling day wanted. Nick must discard this day boundary entirely. What IS transferable: there is a gap in bookable overnight capacity between Chicot State Park and the Morganza area, and the stopgap in that gap is a truck stop — which for a self-supported cyclist means water, food, toilets and shelter, but not a legitimate place to sleep. Nick should plan this stretch around Chicot State Park at one end and confirmed lodging near Morganza or New Roads at the other.

records.summary: CHICOT STATE PARK, LA — bookable state park, ON ROUTE, spots found OPEN on arrival after they had planned to backtrack 15 miles. Rider: 'a very nice state park, our spot was shaded and quiet'
records.detail: Louisiana state park, bookable. Rider explicitly praised it: shaded and quiet site. This was the night BEFORE Day 50 and the departure point for the ride. ARRIVAL DETAIL from page 51: they had been planning to drive backwards about 15 miles to find a spot; on arrival Linda found RV camping spots open at the park itself. Rider: 'now we are right on the route. Score one for Linda.'
records.cyclistIntel: HIGH-VALUE ANCHOR: a bookable public campground with a positive first-hand review, and SHADE — which is the scarce resource in Louisiana, more than water. Chicot State Park has developed sites. Unlike most nights in this journal this one is not RV-dependent; a cyclist can reserve here. Put this on Nick's Louisiana lodging shortlist and book ahead, because Louisiana state parks fill on weekends. *** STRENGTHENED BY p51 ***: this is now a SIXTH instance of the ask-on-arrival pattern, and the most relevant kind for Nick — a bookable public park that showed no availability in advance but had space on the day. The rider also states explicitly that Chicot is ON THE ROUTE, which removes the off-route penalty that spoils most of the RV anchors in this dataset. Combined with shade, water and toilets, this is the strongest Louisiana lodging record in the file.
records.quote: now we are right on the route. Score one for Linda.

records.summary: MORGANZA LA area — RV park reached at the end of the 86-mile day (chosen over a truck-stop boondock at 53 mi)
records.detail: End of Day 50. The crew drove past a 53-mile truck-stop boondock option to reach a proper RV park with hookups in the Morganza area.
records.cyclistIntel: RV-park anchor, hookup-driven. Value to Nick is limited — RV parks near Morganza may or may not take tents — but it establishes that SOMETHING with facilities exists in the Morganza / New Roads area, which matters because the surrounding stretch is agricultural with thin services. Verify tent policy before relying on it.

records.summary: US-61 'SCENIC HIGHWAY' THROUGH BATON ROUGE — busy enough to force shoulder riding all day, and the shoulders are ROUGH. Rider: 'It wasn't my favorite day of the ride.'
records.detail: The rider's summary of the whole day: 'The majority of roads were so busy I had to be on the shoulder most of the day, and the shoulders were rough.' The Scenic Highway is another name for Highway 61. He describes the first 10 miles as too busy and loud to enjoy, then a stretch through a very poor section of town, then downtown. After the levee bike path ended he was 'back on a busy highway with a rough shoulder'.
records.cyclistIntel: TOP-PRIORITY NARROW/ROUGH SHOULDER RECORD for the Louisiana leg — this is exactly the class of warning Nick asked for first. The distinction here is important: the shoulder EXISTS, so this is not a no-shoulder pinch, it is a forced-to-ride-a-bad-surface day. Traffic volume removes the option of taking the lane, and the shoulder surface removes the option of riding it comfortably. Expect rim-and-tyre punishment, debris in the shoulder, and no ability to pick a line. DIRECTION MATTERS HERE: they rode Morganza -> Baton Rouge -> Carville, so the rough US-61 shoulder north of Baton Rouge landed in their morning. Nick rides Carville -> Baton Rouge -> Morganza, which puts that same rough northbound US-61 stretch in his HOT AFTERNOON, on top of a full day's fatigue. That is a worse combination than the journal experienced. Plan Nick's Baton Rouge day short, or start it early enough that US-61 is behind him before the afternoon heat.
records.quote: The majority of roads were so busy I had to be on the shoulder most of the day, and the shoulders were rough. I had a headwind most of the day. It wasn't my favorite day of the ride.
records.to: Morganza (Nick's direction) / Morganza to Baton Rouge (journal direction)

photos.caption: A good share of the day was like this.
photos.shows: Rider on a narrow rough shoulder with no buffer, an oncoming semi truck and a queue of cars in the adjacent lane closing on him; visible cracking and debris on the shoulder surface; red circular regulatory signs on both shoulders further up the road.

records.summary: MISSISSIPPI LEVEE BIKE PATH — close to 20 MILES of off-highway paved path through Baton Rouge. The one good part of a bad day.
records.detail: Rider: 'The nice part of the ride today was a bike path on top of the dike that went for close to 20 miles.' Paved with a painted yellow centerline, atop the levee, water/canal on one side and mowed levee grass on the other.
records.cyclistIntel: THE SINGLE BEST PIECE OF ROUTE INTELLIGENCE ON THE LOUISIANA LEG. Close to 20 continuous miles with zero motor traffic, in the middle of the day's worst road. For Nick this is not merely pleasant, it is a SAFETY SUBSTITUTE for 20 miles of US-61-grade shoulder riding — it should be treated as a hard routing requirement, not an option. Get on it and stay on it as long as it runs. Two caveats that matter: (1) the levee is elevated and completely unshaded and unsheltered, so headwind and sun are worse up there than on the road below — see the page 54 record on closed trail segments; (2) page 54 documents this same trail system further downriver having FENCED-OFF CLOSED SEGMENTS forcing riders down onto no-shoulder River Road. Verify continuity for Nick's riding year before depending on it.
records.quote: The nice part of the ride today was a bike path on top of the dike that went for close to 20 miles.
records.road: Mississippi River levee path / Mississippi River Trail
records.anchorNote: extent applied west→east per the source rule

photos.caption: The bike trail on top of the Mississippi dike. It was nice to see a bike trail again.
photos.shows: Paved path roughly 8-10 ft wide with a yellow centerline running dead straight along the levee crest; chain-link fence and a canal/borrow pit on the left, mowed grass and a distant town on the right; no traffic, no shade anywhere in frame.

records.summary: HEADWIND most of the day for the journal rider heading southeast — which INVERTS TO A TAILWIND for Nick heading northwest
records.detail: Rider: 'I had a headwind most of the day.' Avg speed only 10.6 mph over 6:37 on a day with 755 ft of gain in 70 miles, i.e. effectively flat — the low average is wind and traffic, not terrain. He added: 'It was so hot the headwind was almost welcome.'
records.cyclistIntel: DIRECTION INVERSION, HIGH CONFIDENCE. Their track ran generally south and east down the river; Louisiana spring prevailing wind is from the south/southeast, which is consistent with the headwind they reported. Nick rides this stretch northwest-bound, so the same synoptic pattern gives him a TAILWIND. Do not copy their 10.6 mph average into Nick's planning for this stretch — it is a headwind number and he is unlikely to be paying it.
