The honest caveat: this is one day's wind, and Gulf wind is variable. Treat it as 'Nick is more likely to be helped than hurt here', not as a guarantee. Also carry across the observation that in this heat a headwind provides real evaporative cooling — a tailwind day at 90F+ and 80% humidity means NO airflow relative to the rider and materially worse heat load. Nick's tailwind advantage on this stretch costs him cooling.
records.quote: It was so hot the headwind was almost welcome.

records.summary: Humid and hot: avg 88.8F over the ride, climbing past 100F in the last two hours
records.detail: GPS temperature trace started near 68-70F and rose steadily, crossing 100F in the final stretch; day average 88.8F. Total ascent 755 ft over 70.35 mi.
records.cyclistIntel: The temperature curve here is the argument for Nick's early-finish rule in Louisiana. The last two hours are where the day goes from hot to dangerous, and they are also — in Nick's reversed direction — where the rough US-61 shoulder sits. Two bad things stack in his afternoon. Shorten the Baton Rouge day.

records.summary: First ~10 miles out of Morganza on the Scenic Highway: too busy and loud to be pleasant, then a stretch through a very poor section of town
records.detail: Rider: 'It was too busy and loud for me to enjoy the scenery in the first 10 miles. Then it turned into a tour through a very poor section of town.'
records.cyclistIntel: For Nick this is the FINAL 10 miles of his Baton Rouge-to-Morganza day rather than the first — arriving tired into heavy traffic and noise instead of leaving fresh into it. Worth planning to be off this section before dark. The rider's note about the neighbourhood is his observation, not a hazard claim; the actionable part is that this is an urban-fringe stretch with no services worth stopping for and heavy traffic.

records.summary: Downtown Baton Rouge is genuinely nice, with a vibrant riverfront district — science center and museums, well attended
records.detail: Rider: 'The route did finally get to the downtown area that was quite nice. There was also a very vibrant area near the Mississipi with a science center and other museums.' Photographed the Louisiana State Capitol and the Old State Capitol (now a museum).
records.cyclistIntel: A real rest-and-refuel opportunity mid-day, with shade, food, water, restrooms and air conditioning in a day that otherwise has none of those. If Nick is going to take one long break on the Baton Rouge day, take it here. It is also directly on the route rather than a detour.

photos.caption: The Louisiana State Capitol Building.
photos.shows: Louisiana State Capitol, the art-deco tower.

photos.caption: The 'Old State Capitol' Building. It now is used as a museum. Just across the street from a science center that had a lot of people visiting.
photos.shows: Gothic-revival Old State Capitol, castellated, on the Baton Rouge riverfront.

records.summary: Jersey-recognition effect: kids at a stoplight shouted 'Iowa Hawkeyes!' and 'Caitlyn Clark!' — happens EVERY time he wears the team jersey
records.detail: Rider: 'Every time I have worn my Hawkeye jersey I have gotten a shout out.'
records.cyclistIntel: Minor but real: recognisable kit generates friendly interaction and, more usefully, makes a cyclist a person rather than an obstacle to the drivers around him. Not a hazard record. Worth noting for Nick that a conversation-starting jersey has a measurable effect on how often locals engage helpfully.
records.quote: Every time I have worn my Hawkeye jersey I have gotten a shout out.

records.summary: JOHN JAMES AUDUBON BRIDGE — brown signed Mississippi River crossing on the Day 51 route, photographed with the sign
records.detail: Brown guide sign reading 'John James Audubon Bridge' photographed at the bridge approach. Cable-stayed bridge with a tall white tower; concrete deck, guardrail with a narrow strip outside it, farm field alongside the approach; light two-way traffic in the photo.
records.cyclistIntel: HIGH-PRECISION GEOGRAPHIC ANCHOR — a uniquely named, mapped structure with a single fixed location, which makes it one of the most resolvable records in the Louisiana set. It also pins the Day 51 river crossing: the route leaves Morganza, crosses the Mississippi here on LA-10, then turns south on US-61 for Baton Rouge. The GPS elevation trace confirms it: the day is dead flat except for one bump between roughly 1:20 and 2:05 elapsed, with speed spikes above 20 mph — that is the climb over and descent off this bridge. For Nick this is the Day 51 record's key waypoint and a mandatory shoulder-width verification target, because the ride-quality difference between a bridge with a usable shoulder and one without is the whole safety question on a long high crossing.

photos.caption: (no caption)
photos.shows: Brown 'John James Audubon Bridge' guide sign at the bridge approach; cable-stayed tower ahead; concrete deck rising, guardrail, black-and-yellow chevron object marker; two cars and a truck on the deck.

records.summary: CARVILLE LA area — RV park found five miles off the day's stopping point; crew noted ongoing difficulty finding sites with electrical hookups in Louisiana
records.detail: Rider: 'Linda found an rv park five miles away from today's stopping point. Not bad considering our difficulties finding camping places with electrical hookups.' The rider stopped at Carville and was shuttled the last five miles.
records.cyclistIntel: Hookup-driven and five miles OFF route, so of limited direct use — but the important signal is the crew's stated difficulty: Louisiana between Baton Rouge and New Orleans is THIN on established campground capacity. For a self-supported rider that thinness is worse, not better, because he cannot absorb a five-mile off-route shuttle at the end of a hot 70-mile day. Nick should treat the Baton Rouge -> Carville -> River Ridge corridor as a stretch requiring booked lodging arranged in advance, and should consider a motel here rather than gambling on camping.
records.quote: Not bad considering our difficulties finding camping places with electrical hookups.

records.summary: RIVER ROAD, BATON ROUGE -> NEW ORLEANS: a genuine MIXED BAG — long stretches of heavy traffic with a wide smooth shoulder alternating with heavy traffic on narrow roads with NONE
records.detail: Rider: 'The ride was another mixed bag of heavy traffic/narrow roads, heavy traffic/wide nice shoulder and fun bike trails.' Two photos make the contrast explicit: one captioned 'One of the nicer busy roads. A wide smooth shoulder to ride on', another captioned 'One of the not so nice busy streets. Many times I had to pull off and let a string of upset car drivers pass by.'
records.cyclistIntel: THIS IS THE CENTRAL WARNING FOR NICK'S NEW ORLEANS APPROACH and it is a span, not a point — the character of River Road changes repeatedly over 76 miles with no way to predict it from a map. The critical detail is the second photo's caption: on the bad sections there was not enough room to be passed at all, so he had to STOP AND PULL OFF THE ROAD to let queues of hostile drivers by. That is the worst shoulder situation recorded anywhere in this journal, worse than the West Texas interstate shoulders, because the traffic is dense, local, industrial and impatient rather than fast and sparse. Operational rules for Nick: run a bright rear light in daylight on this whole corridor, use the mirror continuously, and be willing to stop rather than hold a lane — the rider's instinct to pull off was correct. Take the levee path wherever it exists (p54-002) specifically to avoid these sections. This hazard does NOT invert with direction: shoulder width and traffic density are the same whichever way Nick rides. What DOES invert is where in his day it falls — the New Orleans end is his START, so he meets the worst of it fresh and early, which is a real advantage.
records.quote: Many times I had to pull off and let a string of upset car drivers pass by.
records.road: River Road (LA-75 / LA-44 / LA-18 / LA-628 corridor)

photos.caption: One of the nicer busy roads. A wide smooth shoulder to ride on.
photos.shows: Wide clean asphalt shoulder, roughly 6-8 ft, solid white edge line, good surface with no cracking; a white SUV and a box truck in the travel lane ahead; grass verge and scrub to the right.

photos.caption: One of the not so nice busy streets. Many times I had to pull off and let a string of upset car drivers pass by.
photos.shows: Rider in high-visibility yellow on a narrow two-lane street with NO shoulder and no edge line buffer; a large white truck occupying the adjacent lane inches away; parked car, wheelie bin and houses at the roadside.

records.summary: LEVEE BIKE TRAILS along the Mississippi from Carville toward New Orleans — 'fun bike trails', ~30 ft above the surrounding land
records.detail: Rider: 'When I was on top of the levy on the bike trail I was able to look out over the river.' Photo caption: 'Bike trail on the levee. It is about 30 feet higher than either side so I had a bird's eye view of both sides.' Paved path with a yellow centerline, swamp and lily pads on the river side, mowed levee grass on the town side.
records.cyclistIntel: Second confirmation that a usable levee path network exists on this corridor, and the primary means of avoiding the no-shoulder River Road sections in p54-001. ROUTE IT DELIBERATELY. But read this record together with p54-004, which documents the same trail system having fenced closures — the trail is the plan, and River Road is the unavoidable fallback. The 30-ft elevation has two consequences Nick should plan for: total exposure to sun and wind with no shade anywhere on the levee crest, and a climb up and down every time he transitions between the trail and the road, which the closure record shows can happen repeatedly.
records.quote: It is about 30 feet higher than either side so I had a bird's eye view of both sides.

photos.caption: Bike trail on the levee.
photos.shows: Loaded dark blue steel touring bike with rear rack and two bottles parked on a narrow paved path with a yellow centerline; mowed levee grass falling away left, lily-pad swamp and dense tree line right; no shade on the path itself.

photos.caption: Street view of me on the bike trail. There were no other bikes on the trail.
photos.shows: Rider in high-viz yellow with a hydration vest approaching on a paved path; large truck at right, parked white car and buildings behind — the trail here runs immediately alongside street traffic.

records.summary: *** AMENDED BY p56-001 — DOWNGRADED *** Historical account of Mississippi River Trail CLOSED SEGMENTS (fenced, no warning) forcing a drop onto no-shoulder River Road. The rider ACTUALLY RODE this segment two days later and found it OPEN and busy.
records.detail: From a previous ride of the same stretch: 'I hit several places where the trail was closed so I had to drop down to River Road which was very busy and no shoulder. I tried several times to get back on the trail; I would climb back up the levee and ride a quarter mile then hit a fence. Turn around, go back the quarter mile and get back on River Road. I did this three times before I just quit trying and went on the busy street.' He states this openly as a beef with the State of Louisiana, and hoped on this trip that the trail would be open from River Ridge KOA to Audubon Park.
records.cyclistIntel: *** AMENDED. READ THE AMENDMENT FIRST. *** When I first recorded this I rated it severity 4 as a live must-verify hazard. That was wrong to leave standing: page 56 of the same journal has the rider riding this exact segment on 22 May 2025 and finding 13 continuous miles of OPEN, well-used levee trail from River Ridge through to Audubon Park, with no fence and no detour reported. See p56-001. SO: the closure account below is HISTORICAL, from the rider's own earlier ride of this stretch years before, and the 2025 evidence contradicts it as a current condition. Downgraded to severity 2. What still transfers, and why this record is kept rather than deleted: MRT closures are a maintenance phenomenon with a documented precedent on this exact segment, they appear WITHOUT signage, and the fallback when one occurs is busy River Road with NO shoulder. So the correct posture for Nick is not alarm but a five-minute check of current MRT status before his New Orleans day, plus the knowledge that if he does meet a fence, each levee access ramp is a half-mile round-trip commitment and River Road is the answer. DIRECTION: Nick rides this outbound from New Orleans, so any backtracking lands in his fresh, cool morning — the best possible time to absorb it.
records.quote: I did this three times before I just quit trying and went on the busy street.
records.road: Mississippi River Trail levee path, with River Road as forced fallback
records.verifyTarget: Mississippi River Trail closure status, River Ridge to Audubon Park

records.summary: The industrial corridor: giant petroleum and chemical plants on the land side, barge terminals on the river side. 'Dull, drab, industrial' for essentially the whole day.
records.detail: Rider: 'This section of the Mississippi is anything but scenic. On the left side of River Road were giant petroleum and other chemical production sites. On the right side of the road/bike trail the river was just a big industrial district. It was lined with shipping sites with lots of barges and infrastructure to load barges. Dull, drab, industrial.' He climbed the levee expecting a majestic river and photographed the drab industrial view instead.
records.cyclistIntel: Rated 2 rather than 1 because this is not only an aesthetics note. An 80-mile continuous petrochemical corridor means: heavy industrial TRUCK traffic feeding those plants onto the same River Road with the no-shoulder sections (compounding p54-001), plant-gate shift-change traffic surges at predictable hours, air quality worth considering on a day of hard breathing in high heat, and essentially no shade or public services because the land is all industrial. Manage expectations too — there is no scenic payoff to sustain morale on this stretch, so the day should be built around getting through it rather than enjoying it.
records.quote: Dull, drab, industrial.

photos.caption: After climbing to the top of the levee and expecting to see a majestic river I saw a drab industrial area.
photos.shows: View from the levee crest over barge terminals and loading infrastructure on the river.

photos.caption: Big chemical plants on the land side of the levee.
photos.shows: Large petrochemical plant with stacks and process towers immediately adjacent to the levee.

records.summary: *** WATER-CARRY REQUIREMENT *** Supported rider needed resupply EVERY 20-25 MILES on this corridor and was 'drinking a lot of water' — at 91.9F average and over 100F peak
records.detail: Rider: 'Linda meets up with me every 20 to 25 miles. I replentish my water (I am drinking a lot of water) and eat something to keep the calorie train going.' GPS average temperature 91.9F over 6:43, with the trace crossing 100F for most of the second half and spiking near 5:33 elapsed. He also rode a 14 mph headwind and reported 76 miles 'really drained me'.
records.cyclistIntel: THE MOST OPERATIONALLY IMPORTANT NUMBER ON THE LOUISIANA LEG. A rider with a chase vehicle chose 20-25 mile resupply intervals in this heat and humidity. Nick has no chase vehicle. He must either carry enough for 25 miles at Louisiana consumption rates — which is materially more than desert planning suggests, because humidity blocks evaporative cooling so sweat rate goes UP while cooling efficiency goes DOWN — or confirm commercial water stops at that interval along the industrial River Road corridor, where p54-004 establishes the land is almost all private industrial with few public services. Cross-check this interval against the p54-004 services gap when planning. Note also what the crew supplied: COLD grapes, cantaloupe and an ice cream sandwich, which the rider called the highlights of the day. Cold and wet calories, not bars. For Nick that argues for planning stops at places with a freezer or ice, and for treating a gas-station ice stop as a legitimate cooling intervention rather than a luxury. CALIBRATION CAVEAT: this trip ran in an unusually hot spring — see the source heatCalibration field. The 20-25 mile interval is a hot-scenario number, but it is the right one to plan against.
records.quote: Linda meets up with me every 20 to 25 miles. I replentish my water (I am drinking a lot of water)

records.summary: 14 MPH HEADWIND on top of 76 miles and near-100F heat — 'really drained me'. Inverts to a tailwind for Nick.
records.detail: Rider: '76 miles in this heat and humidity, plus a 14 mph headwind really drained me.' Avg speed 11.4 mph over 6:43 on 610 ft of gain in 76.67 mi — flat ground, so the low average is wind.
records.cyclistIntel: Second consecutive day of a quantified headwind on a southeast-bound track, which strengthens the inference in p53-N1: the prevailing Gulf flow on this corridor is from the south/southeast in May. Nick rides northwest-bound and should expect this as a TAILWIND, and should NOT plan against the journal's 11.4 mph average on this stretch. Two honest caveats. First, Gulf wind is variable and a single synoptic pattern is not a rule. Second, and more important operationally: a 14 mph tailwind at 92F and high humidity means near-zero airflow across the rider, which removes his evaporative cooling entirely. The wind that helps Nick's speed on this corridor will hurt his heat management, and on the elevated unshaded levee path there is nothing else to cool him. Plan Nick's Louisiana tailwind days on TIME OF DAY, not on the speed the tailwind seems to promise.
records.quote: 76 miles in this heat and humidity, plus a 14 mph headwind really drained me.

records.summary: NEW ORLEANS ROUTING: the ACA route 'parades you through town, through the French Quarter then out' — advice received was to AVOID the hours when tourists and revelers are out
records.detail: Rider: 'The route parades you through town, through the French Quarter then out. The advice I have received is to avoid the times that the tourists and revelers are out in downtown/French Quarters.' He deliberately rode longer than he wanted (76 mi) to stop 10-15 miles short of the city, then took the next day as a rest day and crossed the city on the day after.
records.cyclistIntel: TIME-OF-DAY ROUTING CONSTRAINT, and it lands early in Nick's trip since he starts at Pensacola and rides west. The French Quarter on a loaded touring bike is a crowd-navigation problem, not a traffic problem: pedestrians stepping off kerbs, rideshare stopping in lanes, and at night intoxicated crowds. The transferable rule is to cross the Quarter EARLY IN THE MORNING. That maps well onto Nick's direction: heading west out of New Orleans, the Quarter is at the very start of his riding day, so an early departure solves it naturally — whereas the journal rider approaching from the east had it at the END of a day and had to spend a whole extra day to sequence it safely. Nick gets this one for free by riding the opposite way. Second transferable point: the rider treated the city crossing as a day of its own with a rest day before it. Nick, with zero spare days in 53, cannot copy that, which makes the early start not optional.
records.quote: The advice I have received is to avoid the times that the tourists and revelers are out in downtown/French Quarters.
records.road: ACA Southern Tier route through downtown New Orleans

records.summary: Plantation tours on the town side of the levee cost $25 to $84 — the crew skipped them for time
records.detail: Rider: 'On the town side of the levy there were a couple amazing plantations to see. Linda found out to tour the plantations it was anywhere from $25.00 to $84.00. With limited time and having seen other old mansions she opted to move on.'
records.cyclistIntel: Cost and time data point for a corridor that otherwise has no attractions. With zero spare days in Nick's 53, this is a skip. Noted only so the decision is already made rather than made at the gate.

records.summary: Egrets and wading birds in the swampy strip between the levee trail and the river
records.detail: Rider was 'entertained by scaring up the egrets and other wading birds' in the swampy area next to the river.
records.cyclistIntel: Harmless and a morale note, but it confirms standing swamp water immediately alongside the levee trail — which means MOSQUITOES at dawn and dusk on exactly the path Nick will want to ride early in the morning. Carry repellent and do not plan long stationary breaks on the levee at first light.

records.summary: UNRESOLVED: at least one Mississippi River crossing on the Day 52 track, bridge identity NOT determinable from the map — and bike legality differs sharply between the candidates
records.detail: The GPS map shows the track running down the river corridor from Carville past Donaldsonville, Convent, Lutcher, Gramercy and Vacherie, through the LaPlace/Reserve area, then past Luling to the red pin at River Ridge, with a black-and-white checkered waypoint marker near the Luling/Destrehan area. The trace appears to change banks at least once, but the map resolution does not establish where or on which structure.
records.cyclistIntel: FLAGGED DELIBERATELY RATHER THAN GUESSED. This matters because the candidate crossings on this stretch are not equivalent for a cyclist: the Gramercy / Veterans Memorial Bridge on LA-3213 is the crossing the ACA route conventionally uses and has a shoulder; the Hale Boggs Memorial Bridge carries I-310 at Luling and interstate bridges are frequently bicycle-prohibited; the Huey P. Long Bridge further downriver is a separate case again. Getting this wrong puts Nick at a bridge he cannot legally or safely ride, with no alternative for many miles. RESOLUTION TASK: overlay the ACA Southern Tier GPX for section 6 on this corridor and identify the crossing, then verify current bicycle access for that specific structure. Do not infer it from this map.
records.road: River Road corridor with at least one Mississippi crossing — structure UNRESOLVED
records.verifyTarget: which Mississippi River bridge the ACA route uses between Carville and River Ridge, and its bicycle legality

records.summary: Miss Leslie's apple pie survived as next-day breakfast: 'Apple pie for breakfast. What a treat.'
records.detail: Photo caption on Day 52 morning, two days after the Bunkie stop on page 52.
records.cyclistIntel: Continuity confirmation for the p52-004 Bunkie record and a small practical point: bought food carried over as a morale breakfast on a corridor with no good early-morning options. Departure from Carville was at 7am.
records.quote: Apple pie for breakfast. What a treat.

records.summary: RIVER RIDGE KOA, LA — 'a very nice KOA' 10-15 miles short of New Orleans, deliberately used as the city-approach staging point. Has a SHUTTLE to the French Quarter.
records.detail: Rider: 'I rode longer than I wanted so we could stay at a very nice KOA 10 or 15 miles out.' The following day was a rest day; the crew took the KOA shuttle to the French Quarter for a steamboat ride and live music. He wanted the WWII Museum but did not have time. The next riding day would cross New Orleans to a second KOA on the east side.
records.cyclistIntel: BEST-DOCUMENTED LODGING ANCHOR IN LOUISIANA and directly useful to Nick. KOAs take tents, which almost none of the RV parks in this journal are confirmed to do, so this is a real self-supported option rather than an RV-only note. Three specific values: (1) it is positioned 10-15 miles outside New Orleans, which is exactly the staging distance needed to cross the city early in the morning per p54-005 — for Nick riding westbound it is the natural FIRST night out of New Orleans instead; (2) it runs a shuttle into the French Quarter, so a rider can see the city without riding a loaded bike through it; (3) it sits at the upriver end of the p54-003 trail-closure segment, so it is the logical place to verify MRT status before committing. Confirm current tent rates and availability — KOAs near New Orleans book up.
records.quote: a very nice KOA 10 or 15 miles out

records.summary: Rest day taken at River Ridge KOA before crossing New Orleans; next riding day planned as a long push through the city to a KOA on the EAST side
records.detail: Wednesday May 21 was a rest day: KOA shuttle to the French Quarter, steamboat ride, live music. The WWII Museum was skipped for lack of time. Riding resumed Thursday with a long day through New Orleans to a KOA east of the city.
records.cyclistIntel: Structural note for Nick's plan. The journal rider spent THREE calendar days on the New Orleans crossing — approach, rest, cross — because the city is a genuine sequencing problem. Nick has zero spare days across 53, so he cannot buy his way out of it the same way. His compensations are that he crosses westbound with the Quarter at the START of a day, and that the River Ridge KOA is his first night OUT rather than his staging night in. Also captured: a second KOA exists east of New Orleans, which is on Nick's approach side coming from Pensacola.

records.summary: *** RESOLVES THE p54-003 CLOSURE WORRY *** The levee trail from River Ridge through Audubon Park WAS OPEN in May 2025 — 13 continuous miles, and BUSY with cyclists and walkers
records.detail: The rider's stated hope on page 54 was that the Mississippi River Trail would be open from River Ridge KOA to Audubon Park. Page 56 answers it: 'The first section was jumping back up on the levee for thirteen miles.' Photo caption: 'A shot of the bike trail. It had lots of bikers and walkers this morning.' He rode it through to the Audubon Park entrance without reporting a single fence or detour.
records.cyclistIntel: THIS IS THE UPDATE THAT MATTERS. On page 54 I recorded the trail-closure account as a severity-4 must-verify hazard; two days later in the same journal the rider actually rode the segment and found it OPEN, CONTINUOUS FOR 13 MILES, and well used. That downgrades p54-003 from a live hazard to a historical one — see the amendment note on that record. For Nick this is now the recommended way OUT of New Orleans westbound: 13 miles of car-free levee path replacing the worst of River Road, ridden at the start of his day. Two residual cautions: MRT closures are a maintenance phenomenon and can recur, so the status is checkable-and-worth-checking rather than settled; and the trail was BUSY with pedestrians that morning, so it is not a fast segment — budget it at walking-pace-tolerant speeds, not trail-cruising speeds.
records.quote: It had lots of bikers and walkers this morning.
records.anchorNote: extent applied west→east per the source rule

photos.caption: A shot of the bike trail.
photos.shows: Handlebar-view down a paved levee path with a yellow centerline, dead straight to the horizon; road and houses down the levee to the left, water and industrial cranes to the right; Garmin head unit and blue handlebar bag in frame.

photos.caption: A typical Mississippi River view to my right along the levee.
photos.shows: River view from the levee crest.

records.summary: AUDUBON PARK — pleasant to ride through but SLOW, heavy pedestrian traffic
records.detail: Rider: 'The entrance to Audubon Park. It was fun to go through there. Slow, since there were so many walkers.'
records.cyclistIntel: The eastern terminus of the 13-mile levee segment and the transition into city streets. Plan it as time, not distance: this is a walk-your-speed-down section, not a place to make up a schedule. It is also a genuine amenity stop — shade, water, restrooms, a park bench — at the point where Nick would be leaving the car-free levee and entering the St Charles Avenue traffic.

photos.caption: The entrance to Audubon Park.
photos.shows: Park entrance.

records.summary: ST CHARLES AVENUE AND CITY STREETS to Jackson Square — 'threw me in with traffic', streetcar corridor, Mardi Gras beads still up in the trees
records.detail: Rider: 'The next part threw me in with traffic on St. Charles Street and other streets to get to Jackson Square.' Photo: Mardi Gras beads visible in the trees along St Charles.
records.cyclistIntel: The hard part of the New Orleans crossing is not the levee, it is the two-to-three miles of city street between Audubon Park and the French Quarter. St Charles carries a streetcar, which means EMBEDDED RAILS in the roadway — a genuine wheel-trap hazard for a loaded touring bike, especially crossing them at a shallow angle, and worse when wet. Cross rails as close to perpendicular as the lane allows. Combine this with the p54-005 timing rule: do this stretch early, when both car and pedestrian volume are lowest.
records.quote: The next part threw me in with traffic on St. Charles Street and other streets to get to Jackson Square.
records.road: St Charles Avenue and connecting streets

photos.caption: This is on St. Charles Street. If you look carefully you can see Mardi Gras beads all over in the tree.
photos.shows: St Charles Avenue with live oaks, Mardi Gras beads caught in the branches.

records.summary: JACKSON SQUARE: BICYCLES ARE NOT ALLOWED IN THE PARK — the rider was thrown out
records.detail: Photo caption: 'Me at Jackson Square. I got thrown out because they don't allow bicycles in the park.'
records.cyclistIntel: A concrete, enforced rule, learned the hard way. If Nick wants the Jackson Square photo he needs to lock the bike outside the fence or have someone hold it — which for a solo self-supported rider with loaded bags means either accepting the risk of leaving it or skipping the square. Worth deciding in advance rather than being turned around at the gate. French Quarter bike theft is also a real consideration; do not leave a loaded touring bike unattended here.
records.quote: I got thrown out because they don't allow bicycles in the park.

records.summary: *** NAVIGATION FAILURE ZONE *** East of Jackson Square the rider 'kept getting off-route through some dicey neighborhoods'
records.detail: Rider: 'When I finally got motivated to move on I kept getting off-route through some dicey neighborhoods.' This is between the French Quarter and the lake country / Chalmette stretch.
records.cyclistIntel: REPEATED off-route errors, not one. That is a signal about the ROUTE ITSELF, not the rider: the ACA cue sheet through east New Orleans has many turns, in a street grid disrupted by canals, rail and industrial parcels, where a missed turn does not self-correct. Practical rules for Nick: have the GPX loaded and follow the track rather than turn cues on this segment, do NOT rely on paper cues here, and do this stretch in daylight with time in hand. The rider's characterisation of the neighbourhoods is his impression and I am not treating it as a hazard claim — the actionable hazard is being lost, at low speed, in an unfamiliar dense area, potentially late in the day, which is a situation to design out with navigation prep rather than route around.
records.quote: I kept getting off-route through some dicey neighborhoods.
records.road: east New Orleans street network — ACA Southern Tier cues

records.summary: *** 1.5-MILE BRIDGE, PLENTY OF TRAFFIC, NO SHOULDER *** — the rider only got over it because roadwork had closed a lane he could ride in. He still had to join the cars on the downhill.
records.detail: Photo caption: 'In the distance you can see a 1.5 mile bridge. Plenty of traffic, no shoulder. Luckily, workers had one of the lanes shut down. I biked in the coned off lane to the top of the bridge where they were working. I only had to join the cars on the downhill side.' The photo shows a green steel truss span at the crest of a long high approach, a lane coned off with orange barrels, and a roadside sign reading 'LA[NE] AT BRIDGE TO BE CLOSED' with blank date fields.
records.cyclistIntel: HIGHEST-SEVERITY SHOULDER RECORD IN THE LOUISIANA SET, and Nick must not read the rider's experience as the normal case. A mile and a half of high bridge deck with dense traffic and NO SHOULDER means no escape route, no place to stop, wind exposure at height, and a concrete barrier on one side — and the only reason it went well is a construction lane closure that happened to be there that day. Nick should assume he gets the bridge WITHOUT the coned lane. Plan accordingly: cross at the lowest-traffic hour available, run a bright rear light in daylight, take the full lane deliberately on the climb rather than inviting squeeze passes, and consider whether the crossing warrants waiting for a gap or asking for a lift. DIRECTION: they climbed and had the closed lane on the up side, joining traffic only on the descent — the easier half. Nick riding westbound gets the reverse: he would ride the traffic-mixed section on the CLIMB, at his slowest, most vulnerable speed, and that is materially worse. This is the single strongest argument in the Louisiana data for building extra caution into Nick's New Orleans-to-Slidell day. RESOLUTION TASK: identify the bridge. Leading candidate is the US-90 crossing of the Rigolets; the Chef Menteur Pass bridge on the same highway is the alternative. A 1.5-mile length and a tall approach favour the Rigolets. Verify current shoulder status and bicycle access before the ride.
records.quote: Plenty of traffic, no shoulder.
records.verifyTarget: which US-90 bridge east of New Orleans is the 1.5-mile no-shoulder crossing, and its current shoulder/bike status

photos.caption: In the distance you can see a 1.5 mile bridge. Plenty of traffic, no shoulder.
photos.shows: Long high bridge approach with a green steel truss span at the crest; nearest lane closed with orange barrels and cones; concrete parapet left, guide sign right reading 'LA_ AT BRIDGE TO BE CLOSED' with empty date blanks; a car and pickup on the open lane; rider's saddle and handlebar in the foreground.

records.summary: FLAT #3 — a SCREW through the REAR tyre, cost about an hour. Rear tyre 'was a bear to pull off'.
records.detail: Rider: 'Then I got a flat. Flat #3 was on the back and was a bear to pull the tire off to change the tube.' Photos show the screw found in the tread and the roadside repair. He notes he had shade and a breeze while working, and captions the screw 'the screw that added an hour onto my trip.'
records.cyclistIntel: Third flat of a 2,500-mile ride so far, which is a good rate — but the operational lesson is the HOUR, not the puncture. A rear flat on a loaded touring bike in the urban-industrial New Orleans corridor cost sixty minutes, and this happened on a day the rider had already lost time to being off-route. For Nick with zero spare days across 53, an hour is a real hit. Two transferable rules: (1) urban and industrial road debris is a different threat profile from the desert goathead problem already recorded — construction screws, glass and metal, concentrated in shoulders and on bridge approaches, exactly where he is forced to ride; (2) the rider deliberately mentions having SHADE AND A BREEZE for the repair, which in Gulf-coast heat is not a luxury but the difference between a controlled repair and a heat incident. When Nick flats in Louisiana, moving to shade before starting work is part of the procedure.
records.quote: There is the screw that added an hour onto my trip.

photos.caption: I didn't have to look too hard to find out why I had a flat.
photos.shows: Screw head visible embedded in the rear tyre tread.

photos.caption: Finally making progress on changing that darn tire. I did have shade and a breeze.
photos.shows: Roadside rear-wheel repair in shade.

photos.caption: There is the screw that added an hour onto my trip.
photos.shows: The extracted screw held up to camera.

records.summary: NASA MICHOUD-type rocket assembly facility on the Day 54 route east of New Orleans — 'a really big NASA building', where the big booster rockets are assembled
records.detail: Rider photographed 'A really big NASA building' and noted 'They assemble the really big booster rockets here.' Also passed a giant Folgers Coffee plant on the same stretch.
records.cyclistIntel: STRONG GEOGRAPHIC ANCHOR — a single, unmistakable, precisely mappable industrial complex directly on the route, visible for miles. Together with the Folgers plant it fixes the eastbound sequence out of New Orleans on the Chef Menteur Highway corridor, which is exactly the segment where the rider repeatedly went off-route (p56-005). For Nick riding westbound these are confirmation landmarks that he is on the correct highway heading INTO the city. Use as a resolution aid for the surrounding unanchored records on this day.
records.road: US-90 / Chef Menteur Highway corridor, east New Orleans

photos.caption: A really big NASA building.
photos.shows: Very large windowless assembly building with NASA markings.

photos.caption: They assemble the really big booster rockets here.
photos.shows: Rocket assembly facility signage/structure.

records.summary: BATTLE OF NEW ORLEANS historical site — the actual battlefield, directly on the Day 54 route
records.detail: Rider: 'I saw the field where the Battle of New Orleans was fought.' Photo caption: 'The Battle of New Orleans historical site. I would have loved to have spent a couple hours there. Maybe next time.'
records.cyclistIntel: MAPPABLE FIXED ANCHOR and a genuinely good stop: a National Park Service unit means restrooms, water, shade and an air-conditioned visitor centre at a point on the route where those are otherwise scarce. It also pins the route's path — the ACA line leaves the French Quarter, runs downriver on the east bank past this site, then turns inland toward the US-90 corridor. For Nick this is a plausible mid-morning water-and-shade stop on his New Orleans day, and it disambiguates the confusing east-New-Orleans street sequence in p56-005.
records.road: downriver from New Orleans on the east bank, Chalmette area

photos.caption: The Battle of New Orleans historical site.
photos.shows: Open battlefield with interpretive site.

records.summary: LAKE COUNTRY approaching Slidell: houses on stilts, fancy houses on stilts, lake views from the bridges, and a finish beneath Spanish moss
records.detail: Rider: 'Then it was lake country which was interesting.' Photos: 'Houses on stilts', 'Some fancy houses on stilts', 'A view of the lake from a bridge', 'Finally finishing the day's ride beneath the Spanish Moss.'
records.cyclistIntel: Positional cue set for the Slidell approach, and a reminder of what stilt houses mean: this is a storm-surge zone at 10-20 ft elevation where the built environment is designed to be flooded. Read together with the hurricane-season note on page 57 — for Nick this is a stretch where weather risk is structural, not incidental. The Spanish moss canopy at the end of the day also means the first real SHADE on the route since the levee, which matters for a hot afternoon finish.

photos.caption: Houses on stilts.
photos.shows: Coastal houses elevated on pilings.

photos.caption: A view of the lake from a bridge.
photos.shows: Open lake water seen from a bridge deck.

photos.caption: Finally finishing the day's ride beneath the Spanish Moss.
photos.shows: Rider in yellow jersey on a quiet lane under live oaks draped with Spanish moss, deep shade.

records.summary: A 56-mile FLAT day that took 5:13 at 10.7 mph and 'just drug on and on' — city navigation, pedestrian traffic and a flat ate the day
records.detail: Rider: '56 flat miles, it should have been one of my easier, quicker days. For whatever reason it didn't happen that way... I was very slow, I think the Louisiana lifestyle has gotten to me. I just dawdled along looking at the scenery.' 492 ft of ascent over 55.99 mi. Departed the River Ridge KOA about 7:30am. Avg temp 87.8F.
records.cyclistIntel: THE MOST USEFUL SCHEDULING LESSON ON THE NEW ORLEANS CROSSING. Every input said this should be a short easy day — 56 miles, dead flat, a rest day behind him — and it still consumed over five hours of moving time plus an hour of repair plus off-route losses. The city is a TIME sink, not a distance one: pedestrian-speed trail sections, streetcar streets, repeated navigation errors, and a mandatory stop-and-look quality that even the rider surrendered to. For Nick with zero spare days, the rule is to plan the New Orleans day at roughly HALF his normal mileage and treat any figure derived from flat-terrain assumptions as fiction. Do not schedule a long onward push out of New Orleans on the same day as the city crossing.
records.quote: All told the day just drug on and on.

records.summary: Continued egrets and wading birds; one raccoon. Otherwise quiet.
records.detail: Rider: 'I continued to see egrets and other wading birds. I saw one raccoon. Not much else in the wildlife department.'
records.cyclistIntel: Low wildlife threat on this corridor — notable mainly as contrast with the dog density recorded further west in rural Louisiana (p52-003). Urban and lake-country Louisiana is a traffic problem, not an animal problem.

records.summary: RIVER RIDGE KOA, LA — second night, the New Orleans REST DAY (shuttle to the French Quarter, steamboat, live music)
records.detail: Rest day Wednesday May 21. Same KOA as night 52. Used the KOA shuttle into the French Quarter. Rider references 'last night's Hurricane' the following morning.
records.cyclistIntel: Chain-completion record: the River Ridge KOA was used for two consecutive nights around the rest day. Reinforces p54-OV52 — this is the New Orleans base camp of choice, tent-friendly, with a shuttle that removes any need to ride into the Quarter at all.

records.summary: KOA SLIDELL, LA — planned target of the day, reached as intended
records.detail: The day's stated plan was to 'parade through New Orleans and skirt around Lake Pontchartrain and stay at a KOA in Slidell.' Achieved.
records.cyclistIntel: SOLID TENT-FRIENDLY ANCHOR and the natural east-side New Orleans staging point. This is the one that matters most for Nick's DIRECTION: riding east-to-west he arrives from Mississippi, so a Slidell overnight lets him cross the city westbound starting first thing in the morning — which is exactly what the French Quarter timing rule in p54-005 requires. Slidell KOA in, River Ridge KOA out, city crossing between them on a deliberately short day. That is the New Orleans plan the journal's data supports.

records.summary: HIGHWAY 90 THROUGH COASTAL MISSISSIPPI: WIDE SMOOTH SHOULDERS. 'Not bad.' A genuine relief after Louisiana.
records.detail: Rider: 'The first part of the day was on highways with wide smooth shoulders. Not bad.' Repeated the next day: 'Today's ride started on Highway 90. Wide smooth shoulder, tall pine trees on both sides.'
records.cyclistIntel: DIRECT AND FAVOURABLE CONTRAST with the Louisiana records. Two consecutive days independently confirm that US-90 in coastal Mississippi carries a wide, smooth, rideable shoulder — the opposite of US-61 through Baton Rouge (p53-001) and River Road (p54-001). For Nick this means the Mississippi coast is where he can bank miles and recover schedule, early in his trip, and it is where the narrow-shoulder warning layer should stay QUIET. Recording the good shoulders explicitly matters as much as recording the bad ones: a warning system that only knows about hazards makes every mile feel equally risky.
records.quote: Wide smooth shoulder, tall pine trees on both sides.

records.summary: *** WIND SHELTER *** Very tall pine trees on both sides of Highway 90 meant 'wind wasn't a factor' — a rare sheltered corridor
records.detail: Rider: 'The highways were surrounded by very tall pine trees so wind wasn't a factor.' Photo caption: 'The pine trees are really tall on Highway 90 in Mississipi.'
records.cyclistIntel: VALUABLE AND UNUSUAL. Almost every wind record in this journal is about exposure — the levee crest, West Texas, the desert. This is the only stretch where the rider reports the terrain and vegetation actively CANCELLING the wind. For Nick that has two consequences: this is a corridor where a forecast headwind may not materialise at road level, so it is a good place to schedule a long day even on a windy forecast; and conversely, a forecast tailwind will not help him much here either, so he should not bank on wind assistance through the pines. The trees also mean SHADE, which given the humidity records on this leg is arguably the more important benefit. Wind shelter from vegetation does NOT invert with direction — this record is equally valid for Nick riding the other way.
records.quote: The highways were surrounded by very tall pine trees so wind wasn't a factor.

photos.caption: The pine trees are really tall on Highway 90 in Mississipi.
photos.shows: US-90 running between walls of very tall pines on both sides.

records.summary: *** THE MISSISSIPPI SOUND BEACH TRAIL *** — HOURS of separated paved path along the Gulf, water on one side, big houses on the other, almost no other users
records.detail: Rider: 'our route took us to the beach trail along the Mississippi Sound. Basically the Gulf of Mexico. I spent hours riding along the beach... It was a very entertaining trip to look out over the water on my right, then look at all the big fancy houses on my left. There wasn't much foot or bike traffic on the bike trail.' The Biloxi Boardwalk is photographed. He notes the beaches are exceptionally soft, almost white sand, and 'really big'.
records.cyclistIntel: SECOND MAJOR OFF-HIGHWAY ASSET ON THE GULF LEG, after the Mississippi levee trail, and it runs for HOURS not miles. Separated from US-90 traffic, flat, paved, with continuous services alongside through Bay St Louis, Pass Christian, Long Beach, Gulfport, Biloxi, Ocean Springs and Gautier — which makes it the best-supported stretch of the entire Gulf leg for water and food. ROUTE IT DELIBERATELY. Cautions: it is completely UNSHADED, unlike the pine corridor; blown SAND on the path is a real surface issue on a windy day and a crash risk in corners; and the beachfront road carries heavy leisure traffic at driveway crossings, so the conflict points are the many places cars cross the path, not the path itself. Direction-neutral.
records.quote: I spent hours riding along the beach.
records.road: US-90 beachfront path along the Mississippi Sound

photos.caption: The beaches were really pretty. Really big.
photos.shows: Wide white-sand beach with the Sound beyond.

photos.caption: The Biloxi Boardwalk.
photos.shows: Boardwalk along the Biloxi beachfront.

photos.caption: (rider at the beach)
photos.shows: Rider standing with his dark blue steel touring bike on a wide concrete beachfront path; white sand, dune fence and sea oats behind him, flat calm Sound water on the horizon; two bottles on the frame, rear rack, long white sun sleeves.

records.summary: UPPER 70s AND 83% HUMIDITY AT 6:30AM — and the humidity was thick enough to FILTER THE SUN for several hours
records.detail: Rider: 'Today was, you guessed it, upper 70's and 83% humidity when I stepped out of the RV at 6:30am... There was so much humidity in the air the sun was filtered for several hours.' Photo caption: 'It was a hazy start to the day.' GPS avg 89.1F over 6:19, starting near 68F and spiking above 100F around 2:05 and again near 4:10 elapsed.
records.cyclistIntel: THE DEFINING CONDITION OF THE GULF LEG, and the second consecutive day at 83% dawn humidity — so this is a pattern, not a one-off. Two operationally opposite effects, and Nick needs both. THE COST: at 83% RH sweat does not evaporate, so cooling fails while sweat rate rises. This is why the 20-25 mile water interval from p54-N1 holds here too, and why the desert playbook of 'start early and beat the heat' only half works — there is no cool window to start in. THE BENEFIT, which is genuinely useful and easy to miss: the same humidity haze FILTERS THE SUN for the first several hours, so direct radiant load in the morning is much lower than a clear desert morning at the same air temperature. Nick's early hours on the Gulf coast are hot and sticky but not sunburning. Plan hydration and electrolytes as the limiter here, and sun exposure as the limiter in Texas and the desert. Note the rider's clothing choice in the beach photo: long white sun sleeves rather than bare arms — the correct answer in filtered high-UV humidity.
records.quote: There was so much humidity in the air the sun was filtered for several hours.

records.summary: *** HURRICANE SEASON *** The rider flags it directly: 'hurricane season officially arrives at Memorial Day', while riding for miles at just 20 to 40 feet above sea level
records.detail: Rider: 'It feels weird riding for miles at just 20 to 40 feet above sea level. And hurricane season officially arrives at Memorial Day.'
records.cyclistIntel: REGION-SCOPE STRUCTURAL RISK, not a day condition — the most important non-route fact on the Gulf leg. Correction to the rider on the date: the Atlantic hurricane season officially runs JUNE 1 to NOVEMBER 30, not Memorial Day, though late May named storms do occur and his instinct about the timing is close enough to matter. What this means for Nick: the Gulf coast portion of his route — Pensacola, Alabama, the Mississippi Sound, Slidell, New Orleans — sits at 10-40 ft elevation in a landfall corridor, and it falls in the FIRST WEEK of his 53-day plan. A tropical system there does not slow him down, it stops him: ferries cancel (see the Dauphin Island ferry dependency on page 58), bridges close, coastal roads flood, and campgrounds evacuate. With zero spare days across 53, Nick has no absorption capacity for that. ACTIONABLE: check the National Hurricane Center outlook before the Gulf days rather than relying on a local forecast, know which inland alternative exists to the beachfront route, and understand that this is the one weather risk on the whole trip that can end it rather than delay it. Also note the built environment already tells the story — the stilt houses recorded in p56-008.
records.quote: And hurricane season officially arrives at Memorial Day.

records.summary: MEMORIAL DAY WEEKEND on the Mississippi coast: lots of CAR traffic but the beach path was still empty on the Friday morning
records.detail: Rider: 'There wasn't much foot or bike traffic on the bike trail. That surprised me, it is the Friday of Memorial Weekend. Lots of car traffic but people had not made it to the beach yet.'
records.cyclistIntel: Timing intelligence for the holiday corridor. Early Friday the path was clear while the ROAD was already loaded — so on a beachfront day the separated path is doubly valuable on a holiday weekend, and the window for a clear path is the morning. Expect the reverse by afternoon: path filling with pedestrians and beach traffic crossing it constantly. This pairs with the sold-out campgrounds recorded on page 58 — Memorial Day weekend on the Gulf coast is a demand event that affects traffic, path congestion and lodging together.

records.summary: LOUISIANA / MISSISSIPPI STATE LINE — signed, photographed, crossed early on Day 55
records.detail: Photo caption: 'Hooray! Good bye, Louisiana. Hello, Mississippi.' Crossed in the first part of the day out of Slidell, before the beach trail section.
records.cyclistIntel: HARD GEOGRAPHIC ANCHOR — a state line on a known highway is one of the most precisely resolvable fixes available, and it segments the whole dataset cleanly. It also marks a real change in road quality: everything west of this line in the Louisiana records is rough or no shoulder, and everything east on US-90 in the Mississippi records is wide and smooth. For Nick riding westbound this sign is the warning that the good shoulders are about to end.

photos.caption: Hooray! Good bye, Louisiana. Hello, Mississippi.
photos.shows: Mississippi state line welcome sign.

records.summary: Blue heron and continued wading birds along the Mississippi Sound
records.detail: Photo caption: 'Linda caught a Blue Heron that didn't fly away before a camera could be pulled out.'
records.cyclistIntel: No hazard. Confirms the wading-bird corridor continues along the Sound.

records.summary: GAUTIER MS — RV overnight at the end of the beach day (RV, hookup-driven)
records.detail: End of Day 55. Rider stepped out of the RV at 6:30am the following morning at this site.
records.cyclistIntel: RV-based, name not given, so of limited direct use — but positionally useful: Gautier sits at the eastern end of the Mississippi Sound beachfront corridor and is a sensible day-end for Nick too. Worth noting that this stretch of coast has dense commercial lodging (Gulfport, Biloxi, Ocean Springs, Gautier), so unlike rural Louisiana this is NOT a lodging-scarce area — a motel is easy here if camping fails.

records.summary: *** TWO VERY TALL BRIDGES *** on the Dauphin Island day — the second one a signed/observed 6% CLIMB onto the island
records.detail: Rider: 'I had two very tall bridges to climb then on to Dauphin Island.' Photo captions: 'The view from the first tall bridge. It is a ship building facility' and 'My view of the 6% climb I will have to get over the bridge to Dauphin Island.' The bridge photo shows a long, steadily rising deck with traffic in the travel lane, a WIDE SMOOTH SHOULDER outside a solid white line, and a concrete parapet on the water side.
records.cyclistIntel: TWO NAMED GRADIENTS AND, CRUCIALLY, A GOOD SHOULDER. The Dauphin Island Bridge photo is the clearest shoulder evidence in the Gulf set: a wide, clean, debris-free shoulder separated by a solid white line, running the full length of the climb, with a barrier between the rider and the water. This is the OPPOSITE of the 1.5-mile no-shoulder Louisiana bridge in p56-006 and Nick should treat them as completely different risk classes. What to actually plan for on this bridge: 6% is steep for a bridge but SHORT, so it is a gear-and-grind for a few minutes rather than a climb; the real factors are CROSSWIND at height over open water, which does not invert with direction and can be strong on the Gulf, and the total absence of shade or bail-out on the deck. The first tall bridge overlooks the Pascagoula shipbuilding yards and is the earlier of the two. DIRECTION: they climbed onto the island from the north. Nick, riding east-to-west and coming off the Fort Morgan ferry, crosses in the reverse sense — he CLIMBS the 6% leaving the island northbound and descends toward Mobile Bay. So he does pay for this climb, in his first few days, with a fully loaded bike. No direction discount.
records.quote: My view of the 6% climb I will have to get over the bridge to Dauphin Island.
records.road: US-90 then AL-193 / Dauphin Island Parkway

photos.caption: My view of the 6% climb I will have to get over the bridge to Dauphin Island.
photos.shows: Long concrete bridge deck rising steadily to a crest with a queue of cars near the top; WIDE smooth shoulder roughly 8-10 ft outside a solid white edge line, clean surface with no debris; solid concrete parapet on the right with open water beyond and a line of light poles; black pickup and an SUV in the travel lane; overcast sky.

photos.caption: The view from the first tall bridge. It is a ship building facility.
photos.shows: Shipbuilding yard with cranes and hulls seen from a high bridge deck — the Pascagoula yards.

records.summary: US-90 into Alabama: wide smooth shoulder and tall pines on both sides, continuing the good Mississippi conditions across the state line
records.detail: Rider: 'Today's ride started on Highway 90. Wide smooth shoulder, tall pine trees on both sides. It wasn't far before we hit the Alabama state line. More tall trees then back to the Gulf of Mexico waters.'
records.cyclistIntel: Third independent confirmation that the US-90 Gulf corridor has good shoulders, now extended across into Alabama. This is the stretch where Nick's warning layer should be quiet and his mileage expectations high. Also confirms the pine-shelter and pine-shade benefit from p57-002 continues east of the Mississippi line.
records.quote: Wide smooth shoulder, tall pine trees on both sides.

records.summary: *** MEMORIAL DAY WEEKEND: EVERY RV PARK THEY TRIED WAS SOLD OUT *** — and then walking in and asking in person found a spot next to the ferry
records.detail: Rider: 'This is a holiday weekend so everywhere we tried the rv parks were sold out. We found a place 7 miles away. But, when I finished my 53 miles in a pouring rain, there was an RV park right next to the ferry we take tomorrow. I went in and asked, they looked and found an open spot for us. Hooray for spontaneous actions.'
records.cyclistIntel: TWO SEPARATE HIGH-VALUE LESSONS, and this is the fifth-plus confirmation of the second one. FIRST: Gulf-coast lodging on a HOLIDAY WEEKEND is a hard constraint, not a soft one — sold out everywhere they phoned, forcing a 7-mile-off-route fallback. Dauphin Island is a barrier island with finite capacity and it is a Memorial Day destination. Nick's Gulf days fall in his FIRST WEEK; if that week overlaps a holiday weekend he must book ahead or plan to be inland. SECOND, and this is now the strongest recurring pattern in the entire journal: ASKING IN PERSON BEATS PHONING AND BEATS THE INTERNET. Every remote source said full; walking through the door found an open spot immediately, at the single best possible location — right next to the ferry terminal they needed the next morning. This is now four-plus-for-four across the trip. For Nick the operational rule is: when lodging shows as unavailable, ride there and ask a human before accepting it, and ask specifically at the place nearest the thing you need tomorrow. Cross-reference this with the six nights in his own 53-day plan that currently have no lodging anchor — this pattern is the main reason those are recoverable rather than fatal.
records.quote: I went in and asked, they looked and found an open spot for us. Hooray for spontaneous actions.

records.summary: *** AMENDED BY p59-001 — TIMING NOW KNOWN *** Ferry dependency, Dauphin Island to Fort Morgan. The crew had no idea how long it would take; page 59 answers it: about a 30-MINUTE crossing, but it still cost TWO HOURS off the riding day.
records.detail: Rider: 'Tomorrow we get to ride the ferry from Dauphin Island to Gulf Shores. We don't know how long that will take so we have no plan for the day. Bike as far as I can, then scrounge up a place to camp.' They deliberately camped at the RV park immediately adjacent to the ferry.
records.cyclistIntel: THE HARDEST SCHEDULE DEPENDENCY ON THE GULF LEG and it lands in NICK'S FIRST FEW DAYS riding east-to-west out of Pensacola — he takes this ferry in the opposite direction, Fort Morgan to Dauphin Island. A ferry is not a road: it has a published schedule that changes seasonally, a finite capacity, a cash or card window, and it cancels for weather and mechanical reasons with no alternative except a very long detour around Mobile Bay through Mobile itself. Note that even a SUPPORTED party with a chase vehicle and a planner treated the ferry day as unplannable. ACTIONABLE FOR NICK: get the current Mobile Bay ferry schedule and bicycle policy before the trip, not during it; know the crossing duration and the first and last sailings; plan to be at the terminal early rather than timing it finely; camp or stay the night immediately adjacent to the terminal as this crew did, so a first sailing is achievable; and identify the land detour around Mobile Bay in advance as the failure plan, because if the ferry is down he needs it the same morning. Combine with the hurricane-season note in p57-N2 — weather cancellation is the realistic failure mode. *** AMENDMENT (from p59-001): the unknown is resolved. First in line for the 8am sailing, off the boat at 8:30 — roughly a 30-minute crossing. But even doing everything right (camped at the terminal, first in the queue, first sailing) the rider's riding day still started TWO HOURS LATE, and that delay alone made it the hottest day of the entire journal at 96.5F average. Budget an hour of day, not thirty minutes. AND THE CRITICAL DIRECTION POINT: for Nick riding east-to-west this ferry is at the END of his day one, not the start. Fort Morgan is a DEAD-END PENINSULA with no road onward. A missed last sailing strands him roughly 20-plus miles out a spur with Gulf Shores as the nearest lodging on a holiday-capacity coast. Get the LAST sailing time and set a hard turnaround at Gulf Shores. ***
records.quote: We don't know how long that will take so we have no plan for the day.
records.verifyTarget: Mobile Bay ferry (Dauphin Island - Fort Morgan) current schedule, duration, bicycle policy and fare; plus the land detour around Mobile Bay as the cancellation fallback

records.summary: Finished 53 miles IN POURING RAIN after riding through sporadic rain; temperature spiked to ~105F mid-ride then crashed as the rain arrived
records.detail: Rider: 'when I finished my 53 miles in a pouring rain'; 'Even after biking in sporatic rain it was a really good day.' GPS avg 84.9F over 4:15; the temperature trace jumps sharply above 100F between roughly 2:13 and 3:20 elapsed, then falls steeply after 3:20 — the storm arriving. He was done biking about noon.
records.cyclistIntel: THE GULF-COAST AFTERNOON CONVECTION PATTERN, visible in the data rather than just the prose: a hot humid morning building to a 100F+ spike, then a sharp temperature collapse as a thunderstorm breaks. This is the normal Gulf summer day shape, and it is a completely different risk from the desert's steady dry heat. For Nick it strongly reinforces the done-early rule on the Gulf leg, for a NEW reason: not the heat, but the storms. Afternoon thunderstorms on the coast bring lightning on exposed elevated bridges and levee paths, standing water, and near-zero visibility to drivers on a corridor where he is already sharing the shoulder. Note the rider finished about NOON and still caught the edge of it. Also practical: rain gear must be accessible without unpacking, and rims and brakes on a loaded bike descending a 6% bridge in the wet behave very differently.
records.quote: Even after biking in sporatic rain it was a really good day.

records.summary: MISSISSIPPI / ALABAMA STATE LINE — signed and photographed, crossed early on Day 56 on US-90
records.detail: Photo caption: 'Another state!' Crossed 'not far' into the day from Gautier, on Highway 90.
records.cyclistIntel: HARD GEOGRAPHIC ANCHOR on a known highway — precisely resolvable, and it brackets the Mississippi records cleanly against the Alabama ones. Useful for resolving the surrounding unanchored spans on Days 55 and 56.

photos.caption: Another state!
photos.shows: Alabama state line sign.

records.summary: DAUPHIN ISLAND services: The Dockside Seafood Restaurant (water views, shrimp baskets) and FORT GAINES, a 200-year-old fort with a well-done walking tour
records.detail: Rider ate at The Dockside Seafood and visited Fort Gaines, 'a 200 year old fort that was the scene of a big Civil War battle. They had a well-done walking tour. Neat history.' He was done riding about noon, which gave the afternoon free. A short trail from the campground reaches the Gulf.
records.cyclistIntel: Named, verified services on a barrier island where options are finite. For Nick this is the arrival or departure point for the ferry, so knowing there is a real restaurant and a genuine attraction here matters for a day whose length is set by a boat schedule he cannot control — if he arrives to a missed sailing, this is a place he can wait. Fort Gaines also sits directly at the ferry terminal end of the island. Beach access is a short walk from the campground.

records.summary: DAUPHIN ISLAND AL — RV park IMMEDIATELY NEXT TO THE FERRY TERMINAL, found by walking in and asking after everywhere else showed sold out on Memorial Day weekend
records.detail: All RV parks tried were sold out for the holiday weekend; a fallback 7 miles away had been arranged. On arrival in pouring rain the rider walked into the RV park adjacent to the ferry and they found an open spot. Camp set up, steak, grilled squash and mashed potatoes cooked, then a short trail walk to the Gulf.
records.cyclistIntel: THE MOST STRATEGICALLY PLACED LODGING RECORD ON THE GULF LEG: a campground immediately beside the Mobile Bay ferry terminal, which is exactly what the p58-003 ferry dependency requires — stay adjacent, catch a first sailing, do not gamble on a morning ride to the boat. Two caveats: capacity is contested on holiday weekends, and the tent policy here is not stated, so verify. The way they got the spot is itself the lesson — see p58-N1.
records.quote: I went in and asked, they looked and found an open spot for us.

records.summary: *** FERRY TIMING RESOLVED *** First in line for the 8am Dauphin Island ferry, OFF THE BOAT AT 8:30 — about a 30-minute crossing, and it still pushed the riding day TWO HOURS LATE
records.detail: Rider: 'Our day today started with a ferry ride from Dauphin Island to Gulf Shores... We didn't get off the ferry until 8:30 so the biking part of the day was about two hours later than normal.' Photo caption: 'First in line for the 8am ferry.' They had camped immediately adjacent to the terminal the night before (see p58-OV56).
records.cyclistIntel: THIS ANSWERS THE OPEN QUESTION IN p58-003 and the answer is worse than it sounds. The crossing itself is only about 30 minutes. But the rider did everything right — camped at the terminal, was FIRST IN LINE, took the first 8am sailing — and still lost two hours off his normal start. The cost is not the boat, it is the boarding, the wait, the unload and the shuttle to the road. And look at what those two hours did to him: this became the HOTTEST day in the entire journal by average temperature, 96.5F, on a mere 45 miles, purely because he rode 10:30am to 2pm instead of 7am to 11am. *** NICK'S DIRECTION MAKES THIS FAR MORE DANGEROUS, NOT LESS *** Nick rides east-to-west from Pensacola, so the ferry falls at the END of his first day, not the start. Fort Morgan is a PENINSULA DEAD END — there is no road onward. If Nick misses the last sailing he is stranded roughly 20-plus miles out a spur with Gulf Shores the nearest lodging, on a holiday-capacity coast, after a full day's riding. That is the worst single failure mode identified anywhere in this dataset for his first week. ACTIONABLE: get the LAST sailing time, not just the schedule; set a hard turnaround time at Gulf Shores beyond which he does not commit to the Fort Morgan spur; and know that the crossing plus boarding is realistically an hour of his day, not thirty minutes.
records.quote: We didn't get off the ferry until 8:30 so the biking part of the day was about two hours later than normal.

photos.caption: First in line for the 8am ferry.
photos.shows: Loaded bike first in the vehicle queue at the Dauphin Island ferry ramp.

photos.caption: Looking back at Dauphin Island.
photos.shows: Dauphin Island receding astern from the ferry deck.

records.summary: *** HOTTEST DAY IN THE JOURNAL: 96.5F AVERAGE *** with spikes near 115F — on only 45 miles, caused entirely by the two-hour late start
records.detail: GPS average temperature 96.5F over 3:34:41 of riding, the highest daily average recorded anywhere in this journal, with the trace climbing steeply after roughly 2:20 elapsed and peaking near 115F around 2:46. Distance was only 45.25 mi with 489 ft of gain. Rider: 'It got pretty old riding with all the traffic and it was getting hot.'
records.cyclistIntel: THE CLEANEST CAUSE-AND-EFFECT LESSON IN THE WHOLE DATASET, and it is worth more than any single hazard record. A short, flat, easy 45-mile day became the hottest day of a 2,500-mile ride for ONE reason: he started two hours late. Nothing about the route changed — only the clock. This is the empirical backing for the done-by-early-afternoon rule that shows up all over this journal, and it converts that rule from a preference into a measurable safety margin: two hours of start delay on the Gulf coast cost roughly ten degrees of average riding temperature and put him in 115F peaks. For Nick, whose first days are on this exact coast, the rule is that the START TIME is the most powerful lever he has, more than mileage, more than fitness, and more than route choice. CALIBRATION CAVEAT: this journal ran in an unusually hot spring — see the source heatCalibration field — so treat 96.5F as the high-end scenario. The mechanism, though, is not calibration-dependent: a late start costs heat everywhere.
records.quote: It got pretty old riding with all the traffic and it was getting hot.

records.summary: FORT MORGAN ROAD off the ferry: tree-lined highway with only SPORADIC traffic — the good half of the day
records.detail: Rider: 'The biking started on a tree lined highway with sporatic traffic.' Photo caption: 'Nice start to the day.' This is the spur road from the Fort Morgan ferry terminal east toward Gulf Shores.
records.cyclistIntel: GOOD-CONDITIONS RECORD covering roughly the first third of the day. Tree-lined means shade, which given p59-N1 is the most valuable thing on this coast, and sporadic traffic means Nick can actually ride it rather than survive it. DIRECTION: for Nick this is the LAST stretch before the ferry rather than the first after it, and that is fortunate — it is quiet, shaded and low-stress, which is what he wants when he is racing a sailing time. Note that the traffic character is holiday-dependent; the same road on Memorial Day Sunday afternoon may be much busier than the morning the rider saw.
records.quote: The biking started on a tree lined highway with sporatic traffic.

photos.caption: Nice start to the day.
photos.shows: Two-lane highway lined with trees, empty of traffic.

photos.caption: There were a lot of oil rigs in the water.
photos.shows: Offshore rigs visible from the Gulf shoreline.

records.summary: *** GULF SHORES / ORANGE BEACH HOLIDAY TRAFFIC *** 'Everyone and his brother were on the highway with their fishing boats' — beaches packed, channels bumper to bumper, and it 'got pretty old riding with all the traffic'
records.detail: Rider: 'That changed when we got to Gulf Shores. Everyone and his brother were on the highway with their fishing boats. The beaches were packed, the channels to the gulf were bumper to bumper with boats. It got pretty old riding with all the traffic and it was getting hot.' This is Memorial Day Sunday. He also describes the scenery for most of the day as 'just a corridor of stores and condos'.
records.cyclistIntel: THE DEFINING HAZARD OF THE ALABAMA-FLORIDA BEACH CORRIDOR, and note what KIND of traffic it is: vehicles TOWING BOAT TRAILERS. That matters specifically for a cyclist. A trailer tracks wider than the tow vehicle, cuts corners tighter, swings on turns, and the driver frequently misjudges how much room the back of the rig needs — so a pass that clears the truck can still bring a trailer fender through the space a cyclist occupies. Add dense driveway and parking-lot turns all along a condo-and-store strip, drivers looking for addresses rather than road, and heat. For Nick this is his FIRST DAY, on unfamiliar roads, possibly with a bike he has not yet ridden fully loaded. RULES: assume every towing vehicle will pass closer than it should; be maximally conservative at every commercial driveway; and if his start date lands on a holiday weekend, seriously consider shifting it, because this corridor on a normal Tuesday is a completely different road. DIRECTION-NEUTRAL for shoulder and traffic, but for Nick this congestion falls in his MORNING rather than his midday, which is a real improvement.
records.quote: Everyone and his brother were on the highway with their fishing boats.

photos.caption: Boats going in and out of the gulf.
photos.shows: Boat traffic queued in a channel to the Gulf.

records.summary: SEVERAL MILES OF SHADED BIKE TRAIL on the Perdido Key / Pensacola approach — 'very pleasant to get off the busy road for a while'
records.detail: Rider: 'My ride today included several miles on a bike trail. It was very pleasant to get off the busy road for a while.' The photo shows a narrow paved path winding through dense woodland under a full tree canopy, dappled shade, leaf litter at the edges, no traffic.
records.cyclistIntel: THE THIRD MAJOR OFF-HIGHWAY ASSET ON THE GULF LEG and the most valuable of the three for heat, because unlike the Mississippi beach path and the New Orleans levee this one is FULLY SHADED under a closed canopy. On a day averaging 96.5F that is not a comfort, it is a physiological intervention. ROUTE IT DELIBERATELY. It also provides direct relief from the boat-trailer traffic in p59-003, so the two records should be read together: where this trail exists, take it. For Nick this falls very early on his first day out of Pensacola — a shaded, car-free start is close to ideal for a rider still settling into a loaded bike. Caveats from the photo: the path is narrow, roughly single-lane, with organic debris at the edges and a canopy that will hold water and slick leaves after rain; and sight lines around the bends are short.
records.quote: It was very pleasant to get off the busy road for a while.
records.road: paved bike trail parallel to the beach highway

photos.caption: My ride today included several miles on a bike trail.
photos.shows: Handlebar view of a narrow paved path curving through dense green woodland; full tree canopy overhead casting heavy dappled shade; leaf and needle litter along both edges; no traffic; the rider's map case and blue bar bag in the foreground.

records.summary: ALABAMA / FLORIDA STATE LINE at Perdido Key — signed and photographed, 'My last state!'
records.detail: Photo caption: 'My last state!' Crossed on the beach highway at Perdido Key, immediately adjacent to the Flora-Bama Bar which straddles the line.
records.cyclistIntel: HARD GEOGRAPHIC ANCHOR, and an unusually precise one because the Flora-Bama sits right on the line and is itself a mapped landmark — the two together fix this point tightly. For NICK this is the most important anchor on the page: Pensacola is his START, so this state line is roughly his first 15-20 miles and marks his exit from Florida into Alabama on day one.

photos.caption: My last state!
photos.shows: Florida/Alabama state line sign on the beach highway.

records.summary: THE FLORA-BAMA BAR on the Alabama/Florida line — rider went in for a Coke and gave up, the lines were too long
records.detail: Photo caption: 'The famous Flora-Bama Bar. I went in to order a Coke but the lines were so long I gave up.' Memorial Day Sunday.
records.cyclistIntel: PRECISE MAPPED ANCHOR sitting on the state line, so it doubles as a route fix. But treat it as a NEGATIVE service record, not a resupply option: on a busy weekend the rider could not even buy a soft drink because of the queues. For Nick, needing water on a hot first day, this is a place to ride past, not to plan a stop at — find a gas station or store instead. Useful confirmation waypoint only.

photos.caption: The famous Flora-Bama Bar.
photos.shows: The Flora-Bama roadhouse on the beach highway.

records.summary: NATIONAL NAVAL AVIATION MUSEUM, PENSACOLA — the rider's chosen end to the day, 1.5 hours, strongly enjoyed. BUT it sits on an active naval air station.
records.detail: Rider: 'I told Linda we were going to stop at the Naval Aviation Museum in Pensacola. Only 45 miles and only 1 1/2 hours at the museum but it was a good way to end the day.' Photos: 'Airplanes everywhere! It was hard to soak it all in', a B-25 and a rare Japanese Zero, and a trainer like the one his father-in-law flew.
records.cyclistIntel: Genuinely worth the stop and it is essentially AT Nick's start point, so it is a day-zero option rather than a mid-ride detour. ONE IMPORTANT PRACTICAL FLAG the journal does not mention: this museum is located aboard NAS Pensacola, and access to the base has been restricted and has changed repeatedly in recent years, with periods when public entry required a pass or was closed entirely, and with security screening at the gate. Do NOT assume a cyclist can simply ride in. VERIFY current public access, entry requirements and whether bicycles are permitted through the gate before planning it into a day. If Nick wants to see it, doing so the day BEFORE he starts riding, by car, is the low-risk version.
records.verifyTarget: current NAS Pensacola public access rules for the Naval Aviation Museum, and whether bicycles may enter the base

records.summary: Brown pelicans and gulls are the whole wildlife picture on the Gulf beach corridor
records.detail: Rider: 'We are seeing a lot of Brown Pelicans and gulls but that's it for wildlife.' Two pelican photos.
records.cyclistIntel: No hazard. Confirms the Gulf beach corridor is a traffic-risk environment rather than an animal-risk one — a useful contrast with the dog density in rural Louisiana (p52-003) and the desert wildlife records further west.

records.summary: *** NICK'S DAY 1, RUN BACKWARDS *** — this page is the single most directly applicable day in the journal, and every element of it inverts
records.detail: Journal Day 57 ran Dauphin Island AL to Pensacola FL: ferry first, then Fort Morgan Road, Gulf Shores holiday traffic, Perdido Key, the AL/FL line at the Flora-Bama, the shaded bike trail, and a finish at Pensacola. 45.25 mi, 489 ft, 12.6 mph, 3:34:41 moving, 96.5F average.
records.cyclistIntel: READ THIS RECORD FIRST WHEN PLANNING NICK'S OPENING DAY. Pensacola is his START, so he rides this exact 45 miles in reverse on day one. The full inversion: (1) FERRY MOVES FROM FIRST TO LAST — the single most consequential change, because Fort Morgan is a dead-end peninsula and a missed last sailing strands him; see p59-001. (2) THE SHADED BIKE TRAIL MOVES FROM LATE TO EARLY — good; he gets car-free shade while settling into a loaded bike. (3) THE HOLIDAY BOAT-TRAILER TRAFFIC THROUGH GULF SHORES AND ORANGE BEACH MOVES FROM MIDDAY TO MORNING — better, but only if he starts early. (4) THE QUIET TREE-LINED FORT MORGAN ROAD MOVES FROM FIRST TO LAST — a calm, shaded run-in to the ferry, which is the right thing to have when watching a clock. (5) THE HEAT LESSON DOES NOT INVERT AT ALL: 96.5F average on 45 flat miles was caused purely by starting two hours late, and Nick has a hard deadline at the far end, so an early start serves both the heat and the boat. Distance-wise this is a gentle opening day — 45 miles and 489 ft — which is appropriate for day one, and the terrain gives him no excuse to be late.
records.road: FL-292 / Perdido Key Dr / AL-182 / AL-180
records.to: Fort Morgan AL then ferry to Dauphin Island

records.summary: PENSACOLA FL area — overnight not named in the journal. GAP, and it matters because Pensacola is NICK'S DAY-ZERO BASE.
records.detail: The rider finished the day at Pensacola after the Naval Aviation Museum stop. No campground, RV park or motel is named on this page.
records.cyclistIntel: FLAGGED AS A GAP RATHER THAN A RECORD. This is the one Gulf-leg overnight Nick most needs and the journal does not supply it, because Pensacola is where his 53 days begin — he needs a place to stay the night BEFORE day one, ideally with somewhere to leave a vehicle or receive a shipped bike box. That has to be researched independently. Note what the journal does establish nearby: the Gulf coast from Gulfport through Pensacola is dense with commercial lodging, so this is a solvable problem, unlike the rural Louisiana stretches.

records.summary: *** "NEAR RECORD HIGHS" — the rider says it outright. This is the single best confirmation of the heat-calibration caveat.
