records.detail: Rider: 'It all sounds good until you hear "Near record highs". Stepping out of the RV at 6am it was already 78 degrees and 83% humidity.' GPS averaged 88.2F over 5:12 with a 93.2F peak.
records.cyclistIntel: THE CALIBRATION QUOTE. Every temperature in this entire dataset should be read through this sentence. The rider is telling you directly that he rode a near-record-heat spring, which is exactly what the source record's heatCalibration field asserts — and this is him confirming it in his own words rather than me inferring it. For Nick: treat every temperature figure in these 489 records as a HIGH-END SCENARIO, not a Gulf-coast baseline. The operational rules (start early, carry more, finish by early afternoon) transfer completely. The numbers do not. Note also the third consecutive 83% dawn humidity reading — that part IS the baseline, and it is what actually limits riding here.
records.quote: It all sounds good until you hear "Near record highs".

records.summary: *** THE DONE-EARLY RULE, STATED BY THE RIDER HIMSELF *** "I was done with the 65 miles by 2:30 so I missed the 90 degree peak."
records.detail: Started out of the RV at 6am at 78F / 83% humidity, rode 64.94 mi at 12.5 mph, finished by 2:30pm and explicitly credits the early finish with dodging the day's peak temperature.
records.cyclistIntel: The clearest single statement of the operating rule that runs through this whole journal, and it pairs exactly with the counter-example on Day 57, where a two-hour ferry delay produced the hottest day of the entire ride on only 45 miles. Same rider, same coast, opposite outcomes, and the only variable was the clock. For Nick this is the rule to build the Gulf and Louisiana legs around: 6am roll-out, 65 miles, done by mid-afternoon. It is achievable on this terrain — 479 ft of climb in 65 miles — and it is the difference between a good day and a dangerous one.
records.quote: I was done with the 65 miles by 2:30 so I missed the 90 degree peak.

records.summary: AN EVERYTHING-GOOD DAY: very flat (479 ft in 65 mi), good roads, NO WIND, cloud cover, light traffic
records.detail: Rider: 'Today's ride was very flat. Under 500 feet of climb in 65 miles. The roads were good, there was no wind, clouds kept the sun off me and traffic was light.' GPS confirms: 64.94 mi, 479 ft ascent, 12.5 mph average.
records.cyclistIntel: Worth recording precisely BECAUSE nothing went wrong — a warning system needs to know where to stay quiet, and this stretch of rural Louisiana is one of those places. Note what made it good: cloud cover doing the same sun-filtering job the humidity haze does elsewhere on this leg, and genuinely still air, which is rare in this dataset. The 12.5 mph average on flat ground with no wind is a useful clean baseline for Nick's own flat-day speed modelling — most other days in the file are contaminated by headwind or heat. Direction-neutral; this is flat enough that no inversion applies.
records.quote: The roads were good, there was no wind, clouds kept the sun off me and traffic was light.
records.road: LA-26 / LA-10 corridor via Mamou and Ville Platte (approx)

records.summary: CRAWFISH AND RICE COUNTRY: flooded fields with cage rows, six-foot corn, dozens of egrets around every corner
records.detail: Rider: 'There was some corn, at least 6 feet tall. There were vast rice fields. And there were flooded fields with cages lined up in a row: Crawfish farms.' Egrets everywhere, plus black long-curved-bill wading birds he could not identify (he guesses curlews; glossy ibis is the likelier candidate for that description in south Louisiana in May).
records.cyclistIntel: Positional cue set for the Atchafalaya-basin approach, and one practical consequence: flooded rice and crawfish fields on both sides of the road for miles means STANDING WATER at road level, which in May means mosquitoes at dawn and dusk. That matters directly against the 6am start this same page recommends. Carry repellent and do not plan stationary breaks at first light here. For Nick riding westbound the sequence reverses — he moves out of cane and corn into rice and crawfish as he heads toward Sugartown.

photos.caption: Crawfish farm.
photos.shows: Flooded field with rows of submerged crawfish traps.

photos.caption: Some type of boat for harvesting crawfish.
photos.shows: Shallow-draft crawfish harvesting boat in a flooded field.

photos.caption: The egrets were everywhere.
photos.shows: White egrets feeding in a flooded field.

records.summary: First cypress trees of the trip, at Chicot State Park
records.detail: Photo caption: 'Our first Cypress trees.' Noted on arrival in the Chicot State Park area.
records.cyclistIntel: Minor positional marker. Cypress means genuine swamp and, more usefully for Nick, means real tree canopy and SHADE — which the Chicot State Park overnight record independently confirms.

records.summary: MAMOU LA — the crew drove back for dinner; the rider's route passed through it
records.detail: After finishing, they drove the RV back to Mamou and met friends for dinner: gumbo with shrimp and okra, sweet tea. The GPS track shows Mamou directly on the day's line between Sugartown and Ville Platte.
records.cyclistIntel: Mamou is ON the route and has restaurants — useful because this day otherwise crosses agricultural country with thin services. Note the meal was reached by vehicle after the ride, so nothing is established about hours or cyclist-friendliness; the transferable fact is that a town with food sits mid-route here.

records.summary: *** THE JOURNAL'S OWN CUMULATIVE MILEAGE IS UNDERSTATED BY 54.3 MI FROM DAY 37 ONWARD *** — author's arithmetic error, verified three ways
records.detail: Day 36 (Marathon->Sanderson, 54.29 mi) ends at a stated total of 1,266.2. Day 37 (Sanderson->Langtry, 60.29 mi) states a total of 1,272.2 — but 1,272.2 minus 1,211.9 (the Big Bend REST DAY total) equals 60.3, exactly Day 37's mileage. The author computed Day 37's running total from the rest-day figure and never added Day 36's ride. Every subsequent day inherits the error: Day 38 correctly adds 95.31 to the wrong 1,272.2. VERIFIED: summing all 49 riding days' mileages gives 2,596.9; the journal's stated Pensacola finish is 2,543.0 (off by +53.9), while the corrected 2,597.3 lands within 0.4 mi of the sum.
records.cyclistIntel: CRITICAL FOR ANCHORING — this is not trivia. The cumulative-offset method (ANCHOR_PILOT.md Tier 0) converts the journal's distance-from-San-Diego into Nick's route mile, so a 54.3 mi error corrupts EVERY record from Day 37 to Day 57 — all of Texas east of Sanderson, plus Louisiana, Mississippi and Alabama. PROOF THAT THE FIX WORKS: testing against Nick's own known route miles, Sanderson and Brackettville implied offsets 55.7 mi apart using the stated figures. Applying the +54.3 correction brings them to 1.4 mi apart. USE cumulativeMiCorrected, NEVER cumulativeMi, for any mile conversion. Both fields are kept on every day record — cumulativeMi preserves what the source actually said, cumulativeMiCorrected is what to compute with.
records.quote: Total so far: 1,272.2 miles (2,047 km)
